- Consolidation and cohesion of important information - Basic timeline -
Timeframe Period / Event Dynasty / Power Key Details / Rulers / Battles / Features
606–647 CE Pushyabhuti Rule Pushyabhuti Dynasty Harshavardhana; Battle of Narmada (618–619 CE) vs. Pulakeshin II; defeated in Deccan expansion; patronage of Buddhism, Nalanda, Xuanzang’s visit.
624–1070 CE Eastern Chalukya Rule Eastern Chalukya Dynasty Founded by Vishnuvardhana at Vengi; frequent wars with Cholas and Rashtrakutas; later allied with Cholas through marriage alliances.
647–750 CE Post-Harsha Fragmentation Rajput Clans Collapse of centralized power; rise of Guhilas, Chandelas, other Rajput clans.
712 CE Arab Conquest of Sindh Arab Invasion Muhammad bin Qasim defeats Raja Dahir at Battle of Aror; first Muslim presence in India.
738 CE Battle of Rajasthan Gurjara-Pratihara Dynasty Nagabhata I repels Arab invasions; early Pratihara resistance.
750–973 CE Rashtrakuta Dominance Rashtrakuta Dynasty Dantidurga founds dynasty; Amoghavarsha; Ellora Kailasa Temple; Tripartite Struggle with Palas, Pratiharas.
753–982 CE Gurjara-Pratihara Peak Gurjara-Pratihara Dynasty Mihira Bhoja; resists Arabs; cultural peak; decline after Rashtrakuta conflicts.
770–1200 CE Pala Empire Flourishes Pala Empire Gopala founds dynasty; Dharmapala, Devapala; Vikramashila, Nalanda; Tripartite Struggle.
848–1070 CE Early Chola Expansion Chola Dynasty Vijayalaya captures Tanjore; Aditya I defeats Pallavas; foundation for imperial phase.
949 CE Battle of Takkolam Chola vs. Rashtrakuta Rashtrakutas defeat Cholas; marks Rashtrakutas ascendancy in South India.
973–1192 CE Western Chalukya Rule Western Chalukyas Tailapa II overthrows Rashtrakutas; Vikramaditya VI; Kalyani capital.
985–1019 CE Chola Imperial Beginnings Chola Dynasty Rajaraja I; Battle of Kalinga (1019 CE); naval conquests begin (Sri Lanka, Maldives).
1000–1027 CE Ghaznavid Invasions Ghaznavid Empire Mahmud of Ghazni; Battle of Peshawar (1001 CE); Somnath raid (1026 CE); weakens North India.
1026–1343 CE Hoysala Emergence Hoysala Empire Vishnuvardhana; Battle of Talakad (1116 CE); Belur, Halebidu temples; rivalry with Cholas, Chalukyas.
1030–1200 CE Rajput Kingdoms Rise Rajput Kingdoms Chauhans (Prithviraj), Solankis, Paramaras; decentralized power in North India.
1054 CE Chola–Chalukya Conflict Chola vs. Western Chalukya Battle of Koppam; Rajadhiraja Chola I killed in battle; Rajendra II led Cholas to victory against Someshvara I.
1070–1230 CE Sena Rule in Bengal Sena Dynasty Vijayasena ousts Palas; Ballala Sena; Hindu rule ends with Muslim conquest.
1070–1279 CE Chola Imperial Peak Chola Dynasty Rajendra I’s Ganga campaign; naval dominance; decline after Pandya resurgence.
1163–1323 CE Kakatiya Rise Kakatiya Dynasty Prataparudra I; Warangal capital; Golconda fort origins; later raided by Khaljis (1310 CE).
1175–1206 CE Ghurid Invasions Ghurid Empire Muhammad Ghori; First Battle of Tarain (1191 CE) lost; Second Battle of Tarain (1192 CE) defeats Prithviraj.
c. 1182 CE Chauhan–Chandela Conflict Chandela vs. Chauhan Battle of Mahoba; Paramardi Deva (Chandela) vs. Prithviraj Chauhan; semi-legendary, remembered through Alha-Udal ballads.
1206–1290 CE Slave Dynasty Delhi Sultanate Qutb-ud-din Aibak; Iltutmish; Battle of Indus (1221 CE) vs. Mongols; Razia Sultana; Qutb Minar.
1296–1316 CE Khalji Sultanate Delhi Sultanate Alauddin Khalji; repelled Mongol invasions; Battle of Jaran-Manjur (1297 CE); major military and economic reforms.
1300–1316 CE Khalji Deccan Campaigns Delhi Sultanate Malik Kafur raids Warangal, Devagiri, Madurai; Kakatiya and Hoysala tribute.
1320–1413 CE Tughlaq Dynasty Delhi Sultanate Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq; Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s Daulatabad shift; Battle of Singoli (1336 CE) vs. Rajputs.
1336–1646 CE Vijayanagara Empire Vijayanagara Empire Harihara I, Bukka I; Krishna Deva Raya (1509–1529 CE); Hampi; resists Bahmani Sultanate.
1347–1518 CE Bahmani Sultanate Bahmani Sultanate Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah; Battle of Adoni (1366 CE); splits into Deccan Sultanates.
1392–1562 CE Malwa Sultanate Malwa Sultanate Dilawar Khan Ghori; Mahmud Khalji; Mandu architecture; later conquered by Gujarat, Mughals.
1398 CE Timur’s Invasion Timurid Empire Timur sacks Delhi; Battle of Delhi vs. Nasir-ud-Din Mahmud Tughlaq; weakens Sultanate.
1399–1757 CE Mysore Kingdom Mysore Kingdom Wodeyar dynasty begins; later Haider Ali (1761 CE); early resistance to external powers.
1407–1573 CE Gujarat Sultanate Gujarat Sultanate Muzaffar Shah I; Mahmud Begada; maritime trade; later annexed by Akbar.
1414–1451 CE Sayyid Dynasty Delhi Sultanate Khizr Khan; weak rule under Timurid influence; regional revolts.
1451–1526 CE Lodi Dynasty Delhi Sultanate Bahlul Lodi; Sikandar Lodi; Ibrahim Lodi; falls at First Battle of Panipat (1526 CE).
1490–1636 CE Ahmadnagar Sultanate Deccan Sultanates Malik Ahmad founds dynasty; resists Mughals; later annexed (1636 CE).
1490–1686 CE Bijapur Sultanate Deccan Sultanates Yusuf Adil Shah; Gol Gumbaz; resists Vijayanagara, Mughals; annexed by Aurangzeb (1686 CE).
1498 CE Portuguese Arrival Portuguese Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut; begins European presence in India.
1509 CE Battle of Diu Portuguese vs. Gujarat Portuguese defeat Gujarat-Mamluk fleet; establishes naval dominance.
1510 CE Goa Captured Portuguese Albuquerque seizes Goa; becomes Portuguese stronghold.
1518–1687 CE Golconda Sultanate Deccan Sultanates Quli Qutb Shah; diamond trade (Koh-i-Noor); Qutb Shahi tombs; falls to Aurangzeb (1687 CE).
1520 CE Battle of Raichur Vijayanagara vs. Bijapur Krishna Deva Raya defeats Bijapur; Vijayanagara peak.
1528–1619 CE Bidar Sultanate Deccan Sultanates Amir Barid; smallest Deccan power; Bidar Fort; annexed by Bijapur (1619 CE).
1538 CE Second Battle of Diu Gujarat vs. Portuguese Portuguese repel Gujarat-Ottoman alliance; solidify control.
1490–1574 CE Berar Sultanate Deccan Sultanates Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk; minor power; absorbed by Ahmadnagar (1574 CE).
1565 CE Battle of Talikota Deccan Sultanates vs. Vijayanagara Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar defeat Vijayanagara; Rama Raya killed; empire declines.
1526 CE First Battle of Panipat Mughal Empire Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi; Mughal rule begins in India.
1527 CE Battle of Khanwa Mughal vs. Rajputs Babur defeats Rana Sanga of Mewar; consolidates North India.
1529 CE Battle of Ghaghra Mughal Empire Babur defeats Afghan chiefs; secures eastern territories.
1539–1540 CE Sur Interregnum Sur Dynasty Sher Shah Suri; Battle of Chausa (1539 CE); Battle of Kannauj (1540 CE); ousts Humayun.
1540–1556 CE Sur Rule Sur Dynasty Sher Shah’s reforms: Grand Trunk Road, revenue system; ends with Humayun’s return.
1556 CE Second Battle of Panipat Mughal Empire Bairam Khan defeats Hemu; Akbar restores Mughal rule.
1556–1605 CE Akbar’s Reign Mughal Empire Battle of Haldighati (1576 CE) vs. Rana Pratap; Mansabdari system; Din-i-Ilahi; empire expands.
1600 CE British East India Company British EIC founded; begins trade in Surat, Madras; early foothold.
1605 CE Dutch Arrival Dutch Dutch East India Company; trade posts in Pulicat, Surat; competes with Portuguese.
1605–1627 CE Jahangir’s Reign Mughal Empire Justice system; Nur Jahan’s influence; patronage of arts.
1612 CE Battle of Swally British vs. Portuguese British defeat Portuguese near Surat; boosts EIC presence.
1620 CE Danish Arrival Danish Danish East India Company; Serampore, Tranquebar; minor trade presence.
1628–1658 CE Shah Jahan’s Reign Mughal Empire Taj Mahal; Battle of Samugarh (1658 CE) leads to Aurangzeb’s rise; architectural peak.
1658–1707 CE Aurangzeb’s Reign Mughal Empire Battle of Deorai (1659 CE); annexes Bijapur (1686 CE), Golconda (1687 CE); Maratha wars.
1664 CE Shivaji Sacks Surat Maratha Empire Shivaji’s early raid on Mughal port; signals Maratha rise.
1664 CE French Arrival French French East India Company founded; later Pondicherry (1674 CE).
1669 CE Jat Uprising Jat Clans Gokula revolts against Aurangzeb; early resistance in North India.
1670 CE Battle of Sinhagad Maratha Empire Shivaji’s forces capture fort; strengthens Maratha power.
1674 CE Shivaji’s Coronation Maratha Empire Shivaji crowned Chhatrapati; formalizes Maratha Empire.
1699 CE Khalsa Founded Sikh Confederacy Guru Gobind Singh forms Khalsa; militarizes Sikh community.
1707 CE Aurangzeb’s Death Mughal Empire Mughal decline begins; rise of Marathas, Sikhs, Europeans.
1709–1716 CE Sikh Revolt Sikh Confederacy Banda Bahadur leads uprising; Battle of Chappar Chiri (1710 CE) vs. Mughals.
1717–1757 CE Bengal Nawabs Bengal Nawabs Murshid Quli Khan; Alivardi Khan; Battle of Giria (1740 CE) vs. Marathas; British influence grows.
1721–1774 CE Rohilla Rise Rohilla Afghans Ali Muhammad Khan founds Rohilkhand; resists Mughals, Marathas.
1722–1757 CE Oudh Nawabs Oudh Nawabs Saadat Ali Khan; Safdarjung; semi-independent from Mughals.
1728 CE Battle of Palkhed Maratha Empire Peshwa Baji Rao I defeats Nizam; Maratha expansion peaks.
1739 CE Battle of Karnal Nadir Shah Nadir Shah defeats Muhammad Shah; sacks Delhi; Mughal treasury looted.
1740 CE Battle of Giria Bengal vs. Marathas Alivardi Khan defeats Maratha raiders; temporary respite for Bengal.
1741 CE Battle of Tiruchirappalli Mysore vs. Marathas Mysore resists Maratha incursion; early Wodeyar strength.
1757 CE Battle of Plassey British vs. Bengal Robert Clive defeats Siraj-ud-Daulah; British East India Company gains Bengal; colonial era begins.
- Kingdoms/dyansties in chronological order -
Kingdom/Empire Dynasty Ruler / Key Figure Period Capital Titles / Notes Key Achievements Policies / Patronage Decline / End
Early Medieval India (~600–1200 CE)
Kanauj Empire Pushyabhuti Prabhakaravardhana 590–606 CE Thanesar Maharajadhiraja (Great King of Kings) Expanded Pushyabhuti influence, defeated Huns Patronized Vedic traditions Died 606 CE, succeeded by Harsha
Harshavardhana 606–647 CE Kannauj Shiladitya (Sun of Virtue) Unified North India, Harsha was defeated by Pulakeshin II (Chalukya) at the Battle of Narmada (618–619 CE), which stopped his southern expansion. Buddhism, Jainism, Sanskrit literature (Banabhatta’s Harshacharita) Died 647 CE, empire fragmented
Eastern Chalukya Kingdom Eastern Chalukya Kubja Vishnuvardhana 624–641 CE Vengi Vishamasiddhi (Achiever of Difficult Tasks) Founded independent rule post-Pulakeshin II Telugu culture, temple construction Succeeded by Jayasimha I
Jayasimha I 641–673 CE Vengi — Consolidated Vengi region Local administration Succeeded by Indra Bhattaraka
Vijayaditya III 848–892 CE Vengi Gunaga (Endowed with Virtues) Longest reign, resisted Rashtrakutas Temple building (e.g., at Biccavolu) Natural death
Chalukya Bhima I 892–921 CE Vengi — Repelled Rashtrakuta invasions Strengthened defenses Succeeded by Vijayaditya IV
Amma II 945–970 CE Vengi — Fought Cholas, maintained independence Military focus Overthrown not directly by Cholas, but his weak reign led to instability, which enabled Chola influence later
Rajaraja Narendra 1018–1061 CE Vengi — Allied with Cholas via marriage Patronized Telugu literature (Mahabharata translation) Succeeded by Kulothunga
Kulothunga Chola I 1070–1120 CE Vengi/Gangaikonda Cholapuram Sungamtavirtta (He Who Abolished Tolls) Merged Eastern Chalukyas with Cholas Trade reforms, administration Chola dominance continued
Vikrama Chola 1120–1135 CE Vengi — Maintained Chola-Chalukya rule Administrative continuity Absorbed into Chola Empire
Rashtrakuta Empire Rashtrakuta Dantidurga 735–756 CE Manyakheta Prithvivallabha (Beloved of the Earth) Overthrew Chalukyas, founded empire Jainism, Ellora caves Succeeded by Krishna I
Krishna I 756–774 CE Manyakheta Subhatunga (Highly Auspicious) Kailasa Temple (Ellora) constructed Shaivism, architecture Natural death
Dhruva 780–793 CE Manyakheta Dharavarsha (Rain of Righteousness) Defeated Pratiharas, Palas Military expansion Natural death
Govinda III 793–814 CE Manyakheta Jagattunga (Eminent in the World) Controlled Kannauj, peak power Centralized rule Natural death
Amoghavarsha 814–878 CE Manyakheta Nripatunga (Eminent Among Kings) Kavirajamarga (Kannada text), built Manyakheta Jainism, literature Abdicated
Krishna II 878–914 CE Manyakheta Akalavarsha (Unseasonal Rain) Fought Cholas, Eastern Chalukyas Military campaigns Natural death
Indra III 914–929 CE Manyakheta Nityavarsha (Eternal Rain) Sacked Kannauj (916 CE) Expansionist policy Natural death
Krishna III 939–967 CE Manyakheta Akalavarsha (Unseasonal Rain) Battle of Takkolam (949 CE), conquered Cholas Shaivism, military His successors weakened, and finally Indra IV (last Rashtrakuta ruler, d. 982 CE) fell to Tailapa II.
Gurjara-Pratihara Empire Gurjara-Pratihara Nagabhata I 730–760 CE Ujjain — Repelled Arab invasions from Sindh Hindu consolidation Succeeded by nephews
Vatsaraja 780–800 CE Ujjain/Kannauj Ranahastin (War Elephant) Tripartite Struggle, captured Kannauj Military expansion Defeated by Dhruva
Nagabhata II 805–833 CE Kannauj Paramabhattaraka (Supreme Lord) Permanently secured Kannauj Vaishnavism, temples Defeated by Govinda III
Mihira Bhoja 836–885 CE Kannauj Adivaraha (Prime Boar, Vishnu Incarnation) Peak power, resisted Palas, Rashtrakutas Temple architecture, Adivaraha coins Natural death
Mahendrapala I 885–910 CE Kannauj — Extended empire, patronized Sanskrit Cultural patronage Succeeded by son
Mahipala I 912–944 CE Kannauj Kshitipala (Protector of Earth) Resisted Rashtrakuta sack (916 CE) Weakened control, literature Empire weakened
Pala Empire Pala Gopala 750–770 CE Gaur — Ended Matsyanyaya (anarchy) in Bengal Buddhist patronage, Odantapuri Succeeded by Dharmapala
Dharmapala 770–810 CE Gaur Vikramashila (Valiant Monk) Tripartite Struggle, Vikramashila founded Mahayana Buddhism, education Defeated but held Bengal
Devapala 810–850 CE Gaur — Peak power, naval ties with Srivijaya Buddhist missions Decline after reign
Mahipala I (different from Gurjara-Pratihara Mahipala I) 977–1027 CE Gaur — Revived Pala power, resisted invaders Buddhist revival Succeeded by successors
Ramapala 1077–1130 CE Gaur — Last significant ruler, recovered Bengal Patronized Ramacharitam Decline, Sena rise
Chola Empire Chola Vijayalaya 848–871 CE Thanjavur — Captured Thanjavur from Muttaraiyars Shaivism, consolidation Succeeded by Aditya I
Aditya I 871–907 CE Thanjavur Kodandarama (Rama with Bow) Defeated Pallavas, annexed Tondaimandalam Temple building along Kaveri Natural death
Parantaka I 907–955 CE Thanjavur Maduraikonda (Conqueror of Madurai) Conquered Pandyas, invaded Sri Lanka Golden roof for Chidambaram Defeated at Takkolam (949 CE)
Gandaraditya 955–957 CE Thanjavur — Short reign, pious ruler Shaivism, hymns Died early
Arinjaya 957–958 CE Thanjavur — Minor ruler, brief reign Weak rule Died soon after
Sundara Chola 957–973 CE Thanjavur Parantaka II Recovered from Rashtrakuta defeat Shaivism, administration Natural death
Rajaraja I 985–1014 CE Thanjavur Mummudi Chola (Lord of Three Worlds) Brihadeeswara Temple, naval conquests Shaivism, bureaucracy Natural death
Rajendra I 1014–1044 CE Gangaikonda Cholapuram Gangaikonda (Conqueror of the Ganga) Ganges expedition, SE Asia campaign Navy, irrigation (Cholagangam) Natural death
Rajadhiraja I 1044–1054 CE Gangaikonda Cholapuram Vijayarajendra (Victorious Rajendra) Ashvamedha, Battle of Koppam Military campaigns Killed in battle (1054 CE)
Rajendra II 1054–1063 CE Gangaikonda Cholapuram — Continued wars with Chalukyas Maintained empire Natural death
Kulothunga I 1070–1120 CE Gangaikonda Cholapuram Sungamtavirtta (He Who Abolished Tolls) Originally he was Eastern Chalukya prince, Unified Chola-Chalukya, land survey Trade, administration Lost Sri Lanka, decline began
Western Chalukya Empire Western Chalukya Tailapa II 973–997 CE Kalyani Ahavamalla (Foe of the Brave) Overthrew Rashtrakutas Deccan consolidation Natural death
Satyashraya 997–1008 CE Kalyani — Fought Cholas, maintained rule Military focus Natural death
Vikramaditya V 1008–1015 CE Kalyani — Short reign, minor ruler Weak rule Succeeded by Jayasimha II
Jayasimha II 1015–1042 CE Kalyani Jagadekamalla (Sole Lord of the World) Resisted Chola invasions Strengthened administration Natural death
Someshvara I 1042–1068 CE Kalyani Trailokyamalla (Lord of Three Worlds) Battle of Koppam (1054 CE) Military campaigns Drowned in Tungabhadra
Vikramaditya VI 1076–1126 CE Kalyani Tribhuvanamalla (Lord of Three Worlds) Chalukya-Vikrama era, Bilhana’s works Arts, law (Mitakshara) Decline after reign
Hoysala Empire Hoysala Sala ~1026–1047 CE Dwarasamudra — Founded Hoysala dynasty (legendary) Local consolidation Succeeded by Vinayaditya
Vinayaditya 1047–1098 CE Dwarasamudra — Strengthened Hoysala base Minor patronage Succeeded by Vishnuvardhana
Vishnuvardhana 1108–1152 CE Dwarasamudra — Battle of Talakad, Belur temples Vaishnavism, architecture Natural death
Narasimha I 1152–1173 CE Dwarasamudra — Consolidated power Temple building Succeeded by Ballala II
Vira Ballala II 1173–1220 CE Dwarasamudra — Peak influence, defeated Cholas Military, cultural patronage Decline began later
Sena Kingdom Sena Hemantasena 1070–1096 CE Vikramapura — Founded Sena rule Hindu consolidation Succeeded by Vijayasena
Vijayasena 1096–1159 CE Vikramapura — Ousted Palas, unified Bengal Hinduism, Sanskrit Natural death
Ballala Sena 1159–1179 CE Vikramapura — Cultural peak, social reforms Legal texts, caste system Natural death
Lakshmana Sena 1179–1206 CE Vikramapura — Patronized literature (Jayadeva) Cultural patronage Overthrown by Bakhtiyar Khalji
Kakatiya Kingdom Kakatiya Beta II 1076–1110 CE Warangal — Early ruler, feudatory of Chalukyas Local consolidation Succeeded by Prola II
Prola II 1110–1158 CE Warangal — Gained independence Telugu culture Succeeded by Prataparudra I
Prataparudra I 1158–1195 CE Warangal — Strengthened Kakatiya rule Military focus Natural death
Rudrama Devi 1262–1289 CE Warangal Rani (Queen) Female ruler, resisted invasions Temple building Died in battle
Prataparudra II 1289–1323 CE Warangal — Warangal Fort, resisted Khaljis Telugu arts Defeated by Tughlaqs (1323 CE)
Importantn Rajputana kingdoms
Mewar Guhila (later Sisodia) Bappa Rawal ~728–764 CE Chittor (initially Nagda) Rawal, Founder of Mewar
  • Founded Mewar dynasty, uniting Rajput clans.
  • Resisted Arab invasions, strengthening regional control.
  • Patronized Shaivite temples, promoting Hindu culture.
  • Established strong administrative base for Mewar.
 Early Guhila rule faced vassalage under Pratiharas, Paramaras, and Chahamanas.
Rana Kumbha 1433–1468 CE Chittor Maharana
  • Built Kumbhalgarh Fort (UNESCO World Heritage Site).
  • Defeated Malwa and Gujarat Sultanates in multiple battles (e.g., Sarangpur, Mandalgarh).
  • Erected Vijay Stambha (Victory Tower) in Chittor.
  • Patronized Sanskrit literature, music, and architecture.
  • Promoted Jainism and Hinduism, built temples.
  • Strengthened fort network for defense.
 Assassinated by son Udai Singh I, leading to temporary instability.
Maharana Sanga 1508–1528 CE Chittor Maharana
  • Expanded Mewar’s territory, controlling parts of Rajasthan, Malwa, and Gujarat.
  • Fought Battle of Khanwa (1527) against Babur, uniting Rajput confederacy.
  • Vassalized neighboring Hindu kingdoms.
  • Formed alliances with Rajput states for collective resistance.
  • Patronized warriors and local governance structures.
 Died in 1528, possibly poisoned; Mewar weakened after Khanwa defeat.
Maharana Pratap 1572–1597 CE Udaipur (after Chittor’s fall in 1568) Maharana
  • Fought Battle of Haldighati (1576) against Mughals, showcasing guerrilla warfare.
  • Reclaimed parts of Mewar, maintaining independence.
  • Promoted Rajput honor and resistance against Mughal assimilation.
  • Relied on local tribal support for guerrilla tactics.
 Died in 1597; Mewar became Mughal tributary post-1615 under Amar Singh I.
Marwar Rathore Rao Chunda ~1390–1421 CE Mandore (later Jodhpur) Rao, Founder of Marwar
  • Established Rathore rule in Marwar, consolidating power around Mandore.
  • Secured control over Nagaur and surrounding areas.
  • Strengthened clan alliances through marriage and diplomacy.
  • Promoted Rajput martial traditions.
 Killed in battle against Khichi Chauhans; early Rathore rule faced regional rivalries.
Rao Jodha 1438–1489 CE Jodhpur Rao
  • Founded Jodhpur (1459), establishing it as Marwar’s capital.
  • Built Mehrangarh Fort, a key defensive structure.
  • Expanded Rathore influence in western Rajasthan.
  • Patronized local governance and fort construction.
  • Maintained autonomy against Delhi Sultanate.
 Succession disputes weakened early stability.
Maharaja Jaswant Singh 1626–1678 CE Jodhpur Maharaja
  • Fought for Mughals as a key ally under Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb.
  • Expanded Marwar’s influence through Mughal campaigns.
  • Balanced Mughal allegiance with Rajput autonomy.
  • Patronized art and architecture, including Jaswant Thada.
 Died in 1678; Mughal intervention under Aurangzeb annexed Marwar temporarily.
Malwa (Rajput) Paramara Siyaka II ~949–972 CE Dhar Maharaja
  • Established Paramara independence from Pratiharas.
  • Defeated Rashtrakutas, expanding Malwa’s influence.
  • Patronized Jainism and Hinduism, supporting temple construction.
  • Encouraged scholarly works in Sanskrit.
 Succession struggles weakened dynasty post-Siyaka.
Bhoja ~1010–1055 CE Dhar Maharaja, Scholar-King
  • Expanded Malwa to its zenith, controlling parts of Gujarat and Rajasthan.
  • Authored works on philosophy, grammar, and architecture (e.g., Samarangana Sutradhara).
  • Built Bhojeshwar Temple in Bhojpur.
  • Patronized education, establishing Bhoj Shala (school).
  • Promoted Jain and Hindu religious institutions.
 Killed in battle against Chalukyas and Kalachuris; Malwa declined post-Bhoja.
Vikramaditya ~1076–1126 CE Dhar Maharaja
  • Restored Paramara power after decline.
  • Defended Malwa against Chalukya invasions.
  • Supported local governance and military reforms.
  • Patronized regional art and culture.
 Paramara rule ended with Delhi Sultanate’s conquest in 1305.
Malwa (Sultanate) Ghorid (later independent) Hoshang Shah 1406–1435 CE Mandu (initially Dhar) Sultan
  • Established Malwa Sultanate after Delhi Sultanate’s weakening.
  • Built Jama Masjid and Hindola Mahal in Mandu.
  • Adopted religious tolerance, granting jagirs to Rajputs.
  • Patronized Jain scholars like Nardeva Soni.
 Internal succession disputes weakened early rule.
Mahmud Khalji 1436–1469 CE Mandu Sultan
  • Expanded Malwa’s influence through campaigns against Mewar, Gujarat, and Delhi.
  • Built Jahaz Mahal in Mandu.
  • Focused on military campaigns, often destroying temples in conflicts.
  • Encouraged urban development in Mandu.
 Defeated by Rana Kumbha; Malwa Sultanate annexed by Mughals in 1562.
Delhi Sultanate and Regional Powers (1206–1526 CE)
Delhi Sultanate Slave Dynasty Qutb-ud-din Aibak 1206–1210 CE Delhi Sultan (Ruler) Founded Sultanate, began Qutb Minar Islamic governance, military Died in polo accident
Aram Shah 1210–1211 CE Delhi — Brief, weak rule Minor administration Overthrown by Iltutmish
Shams-ud-din Iltutmish 1211–1236 CE Delhi Sultan-i-Azam (Great Sultan) Completed Qutb Minar, Mongol resistance Coinage, iqta system Natural death
Rukn-ud-din Firuz 1236 CE Delhi — Short reign, incompetent Weak rule Deposed by Razia
Razia Sultana 1236–1240 CE Delhi Sultana (Female Ruler) First female Muslim ruler, effective governance Education, justice Deposed, killed
Muiz-ud-din Bahram 1240–1242 CE Delhi — Weak ruler, controlled by nobles Unstable rule Deposed, killed
Ala-ud-din Masud 1242–1246 CE Delhi — Weak ruler, puppet of nobles Minor administration Deposed
Nasir-ud-din Mahmud 1246–1266 CE Delhi — Stable reign under Balban’s regency Pious rule Natural death
Ghiyas-ud-din Balban 1266–1287 CE Delhi Sultan (Ruler) Strengthened sultanate, Mongol defense Persian court, iron rule Natural death
Muiz-ud-din Qaiqabad 1287–1290 CE Delhi — Weak ruler, paralyzed later Puppet of nobles Deposed, killed by Khaljis
Khalji Dynasty Jalal-ud-din Khalji 1290–1296 CE Delhi Sultan (Ruler) Founded Khalji rule, lenient ruler Moderate policies Assassinated by Alauddin
Alauddin Khalji 1296–1316 CE Delhi Sikandar-i-Sani (Second Alexander) Siege of Chittor, Mongol defeats Market reforms, military Natural death
Shihab-ud-din Umar 1316 CE Delhi — Child ruler, puppet Weak rule Deposed, blinded
Qutb-ud-din Mubarak 1316–1320 CE Delhi — Reversed Alauddin’s reforms Liberal policies Assassinated by Tughlaqs
Khusro Khan 1320 CE Delhi — Usurper, brief reign Chaos, Hindu convert leading Baradu nobles, overthrown by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq Overthrown by Ghiyas-ud-din
Tughlaq Dynasty Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq 1320–1325 CE Delhi Sultan (Ruler) Founded Tughlaqabad Restored order Died in pavilion collapse
Muhammad bin Tughlaq 1325–1351 CE Delhi/Daulatabad — Daulatabad shift, token currency Ambitious reforms Natural death
Firuz Shah Tughlaq 1351–1388 CE Delhi — Built Firozabad, canals Public works, Sharia Natural death
Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq II 1388–1389 CE Delhi — Brief reign, weak ruler Unstable rule Assassinated
Nasir-ud-din Mahmud 1394–1413 CE Delhi — Last Tughlaq ruler, faced Timur's sack of Delhi, reduced to nominal power Weak administration Timur’s invasion (1398 CE)
Sayyid Dynasty Khizr Khan 1414–1421 CE Delhi Rayat-i-Ala (Exalted Banner) Founded Sayyid rule, Timurid vassal Weak central authority Natural death
Mubarak Shah 1421–1434 CE Delhi Muizz-ud-Din (Strengthener of Faith) Built Mubarakabad Minor stability Assassinated
Muhammad Shah 1434–1445 CE Delhi — Weak ruler, lost territories Nominal rule Natural death

Vijayanagara Empire Sangama Harihara I 1336–1356 CE Hampi Raya, Co-founder
  • Founded Vijayanagara Empire with brother Bukka I.
  • Established control over Tungabhadra region.
  • Initiated irrigation projects, including early canals for agriculture.
  • Promoted Hindu revival against Muslim invasions.
  • Patronized Shaivite and Vaishnavite temples.
 Succeeded by Bukka I; empire faced early Bahmani conflicts.
Bukka I 1356–1377 CE Hampi Raya
  • Expanded empire to Madurai and Goa.
  • Fought Bahmani Sultanate, securing northern Deccan.
  • Built dams and tanks to support agriculture in Hampi region.
  • Patronized Telugu and Kannada literature.
  • Strengthened administrative systems (Nayankara).
 Natural death; empire stabilized.
Harihara II 1377–1404 CE Hampi Maharaya
  • Conquered southern India, including Tamil regions.
  • Strengthened coastal control, engaging with Arab traders.
  • Expanded irrigation systems, including anicuts on Tungabhadra.
  • Promoted Vaishnavism and temple construction.
  • Encouraged trade with Persian Gulf merchants.
 Natural death; succession disputes emerged.
Deva Raya I 1406–1422 CE Hampi Maharaya
  • Defeated Bahmanis in key battles, stabilizing empire.
  • Constructed major dam on Tungabhadra River, boosting agriculture.
  • Welcomed Persian embassy, strengthening diplomatic ties.
  • Patronized irrigation infrastructure for agrarian economy.
  • Supported Shaivite and Jain institutions.
 Natural death; Bahmani conflicts persisted.
Deva Raya II 1422–1446 CE Hampi Maharaya
  • Strengthened army with Muslim archers and cavalry.
  • Hosted Persian and Portuguese envoys, initiating European contact.
  • Expanded irrigation networks, including canals in Krishna basin.
  • Patronized Sanskrit, Telugu, and Kannada literature (e.g., poet Srinatha).
  • Promoted religious tolerance, supporting Jainism and Islam.
 Natural death; empire faced internal strife.
Saluva Saluva Narasimha 1485–1491 CE Hampi Raya, Founder of Saluva dynasty
  • Usurped throne, restoring Vijayanagara’s stability post-Sangama decline.
  • Repelled Bahmani and Gajapati invasions.
  • Built irrigation tanks and temples in Tamil regions.
  • Patronized Vaishnavite temples, especially Tirupati.
  • Reorganized Nayankara system for better governance.
 Natural death; weak successors led to Tuluva rise.
Immadi Narasimha 1491–1505 CE Hampi Raya
  • Maintained empire under regent Tuluva Narasa Nayaka.
  • Supported minor irrigation projects in core territories.
  • Limited patronage due to weak rule.
  • Relied on Nayakas for military and administration.
 Deposed by Tuluva Narasa Nayaka; Saluva dynasty ended.
Tuluva Viranarasimha Raya 1505–1509 CE Hampi Raya
  • Usurped throne from Saluva dynasty.
  • Consolidated power in southern territories.
  • Initiated canal repairs for agricultural stability.
  • Strengthened Nayankara system for loyalty.
  • Patronized Vaishnavite institutions.
 Natural death; succeeded by Krishna Deva Raya.
Krishna Deva Raya 1509–1529 CE Hampi Maharaya
  • Won Battle of Raichur (1520) against Bijapur, achieving peak power.
  • Built major dams and irrigation systems (e.g., Krishnarajasagara dam).
  • Granted trading rights to Portuguese, establishing factories at Bhatkal.
  • Constructed Vitthala and Hazara Rama temples.
  • Patronized Telugu literature (Amuktamalyada) and eight poets (Ashtadiggajas).
  • Promoted religious tolerance, supporting Shaivism and Vaishnavism.
  • Encouraged overseas trade with Portuguese and Arabs.
 Natural death; succession disputes weakened empire.
Achyuta Deva Raya 1529–1542 CE Hampi Raya
  • Maintained empire’s territorial integrity.
  • Repaired irrigation systems to sustain agriculture.
  • Engaged with Portuguese for coastal trade.
  • Patronized temple festivals and cultural continuity.
  • Supported Nayakas for decentralized governance.
 Natural death; internal rebellions emerged.
Aravidu Sadasiva Raya 1542–1570 CE Hampi (later Penukonda) Raya
  • Ruled under regent Aliya Rama Raya.
  • Lost Battle of Talikota (1565), leading to Hampi’s sack.
  • Shifted capital to Penukonda post-Talikota.
  • Limited patronage due to regency and weak rule.
  • Relied on Portuguese for military supplies.
 Deposed; empire fragmented after Talikota.
Tirumala Deva Raya 1565–1572 CE Penukonda Raya
  • Consolidated remnants of empire post-Talikota.
  • Strengthened fortifications and irrigation in Penukonda.
  • Maintained trade with Portuguese for economic stability.
  • Patronized Hindu temples to restore legitimacy.
  • Reorganized administration to curb Nayaka rebellions.
 Abdicated; empire continued decline under successors.

- Battles and campaigns -
Conflict / Battle Name Time (Approx.) Location Participants Purpose / Context Outcome Key Commanders / Notes
Battles of Rajasthan (Arab Campaigns) ~738 CE Rajasthan / Gujarat border regions Indian Confederacy (Pratiharas, Chalukyas, etc.) vs. Umayyad Caliphate Arab governor Muhammad bin Qasim aimed to expand eastward from Sindh into Rajput territories for wealth and strategic control. Decisive Indian victory. Arab advance halted. Nagabhata I (Pratihara), Vikramaditya II (Chalukya), Bappa Rawal (Guhila). Unified resistance key.
Battle of Takkolam 949 CE Takkolam (near Arkonam, Tamil Nadu) Rashtrakuta Empire vs. Chola Empire Rashtrakuta king Krishna III sought to crush Chola resurgence under Parantaka I to maintain dominance over South India’s trade routes. Rashtrakuta victory. Chola prince Rajaditya killed. Krishna III (Rashtrakuta), Parantaka I (Chola). Delayed Chola expansion.
Sack of Somnath 1025–1026 CE Somnath Temple, Gujarat Ghaznavid Empire vs. Local Rajput rulers Mahmud of Ghazni raided the wealthy Somnath temple to fund his empire and enhance his prestige as a Muslim conqueror. Ghaznavid victory. Temple looted, thousands killed. Mahmud of Ghazni (Ghaznavid), Bhimadeva I (Chaulukya). Culturally devastating.
Battle of Koppam 1054 CE Koppam, Tungabhadra River (Andhra/Karnataka border) Chola Empire vs. Western Chalukyas Chola king Rajendra II aimed to assert supremacy over Western Chalukyas in a rivalry over Deccan control and resources. Inconclusive; Chalukya tactical edge, Cholas regrouped. Rajendra Chola II (Chola), Someshvara I (Chalukya). Rajendra wounded.
Battle of Vijayawada (Chola–Chalukya wars) ~1062 CE Vijayawada, Andhra region Chola Empire vs. Eastern Chalukyas Chola king Virarajendra sought to secure influence over Vengi region, contested by Eastern Chalukyas. Chola victory. Vijayaditya VII subdued. Virarajendra Chola (Chola), Vijayaditya VII (Chalukya). Strengthened Chola hold.
Battle of Kasahrada 1178 CE Kasahrada (near Mount Abu, Rajasthan) Chaulukya Dynasty vs. Ghurid Sultanate Muhammad Ghori invaded Gujarat to expand Ghurid influence, opposed by Chaulukya king Mularaja II defending his realm. Chaulukya victory. Ghori repelled. Mularaja II (Chaulukya), Muhammad Ghori (Ghurid). Delayed Ghurid expansion.
First Battle of Tarain 1191 CE Tarain (Taraori, Haryana) Chahamana (Chauhan) vs. Ghurid Sultanate Ghori aimed to conquer North India and establish a foothold beyond Punjab, resisted by Prithviraj Chauhan’s Rajput coalition. Rajput victory. Ghori wounded, retreated. Prithviraj Chauhan III (Chahamana), Muhammad Ghori (Ghurid). Temporary setback.
Second Battle of Tarain 1192 CE Tarain (Taraori, Haryana) Ghurid Sultanate vs. Chah ,(Chahamana (Chauhan) Ghori returned with a larger army to avenge his defeat and secure North India, facing a weakened Prithviraj after allies deserted. Ghurid victory. Prithviraj executed. Muhammad Ghori (Ghurid), Prithviraj Chauhan III (Chahamana). Led to Delhi Sultanate.
Battle of Chandawar 1194 CE Near Chandawar, Uttar Pradesh Ghurid Sultanate vs. Gahadavala Dynasty Ghori targeted Gahadavalas to extend control over the fertile Gangetic plains, a key economic and political prize. Ghurid victory. Jayachandra killed. Muhammad Ghori (Ghurid), Jayachandra (Gahadavala). Consolidated Ghurid power.
Battle of Ranthambore 1301 CE Ranthambore Fort, Rajasthan Delhi Sultanate vs. Chauhan Rajputs Alauddin Khalji aimed to subdue Rajput strongholds like Ranthambore to secure his empire’s western flank. Sultanate victory. Fort captured. Alauddin Khalji (Sultanate), Hammiradeva (Chauhan). Expanded Khalji control.
Siege of Chittorgarh 1303 CE Chittorgarh Fort, Rajasthan Delhi Sultanate vs. Guhila Rajputs Alauddin Khalji sought to crush Rajput resistance and secure Rajasthan’s forts to protect against Mongol threats. Sultanate victory. Fort sacked, mass jauhar. Alauddin Khalji (Sultanate), Ratnasimha (Guhila). Brutal conquest.
Battle of Amroha 1305 CE Amroha, Uttar Pradesh Delhi Sultanate vs. Mongol invaders Mongols raided North India for plunder, prompting Alauddin Khalji to defend his empire’s heartland. Sultanate victory. Mongols repelled. Malik Kafur (Sultanate), Mongol commanders. Bolstered Khalji defenses.
Battle of Jalore 1310–1311 CE Jalore Fort, Rajasthan Delhi Sultanate vs. Chahamana of Jalore Alauddin Khalji aimed to eliminate Rajput resistance in Jalore to secure his western territories. Sultanate victory. Kanhadadeva killed. Alauddin Khalji (Sultanate), Kanhadadeva (Chahamana). Epic resistance noted.
Battle of Madurai 1311 CE Madurai, Tamil Nadu Delhi Sultanate vs. Pandya Kingdom Alauddin Khalji sent Malik Kafur to raid Madurai for tribute and to weaken southern resistance to Delhi’s authority. Sultanate victory. Madurai sacked. Malik Kafur (Sultanate), Sundara Pandya (Pandya). Temporary Sultanate control.
Battle of Delhi 1398 CE Near Delhi Tughlaq Dynasty vs. Timurid Empire Timur invaded to plunder Delhi’s wealth and exploit Tughlaq instability after years of internal strife. Timurid victory. Delhi devastated. Timur (Timurid), Mahmud Shah (Tughlaq). Hastened Tughlaq decline.
Battle of Raichur 1520 CE Raichur, Karnataka Vijayanagara Empire vs. Bijapur Sultanate Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara laid siege to Raichur fort, controlled by Adil Shah of Bijapur, due to its strategic importance between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers. Vijayanagara victory. Raichur fort captured. Krishnadevaraya (Vijayanagara), Ismail Adil Shah (Bijapur). Marked Vijayanagara’s military supremacy in the Deccan.
Battle of Panipat 1526 CE Panipat, Haryana Mughal Empire vs. Delhi Sultanate (Lodi) Babur invaded to establish a new empire, challenging Ibrahim Lodi’s weakening rule amid noble discontent. Mughal victory. Ibrahim Lodi killed. Babur (Mughal), Ibrahim Lodi (Sultanate). Artillery decisive.
Battle of Khanwa 1527 CE Khanwa, Rajasthan Mughal Empire vs. Rajput Confederacy Rana Sanga led Rajputs to resist Babur’s consolidation, aiming to restore Rajput dominance in North India. Mughal victory. Rana Sanga defeated. Babur (Mughal), Rana Sanga (Mewar). Mughal rule entrenched.
Battle of Chanderi 1528 CE Chanderi, Madhya Pradesh Mughal Empire vs. Rajputs of Malwa Babur targeted Chanderi to eliminate Rajput resistance in Malwa and secure central India. Mughal victory. Fort captured. Babur (Mughal), Medini Rai (Rajput). Mass jauhar followed.
Battle of Ghaghra 1529 CE Ghaghra River, Bihar Mughal Empire vs. Afghan Confederacy Babur aimed to crush Afghan remnants under Mahmud Lodi and secure eastern India against Bengal’s support. Mughal victory. Afghan power diminished. Babur (Mughal), Mahmud Lodi (Afghan). Eastern frontiers secured.
Battle of Surajgarh 1534 CE Surajgarh, Gujarat Sher Shah Suri vs. Bengal Sultanate Sher Shah aimed to consolidate control over Bihar and weaken Bengal’s influence in the region. Sher Shah victory. Bihar consolidated. Sher Shah Suri, Bengal commanders. Strengthened Sur power.
Battle of Chausa 1539 CE Chausa, Bihar Mughal Empire vs. Sur Empire Sher Shah Suri challenged Humayun to seize North India, exploiting Mughal vulnerabilities after Gujarat losses. Sur victory. Humayun defeated. Humayun (Mughal), Sher Shah Suri (Sur). Sher Shah’s rise began.
Battle of Kannauj 1540 CE Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh Mughal Empire vs. Sur Empire Humayun attempted to reclaim his throne from Sher Shah Suri after regrouping from Chausa defeat. Sur victory. Humayun exiled. Humayun (Mughal), Sher Shah Suri (Sur). End of early Mughal rule.
Battle of Sirhind 1555 CE Sirhind, Punjab Mughal Empire vs. Sur Empire Humayun, aided by Persian support, sought to recover the Mughal throne from the declining Sur dynasty. Mughal victory. Humayun restored. Humayun (Mughal), Sikandar Suri (Sur). Paved way for Akbar’s rule.
Battle of Tughlaqabad 1556 CE Tughlaqabad, near Delhi Mughal Empire vs. Hemu (Afghan–Sur) Hemu marched to capture Delhi after Humayun’s death, opposed by Akbar’s regent Bairam Khan. Hemu’s victory. Delhi captured. Hemu (Sur), Tardi Beg Khan (Mughal). Set stage for Second Panipat.
Second Battle of Panipat 1556 CE Panipat, Haryana Mughal Empire vs. Sur Empire Akbar’s regent Bairam Khan fought to reclaim Mughal rule from Hemu, who had crowned himself king. Mughal victory. Hemu killed. Bairam Khan (Mughal), Hemu (Sur). Restored Mughal dominance.
Battle of Talikota 1565 CE Near Talikota, Karnataka Vijayanagara Empire vs. Deccan Sultanates Sultanates allied to destroy Vijayanagara’s dominance in the Deccan, fearing its growing power. Sultanate victory. Vijayanagara sacked. Rama Raya (Vijayanagara), Hussain Nizam Shah (Sultanates). End of Vijayanagara’s glory.
Battle of Dharmat 15 April 1658 CE Dharmat (near Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh) Aurangzeb & Murad Baksh vs. Dara Shikoh (Mughal succession struggle) Battle fought during the Mughal War of Succession after Shah Jahan’s illness. Dara Shikoh, the crown prince, marched with imperial forces to check Aurangzeb’s advance. Despite larger numbers, Dara’s army was poorly organized and demoralized. Aurangzeb–Murad victory. Dara Shikoh fled to Agra. Aurangzeb, Murad Baksh, Dara Shikoh. Paved way for Aurangzeb’s eventual capture of the throne.
Battle of Samugarh 1658 CE Samugarh, near Agra Mughal factions (Aurangzeb vs. Dara Shikoh) Aurangzeb and Dara Shikoh fought for the Mughal throne after Shah Jahan’s illness, a brutal succession struggle. Aurangzeb’s victory. Dara defeated. Aurangzeb (Mughal), Dara Shikoh (Mughal). Aurangzeb crowned.
Battle of Deorai 1659 CE Deorai, near Ajmer Mughal Empire vs. Mughal rebels (Shuja) Aurangzeb aimed to eliminate his brother Shah Shuja’s claim to the throne after Samugarh. Mughal victory. Shuja fled. Aurangzeb (Mughal), Shah Shuja (rebel). Ended succession threats.
Battle of Khajwa 1659 CE Khajwa, Uttar Pradesh Mughal Empire vs. Mughal rebels (Shuja) Aurangzeb pursued Shah Shuja to crush his rebellion and secure eastern Mughal territories. Mughal victory. Shuja defeated. Aurangzeb, Mir Jumla (Mughal), Shah Shuja (rebel). Consolidated Aurangzeb’s rule.
Battle of Purandar 1665 CE Purandar Fort, Maharashtra Maratha Empire vs. Mughal Empire Aurangzeb aimed to subdue Shivaji’s growing Maratha power by capturing key forts in the Deccan. Mughal victory. Treaty of Purandar signed. Jai Singh I (Mughal), Shivaji (Maratha). Shivaji ceded forts, agreed to Mughal service.
Battle of Sinhagad 1670 CE Sinhagad Fort, Maharashtra Maratha Empire vs. Mughal Empire Shivaji aimed to reclaim key forts from Mughals to strengthen Maratha control in the Deccan. Maratha victory. Fort recaptured. Tanaji Malusare (Maratha), Udaybhan Rathod (Mughal). Legendary feat.
Battle of Saraighat 1671 CE Brahmaputra River, Assam Ahom Kingdom vs. Mughal Empire Mughals under Aurangzeb sought to conquer Assam, opposed by Ahoms defending their independence. Ahom victory. Mughals repelled. Lachit Borphukan (Ahom), Ram Singh (Mughal). Riverine tactics decisive.
Battle of Salher 1672 CE Salher Fort, Maharashtra Maratha Empire vs. Mughal Empire Marathas under Shivaji aimed to capture Salher to disrupt Mughal control in the northern Deccan. Maratha victory. First major open battle won. Moropant Pingle (Maratha), Mughal garrison. Boosted Maratha morale.
Battle of Bijapur 1686 CE Bijapur, Karnataka Mughal Empire vs. Bijapur Sultanate Aurangzeb aimed to annex Bijapur to complete Mughal domination of the Deccan Sultanates. Mughal victory. Bijapur annexed. Aurangzeb (Mughal), Sikandar Adil Shah (Bijapur). Ended Adil Shahi dynasty.
Battle of Golconda 1687 CE Golconda Fort, Telangana Mughal Empire vs. Golconda Sultanate Aurangzeb sought to annex Golconda, the last major Deccan Sultanate, to consolidate Mughal rule in South India. Mughal victory. Golconda annexed. Aurangzeb (Mughal), Abul Hasan Qutb Shah (Golconda). Ended Qutb Shahi dynasty.
Battle of Haldighati 1576 CE Haldighati, Rajasthan Mughal Empire vs. Mewar Kingdom Aurangzeb aimed to subdue Maharana Pratap’s resistance to Mughal hegemony in Rajasthan. Mughal victory. Pratap escaped. Man Singh I (Mughal), Maharana Pratap (Mewar). Guerrilla warfare followed.
Battle of Shivneri 1670 CE Shivneri Fort, Maharashtra Maratha Empire vs. Mughal Empire Shivaji aimed to recapture Shivneri, his birthplace, to bolster Maratha defenses against Mughal expansion. Maratha victory. Fort recaptured. Shivaji (Maratha), Mughal garrison. Symbolic Maratha victory.
Battle of Satara 1700 CE Satara, Maharashtra Maratha Empire vs. Mughal Empire Aurangzeb aimed to crush Maratha resistance under Rajaram by capturing their new capital at Satara. Maratha victory. Mughals repelled. Rajaram (Maratha), Aurangzeb (Mughal). Prolonged Mughal campaign.
Battle of Khelna 1702 CE Khelna Fort, Maharashtra Mughal Empire vs. Maratha Empire Aurangzeb sought to capture key Maratha forts to weaken their guerrilla campaigns in the Deccan. Mughal victory. Fort captured. Aurangzeb (Mughal), Tarabai (Maratha). Temporary Mughal gain.
Battle of Jajau 20 June 1707 CE Jajau (near Agra, Uttar Pradesh) Bahadur Shah I (Prince Muazzam) vs. Muhammad Azam Shah (both sons of Aurangzeb) After Aurangzeb’s death in February 1707, a war of succession broke out among his sons. Prince Muazzam (Governor of Kabul) advanced with support, while Azam Shah crowned himself emperor at Ahmadnagar and marched north. Bahadur Shah I’s victory. Azam Shah and his son Bidar Bakht were killed in battle. Bahadur Shah I (Prince Muazzam), Muhammad Azam Shah, Bidar Bakht. Resulted in Bahadur Shah’s accession to the Mughal throne.
Battle of Jajmau December 1707 CE Jajmau (near Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh) Bahadur Shah I (Prince Muazzam) vs. Kam Baksh (youngest son of Aurangzeb) After Bahadur Shah’s victory at Jajau, his younger brother Kam Baksh proclaimed himself emperor in the Deccan. Bahadur Shah marched south to eliminate him and secure the throne. Bahadur Shah I’s victory. Kam Baksh was defeated, captured, and later died of wounds. Throne consolidated under Bahadur Shah I. Bahadur Shah I (Prince Muazzam), Kam Baksh. Marked the end of immediate Mughal succession struggles after Aurangzeb’s death.
Battle of Kirtipur / First Sikh Wars 1708–1716 CE Punjab region (notably Chappar Chiri, Sirhind, Gurdaspur) Mughal Empire under Bahadur Shah I & successors vs. Sikhs under Guru Gobind Singh (till 1708) and Banda Singh Bahadur Following Aurangzeb’s death, the Khalsa under Guru Gobind Singh and later Banda Singh Bahadur challenged Mughal authority. Key clash at Chappar Chiri (1710) saw the Mughal governor of Sirhind defeated, leading to Sikh control over parts of Punjab. Mixed outcome. Sikhs initially victorious (Sirhind captured, Wazir Khan slain), but Banda Singh Bahadur was later besieged and executed by the Mughals in 1716. Punjab remained unstable. Bahadur Shah I, Banda Singh Bahadur, Guru Gobind Singh (spiritual leadership till 1708). Beginning of prolonged Mughal–Sikh conflict.
Battle of Palkhed 1728 CE Palkhed, Maharashtra Maratha Empire vs. Nizam of Hyderabad Marathas under Bajirao I confronted the Nizam, who opposed their collection of chauth in the Deccan. Maratha victory. Treaty signed. Bajirao I (Maratha), Nizam-ul-Mulk (Hyderabad). Cemented Maratha authority.
Battle of Delhi (1737) 1737 CE Delhi Maratha Empire vs. Mughal Empire Marathas under Bajirao I raided Delhi to demonstrate Mughal weakness and assert dominance in North India. Maratha victory. Mughal defenses overrun. Bajirao I (Maratha), Mughal garrison. Highlighted Mughal decline.
Battle of Bhopal 1737 CE Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh Maratha Empire vs. Mughal allies & Nizam Marathas aimed to force the Nizam and Mughal vassals to cede Malwa, expanding their central Indian influence. Maratha victory. Nizam surrendered. Bajirao I (Maratha), Nizam-ul-Mulk (Nizam). Malwa ceded to Marathas.
Battle of Vasai 1739 CE Vasai, Maharashtra Maratha Empire vs. Portuguese Marathas under Chimaji Appa aimed to expel Portuguese from the Konkan coast to secure western trade routes. Maratha victory. Portuguese stronghold captured. Chimaji Appa (Maratha), Portuguese garrison. Ended Portuguese dominance.
First Battle of Katwa 1744 CE Katwa, Bengal Maratha Empire vs. Nawab of Bengal Marathas raided Bengal to extract tribute (chauth) from Nawab Alivardi Khan, exploiting Mughal decline. Maratha victory. Bengal plundered. Bhaskar Pandit (Maratha), Alivardi Khan (Bengal). Part of Bargi invasions.
Battle of Plassey 1757 CE Plassey, Bengal East India Company vs. Nawab of Bengal Robert Clive aimed to oust Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah and install a puppet ruler to control Bengal’s wealth and trade. British victory. Siraj-ud-Daulah defeated. Robert Clive (EIC), Siraj-ud-Daulah (Bengal). Treachery by Mir Jafar pivotal.
Battle of Buxar 1764 CE Buxar, Bihar East India Company vs. Mughal Empire & allies The EIC aimed to defeat the combined forces of Mughal emperor Shah Alam II, Nawab of Bengal, and Nawab of Awadh to secure Bengal and Bihar. British victory. Mughal allies defeated. Hector Munro (EIC), Mir Qasim, Shah Alam II (Mughal allies). Treaty of Allahabad granted EIC diwani rights.
Third Battle of Panipat 1761 CE Panipat, Haryana Maratha Empire vs. Durrani Empire Marathas aimed to dominate North India and install Vishwasrao as Mughal emperor, opposed by Ahmad Shah Durrani to protect his Punjab influence. Durrani victory. Maratha expansion halted. Sadashivrao Bhau (Maratha), Ahmad Shah Durrani (Durrani). Massive casualties.
First Anglo-Mysore War 1767–1769 CE Mysore, Tamil Nadu East India Company vs. Mysore The EIC aimed to curb Hyder Ali’s growing power in Mysore and secure southern trade routes. Mysore victory. Treaty of Madras signed. Hyder Ali (Mysore), EIC commanders. EIC forced to negotiate.
Second Anglo-Mysore War 1780–1784 CE Mysore, Tamil Nadu East India Company vs. Mysore Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan resisted EIC expansion, allied with the French, to protect Mysore’s sovereignty. Inconclusive; Treaty of Mangalore signed. Hyder Ali, Tipu Sultan (Mysore), Warren Hastings (EIC). Stalemate; Mysore remained independent.
Campaigns (738–1800 CE)
Tripartite Struggle Campaigns ~Late 8th / Early 9th C. CE Kannauj & Ganges Valley Gurjara-Pratiharas vs. Palas vs. Rashtrakutas Three dynasties vied for control of Kannauj, the symbolic and economic heart of North India, in a decades-long power struggle. Pratiharas dominated; all weakened. Vatsaraja, Nagabhata II (Pratihara); Dharmapala (Pala); Dhruva, Govinda III (Rashtrakuta). Multi-decade rivalry.
Ghaznavid Campaigns into Punjab ~1001–1026 CE Punjab, Northwest India Ghaznavid Empire vs. Hindu Shahi & local rulers Mahmud of Ghazni launched 17 raids to plunder wealth, weaken Hindu Shahi resistance, and expand Ghaznavid influence. Ghaznavid victories. Punjab annexed. Mahmud of Ghazni (Ghaznavid), Jayapala, Anandapala (Hindu Shahi). Included Somnath raid.
Chola Expedition to Srivijaya ~1025 CE Malay Peninsula, Sumatra Chola Empire vs. Srivijaya Empire Rajendra Chola I aimed to secure maritime trade routes in Southeast Asia, targeting Srivijaya’s rival dominance. Chola victory. Srivijaya ports raided. Rajendra Chola I (Chola), Sangrama Vijayatunggavarman (Srivijaya). Naval supremacy shown.
Khalji Southern Campaigns 1305–1318 CE Deccan & South India Delhi Sultanate vs. Kakatiya, Pandya, etc. Alauddin Khalji sent Malik Kafur on multiple raids to extract tribute, weaken southern kingdoms, and secure resources. Sultanate victories. Tribute imposed. Alauddin Khalji, Malik Kafur (Sultanate), Prataparudra (Kakatiya). Temporary control.
Tughlaq Campaigns against Mongols 1320s–1330s CE Northwest India & Punjab Delhi Sultanate vs. Mongol invaders Muhammad bin Tughlaq launched defensive campaigns to repel recurring Mongol raids threatening North India. Mixed results; temporary repulsions. Muhammad bin Tughlaq (Sultanate), Mongol khans. Strengthened frontier defenses.
Timur’s Invasion of India 1398 CE Delhi & Northwest India Timurid Empire vs. Tughlaq Dynasty Timur aimed to plunder Delhi’s wealth and exploit Tughlaq instability, seeking to emulate earlier conquerors. Timurid victory. Delhi sacked. Timur (Timurid), Mahmud Shah (Tughlaq). Devastating campaign.
Akbar’s Northwest Campaigns 1572–1586 CE Kabul, Kandahar, Northwest Frontier Mughal Empire vs. Afghan tribes & Mirza Hakim Akbar aimed to secure the northwest frontier, subdue his half-brother Mirza Hakim’s rebellion, and protect trade routes to Central Asia. Mughal victories. Akbar, Man Singh I (Mughal), Mirza Hakim (rebel). Frontier stabilized.
Akbar’s Deccan Campaign 1595–1601 CE Khandesh, Ahmadnagar, Deccan Mughal Empire vs. Deccan Sultanates Akbar sought to extend Mughal rule into the Deccan, targeting Khandesh and Ahmadnagar for their strategic and economic value. Mughal victory. Khandesh annexed. Akbar, Abul Fazl (Mughal), Chand Bibi (Ahmadnagar). Siege of Asirgarh key.
Jahangir’s Kangra Campaign 1615–1620 CE Kangra Fort, Himachal Pradesh Mughal Empire vs. Kangra Raja Jahangir aimed to subdue the northwest hill states, capturing Kangra Fort to assert Mughal authority in the region. Mughal victory. Fort captured (1620). Jahangir, Khurram (Mughal), Raja of Kangra. Extended Mughal control.
Jahangir’s Mewar Campaign 1613–1615 CE Mewar, Rajasthan Mughal Empire vs. Mewar Kingdom Jahangir sought to force Rana Amar Singh to submit to Mughal authority, ending decades of Rajput resistance. Mughal diplomatic victory. Amar Singh submitted. Jahangir, Khurram (Mughal), Amar Singh (Mewar). Peace treaty signed.
Shah Jahan’s Balkh Campaign 1646–1647 CE Balkh, Badakhshan (Afghanistan) Mughal Empire vs. Uzbek rulers Shah Jahan aimed to reclaim ancestral Timurid lands and install a friendly ruler in Balkh. Temporary occupation; withdrawn due to costs. Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb (Mughal), Nazr Muhammad (Uzbek). Limited success.
Shah Jahan’s Kandahar Campaigns 1638–1653 CE Kandahar, Afghanistan Mughal Empire vs. Safavid Persia Shah Jahan sought to secure Kandahar, a strategic northwest fortress, from Safavids over three campaigns. Mixed: Captured 1638, lost 1649, failed 1653. Shah Jahan, Ali Mardan Khan (Mughal), Shah Abbas II (Safavid). Prestige blow after failures.
Shah Jahan’s Deccan Campaign 1636–1656 CE Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, Golconda Mughal Empire vs. Deccan Sultanates Shah Jahan aimed to annex Ahmadnagar and force tribute from Bijapur and Golconda to extend Mughal rule southward. Mughal victory. Ahmadnagar annexed. Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb (Mughal), Adil Shah, Qutb Shah. Extended Mughal reach.
Aurangzeb’s Deccan Campaigns 1658–1687 CE Deccan (Bijapur, Golconda, Marathas) Mughal Empire vs. Deccan Sultanates & Marathas Aurangzeb aimed to annex Bijapur and Golconda and crush Maratha resistance to consolidate Mughal rule in the south. Mughal victories (Bijapur 1686, Golconda 1687). Aurangzeb, Jai Singh (Mughal), Shivaji (Maratha). Resource drain.
Aurangzeb’s Northwest Campaigns 1660s–1690s CE Khyber Pass, Swat, tribal areas Mughal Empire vs. Pashtun & Afghan tribes Aurangzeb launched campaigns to pacify rebellious tribes (e.g., Afridi, Yusufzai) and secure the northwest frontier. Mixed; temporary control, constant revolts. Aurangzeb, Diler Khan (Mughal), tribal leaders (Afridi, Yusufzai). Costly stalemate.
Aurangzeb’s Maratha Campaigns 1681–1707 CE Deccan, Maharashtra Mughal Empire vs. Maratha Empire Aurangzeb aimed to crush the Maratha rebellion under Shivaji and his successors to assert Mughal dominance in the Deccan. Mixed; Marathas persisted via guerrilla warfare. Aurangzeb (Mughal), Shivaji, Rajaram, Tarabai (Maratha). Drained Mughal resources.
Maratha Campaigns in the North 1737–1744 CE Delhi, Malwa, Bengal Maratha Empire vs. Mughal Empire & allies Marathas under Bajirao I aimed to expand northward, extract tribute, and dominate a declining Mughal empire. Maratha victories (e.g., Bhopal 1737, Katwa 1744). Bajirao I, Bhaskar Pandit (Maratha), Nizam-ul-Mulk (Mughal ally). Weakened Mughals.
Later Mughal Campaigns 1710s–1750s CE North India, Deccan Mughal Empire vs. Marathas, Sikhs, regional powers Later Mughals (e.g., Bahadur Shah I, Muhammad Shah) fought to maintain control amid Maratha expansion, Sikh uprisings, and invasions (e.g., Nadir Shah). Mixed; Mughal decline accelerated. Bahadur Shah I, Muhammad Shah (Mughal), Balaji Bajirao (Maratha). Mughal authority eroded.
Nadir Shah’s Invasion 1739 CE Delhi, Northwest India Persian Empire vs. Mughal Empire Nadir Shah invaded to plunder Mughal wealth and exploit their weakness after Maratha raids. Persian victory. Delhi sacked. Nadir Shah (Persian), Muhammad Shah (Mughal). Mughal treasury looted.
- Invasions and European companies -
Invading Group Approximate Period Region(s) Affected Key Leaders/Events Impact/Significance
Umayyad Caliphate (Arabs) ~711–738 CE Sindh, Rajasthan, Gujarat border regions Muhammad bin Qasim; conquest of Sindh (711–712 CE); Battles of Rajasthan (738 CE). First Muslim foothold in India (Sindh); introduction of Islam; halted by Indian confederacy; limited territorial gain but notable cultural exchange.
Ghaznavid Empire ~1001–1026 CE or until 1186 (for Punjab) Northwest India (Punjab, Rajasthan, Gujarat) Mahmud of Ghazni; 17 raids, including Sack of Somnath (1025–1026 CE); battles against Hindu Shahi. Punjab annexed (ruled until 1186 CE); massive plunder; weakened Hindu Shahi; cultural disruption; paved way for later Muslim invasions.
Ghurid Sultanate ~1175–1206 CE Northwest and Northern India (Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan) Muhammad Ghori; First Battle of Tarain (1191 CE), Second Battle of Tarain (1192 CE), Battle of Chandawar (1194 CE). Established Muslim rule; foundation of Delhi Sultanate; end of Rajput dominance in North India; major political and cultural shift.
Mongol Invasions ~1221–1327 CE (13th–14th centuries) Northwest India (Punjab, Sindh, Delhi region)
  • 1221 CE: Genghis Khan pursued Khwarazm prince Jalal al-Din into Punjab (Battle of Indus).
  • 1241 CE: Sack of Lahore.
  • 1257–1260 CE: Raids during Nasiruddin Mahmud’s reign.
  • 1299 CE: Major attack during Alauddin Khalji’s reign; Battle of Kili.
  • 1305 CE: Battle of Amroha (Alauddin’s forces repulsed Mongols).
  • 1306 CE: Mongols crushed near Ravi river.
  • 1327 CE: Last major Mongol attempt under Tughlaq rule.
  • Repeated raids devastated Punjab and the northwestern frontier.
  • Alauddin Khalji fortified Siri city and created a permanent standing army.
  • Frontier forts were strengthened; defensive policies became central to the Sultanate.
  • No permanent Mongol conquest, but invasions strained Delhi’s economy and military.
Timurid Empire 1398 CE Northwest India, Delhi Timur (Tamerlane); Battle of Delhi (1398 CE); sack of Delhi. Massive destruction; Delhi devastated; Tughlaq dynasty weakened; regional fragmentation; temporary power vacuum.
Portuguese ~1498–17th century CE Western Coast (Goa, Diu, Daman, Bombay, Malabar) Vasco da Gama (1498 arrival); Afonso de Albuquerque; capture of Goa (1510 CE), Battle of Diu (1509 CE). Established coastal enclaves (Goa as capital); monopolized spice trade; introduced Christianity and European naval power; disrupted local trade networks; long-term colonial presence.
Mughal–Timurid forces (Babur’s army) 1526 CE Northwest and Northern India (Punjab, Haryana, Delhi) Babur; Battle of Panipat (1526 CE); defeat of Ibrahim Lodi. Founded Mughal Empire; end of Delhi Sultanate (Lodi); Central Asian tactics introduced; basis for a Persian-Indian cultural synthesis.
East India Company (British) 1600 CE (charter), 1613 CE (Surat factory), 1757 CE onwards (political control) Surat, later Madras, Bombay, Calcutta; Bengal after Plassey
  • Chartered by Queen Elizabeth I (1600).
  • William Hawkins: 1608–1611 CE, Agra, first English envoy to Jahangir’s court, failed to secure factory rights due to Portuguese influence.
  • Sir Thomas Roe: 1615–1619 CE, Ajmer/Agra, ambassador of King James I, secured firman from Emperor Jahangir for factory at Surat (1613 CE) and trading rights with no inland tariffs.
  • Jean-Baptiste Tavernier: 1638–1668 CE (multiple visits), French merchant/traveler, traded gems, documented Mughal court under Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb, no direct factory rights.
  • Niccolao Manucci: 1656–1717 CE, Venetian traveler, served in Mughal court (under Dara Shikoh and Aurangzeb), wrote detailed accounts (Storia do Mogor), no factory involvement.
  • First factory at Surat (1613 CE, Jahangir’s permission).
  • Robert Clive’s victory at Plassey (1757 CE) against Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah.
  • Initial phase: commercial trade, rivalry with Portuguese/Dutch/French; factories at Surat, Madras (1639), Bombay (1668), Calcutta (1690).
  • Roe’s firman enabled duty-free trade, strengthening British presence.
  • Tavernier and Manucci provided cultural insights, aiding European understanding of India.
  • Later phase: territorial control after Plassey, beginning of British colonial dominance, control of Bengal’s wealth, end of Nawabi independence.
Dutch (VOC) ~1605–17th century CE Coromandel Coast, Bengal, Malabar, Gujarat
  • Dutch East India Company (VOC) founded 1602.
  • Trading posts established (e.g., Pulicat 1610 CE, under permission from Vijayanagara rulers; Surat 1616 CE, under Jahangir).
  • Conflicts with Portuguese and locals; no major leaders like Roe for diplomacy.
  • Trade-focused presence; no large-scale conquest.
  • Factories at Pulicat, Surat, Chinsura (Bengal); competed with Portuguese and British.
  • Limited territorial impact but influenced commerce, especially textiles and spices.
Danes (Danish East India Company) ~1616–17th century CE Eastern Coast (Tranquebar), Bengal
  • Ove Gjedde; established Tranquebar (1620 CE, permission from Raghunatha Nayak of Thanjavur).
  • Minor trading posts in Bengal.
  • Small-scale trade presence (Tranquebar as main base).
  • Minimal military impact; focused on commerce.
  • Marginal influence compared to British, Dutch; brief missionary activity.
French ~1664–1760 CE Eastern Coast (Pondicherry), Bengal, Malabar
  • François Caron; French East India Company founded 1664.
  • Pondicherry founded (1674 CE, permission from Sher Khan Lodi, Bijapur governor).
  • Skirmishes with locals and rivals; no prominent individual diplomats like Roe.
  • Trade settlements established (Pondicherry as base; Chandernagore in Bengal).
  • Competed with British and Dutch; minor territorial control.
  • Set stage for later 18th-century conflicts; introduced French cultural influence.
Safavid Persia ~16th–17th centuries CE Northwest India (Kandahar region) Shah Abbas I, Shah Abbas II; Kandahar campaigns (e.g., 1649 CE capture from Shah Jahan). No permanent Indian conquest; Kandahar contested; strained Mughal resources; highlighted Mughal-Safavid rivalry; limited cultural impact.
Durrani Empire ~1748–1769 CE Northwest and Northern India (Punjab, Haryana, Delhi) Ahmad Shah made nine invasions (1748–1769 CE), though Panipat (1761) was decisive; multiple invasions; Third Battle of Panipat (1761 CE) against Marathas. Punjab briefly annexed; Maratha expansion halted; Mughal empire weakened; opened path for British influence; Afghan presence in northwest.
- Historians, shcolars, artists and other -
Figure / Text Time (Approx.) Location / Region Works / Description & Key Details Contemporary Ruler(s) / Period
Vakpati ~Late 8th Century CE Kannauj (Gurjara-Pratihara court) Poetry (Mahakavya):
  • Gaudavaho – Epic poem in Prakrit celebrating Yashovarman’s victory over the Gauda king; blends historical narrative with poetic artistry, reflecting early medieval literary trends.
One of the earliest known poets associated with the Gurjara-Pratihara court; possibly linked to early Paramaras. 		Yashovarman of Kannauj / Early Paramaras
Rajashekhara ~Late 9th–Early 10th Century CE Manyakheta (Rashtrakuta court), Kannauj Plays & Poetry:
  • Karpuramanjari (Prakrit romantic comedy, notable for its use of a regional language over Sanskrit).
  • Balaramayana (Sanskrit play on Rama’s life), Viddhashalabhanjika (Courtly drama with intricate characters).
  • Kavyamimamsa (Treatise on poetics, analyzing literary theory, structure, and aesthetics).
Served multiple royal courts; bridged Sanskrit and Prakrit literary traditions. 		Rashtrakutas (Krishna III) / Gurjara-Pratiharas
Somadeva 11th Century CE Kashmir Books (Narrative):
  • Kathasaritsagara (Ocean of the Streams of Stories - A vast Sanskrit anthology of folk tales, fables, and legends compiled for Queen Suryamati, preserving oral traditions).
Influenced later storytelling traditions across South Asia. 		Lohara Dynasty (Kashmir)
Krishnamishra ~11th Century CE Kannauj under Gahadavala Plays (Allegorical Drama):
  • Prabodhachandrodaya (Sanskrit play depicting Vedantic wisdom triumphing over rival philosophies like Buddhism and Jainism through personified virtues and vices).
Philosophical dramatist reflecting medieval intellectual debates. 		Karnata Dynasty (Mithila)
Minhaj-us-Siraj 1193–1259 CE Delhi (Delhi Sultanate) Books (History):
  • Tabaqat-i-Nasiri (Detailed chronicle of Muslim rulers from Central Asia to India up to 1260 CE, dedicated to Sultan Nasiruddin Mahmud; a primary source for early Sultanate history).
Early historian providing insights into the Slave Dynasty. 		Iltutmish, Nasiruddin Mahmud (Delhi Sultanate)
Jnanesvara (Jnanadeva) 1275–1296 CE Maharashtra (Alandi) Poetry/Philosophy:
  • Jnanesvari (Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, one of the earliest major works in Marathi, blending Bhakti and Advaita philosophy).
  • Amritanubhava (Treatise on divine experience and non-dualism).
Pioneered Varkari Bhakti tradition; died at 21 but left a profound legacy. 		Yadava Dynasty (Ramachandra)
Ziauddin Barani 1285–1357 CE Delhi (Delhi Sultanate) Books (History):
  • Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi (Narrative history of Delhi Sultanate from Balban to Firoz Shah Tughlaq, rich with political analysis and social observations).
  • Fatawa-i-Jahandari (Treatise on ideal Muslim governance, offering practical and theoretical insights).
Court historian; critical of rulers like Muhammad bin Tughlaq. 		Firoz Shah Tughlaq (Delhi Sultanate)
Namdev ~1270–1350 CE Maharashtra Poetry (Bhakti):
  • Abhangas (devotional songs in Marathi and Hindi) dedicated to Vithoba, emphasizing direct devotion; some works included in the Sikh Guru Granth Sahib.
Key Varkari saint; bridged Marathi and northern Bhakti traditions. 		Early Delhi Sultanate (contemporary of Alauddin Khilji)
Isami ~14th Century CE Daulatabad (Bahmani Sultanate) Books (History/Poetry):
  • Futuh-us-Salatin (Persian verse chronicle of Muslim conquests in India from Ghaznavids to Tughlaqs, inspired by Firdausi’s Shahnameh).
Early Deccan historian; reflects Bahmani cultural identity. 		Muhammad bin Tughlaq / Early Bahmani
Ramananda ~14th–15th Century CE Varanasi (North India) Philosophy/Poetry:
  • Founded Ramanandi sect; composed Hindi devotional hymns to Rama, making Bhakti accessible across castes; influenced Kabir, Tulsidas, and the broader Bhakti movement.
Key figure in spreading Rama devotion northward. 		Late Delhi Sultanate
Vidyapati ~1352–1448 CE Mithila (Bihar), Bengal Poetry:
  • Padavali (Maithili love songs on Radha-Krishna, blending eroticism and devotion; influenced Vaishnava poetry).
  • Sanskrit works like Likhanavali (on law and erotics).
Known as ‘Maithil Kavi Kokil’ (Nightingale of Mithila); shaped eastern Indian literature. 		Oiniwar Dynasty of Mithila
Kabir ~1398–1518 CE Varanasi (North India) Poetry (Bhakti/Sufi):
  • Dohas, padas, and shabdas in Hindi, critiquing religious orthodoxy and promoting a formless God; preserved in Guru Granth Sahib and Kabir Panth texts.
Syncretic saint; influenced Hindu and Muslim spiritual traditions. 		Lodi Dynasty / Early Mughal Period
Nund Rishi (Sheikh Nooruddin) 1377–1438 CE Kashmir Poetry (Sufi/Mystical):
  • Shruks (Kashmiri verses blending Sufi mysticism with local Shaivism, advocating peace, simplicity, and devotion).
Founder of Rishi order; revered as Kashmir’s patron saint. 		Zain-ul-Abidin (Kashmir Sultanate)
Babur 1483–1530 CE (Reigned 1526–1530 CE) Northern India (Mughal Empire) Books (Autobiography):
  • Baburnama (Memoirs in Chagatai Turkish, chronicling his conquests, personal life, and detailed observations of India’s nature and culture).
Founder of Mughal Empire; poet and calligrapher. 		Babur (Self) / Defeated Ibrahim Lodi
Mirabai ~1498–1546 CE Rajasthan (Mewar) Poetry (Bhakti):
  • Devotional songs in Rajasthani and Braj Bhasha to Krishna, expressing ecstatic love and defiance of societal norms; widely sung in Indian tradition.
Royal poetess; icon of feminine devotion in Bhakti movement. 		Rana Sanga (Mewar) / Early Mughal Period
Guru Nanak 1469–1539 CE Punjab (Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib) Religious Texts / Poetry:
  • Compositions in Guru Granth Sahib (e.g., Japji Sahib, Asa di Var), blending Bhakti and Sufi ideas in Punjabi, advocating equality and devotion.
Founder of Sikhism; traveled widely to spread his message. 		Lodi Dynasty / Babur (Early Mughal)
Raskhan ~1548–1628 CE Braj region (North India) Poetry (Bhakti):
  • Prem Vatika, Sujan Raskhan (Braj Bhasha poems expressing passionate devotion to Krishna; a Muslim poet who converted to Vaishnavism after a vision).
Celebrated for his intense Krishna bhakti; exemplifies Hindu-Muslim syncretism. 		Akbar, Jahangir (Mughal Empire)
Surdas ~1478–1583 CE Braj region (North India) Poetry (Bhakti):
  • Sur Sagar (Braj Bhasha poems on Krishna’s life, especially his childhood; traditionally said to include over 100,000 verses, though fewer survive).
Blind poet; one of the Ashtachap poets of Vallabhacharya’s sect. 		Akbar (Mughal Empire)
Tansen ~1506–1589 CE Gwalior, Agra (Mughal Empire) Music:
  • Legendary musician; developed ragas like Miyan ki Todi, Darbari Kanada, and Malhar (said to invoke rain); composed dhrupad songs in praise of Krishna and Akbar.
  • Trained under Swami Haridas in Gwalior; blended Hindustani classical traditions with Persian influences at Akbar’s court; known for his vocal prowess and innovation.
One of Akbar’s Nine Jewels; considered the greatest musician of medieval India. 		Akbar (Mughal Empire)
Tulsidas 1532–1623 CE Varanasi, Chitrakoot Poetry (Devotional):
  • Ramcharitmanas (Awadhi epic retelling Ramayana, making it accessible to common people).
  • Hanuman Chalisa, Vinaya Patrika (Hymns of devotion to Rama).
Revived Rama bhakti; cornerstone of Hindi devotional literature. 		Akbar (Mughal Empire)
Abul Fazl 1551–1602 CE Agra, Fatehpur Sikri (Mughal Empire) Books (History/Biography):
  • Akbarnama (Three-volume history of Akbar’s reign in Persian, detailing his conquests and policies).
  • Ain-i-Akbari (Detailed record of Akbar’s administration, culture, and statistics).
Akbar’s vizier; one of Nine Jewels; assassinated by Bir Singh Bundela. 		Akbar (Mughal Empire)
Faizi 1547–1595 CE Agra, Fatehpur Sikri (Mughal Empire) Poetry/Translation:
  • Persian poetry (e.g., Nal wa Daman); translated Sanskrit texts like Mahabharata and Lilavati into Persian for Akbar’s court.
Abul Fazl’s brother; one of Akbar’s Nine Jewels. 		Akbar (Mughal Empire)
Badauni (Abdul Qadir) 1540–1615 CE Agra, Delhi (Mughal Empire) Books (History):
  • Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh (Three-volume history critical of Akbar’s religious liberalism, offering a contrasting view to Abul Fazl).
Orthodox scholar; provides an alternative Mughal narrative. 		Akbar (Mughal Empire)
Ibrahim Adil Shah II 1556–1627 CE (Reigned 1580–1627 CE) Bijapur (Adil Shahi Sultanate) Books (Poetry/Music):
  • Kitab-i-Nauras (Dakhni Urdu poems blending Hindu-Muslim themes, celebrating music and the nine rasas; reflects Deccan syncretism).
Patron of arts; built Ibrahim Rauza; resisted Mughal dominance. 		Ibrahim Adil Shah II (Self) / Mughal influence
Jahangir 1569–1627 CE (Reigned 1605–1627 CE) Agra, Lahore (Mughal Empire) Books (Autobiography):
  • Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (Persian memoirs detailing his reign, justice system, love for nature, and patronage of arts like miniature painting).
Mughal emperor; documented his rule personally. 		Jahangir (Self)
Ferishta (Muhammad Qasim) ~1560–1620 CE Bijapur, Ahmadnagar Books (History):
  • Tarikh-i-Ferishta (Comprehensive Persian history of India from early Islamic invasions to the Deccan Sultanates and Mughals; widely referenced).
One of the most detailed medieval Indian historians. 		Adil Shahi / Nizam Shahi / Early Mughal
Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khana 1556–1627 CE Agra, Delhi (Mughal Empire) Poetry:
  • Dohas in Braj Bhasha and Hindi (e.g., on ethics and devotion); Persian poetry; translated Baburnama into Persian; composed verses to Krishna.
One of Akbar’s Nine Jewels; general and poet known as ‘Rahim’. 		Akbar, Jahangir (Mughal Empire)
Mian Mir 1550–1635 CE Lahore (Mughal Empire) Sufi Poetry/Philosophy:
  • Mystical verses in Persian and Punjabi; spiritual guide to Dara Shikoh; laid the foundation of the Golden Temple’s sanctum, symbolizing interfaith harmony.
Qadiri Sufi saint; revered across communities. 		Jahangir, Shah Jahan (Mughal Empire)
Abdul Hamid Lahori d. 1654 CE Mughal Court (Delhi, Agra) Works (Court Historian):
  • Padshahnama (official chronicle of Shah Jahan’s reign, written in Persian).
  • Detailed descriptions of Shah Jahan’s campaigns, administration, and architectural projects (including Taj Mahal, Red Fort).
  • Modeled on Abul Fazl’s Akbarnama, but limited to Shah Jahan’s era.
Court historian; documented Mughal grandeur and imperial ideology under Shah Jahan. 		Shah Jahan (Mughal)
Dara Shikoh 1615–1659 CE Agra, Delhi (Mughal Empire) Books (Philosophy/Sufism):
  • Majma-ul-Bahrain (Synthesis of Hindu and Islamic mysticism).
  • Translated Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita into Persian as Sirr-i-Akbar; wrote Safinatul Awliya (Sufi biographies).
Mughal prince; scholar of comparative religion; executed by Aurangzeb. 		Shah Jahan (Mughal Empire)
Sarmad Kashani ~1590–1661 CE Delhi (Mughal Empire) Poetry (Sufi):
  • Rubaiyat (Persian quatrains, mystical and rebellious, rejecting orthodoxy; lived as a naked fakir).
Sufi poet; executed by Aurangzeb for heresy. 		Aurangzeb (Mughal Empire)
Bulleh Shah 1680–1757 CE Punjab (Kasur, Lahore) Poetry (Sufi):
  • Kafis (Punjabi mystical poems expressing divine love and defiance of religious norms; e.g., “Bulleh! Ki Jaana Main Kaun”).
Sufi poet; bridged folk and mystical traditions. 		Aurangzeb / Later Mughals
Shah Waliullah Dehlawi 1703–1762 CE Delhi (Late Mughal Empire) Books (Theology):
  • Hujjat Allah al-Baligha (Rational interpretation of Islamic principles).
  • Translated Quran into Persian; wrote Fathur Rahman (commentary).
Islamic reformer; influenced later Muslim thought in India. 		Ahmad Shah Bahadur (Mughal Empire)
Mir Taqi Mir 1723–1810 CE Delhi, Lucknow Poetry:
  • Urdu ghazals (e.g., Dikhayi Diye Yun) reflecting Mughal decline and personal melancholy; foundational figure in Urdu poetry.
Known as ‘Khuda-e-Sukhan’ (God of Poetry). 		Late Mughals / Nawabs of Awadh
Mirza Ghalib 1797–1869 CE Delhi (Late Mughal Empire) Poetry:
  • Diwan-e-Ghalib (Urdu and Persian ghazals exploring love, loss, and existential themes; e.g., “Hazaron Khwahishen Aisi”); witnessed 1857 uprising.
Iconic poet; chronicled the end of Mughal culture. 		Bahadur Shah Zafar (Mughal Empire)
- Literature work -
Text/Work Time (Approx.) Language/Region Description & Key Details Category/Subcategory
Hindu Literature (~6th–18th Century CE)
Gaudavaho (Vakpati) ~Late 8th Century CE Prakrit / Malwa (Dhara) By Vakpati. Epic poem celebrating Yashovarman of Kannauj’s victory over the Gauda king; patronized by Gurjara-Pratihara ruler Vatsraja. Reflects early medieval literary style with historical narrative, blending martial themes with poetic flair. Hindu Literature / Mahakavya
Karpuramanjari ~Late 9th–Early 10th Century CE Prakrit / Manyakheta, Kannauj By Rajashekhara. Romantic comedy play in Prakrit, notable for its use of a regional language over Sanskrit. Composed in the Rashtrakuta and Gurjara-Pratihara courts; showcases courtly love and humor, a rarity in medieval drama. Hindu Literature / Drama
Kathasaritsagara 11th Century CE Sanskrit / Kashmir By Somadeva. Vast anthology of tales compiled for Queen Suryamati of the Lohara dynasty. Known as the "Ocean of the Streams of Stories," it preserves folk narratives, fables, and legends, influencing later Indian storytelling traditions. Hindu Literature / Narrative Collections
Prabodhachandrodaya ~11th Century CE Sanskrit By Krishnamishra. Allegorical play depicting Vedantic wisdom triumphing over rival philosophies (e.g., Buddhism, Jainism) through personified virtues and vices. Composed in the Gahadavala dynasty of Kannauj; reflects medieval intellectual debates. Hindu Literature / Drama
Gita Govinda 12th Century CE Sanskrit / Bengal or Odisha By Jayadeva. Lyric poem on the love between Krishna and Radha, composed under the Sena dynasty (possibly Lakshmana Sena). Its musical and devotional verses became central to Vaishnava Bhakti and Odissi dance traditions. Hindu Literature / Bhakti Poetry
Jnanesvari ~1290 CE Marathi / Maharashtra (Alandi) By Jnanesvara (Jnanadeva). Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, blending Bhakti and Advaita philosophy. Composed under the Yadava dynasty; one of the earliest major vernacular works, foundational to the Varkari Bhakti tradition. Hindu Literature / Bhakti Texts
Padavali ~14th–15th Century CE Maithili / Mithila (Bihar), Bengal By Vidyapati. Collection of love songs on Radha and Krishna, blending eroticism and devotion. Composed under the Oinwara dynasty and later Jaunpur Sultanate; influenced Vaishnava poetry and the Bhakti movement in eastern India. Hindu Literature / Bhakti Poetry
Sur Sagar ~16th Century CE Braj Bhasha / Braj (North India) By Surdas. Extensive collection of poems on Krishna’s life, especially his childhood exploits in Vrindavan. Composed under Mughal rule (Akbar’s reign); traditionally said to include over 100,000 verses, a cornerstone of Krishna Bhakti. Hindu Literature / Bhakti Poetry
Ramcharitmanas ~1574–1577 CE Awadhi / Varanasi, Chitrakoot By Tulsidas. Epic retelling of the Ramayana in Awadhi, making Rama’s story accessible to the masses. Composed during Akbar’s reign; emphasizes Rama bhakti and moral values, widely recited in North India. Hindu Literature / Epics (Bhakti)
Prem Vatika ~16th–Early 17th Century CE Braj Bhasha / Braj (North India) By Raskhan. Collection of devotional poems expressing intense love for Krishna, written by a Muslim poet who embraced Vaishnavism. Composed during Akbar and Jahangir’s reigns; exemplifies Hindu-Muslim literary syncretism. Hindu Literature / Bhakti Poetry
Islamic Literature (~13th–18th Century CE)
Tabaqat-i-Nasiri ~1260 CE Persian / Delhi (Delhi Sultanate) By Minhaj-us-Siraj. Chronicle of Muslim rulers from Central Asia to India, dedicated to Sultan Nasiruddin Mahmud. Covers the Slave Dynasty (e.g., Iltutmish); a primary historical source for the early Delhi Sultanate. Islamic Literature / Historical Chronicles
Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi ~1357 CE Persian / Delhi (Delhi Sultanate) By Ziauddin Barani. Narrative history of the Delhi Sultanate from Balban to Firoz Shah Tughlaq, offering political insights and social commentary. Written under the Tughlaq dynasty; critical of rulers like Muhammad bin Tughlaq. Islamic Literature / Historical Chronicles
Futuh-us-Salatin ~14th Century CE Persian / Daulatabad (Bahmani Sultanate) By Isami. Verse chronicle of Muslim conquests in India from the Ghaznavids to the Tughlaqs, modeled after Firdausi’s Shahnameh. Composed in the early Bahmani Sultanate; reflects Deccan pride and historical memory. Islamic Literature / Historical Poetry
Baburnama ~1526–1530 CE Chagatai Turkish / Northern India By Babur. Autobiographical memoirs detailing his conquests (e.g., Panipat), personal life, and observations of India’s flora, fauna, and culture. Written during the founding of the Mughal Empire; a rare ruler’s personal account. Islamic Literature / Autobiographies
Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh ~Late 16th Century CE Persian / Agra, Delhi (Mughal Empire) By Abdul Qadir Badauni. Three-volume history critical of Akbar’s religious policies, contrasting Abul Fazl’s views. Composed under Akbar; offers an orthodox perspective on Mughal rule. Islamic Literature / Historical Chronicles
Akbarnama ~1590–1602 CE Persian / Agra, Fatehpur Sikri By Abul Fazl. Three-volume official history of Akbar’s reign, detailing his conquests, administration, and policies. Written under Akbar; a key source for Mughal history, reflecting his vision of governance. Islamic Literature / Historical Chronicles
Ain-i-Akbari ~1590s CE Persian / Agra, Fatehpur Sikri By Abul Fazl. Detailed record of Akbar’s administration, culture, geography, and statistics (e.g., revenue systems, military organization). Part of Akbarnama; an encyclopedic work of Mughal governance. Islamic Literature / Administrative Texts
Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri ~1605–1627 CE Persian / Agra, Lahore By Jahangir. Autobiographical memoirs of his reign, covering justice, nature, and art patronage (e.g., miniature painting). Written during his rule; provides a personal glimpse into Mughal court life. Islamic Literature / Autobiographies
Kitab-i-Nauras ~Late 16th–Early 17th Century CE Dakhni Urdu / Bijapur By Ibrahim Adil Shah II. Collection of poems celebrating music, art, and the nine rasas, blending Hindu-Muslim themes. Composed in the Adil Shahi Sultanate; reflects Deccan syncretism and cultural richness. Islamic Literature / Poetry
Tarikh-i-Ferishta ~Early 17th Century CE Persian / Bijapur, Ahmadnagar By Ferishta (Muhammad Qasim). Comprehensive history of India from early Islamic invasions to the Deccan Sultanates and Mughals. Written under Adil Shahi and Nizam Shahi patronage; a vital medieval chronicle. Islamic Literature / Historical Chronicles
