Majma-ul-Bahrain ~1655 CE Persian / Agra, Delhi By Dara Shikoh. Philosophical treatise synthesizing Hindu and Islamic mysticism (e.g., Vedanta and Sufism). Written under Shah Jahan; reflects his pursuit of religious unity, later condemned by Aurangzeb. Islamic Literature / Sufi Philosophy
Diwan-e-Ghalib ~19th Century CE (Late Mughal) Urdu, Persian / Delhi By Mirza Ghalib. Collection of ghazals exploring love, loss, and existential themes (e.g., “Hazaron Khwahishen Aisi”). Composed during Bahadur Shah Zafar’s reign; chronicled the 1857 uprising and Mughal decline. Islamic Literature / Poetry
Sikh Literature (~15th–18th Century CE)
Guru Granth Sahib ~1469–1708 CE (Compiled 1604) Punjabi (Gurmukhi script) / Punjab Compiled by Guru Arjan (5th Guru) and finalized by Guru Gobind Singh (10th Guru). Sacred Sikh scripture with hymns by Guru Nanak, Kabir, Namdev, and others, emphasizing devotion, equality, and one God. Central to Sikh worship. Sikh Literature / Sacred Texts
Regional Vernacular Literature (~13th–18th Century CE)
Abhangas of Namdev ~13th–14th Century CE Marathi, Hindi / Maharashtra By Namdev. Devotional songs to Vithoba, emphasizing direct devotion over ritual. Composed in the later Yadava dynasty and early Delhi Sultanate; some included in Guru Granth Sahib, reflecting Varkari Bhakti. Regional Vernacular Literature / Bhakti Poetry
Shruks of Nund Rishi ~14th–15th Century CE Kashmiri / Kashmir By Nund Rishi (Sheikh Nooruddin). Mystical verses blending Sufism and local Shaivism, advocating peace and simplicity. Composed under the Kashmir Sultanate (Zain-ul-Abidin); foundational to Kashmiri Sufi tradition. Regional Vernacular Literature / Sufi Poetry
Kabir’s Dohas ~15th–16th Century CE Hindi / Varanasi By Kabir. Couplets and songs critiquing religious orthodoxy and promoting a formless God. Composed under Lodi and early Mughal rule; preserved in Guru Granth Sahib and Kabir Panth, embodying syncretic Bhakti-Sufi ideals. Regional Vernacular Literature / Bhakti-Sufi Poetry
Mirabai’s Bhajans ~16th Century CE Rajasthani, Braj Bhasha / Rajasthan By Mirabai. Devotional songs to Krishna expressing ecstatic love and defiance of norms. Composed in Mewar under Rana Sanga and early Mughal influence; widely sung, symbolizing feminine Bhakti. Regional Vernacular Literature / Bhakti Poetry
Kafis of Bulleh Shah ~18th Century CE Punjabi / Punjab (Kasur, Lahore) By Bulleh Shah. Mystical Sufi poems expressing divine love and rebellion against orthodoxy (e.g., “Bulleh! Ki Jaana Main Kaun”). Composed under Aurangzeb and later Mughals; influential in Punjabi folk culture. Regional Vernacular Literature / Sufi Poetry
- Religion -
Religion/Movement Time Period Origin (Location) Core Principles Rise & Development Key Figures (Time, Location, Background) Primary Texts Major Sects/Schools Key Concepts/Figures (Salvation/Guidance) Significant Councils/Assemblies (Time, Location, Patron) Important Sites Patron Rulers/Dynasties Factors of Decline
Bhakti Movement (Hinduism) ~7th–17th Century CE South India (Tamil Nadu), later North India
  • Devotion (Bhakti): Personal, emotional connection to a deity.
  • Equality: Rejection of caste, gender, and ritual hierarchies.
  • Moksha: Liberation through love and surrender to God.
  • Monotheism/Personal God: Focus on Vishnu (Krishna, Rama), Shiva, or Devi.
  • Simplicity: Emphasis on direct devotion over complex rituals.
  • Originated with Alvars (Vaishnava) and Nayanars (Shaiva) in Tamil Nadu (~7th–10th CE).
  • Spread to North India via Ramananda (~14th CE), emphasizing vernacular languages.
  • Peaked during Mughal era (16th–17th CE) with poets like Tulsidas, Mirabai, and Tyagaraja.
  • Influenced by and syncretized with Sufism (e.g., Kabir’s teachings).
  • Gained mass appeal among lower castes and women.
  • Alvars: ~7th–10th CE, Tamil Nadu, 12 Vaishnava saints (e.g., Andal, female poet, daughter of Periyalvar, Brahmin; Nammalvar, Shudra poet, mystic visionary).
  • Nayanars: ~6th–9th CE, Tamil Nadu, 63 Shaiva saints (e.g., Appar, ex-Jain monk turned poet; Sundarar, Brahmin, temple singer; Manikkavacakar, Brahmin minister turned ascetic).
  • Siddhas (Sittars): ~8th–13th CE, Tamil Nadu, mystic poet-saints (e.g., Tirumular, Shaiva yogi; Sivavakkiyar, anti-caste poet), emphasized spiritual liberation through yoga and poetry.
  • Basava: ~1131–1196 CE, Bagewadi (Karnataka), poet and social reformer, born to a Brahmin family (later rejected caste), founded Lingayat sect, promoted Shaiva Bhakti and anti-caste equality.
  • Nimbarka: ~11th–12th CE (disputed, possibly 6th–7th CE), Mathura (Uttar Pradesh), Brahmin philosopher, founded Nimbarka Sampradaya, preached Dvaitadvaita (dualistic monism) and Radha-Krishna devotion.
  • Ramananda: ~1360–1470 CE, Prayag (Uttar Pradesh), Brahmin scholar, disciple of Ramanuja lineage, opened Bhakti to all castes, teacher to many saints.
  • Namdev: ~1270–1350 CE, Maharashtra, tailor, born in a Shudra tailor family, preached devotion to Vitthal (Vishnu), traveled widely.
  • Jnaneshwar: ~1275–1296 CE, Alandi (Maharashtra), poet/philosopher, born to Brahmin parents (outcasted initially), wrote Jnaneshwari (Bhagavad Gita commentary), Vitthal devotee.
  • Kabir: ~1440–1518 CE, Varanasi, weaver, born to Muslim weaver family but raised with Hindu influences, preached Nirguna (formless God), mystic poet.
  • Ravidas: ~1450–1520 CE, Varanasi, cobbler, born in a Chamar (leatherworker) Shudra family, Krishna devotee, emphasized equality.
  • Sena: ~14th–15th CE, Punjab, barber, born in a lower-caste barber family, disciple of Ramananda, composed devotional songs to Vishnu.
  • Pipa: ~14th CE, Gagron (Rajasthan), ex-Rajput king turned poet, born into royalty, became Ramananda’s disciple, preached Krishna devotion.
  • Chaitanya Mahaprabhu: ~1486–1534 CE, Nadia (Bengal), Brahmin scholar, born to Jagannath Mishra (priest), founded Gaudiya Vaishnavism, ecstatic Krishna devotion.
  • Vallabhacharya: ~1479–1531 CE, Champaran (Andhra Pradesh origin, active in North India), Brahmin philosopher, born to a Telugu Brahmin family, founded Pushti Marg, Krishna Bhakti through grace.
  • Mirabai: ~1498–1546 CE, Rajasthan, Rajput princess, married into Mewar royal family, Krishna devotee, defied social norms with ecstatic poetry.
  • Surdas: ~1478–1583 CE, Braj (Uttar Pradesh), blind poet, uncertain family background (possibly Brahmin), Krishna devotee, composed Sursagar.
  • Dadu Dayal: ~1544–1603 CE, Ahmedabad (Gujarat), cotton carder, born to a lower-caste family, preached Nirguna Bhakti, founded Dadu Panth.
  • Tulsidas: ~1532–1623 CE, Rajapur (Uttar Pradesh), Brahmin poet, born to poor Brahmin parents, composed Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, Rama devotee.
  • Eknath: ~1533–1599 CE, Paithan (Maharashtra), Brahmin scholar, born to a scholarly family, wrote Eknathi Bhagavat, promoted Vitthal devotion.
  • Tukaram: ~1608–1650 CE, Dehu (Maharashtra), farmer/trader, born in a Shudra Kunbi family, Vitthal devotee, wrote Abhangas (devotional poems).
  • Tyagaraja: 1767–1847 CE, Tiruvarur (Tamil Nadu), Brahmin composer, born to a Telugu Brahmin family, Krishna devotee, composed thousands of Carnatic music kritis.
  • Guru Nanak: 1469–1539 CE, Talwandi (Punjab, now Pakistan), accountant/clerk, born in a Khatri merchant family, founded Sikhism, preached Nirguna Bhakti.
  • Primary Texts:
    • Nalayira Divya Prabandham (Alvars’ Tamil hymns).
    • Tevaram (Nayanars’ Shaiva hymns).
    • Tirumandiram (Tirumular, Siddha text).
    • Vachanas (Basava, Lingayat poetry).
    • Vedanta-Parijata-Saurabha (Nimbarka’s Brahma Sutras commentary).
    • Jnaneshwari (Jnaneshwar’s Gita commentary).
    • Ramcharitmanas (Tulsidas’ Hindi Ramayana).
    • Bijak (Kabir’s couplets).
    • Mirabai’s bhajans (devotional songs).
    • Krishna poetry (Surdas’ Sursagar).
    • Dadu Vani (Dadu Dayal’s hymns).
    • Tyagaraja’s kritis (Carnatic music compositions).
  • Literature & Architecture Highlights:
    • Tamil poetry: Tiruppavai (Andal), Tiruvacakam (Manikkavacakar), Tirumandiram (Tirumular).
    • Hindi/Awadhi works: Ramcharitmanas, Kabir’s dohas.
    • Braj poetry: Surdas’ Krishna songs.
    • Kannada Vachanas: Basava’s anti-caste poetry.
    • Temples: Srirangam (Vaishnava), Chidambaram (Shaiva), Jagannath Puri (Ramananda influence).
  • Vaishnava Bhakti: Vishnu/Krishna/Rama worship (Alvars, Ramananda, Tulsidas, Nimbarka, Chaitanya, Vallabhacharya).
  • Shaiva Bhakti: Shiva devotion (Nayanars, Siddhas).
  • Lingayat Sect: Shaiva, anti-caste, Basava’s leadership.
  • Nirguna Bhakti: Formless God (Kabir, Dadu Dayal, Guru Nanak, influenced by Advaita and Sufism).
  • Saguna Bhakti: God with attributes (Mirabai, Surdas, Tyagaraja).
  • Moksha: Attained through Bhakti (devotion) rather than Jnana (knowledge) alone.
  • Key Figures: Krishna (lover/guide), Rama (ideal king), Shiva (ascetic/lord).
  • Guru: Spiritual teacher as guide (e.g., Ramananda, Nimbarka, Chaitanya).
  • No formal councils; informal gatherings prominent.
  • Kumbh Mela: Periodic (e.g., 12th–17th CE, Prayag), Bhakti saints’ gatherings, no single patron.
  • Kabir’s followers’ assemblies: ~15th–16th CE, Varanasi, self-organized.
  • Chaitanya’s Sankirtan gatherings: ~16th CE, Bengal, led by Chaitanya, no royal patron.
  • Srirangam Temple (Tamil Nadu, Vishnu).
  • Chidambaram Temple (Tamil Nadu, Shiva).
  • Ayodhya (Rama devotion).
  • Mathura/Vrindavan (Krishna devotion, Nimbarka, Chaitanya).
  • Varanasi (Kabir, Ravidas).
  • Puri (Jagannath Temple).
  • Basavakalyan (Lingayat center, Karnataka).
  • Cholas: ~9th–13th CE, temple builders (e.g., Rajaraja I).
  • Vijayanagara Empire: ~14th–16th CE (Krishna Deva Raya, patron of Tulsidas’ style).
  • Mughals: Akbar (1556–1605 CE), tolerated and engaged with Bhakti saints.
  • Integration into mainstream Hinduism by 18th CE.
  • Colonial disruptions (British suppression of regional cultures).
  • Shift to orthodoxy in some regions post-Mughal decline.
Sufi Movement (Islam) ~12th–17th Century CE Northwest India (Sindh, Punjab), later Delhi
  • Ishq: Divine love as path to God.
  • Tasawwuf: Mystical inner journey.
  • Tauhid: Unity of God beyond formal worship.
  • Equality: Universal brotherhood, transcending social divides.
  • Zikr: Remembrance of God through chants/music.
  • Introduced via Arab traders (~8th CE), matured with Sufi saints post-12th CE.
  • Rose under Delhi Sultanate (13th CE) with Chishti order.
  • Flourished under Mughals (16th–17th CE) with patronage and syncretism.
  • Spread through khanqahs, poetry, and music (e.g., Qawwali).
  • Interacted with Bhakti, influencing poets like Kabir.
  • Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti: 1142–1236 CE, Ajmer, Persian Sufi from Chisht (Afghanistan), founded Chishti order in India.
  • Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki: 1173–1235 CE, Delhi, disciple of Moinuddin, spread Chishti order.
  • Sheikh Nasiruddin Chirag-i-Dehlavi: 1274–1356 CE, Delhi, Chishti saint, disciple of Nizamuddin, emphasized spiritual discipline and charity.
  • Nizamuddin Auliya: 1238–1325 CE, Delhi, Chishti saint, emphasized love and charity.
  • Amir Khusrau: 1253–1325 CE, Delhi, poet-musician, Nizamuddin’s disciple, pioneered Qawwali.
  • Sheikh Ahmad Sarhindi: 1564–1624 CE, Sirhind (Punjab), Naqshbandi saint, born to a scholarly Muslim family, emphasized orthodox Sufism, opposed Akbar’s syncretism.
  • Sheikh Salim Chishti: 1478–1572 CE, Fatehpur Sikri, Chishti saint, born in Delhi, spiritual guide to Akbar, known for blessings and tolerance.
  • Sheikh Niamutullah: ~14th–15th CE, Delhi/Kashmir, founder of Niamatullahi order, emphasized mystical unity, limited influence in India.
  • Makhdum Muhammad Jilani: ~15th CE, Uch (Punjab), Qadiri saint, spread Qadiri order, focused on charity and spiritual guidance.
  • Bahauddin Zakariya: 1170–1262 CE, Multan, founded Suhrawardi order in India.
  • Bulleh Shah: 1680–1757 CE, Kasur (Punjab), Punjabi Sufi poet, disciple of Shah Inayat Qadiri.
  • Primary Texts:
    • Kashf-ul-Mahjub (Data Ganj Bakhsh, 11th CE).
    • Fawaid-ul-Fuad (Nizamuddin’s discourses, 14th CE).
    • Awarif-ul-Ma’arif (Suhrawardi teachings).
    • Maktubat-i-Imam Rabbani (Ahmad Sarhindi’s letters).
    • Bulleh Shah’s Kafis (Punjabi poetry).
    • Amir Khusrau’s ghazals and masnavis.
  • Literature & Architecture Highlights:
    • Persian poetry (Khusrau’s Diwan).
    • Punjabi Sufi poetry (Bulleh Shah).
    • Qawwali music tradition.
    • Dargahs: Ajmer Sharif, Nizamuddin Dargah, Multan shrines, Fatehpur Sikri (Salim Chishti).
  • Chishti: Emphasis on love, tolerance, poverty (Moinuddin, Nizamuddin, Nasiruddin, Salim Chishti).
  • Suhrawardi: Discipline, wealth acceptance (Bahauddin Zakariya).
  • Naqshbandi: Silent meditation, orthodoxy (Ahmad Sarhindi).
  • Qadiri: Charity, humility (Makhdum Jilani, Shah Inayat).
  • Niamatullahi: Mystical unity, limited spread (Niamutullah).
  • Fana: Annihilation of self in God.
  • Baqa: Subsistence in divine presence.
  • Pirs/Murshids: Spiritual guides (e.g., Nizamuddin, Ahmad Sarhindi).
  • Urs Festivals: Annual celebrations at dargahs (e.g., Ajmer, 13th CE onwards, Mughal patronage).
  • Chishti gatherings: ~13th–14th CE, Delhi/Ajmer, led by saints like Nizamuddin, Nasiruddin.
  • Ajmer Sharif Dargah (Moinuddin Chishti).
  • Nizamuddin Dargah (Delhi).
  • Hazrat Data Ganj Bakhsh (Lahore).
  • Bahauddin Zakariya Tomb (Multan).
  • Fatehpur Sikri (Salim Chishti shrine).
  • Uch Sharif (Makhdum Jilani).
  • Delhi Sultanate: Iltutmish (1211–1236 CE), early Chishti patron.
  • Mughals: Akbar (1556–1605 CE, patron of Salim Chishti), Jahangir, Dara Shikoh (Sufi sympathizer).
  • Rise of orthodox Islam under Aurangzeb (1658–1707 CE).
  • Colonial policies disrupted syncretic traditions (18th CE).
  • Shift to political Islam post-Mughal decline.
Sikhism ~15th–18th Century CE Punjab (Northwest India)
  • Ik Onkar: One Supreme Creator.
  • Equality: No caste, creed, or gender distinctions.
  • Seva: Selfless service to humanity.
  • Simran: Meditation on God’s name.
  • Five Ks: Kesh (hair), Kangha (comb), Kara (bracelet), Kachera (undergarment), Kirpan (sword), formalized by Guru Gobind Singh.
  • Guru-Shishya: Guru as divine guide.
  • Founded by Guru Nanak (1469 CE) rejecting Hindu/Muslim ritualism.
  • Evolved through 10 Gurus (1469–1708 CE), each adding institutions.
  • Militarized under Guru Hargobind (17th CE) amid Mughal tensions.
  • Khalsa established by Guru Gobind Singh (1699 CE) as a warrior order.
  • Scripture made eternal Guru (1708 CE), ending human Guruship.
  • Guru Nanak: 1469–1539 CE, Talwandi (Nankana Sahib), Khatri caste, founded Sikhism, traveled widely.
  • Guru Angad: 1504–1552 CE, Khadur (Punjab), Khatri, standardized Gurmukhi script.
  • Guru Amar Das: 1479–1574 CE, Goindval (Punjab), Khatri, institutionalized langar (community kitchen).
  • Guru Ram Das: 1534–1581 CE, Lahore, Sodhi Khatri, founded Amritsar (1577 CE).
  • Guru Arjan: 1563–1606 CE, Goindval, Sodhi, compiled Adi Granth (1604), martyred by Jahangir.
  • Guru Hargobind: 1595–1644 CE, Amritsar, Sodhi, introduced militancy, built Akal Takht.
  • Guru Har Rai: 1630–1661 CE, Kiratpur (Punjab), Sodhi, maintained peace, aided Dara Shikoh.
  • Guru Har Krishan: 1656–1664 CE, Delhi, Sodhi, died at 8 aiding plague victims.
  • Guru Tegh Bahadur: 1621–1675 CE, Anandpur, Sodhi, martyred by Aurangzeb in Delhi for resisting forced conversions.
  • Guru Gobind Singh: 1666–1708 CE, Patna/Anandpur, Sodhi, founded Khalsa (1699), declared Guru Granth Sahib as eternal Guru.
  • Primary Texts:
    • Guru Granth Sahib (compiled by Guru Arjan, 1604; finalized 1708).
    • Dasam Granth (Guru Gobind Singh’s compositions).
    • Janamsakhis (Nanak’s biographies).
  • Literature & Architecture Highlights:
    • Gurbani hymns (e.g., Japji Sahib by Nanak).
    • Dasam Granth poetry (e.g., Zafarnama).
    • Golden Temple (Amritsar, founded 1577, gilded 19th CE).
    • Akal Takht (military/political seat, 1606).
    • Gurdwaras: Anandpur Sahib, Patna Sahib.
  • Nanak Panthis: Early followers of Nanak, non-militant.
  • Khalsa: Warrior order founded by Guru Gobind Singh (1699).
  • Udasis: Ascetic sect linked to Guru Nanak’s son Sri Chand.
  • Later Sects (post-medieval): Namdharis (19th CE), Nirankaris (19th CE).
  • Mukti: Liberation through devotion, ethics, and service.
  • Ten Gurus: Divine guides, culminating in Guru Granth Sahib.
  • Khalsa Ideals: Purity, courage, equality.
  • Khalsa Formation: 1699 CE, Anandpur, Guru Gobind Singh, Baisakhi assembly.
  • Guru Granth Sahib Installation: 1708 CE, Nanded, Guru Gobind Singh, declared scripture as Guru.
  • Golden Temple (Amritsar).
  • Akal Takht (Amritsar).
  • Anandpur Sahib (Khalsa birthplace).
  • Takht Sri Patna Sahib (Guru Gobind Singh’s birthplace).
  • Hazur Sahib (Nanded, Guru Gobind Singh’s death).
  • Fatehgarh Sahib (martyrdom site of Guru Gobind Singh’s sons).
  • Mughals: Akbar (1556–1605 CE) tolerated early Sikhs; Jahangir and Aurangzeb persecuted (Guru Arjan, Tegh Bahadur).
  • Sikh Misls: 18th CE, post-Mughal self-rule.
  • Ranjit Singh: 19th CE, later consolidated Sikh power.
  • Mughal persecution (e.g., executions of Guru Arjan, Tegh Bahadur).
  • Afghan invasions (18th CE) disrupted Punjab.
  • British annexation (1849 CE) ended Sikh sovereignty.
- Art and culture -
Category Details
Gardens
  • Shalimar Bagh
    • Time: 1619 CE
    • Location: Srinagar, Kashmir
    • Purpose: Mughal pleasure garden, imperial retreat
    • Features: Three terraces (public, private, zenana), Chini Khanas (tiled niches), central water channel with black marble pavilion
    • Patronage: Jahangir (Mughal), expanded by Shah Jahan
    • Notable Event: Jahangir’s poetic inscriptions on beauty of Kashmir
  • Nishat Bagh
    • Time: 1633 CE
    • Location: Srinagar, Kashmir
    • Purpose: Scenic retreat for Mughal nobility
    • Features: 12 terraces (zodiac-inspired), fountains, panoramic Dal Lake view, rose gardens
    • Patronage: Asaf Khan (Jahangir’s brother-in-law), Mughal
    • Notable Event: Shah Jahan’s envy led to temporary water supply cut
  • Pinjore Gardens (Yadavindra Gardens)
    • Time: ~17th CE
    • Location: Pinjore, Haryana
    • Purpose: Summer retreat for Mughal governors
    • Features: Seven terraces, Sheesh Mahal, Rang Mahal, water channels, Rajput-Mughal blend
    • Patronage: Fidai Khan (Aurangzeb’s foster brother)
    • Notable Detail: Reflects Mughal adaptation to hilly terrain
  • Babur’s Garden (Ram Bagh)
    • Time: 1528 CE
    • Location: Agra, Uttar Pradesh
    • Purpose: First Mughal garden in India, Babur’s resting place
    • Features: Charbagh (four-part) layout, Persian style, step wells, fruit trees
    • Patronage: Babur (Mughal)
    • Notable Event: Babur’s burial here before transfer to Kabul
Temples
  • Brihadeeswara Temple
    • Time: 1010 CE
    • Location: Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu
    • Purpose: Shiva worship, symbol of Chola power
    • Features: 216-ft vimana (tower), 13-tonne monolithic Nandi, frescoes, Dravidian style
    • Patronage: Rajaraja Chola I
    • Notable Detail: Shadowless at noon, engineering marvel
  • Khajuraho Temples
    • Time: ~950–1050 CE
    • Location: Chhatarpur, Madhya Pradesh
    • Purpose: Hindu (Shiva, Vishnu) and Jain worship
    • Features: Nagara style, erotic sculptures (10% of total), Kandariya Mahadev (102-ft tall), tantric influences
    • Patronage: Chandela dynasty
    • Notable Event: Survived Muslim invasions due to remote location
  • Kandariya Mahadeo Temple
    • Time: ~1025–1050 CE
    • Location: Khajuraho, Madhya Pradesh
    • Purpose: Shiva worship
    • Features: Nagara style, 102-ft shikhara, 900+ sculptures, intricate friezes
    • Patronage: Vidyadhara (Chandela dynasty)
    • Notable Detail: Pinnacle of Khajuraho’s architectural grandeur
  • Dilwara Temples
    • Time: ~11th–13th CE
    • Location: Mount Abu, Rajasthan
    • Purpose: Jain Tirthankara worship
    • Features: Intricate marble carvings, Vimal Vasahi (1031 CE), Luna Vasahi (1230 CE)
    • Patronage: Chalukyas of Gujarat (Vimal Shah, Tejpal)
    • Notable Detail: Marble sourced from Makrana, Rajasthan
  • Sun Temple, Konark
    • Time: 1250 CE
    • Location: Konark, Odisha
    • Purpose: Surya (Sun God) worship
    • Features: Chariot with 24 wheels, Kalinga architecture, sundial, erotic reliefs
    • Patronage: Narasimhadeva I (Eastern Ganga)
    • Notable Event: Partially collapsed due to structural flaws
  • Meenakshi Temple
    • Time: ~12th–17th CE (expanded)
    • Location: Madurai, Tamil Nadu
    • Purpose: Meenakshi (Parvati) and Sundareswarar (Shiva) worship
    • Features: 14 gopurams (tallest 170 ft), Thousand Pillar Hall, temple tank
    • Patronage: Pandya dynasty, Nayaks of Madurai
    • Notable Detail: Annual Meenakshi Tirukalyanam festival
  • Tirupati (Sri Venkateswara Temple)
    • Time: ~10th–17th CE (expanded)
    • Location: Tirupati, Andhra Pradesh
    • Purpose: Vishnu (Venkateswara) worship
    • Features: Dravidian style, gold-plated vimana, seven hills setting, temple tank
    • Patronage: Cholas, Vijayanagara (Krishna Deva Raya), Pallavas
    • Notable Detail: Richest temple in India, major Vaishnava pilgrimage
  • Mahabalipuram (Shore Temple)
    • Time: ~7th–8th CE
    • Location: Mahabalipuram, Tamil Nadu
    • Purpose: Shiva and Vishnu worship
    • Features: Dravidian style, rock-cut architecture, shore location, rathas, bas-reliefs
    • Patronage: Narasimhavarman I (Pallava dynasty)
    • Notable Detail: UNESCO site, survived tsunami erosion
  • Vidyashankara Temple
    • Time: 1338 CE
    • Location: Sringeri, Karnataka
    • Purpose: Shiva worship, Advaita center
    • Features: Hoysala-Vijayanagara style, 12 zodiac pillars, stone carvings
    • Patronage: Vijayanagara Empire (Harihara II)
    • Notable Detail: Linked to Shankaracharya’s Sringeri Math
  • Rajarani Temple
    • Time: ~11th CE
    • Location: Bhubaneswar, Odisha
    • Purpose: Shiva worship (originally)
    • Features: Kalinga style, ornate deul (tower), erotic carvings, no deity now
    • Patronage: Somavamshi dynasty
    • Notable Detail: Known for aesthetic elegance, nicknamed “love temple”
  • Bhimesvara Temple
    • Time: ~8th–12th CE
    • Location: Bhubaneswar, Odisha
    • Purpose: Shiva worship
    • Features: Kalinga style, simple shikhara, intricate carvings
    • Patronage: Eastern Ganga dynasty
    • Notable Detail: Smaller but significant in Bhubaneswar’s temple cluster
  • Virupaksha Temple
    • Time: ~7th–14th CE (expanded)
    • Location: Hampi, Karnataka
    • Purpose: Shiva worship
    • Features: Dravidian style, nine-story gopuram, Hampi’s main temple
    • Patronage: Vijayanagara Empire (Krishna Deva Raya)
    • Notable Detail: Still active, central to Hampi’s cultural identity
  • Vijaya Vittala Temple
    • Time: ~15th–16th CE
    • Location: Hampi, Karnataka
    • Purpose: Vishnu (Vitthal) worship
    • Features: Dravidian style, stone chariot, musical pillars
    • Patronage: Vijayanagara Empire (Krishna Deva Raya)
    • Notable Detail: UNESCO site, architectural marvel
  • Sri Mariamman Temple
    • Time: ~17th CE
    • Location: Samayapuram, Tamil Nadu
    • Purpose: Mariamman (goddess of rain) worship
    • Features: Dravidian style, colorful gopuram, festival processions
    • Patronage: Nayaks of Madurai
    • Notable Detail: Major folk deity worship site
  • Kamakhya Temple
    • Time: ~8th–17th CE (rebuilt)
    • Location: Guwahati, Assam
    • Purpose: Shakti (Kamakhya) worship
    • Features: Tantric shrine, beehive-shaped dome, animal sacrifices
    • Patronage: Koch dynasty (rebuilt by Nara Narayan)
    • Notable Detail: Ambubachi Mela, major tantric pilgrimage
  • Lingaraja Temple
    • Time: ~11th CE
    • Location: Bhubaneswar, Odisha
    • Purpose: Shiva (Harihara) worship
    • Features: Kalinga style, 180-ft deul, 700+ smaller shrines
    • Patronage: Somavamshi dynasty
    • Notable Detail: Syncretic Shiva-Vishnu worship
Forts
  • Red Fort
    • Time: 1639–1648 CE
    • Location: Delhi
    • Purpose: Mughal imperial residence and defense
    • Features: Red sandstone, Diwan-i-Aam, Diwan-i-Khas, Rang Mahal, 2.5 km wall
    • Patronage: Shah Jahan (Mughal)
    • Notable Event: Peacock Throne housed here until Nadir Shah’s raid (1739)
  • Golconda Fort
    • Time: ~13th–16th CE (expanded)
    • Location: Hyderabad, Telangana
    • Purpose: Qutb Shahi defense, diamond trade hub
    • Features: Acoustic system, Fateh Darwaza, 87 bastions, granite construction
    • Patronage: Qutb Shahi dynasty
    • Notable Detail: Source of Koh-i-Noor and Hope diamonds
  • Mehrangarh Fort
    • Time: 1459 CE (expanded 17th CE)
    • Location: Jodhpur, Rajasthan
    • Purpose: Rathore Rajput defense
    • Features: 120-ft walls, Moti Mahal, Phool Mahal, cannon marks from battles
    • Patronage: Rao Jodha, later Rathore rulers
    • Notable Event: Impregnable except for Aurangzeb’s brief occupation
  • Gwalior Fort
    • Time: ~8th–14th CE (expanded)
    • Location: Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh
    • Purpose: Strategic defense, royal residence
    • Features: Man Mandir Palace, 10th-century Teli ka Mandir, Jain rock sculptures
    • Patronage: Tomars, later Mughals and Marathas
    • Notable Detail: Described as “pearl among fortresses” by Babur
  • Chittorgarh Fort
    • Time: ~7th–16th CE (expanded)
    • Location: Chittor, Rajasthan
    • Purpose: Sisodia Rajput stronghold
    • Features: 13 km wall, Vijay Stambh (148 ft), Kirti Stambh, seven gates
    • Patronage: Sisodia dynasty (Rana Kumbha)
    • Notable Event: Three jauhars (self-immolation) during sieges (1303, 1535, 1568)
  • Siri Fort
    • Time: ~1303 CE
    • Location: Delhi
    • Purpose: Defense against Mongol invasions
    • Features: Fortified walls, Hauz Khas reservoir, rubble construction
    • Patronage: Alauddin Khalji (Delhi Sultanate)
    • Notable Detail: Second city of Delhi, now largely in ruins
Mosques
  • Jama Masjid, Delhi
    • Time: 1650–1656 CE
    • Location: Delhi
    • Purpose: Friday congregational prayers
    • Features: Red sandstone, white marble, three domes, 40m minarets, capacity 25,000
    • Patronage: Shah Jahan (Mughal)
    • Notable Detail: Built opposite Red Fort, symbol of Mughal piety
  • Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque
    • Time: 1193 CE
    • Location: Delhi
    • Purpose: First mosque in North India, victory monument
    • Features: Reused Jain/Hindu temple pillars, arched screen, Qutub Minar
    • Patronage: Qutbuddin Aibak (Delhi Sultanate)
    • Notable Event: Marks start of Islamic architecture in India
  • Moti Masjid
    • Time: 1659 CE
    • Location: Agra Fort, Uttar Pradesh
    • Purpose: Private imperial prayer
    • Features: White marble, three small domes, pearl-like finish
    • Patronage: Aurangzeb (Mughal)
    • Notable Detail: Contrast to Shah Jahan’s opulence
  • Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra
    • Time: ~1192–13th CE
    • Location: Ajmer, Rajasthan
    • Purpose: Mosque from converted Jain temple
    • Features: Seven-arched screen, calligraphic inscriptions, Indo-Islamic fusion
    • Patronage: Qutbuddin Aibak (Delhi Sultanate)
    • Notable Detail: Name suggests rapid construction (2.5 days, likely symbolic)
  • Atala Masjid
    • Time: 1408 CE
    • Location: Jaunpur, Uttar Pradesh
    • Purpose: Friday prayers
    • Features: Massive pishtaq (portal), Sharqi style, three domes
    • Patronage: Ibrahim Shah Sharqi (Jaunpur Sultanate)
    • Notable Detail: Known as “Jaunpur’s Taj Mahal”
Tombs
  • Taj Mahal
    • Time: 1632–1653 CE
    • Location: Agra, Uttar Pradesh
    • Purpose: Mausoleum for Mumtaz Mahal
    • Features: White Makrana marble, perfect symmetry, 42-acre complex, Charbagh garden
    • Patronage: Shah Jahan (Mughal)
    • Notable Detail: 20,000 artisans, designed by Ustad Ahmad Lahauri
  • Humayun’s Tomb
    • Time: 1565–1572 CE
    • Location: Delhi
    • Purpose: Tomb for Emperor Humayun
    • Features: Red sandstone, double dome (Persian), Charbagh layout
    • Patronage: Bega Begum (Humayun’s widow), Mughal
    • Notable Detail: First garden-tomb in India, UNESCO site
  • Safdarjung Tomb
    • Time: 1754 CE
    • Location: Delhi
    • Purpose: Tomb for Safdarjung (Mughal viceroy)
    • Features: Red sandstone, marble, late Mughal style, asymmetrical design
    • Patronage: Ahmad Shah Bahadur (Mughal)
    • Notable Detail: Reflects Mughal decline in grandeur
  • Gol Gumbaz
    • Time: 1656 CE
    • Location: Bijapur, Karnataka
    • Purpose: Tomb for Muhammad Adil Shah
    • Features: 44m-wide dome (second largest pre-modern), whispering gallery
    • Patronage: Adil Shahi dynasty
    • Notable Detail: Echoes repeat 7–10 times
  • Akbar’s Tomb
    • Time: 1605–1613 CE
    • Location: Sikandra, Uttar Pradesh
    • Purpose: Tomb for Emperor Akbar
    • Features: Red sandstone, marble inlay, four-tiered pyramid, Charbagh
    • Patronage: Jahangir (Mughal)
    • Notable Detail: Akbar designed it himself, completed by son
Paintings
  • Ellora Caves
    • Time: ~6th–9th CE
    • Location: Maharashtra
    • Features: Hindu (Shiva, Vishnu), Buddhist, Jain murals, frescoes of Krishna’s life
    • Patronage: Rashtrakutas
    • Notable Detail: Use of natural pigments, fading due to time
  • Sittanavasal Caves
    • Time: ~7th–9th CE
    • Location: Tamil Nadu
    • Features: Jain paintings, lotus pond with fish, floral motifs, tempera technique
    • Patronage: Pandyas
    • Notable Detail: Rare surviving Jain art
  • Mughal Miniatures
    • Time: ~16th–17th CE
    • Location: Mughal courts (Delhi, Agra, Lahore)
    • Features: Persian-Indian fusion, detailed portraits, Hamzanama (1,400 folios), Baburnama
    • Patronage: Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan (Mughal)
    • Notable Artists: Basawan, Daswanth, Abdus Samad
  • Rajasthani Miniatures
    • Time: ~16th–18th CE
    • Location: Rajasthan (Mewar, Marwar, Bundi)
    • Features: Krishna Leela, Ragamala series, vibrant colors, Bhakti themes
    • Patronage: Rajput rulers (Sisodia, Rathore)
    • Notable Detail: Mewar school known for bold outlines
  • Pahari Paintings
    • Time: ~17th–18th CE
    • Location: Himachal Pradesh, Jammu
    • Features: Krishna-Radha themes, delicate brushwork, Basohli and Kangra schools
    • Patronage: Hill Rajput kings (e.g., Raja Kirpal Pal of Basohli)
    • Notable Detail: Kangra school’s lyrical softness
Painting Schools
  • Mughal School
    • Time: ~16th–17th CE
    • Location: Mughal courts (Delhi, Agra, Lahore)
    • Purpose: Illustrate imperial chronicles, portraits
    • Features: Realism, Persian influence, fine detailing, gold leaf
    • Key Artists: Mir Sayyid Ali, Abdus Samad, Basawan, Mansur (Jahangir’s favorite)
    • Patronage: Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan
    • Notable Works: Akbarnama, Jahangirnama
  • Rajput School
    • Time: ~16th–18th CE
    • Location: Rajasthan (Mewar, Marwar, Bundi, Kishangarh)
    • Purpose: Depict Bhakti themes, court life
    • Features: Bold colors, emotional expression, Krishna stories
    • Key Artists: Sahibdin (Mewar), Nihal Chand (Kishangarh’s Bani Thani)
    • Patronage: Rajput rulers
    • Notable Works: Ragamala, Rasikapriya
  • Pahari School
    • Time: ~17th–18th CE
    • Location: Himachal Pradesh, Jammu (Basohli, Kangra, Guler)
    • Purpose: Illustrate Krishna legends, love poetry
    • Features: Soft colors, naturalistic style, Basohli’s bold contrasts
    • Key Artists: Nainsukh (Kangra), Manaku
    • Patronage: Hill Rajput kings
    • Notable Works: Gita Govinda series
  • Deccan School
    • Time: ~16th–17th CE
    • Location: Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar)
    • Purpose: Courtly art, poetic illustrations
    • Features: Vibrant palette, Persian-Turkish influence, lyrical themes
    • Key Artists: Unknown masters, often anonymous
    • Patronage: Adil Shahi, Qutb Shahi rulers
    • Notable Works: Ragamala, portraits of Ibrahim Adil Shah II
Music
  • Hindustani Classical Music
    • Time: ~13th–17th CE
    • Location: North India (Delhi, Agra, Gwalior, Jaipur)
    • Purpose: Courtly entertainment, spiritual devotion
    • Features:
      • Raga: Melodic framework with specific notes (e.g., Miyan ki Malhar, Bhairav), time-specific moods
      • Tala: Rhythmic cycles (e.g., Teental: 16 beats, Jhaptaal: 10 beats), played on pakhawaj or tabla
      • Dhrupad: Oldest form, slow, meditative, 4-part (Alap, Jor, Jhala, Bandish), minimal ornamentation, pakhawaj accompaniment
      • Khayal: Expressive, improvisational, 2-part (Vilambit, Drut), elaborate taans, tabla accompaniment
    • Key Figures:
      • Amir Khusrau (1253–1325 CE, Delhi): Poet-musician, credited with Khayal foundation, fused Persian-Indian styles
      • Swami Haridas (~15th–16th CE, Vrindavan): Dhrupad master, Tansen’s guru, Bhakti influence
      • Tansen (1500–1586 CE, Gwalior/Akbar’s court): Master of Dhrupad, composed ragas (e.g., Miyan ki Todi, Darbari), legendary lamp-lighting with Raga Deepak
      • Baiju Bawra (~16th CE, legendary): Rival of Tansen, Dhrupad singer, possibly apocryphal
    • Patronage: Delhi Sultanate (e.g., Alauddin Khilji), Mughals (Akbar, Jahangir, Muhammad Shah Rangila)
    • Notable Detail:
      • Dhrupad declined post-17th CE as Khayal gained favor
      • Tansen ennobled as one of Akbar’s “Nine Jewels”
      • UPSC Note: Contrast Dhrupad (austere) vs. Khayal (flexible), Tansen’s ragas often in questions
  • Carnatic Music
    • Time: ~13th–17th CE
    • Location: South India (Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh)
    • Purpose: Temple devotion, court performances
    • Features:
      • Raga: Melodic base (e.g., Shankarabharanam), gamakas (ornamentations)
      • Tala: Rhythmic cycles (e.g., Adi Tala: 8 beats), mridangam accompaniment
      • Kriti: Structured compositions, devotional lyrics
      • Less improvisation than Hindustani, rooted in Natya Shastra
    • Key Figures:
      • Annamacharya (1408–1503 CE, Tallapaka): Composed 32,000 Telugu kirtanas for Venkateswara
      • Purandara Dasa (1484–1564 CE, Vijayanagara): “Father of Carnatic Music,” structured pedagogy (e.g., Sarali Varisai exercises), 475,000 compositions (mostly lost)
    • Patronage: Vijayanagara Empire (Krishna Deva Raya), Nayaks of Tanjore
    • Notable Detail:
      • Purandara’s beginner exercises still foundational
      • UPSC Note: Asked as South India’s musical contribution vs. Hindustani
  • Qawwali
    • Time: ~13th–17th CE
    • Location: North India (Delhi, Ajmer, Punjab)
    • Purpose: Sufi devotional music for spiritual ecstasy
    • Features:
      • Group singing, harmonium, dholak, rhythmic clapping
      • Persian/Urdu poetry praising God or saints
      • Repetition for trance-like states
    • Key Figures:
      • Amir Khusrau (1253–1325 CE, Delhi): Pioneer, linked to Chishti Sufis (Nizamuddin Auliya)
      • Sabir Brothers (later tradition, rooted in medieval style)
    • Patronage: Delhi Sultanate, Mughals, Sufi orders (Chishti, Suhrawardi)
    • Notable Detail:
      • Performed at dargahs (e.g., Ajmer Sharif)
      • UPSC Note: Syncretism with Bhakti (e.g., Kabir’s influence), cultural fusion
Dance
  • Kathak
    • Time: ~15th–17th CE
    • Location: North India (Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan)
    • Purpose: Storytelling, court entertainment
    • Features: Footwork (tatkar), spins (chakkars), Bhakti and Mughal influences
    • Key Figures: Linked to Bhakti poets (e.g., Mirabai), refined under Wajid Ali Shah (19th CE)
    • Patronage: Mughals (Akbar, Jahangir), Rajput courts
    • Notable Detail: Transition from temple to courtly form
  • Bharatanatyam
    • Time: ~10th–17th CE
    • Location: Tamil Nadu
    • Purpose: Temple worship, later court performance
    • Features: Natya Shastra-based, mudras, abhinaya (expression)
    • Key Figures: Devadasis (temple dancers), formalized by Chola/Nayak patronage
    • Patronage: Cholas, Nayaks of Tanjore
    • Notable Detail: Sculptures at Brihadeeswara depict poses
  • Kuchipudi
    • Time: ~15th–17th CE
    • Location: Andhra Pradesh
    • Purpose: Dance-drama, Krishna devotion
    • Features: Solo and group performances, tarangam (dancing on brass plate)
    • Key Figures: Siddhendra Yogi (15th CE), codified the form
    • Patronage: Vijayanagara, Golconda rulers
    • Notable Detail: Bhakta Prahlada story central
  • Odissi
    • Time: ~12th–17th CE
    • Location: Odisha
    • Purpose: Temple worship (Jagannath)
    • Features: Tribhangi posture, soft movements, Gotipua tradition
    • Key Figures: Maharis (temple dancers)
    • Patronage: Eastern Ganga, Gajapati kings
    • Notable Detail: Carvings at Konark inspire poses
Other Structures
  • Qutub Minar
    • Time: 1199–13th CE
    • Location: Delhi
    • Purpose: Victory tower, call to prayer
    • Features: 73m tall, five storeys, red sandstone, Quranic inscriptions
    • Patronage: Qutbuddin Aibak, Iltutmish (Delhi Sultanate)
    • Notable Detail: Tallest brick minaret in world
  • Gomateshwara Statue
    • Time: 983 CE
    • Location: Shravanabelagola, Karnataka
    • Purpose: Jain Bahubali worship
    • Features: 57-ft monolithic statue, nude ascetic form
    • Patronage: Ganga dynasty (Chamundaraya)
    • Notable Event: Mahamastakabhisheka every 12 years
  • Vijayanagara Hampi
    • Time: ~14th–16th CE
    • Location: Hampi, Karnataka
    • Purpose: Capital city with temples, markets
    • Features: Virupaksha Temple, stone chariot, Lotus Mahal, aqueducts
    • Patronage: Vijayanagara Empire (Krishna Deva Raya)
    • Notable Event: Sacked by Deccan Sultanates (1565)
  • Charminar
    • Time: 1591 CE
    • Location: Hyderabad, Telangana
    • Purpose: Monument marking end of plague
    • Features: Four 56m minarets, Indo-Islamic arches, clock added later
    • Patronage: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah (Qutb Shahi)
    • Notable Detail: Centerpiece of Hyderabad’s old city
  • Golden Temple
    • Time: 1577 CE (rebuilt 1764)
    • Location: Amritsar, Punjab
    • Purpose: Sikh worship, community hub
    • Features: Gold-plated dome, marble structure, Amrit Sarovar (pool)
    • Patronage: Guru Ram Das, rebuilt by Ranjit Singh
    • Notable Detail: Houses Guru Granth Sahib
  • Fatehpur Sikri
    • Time: 1571–1585 CE
    • Location: Uttar Pradesh
    • Purpose: Mughal capital city
    • Features: Buland Darwaza (54m), Jama Masjid, Panch Mahal, Salim Chishti’s tomb
    • Patronage: Akbar (Mughal)
    • Notable Detail: Abandoned due to water scarcity
  • Tungabhadra Dam
    • Time: ~14th–16th CE
    • Location: Hampi, Karnataka
    • Purpose: Irrigation for Vijayanagara agriculture
    • Features: Stone and earth dam, extensive canal system, reservoir
    • Patronage: Vijayanagara Empire (Krishna Deva Raya)
    • Notable Detail: Supported Hampi’s agrarian economy
  • Firuz Shah’s Canal System
    • Time: ~1350s CE
    • Location: Delhi, Haryana
    • Purpose: Irrigation and water supply
    • Features: Western Yamuna Canal, extended to Hisar and Hansi
    • Patronage: Firuz Shah Tughlaq (Delhi Sultanate)
    • Notable Detail: Revived by Mughals and British
  • Sher Shah’s Trunk Road
    • Time: ~1540–1545 CE
    • Location: Bengal to Peshawar (Grand Trunk Road)
    • Purpose: Trade, military, and administrative connectivity
    • Features: 2,500 km road, rest houses (sarais), milestones, tree-lined
    • Patronage: Sher Shah Suri (Suri dynasty)
    • Notable Detail: Later expanded by Mughals and British
Languages
  • Classical Sanskrit
    • Time: ~500 CE–1200 CE (continued use)
    • Location: Pan-India
    • Features: Refined by Panini’s grammar, used in courtly and religious texts
    • Notable Works:
      • Bana’s “Kadambari” (~7th CE)
      • Rajatarangini by Kalhana (12th CE, Kashmir)
    • Patronage: Guptas, Cholas, Vijayanagara
    • UPSC Note: Transition to vernaculars in medieval period
  • Persian
    • Time: ~12th–17th CE
    • Location: North India (Delhi, Agra, Lahore)
    • Features: Official language of Delhi Sultanate and Mughals, poetic and administrative use
    • Notable Works:
      • Amir Khusrau’s “Khamsa” (~13th CE)
      • Ain-i-Akbari by Abul Fazl (16th CE)
      • Baburnama (16th CE)
    • Patronage: Delhi Sultanate (e.g., Iltutmish), Mughals (Akbar, Shah Jahan)
    • UPSC Note: Symbol of Islamic rule, cultural fusion
  • Tamil
    • Time: ~500 CE–1750 CE (continued development)
    • Location: South India (Tamil Nadu)
    • Features: Dravidian, Bhakti poetry, temple inscriptions
    • Notable Works:
      • Tevaram (Nayanars, 6th–9th CE)
      • Nalayira Divya Prabandham (Alvars, 7th–10th CE)
      • Kamba Ramayanam (12th CE)
    • Patronage: Cholas, Pandyas, Nayaks
    • UPSC Note: Bhakti movement’s literary base
  • Hindi (Early Forms: Apabhramsa, Awadhi, Braj)
    • Time: ~10th–17th CE
    • Location: North India (Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan)
    • Features: Vernacular evolution from Prakrit, Bhakti and Sufi poetry
    • Notable Works:
      • Padmavat by Malik Muhammad Jayasi (1540 CE, Awadhi)
      • Ramcharitmanas by Tulsidas (1574 CE, Awadhi)
      • Sursagar by Surdas (16th CE, Braj)
    • Patronage: Regional rulers, Mughal tolerance (e.g., Akbar)
    • UPSC Note: Rise of vernacular literature
  • Urdu (Early Form: Dehlavi)
    • Time: ~14th–17th CE
    • Location: North India (Delhi, Deccan)
    • Features: Blend of Persian, Arabic, Turkish, and Hindi, Sufi poetry
    • Notable Works:
      • Amir Khusrau’s ghazals (~13th CE)
      • Bulleh Shah’s Kafis (17th CE, Punjab)
    • Patronage: Delhi Sultanate, Mughals, Deccan Sultanates
    • UPSC Note: Syncretic language, precursor to modern Urdu
  • Telugu
    • Time: ~11th–17th CE
    • Location: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana
    • Features: Dravidian, courtly and devotional poetry
    • Notable Works:
      • Amuktamalyada by Krishna Deva Raya (16th CE)
      • Annamacharya’s kirtanas (15th CE)
    • Patronage: Vijayanagara Empire, Qutb Shahi
    • UPSC Note: Literary peak under Vijayanagara
  • Kannada
    • Time: ~9th–17th CE
    • Location: Karnataka
    • Features: Dravidian, Jain and Bhakti literature
    • Notable Works:
      • Kavirajamarga by Amoghavarsha (9th CE)
      • Vachanas by Basava (12th CE)
      • Purandara Dasa’s songs (16th CE)
    • Patronage: Rashtrakutas, Hoysalas, Vijayanagara
    • UPSC Note: Lingayat movement’s contribution
- Political, administrative, economic, etc systems -
Political Entity System Type Time Period (Approximate) Location/Region Detailed Features, Structures & Systems Key Figures, Posts, Ranks & Roles (Linked to Systems)
Delhi Sultanate Administration & Key Systems (Iqta) ~1206 CE - 1526 CE North India, parts of Deccan (Capital: Delhi, Daulatabad briefly)
  • Central Administration: Headed by the Sultan. Key departments: Diwan-i-Wizarat (Finance - Wazir), Diwan-i-Arz (Military - Ariz-i-Mumalik), Diwan-i-Risalat (Religious Affairs - Sadr-us-Sudur), Diwan-i-Insha (Correspondence - Dabir-i-Khas).
  • Iqta System: Core administrative/revenue assignment. Revenue rights of territories (Iqtas) assigned to officials (Iqtadars/Muqtis/Walis) who collected revenue, maintained troops, managed local admin, remitted surplus (fawazil). Generally non-hereditary and transferable.
  • Provincial/Local Structure: Provinces (Vilayats/Iqlims) often aligned with major Iqtas, subdivided into Shiqs (districts) and Parganas (sub-districts).
  • Intelligence System (Barids) for oversight.
  • Sultan: Supreme ruler.
  • Wazir: Chief minister (Finance/Civil Admin).
  • Ariz-i-Mumalik: Head of Military Dept.
  • Sadr-us-Sudur: Head of Religious Affairs.
  • Dabir-i-Khas: Head of Correspondence.
  • Iqtadar / Muqti / Wali: Holder of an Iqta; key provincial/regional administrator.
  • Shiqdar: Head of a Shiq (district).
  • Amil / Nazir: Revenue officials (Pargana).
  • Barid: Intelligence officer.
  • Chaudhari / Khut / Muqaddam: Village headmen/intermediaries.
Military System ~1206 CE - 1526 CE North India, Deccan
  • Composition: Strong cavalry focus; Infantry and war elephants significant.
  • Recruitment & Maintenance: Troops primarily supplied by Iqtadars. Central standing army (Hashm-i-Qalb) paid directly by state, expanded under rulers like Alauddin Khalji.
  • Organization: Managed by Diwan-i-Arz. Use of branding (Dagh) and descriptive rolls (Chehra) under some rulers.
  • Tactics & Fortification: Skilled cavalry tactics, siege warfare. Numerous forts.
  • Sultan: Supreme Commander.
  • Ariz-i-Mumalik: Managed military administration.
  • Iqtadars/Muqtis: Provided and commanded large cavalry contingents.
  • Sipah Salar / Sar-i-Khail: Military commanders.
  • Kotwal: Commander of fort/town garrison.
Economic System & Revenue ~1206 CE - 1526 CE North India, Deccan
  • Revenue Sources: Land Revenue (Kharaj, Ushraf) collected mainly via Iqta system; Jizya (poll tax); Zakat (charity tax); Khums (war booty share); Trade Taxes.
  • Assessment Methods: Varied - sharing (Batai), estimation (Kankut), measurement (Masahat).
  • Coinage: Standardized Silver Tanka and Copper Jital. Gold Mohurs also used.
  • Trade & Urbanization: Growth of cities, active internal/overland trade. State workshops (Karkhanas).
  • Wazir / Diwan-i-Wizarat: Oversaw finance.
  • Iqtadar/Muqti: Primary revenue administrator in Iqta.
  • Amil / Karkun / Mutsarrif: Local revenue officials.
  • Chaudhari / Khut / Muqaddam: Village intermediaries.
  • Shahna-i-Mandi: Market superintendent.
Judicial & Social Systems ~1206 CE - 1526 CE North India, Deccan
  • Judicial: Sultan highest court. Islamic Law (Sharia) applied by Qazis, esp. for Muslims/criminal cases. Local customs influential. Chief Qazi at the center.
  • Social: Muslim ruling elite over predominantly Hindu population. Caste system persisted. Rise of Sufism. Slavery existed.
  • Sultan: Highest Judge.
  • Qazi-ul-Quzzat: Chief Justice.
  • Qazi: Judge.
  • Ulema: Religious scholars.
  • Sufi Saints: Religious figures.
  • Nobility (Amirs, Maliks): Elite.
Vijayanagara Empire Administration & Key Systems (Nayankara, Ayagar) ~1336 CE - 1646 CE South India (Capital: Vijayanagara/Hampi)
  • Central Administration: Headed by Emperor (Raya), assisted by ministers. Secretariat organized.
  • Provincial Structure: Divided into Mandalams (provinces), Nadus (districts), etc.
  • Nayankara System: Key politico-military structure. Military chiefs (Nayakas) granted territories (Amaram), owed revenue, troops, admin duties. Often hereditary.
  • Ayagar System: Governed village administration via hereditary village functionaries (Ayagars) managing local affairs, paid via tax-free lands (Manyams).
  • Raya: Emperor.
  • Pradhani: Prime Minister.
  • Mahamandaleshvara: Provincial governor.
  • Nayaka: Holder of Amaram grant; military chief/regional administrator.
  • Ayagars: Hereditary village officials (Karanikam - accountant, Talaiyari - watchman).
Military System ~1336 CE - 1646 CE South India
  • Structure: Dependent on contingents from Nayakas (Nayankara System). Raya (king) maintained standing army.
  • Composition: Infantry, strong cavalry (imported horses vital), elephants, some artillery.
  • Fortification: Extensive network of powerful forts.
  • Raya: Supreme commander.
  • Nayakas: Supplied bulk of troops, commanded contingents.
  • Kandachara Department: Military administration.
Economic System & Revenue ~1336 CE - 1646 CE South India
  • Base: Agrarian; advanced irrigation.
  • Revenue: Land Revenue main source, collection often managed by Nayakas. Other taxes: trade, professions, etc.
  • Trade: Active internal/overseas trade. Guilds prominent.
  • Temple Economy: Significant role (land owner, employer, banker).
  • Coinage: Standard Gold Varaha (Pagoda).
  • Athavane: Central Revenue Department.
  • Nayakas: Collected revenue.
  • Karanikam (Ayagar): Village accountant.
  • Guild Leaders (Settis): Organized trade.
Judicial & Social Systems ~1336 CE - 1646 CE South India
  • Judicial: Raya (king) highest court. Local justice by governors, Nayakas, village assemblies based on Hindu law/custom.
  • Social: Hierarchical caste-based society. Brahmins influential. Nayakas formed landed aristocracy. Temples central to social life.
  • Raya: Highest Judge.
  • Nayakas/Governors: Dispensed local justice.
  • Brahmins: Advisors, scholars.
  • Village Assemblies/Caste Panchayats: Handled local disputes.
Mughal Empire Administration & Key Systems (Mansabdari, Jagirdari) ~1526 CE - c. 1857 CE (Peak ~1556-1707) Most of the Indian Subcontinent (Capital: Agra, Delhi, Fatehpur Sikri, Lahore)
  • Central Administration: Highly centralized bureaucracy under Emperor (Badshah). Key departments: Diwan-i-Ala (Revenue/Finance - Wazir), Mir Bakshi (Military Admin/Pay), Mir Saman (Household/Workshops), Sadr-us-Sudur (Religious Affairs).
  • Mansabdari System: Cornerstone integrating military/civil bureaucracy. Rank (Mansab) denoted by Zat (status/salary) and Sawar (cavalry contingent). Unified nobility; rank determined pay, status, military obligation. Managed by Mir Bakshi.
  • Jagirdari System: Primary method of paying Mansabdars. Assignment of land revenue rights (Jagir) in lieu of cash salary. Jagirdars collected revenue via agents. Distinct from Khalisa (crown) lands. Frequently transferred (except Watan Jagirs).
  • Provincial/Local Structure: Subahs (provinces: Subedar, Diwan), Sarkars (districts: Faujdar, Amalguzar), Parganas (sub-districts: Shiqdar, Amin, Qanungo).
  • Badshah: Emperor.
  • Diwan-i-Ala / Wazir: Chief Revenue/Finance Minister.
  • Mir Bakshi: Head of Military Admin / Paymaster General.
  • Mir Saman: Head of Imperial Household.
  • Sadr-us-Sudur: Head of Religious Affairs.
  • Mansabdar: Holder of a Mansab rank.
  • Jagirdar: Holder of a Jagir.
  • Subedar: Provincial Governor.
  • Diwan (Provincial): Provincial Revenue Head.
  • Faujdar: District military/police head.
  • Amalguzar / Krori: Revenue collector.
  • Amin / Shiqdar / Qanungo: Pargana level officials.
  • Kotwal: Urban administrator.
  • Muqaddam / Patwari: Village headman / accountant.
Military System ~1526 CE - c. 1750s CE Pan-India
  • Structure & Recruitment: Organized via Mansabdari system. Mansabdars provided cavalry (Tabinan) based on Sawar rank. Strict inspections (Dagh system).
  • Components: Strong artillery (Topkhana); disciplined Cavalry; Infantry (Ahsham - matchlockmen); War Elephants; River flotillas (Nawwara).
  • Logistics & Forts: Efficient logistics; extensive use of large forts.
  • Mir Bakshi: Oversaw military admin, Mansabdari adherence.
  • Mansabdars: Commanded contingents.
  • Mir Atish: Commander of Artillery.
  • Faujdar: Commanded local forces.
  • Qiladar: Fort commander.
Economic System & Revenue ~1526 CE - c. 1750s CE Pan-India
  • Revenue Sources: Land Revenue (primarily via Zabti/Dahsala, Nasaq, Batai systems); Trade Taxes; Jizya (under Aurangzeb); monopolies; Peshkash.
  • Zabti/Dahsala System: Introduced by Raja Todar Mal (1580 CE). Based on average produce and prices over 10 years. One-third of produce (Mal) fixed in rupees per bigha as state share; two-thirds (Kharaj) left for cultivators. Used bamboo jarid for accurate land measurement. Applied in Lahore to Allahabad, Malwa, Gujarat; later Deccan under Shah Jahan. Lands classified as Polaj (regularly cultivated), Parauti (fallow to regain fertility), Chachar (uncultivated 3-4 years), Banjar (uncultivated >4 years). Dastur-i-amal (cash rates schedule) set per crop/region.
  • Batai/Ghalla-Bakhshi System: Crop-sharing system where produce divided into heaps, state took one-third. Peasants could pay in cash or kind. Prevalent where Zabti not applied.
  • Nasaq System: Rough estimation of revenue based on past receipts, avoiding detailed measurement. Common in Bengal and other regions.
  • Note on Zadti, Atnat, Sasaq: No historical evidence found for these as distinct revenue systems in medieval India. Possibly misspellings or local terms not widely documented.
  • Revenue Assignment: Mostly via Jagirdari System (Jagirdars collect); direct collection in Khalisa lands.
  • Coinage: Standardized silver Rupiya, gold Mohur, copper Dam.
  • Trade & Commerce: Flourishing internal/external trade (textiles, indigo, etc.). Roads, sarais. Hundi system used. European companies active.
  • Agriculture & Crafts: Extensive cultivation; high craft skills; imperial Karkhanas.
  • Diwan-i-Ala: Head of finance/revenue.
  • Raja Todar Mal: Architect of Zabti/Dahsala system.
  • Jagirdar: Collected revenue from Jagirs.
  • Amalguzar / Krori: Revenue collector (Khalisa).
  • Amin / Qanungo / Patwari: Local revenue officials.
  • Chaudhari / Muqaddam: Village intermediaries.
  • Sarrafs / Sahukars: Bankers, money-changers.
Judicial & Social Systems ~1526 CE - c. 1857 CE Pan-India
  • Judicial: Emperor highest court. Hierarchy under Qazi-ul-Quzzat. Qazis applied Islamic law; Mir Adl ensured procedures. Customary law influential locally.
  • Social: Emperor and Mansabdar nobility elite. Complex ethnic mix. Caste system structured Hindu society. Syncretic culture. Status of women varied; Purdah common among elite. Akbar's tolerance vs Aurangzeb's orthodoxy.
  • Badshah: Highest Judge.
  • Qazi-ul-Quzzat: Chief Justice.
  • Qazi: Judge.
  • Mir Adl: Judicial procedure officer.
  • Mufti: Expounder of Islamic law.
  • Ulema / Brahmins: Religious scholars.
  • Mansabdars / Jagirdars: Social/political elite.
Maratha Confederacy Administration & Key Systems (Ashtapradhan, Chauth/Sardeshmukhi) ~1674 CE - c. 1818 CE Deccan, expanding across large parts of India (Capitals: Raigad, Satara, Pune)
  • Central Admin (Shivaji): Headed by Chhatrapati. Assisted by Ashtapradhan (Council of Eight Ministers - advisory): Peshwa (PM), Amatya (Finance), Mantri (Chronicler), Sachiv (Correspondence), Sumant (Foreign), Senapati (Army), Panditrao (Religion), Nyayadhish (Justice).
  • Central Admin (Peshwa Era): Peshwa became de facto head (Pune), Chhatrapati nominal (Satara). Peshwa's secretariat (Huzur Daftar) central hub.
  • Provincial/Local: Prants (provinces), Tarfs/Mahals administered by Subedar, Mamlatdar, Kamavisdar. Hereditary Deshmukhs/Deshpandes powerful regionally. Forts key centers.
  • Saranjam System (Mokasa): Assignment of land revenue rights for military/civil service.
  • Chhatrapati: King.
  • Peshwa: Prime Minister (later de facto ruler).
  • Ashtapradhan Ministers: Heads of departments under Shivaji.
  • Mamlatdar / Kamavisdar: District/provincial officials.
  • Subedar: Governor.
  • Deshmukh / Deshpande: Hereditary regional officials.
  • Patil / Kulkarni: Village headman / accountant.
  • Killedar: Fort commander.
  • Saranjamdar / Mokasdar: Holder of Saranjam/Mokasa grant.
Military System ~1640s CE - c. 1818 CE Deccan, Pan-India
  • Shivaji's Era: Light cavalry; guerrilla tactics (ganimi kava); hill forts; locally recruited infantry (Mavales).
  • Troop Types: Bargirs (state-paid cavalry) and Shiledars (brought own equipment).
  • Peshwa Era: Shift towards conventional army; European-style infantry; developed artillery. Large armies dependent on contingents from major chiefs (Scindia, Holkar etc.) holding large Saranjams.
  • Senapati / Sar-i-Naubat: Commander-in-Chief.
  • Peshwa: Often led campaigns.
  • Major Maratha Chiefs (Scindia, Holkar, etc.): Commanded armies.
  • Saranjamdar/Mokasdar: Supplied troops.
  • Killedar: Fort commander.
Economic System & Revenue ~1674 CE - c. 1818 CE Deccan, Pan-India
  • Revenue (Swarajya): Land revenue primary source.
  • Revenue (External): Crucial income from Chauth (1/4th revenue demand for protection) and Sardeshmukhi (additional 1/10th claim) levied over vast territories.
  • Other Revenue: Trade taxes, professional taxes.
  • Land Grants: Saranjam/Mokasa system supported officials/military.
  • Amatya / Majumdar: Finance Minister.
  • Peshwa: Controlled central finances later.
  • Mamlatdar / Kamavisdar: District collectors.
  • Deshmukh / Deshpande: Hereditary officers key for external levy collection.
  • Saranjamdar/Mokasdar: Collected revenue from assigned lands.
  • Patil / Kulkarni: Village level functionaries.
Judicial & Social Systems ~1674 CE - c. 1818 CE Deccan, Pan-India
  • Judicial: Chhatrapati/Peshwa highest court. Nyayadhish (Chief Justice) based on Hindu law/customs. Local justice by officials (Mamlatdar) or Panchayats/Patils.
  • Social: Hierarchical society; Brahmin dominance under Peshwas. Maratha chiefs formed aristocracy. Strong Maratha identity. Caste system prevalent.
  • Chhatrapati / Peshwa: Highest Judge.
  • Nyayadhish: Chief Justice.
  • Mamlatdar / Patil / Panchayat: Dispensed local justice.
  • Brahmins: Held high positions.
  • Maratha Chiefs/Sardars: Elite.
- Ports, trade routes, etc -
Category Time Period (Approximate) Location/Region Core Features & Trade Details Key Ports & Routes Associated Dynasties & Figures/Groups
Major Ports of Medieval India
Cambay (Khambhat) ~8th CE - 17th CE (peak before Surat's rise) Gujarat (Gulf of Khambhat)
  • Major international port, known for textiles, indigo, agate/carnelian beads.
  • Visited by travellers like Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta.
  • Declined later due to silting and the rise of Surat.
  • Trade with: Persia, Arabia, East Africa, Southeast Asia.
 Western coastal routes; linked to North Indian land routes Chaulukyas (Solankis), Delhi Sultanate, Gujarat Sultanate
Surat ~15th CE - 18th CE (peak under Mughals) Gujarat (Tapti River mouth)
  • Premier port of the Mughal Empire, major Haj pilgrimage embarkation point.
  • Exported: Textiles (cotton, silk), indigo, spices.
  • Imported: Bullion (silver, gold), horses, metals, luxury goods.
  • Hub for Indian merchants (Baniyas); English & Dutch established factories. Sacked by Shivaji. Declined with Bombay's rise.
 Western coastal routes; linked to Agra/Delhi land routes Gujarat Sultanate, Mughal Empire (esp. Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan), Marathas (Shivaji), English EIC, Dutch VOC
Calicut (Kozhikode) ~13th CE - 18th CE Kerala (Malabar Coast)
  • Major hub for spice trade (esp. pepper), controlled by the Zamorin.
  • First landing point for Vasco da Gama (1498).
  • Exported: Pepper, ginger, cardamom, cinnamon, textiles.
  • Imported: Gold, silver, horses.
  • Trade with: Arabs, Persians, Chinese (initially), Portuguese, Dutch, English.
 Indian Ocean maritime routes Zamorins of Calicut, Portuguese, Dutch VOC, English EIC
Goa ~11th CE onwards (Portuguese stronghold from 1510) Konkan Coast
  • Important port under Bahmanis/Bijapur; captured by Portuguese (Albuquerque, 1510).
  • Became capital of Portuguese Estado da India.
  • Center for horse trade, spices, religious activities (St. Francis Xavier).
  • Issued 'cartazes' (permits) to control shipping.
 Western coastal routes; center of Portuguese maritime network Kadambas, Bahmanis, Bijapur Sultanate, Portuguese Estado da India
Masulipatnam (Machilipatnam) ~15th CE - 18th CE Andhra Pradesh (Coromandel Coast)
  • Major port for Golconda kingdom, famous for textiles (kalamkari, chintz).
  • Exported: Textiles, diamonds (from Golconda mines), iron, saltpeter.
  • Imported: Copper, spices (from SE Asia).
  • Important center for English, Dutch, French trade factories.
 Bay of Bengal routes; linked to Golconda/Hyderabad Qutb Shahi Dynasty (Golconda), Mughals, English EIC, Dutch VOC, French Compagnie
Hooghly / Satgaon ~16th CE - 18th CE Bengal (Hooghly River delta)
  • Major trade centers in Bengal, replacing earlier ports like Tamralipti. Satgaon declined, Hooghly rose.
  • Portuguese established base at Hooghly, later expelled by Mughals.
  • Exported: Textiles (muslin, silk), sugar, rice, saltpeter.
  • English, Dutch, French established factories nearby (leading to Calcutta, Chinsurah, Chandernagore).
 Bay of Bengal routes; linked to Gangetic plains Bengal Sultanate, Mughal Empire, Portuguese, Dutch VOC, English EIC, French Compagnie
Pulicat ~15th CE - 17th CE Tamil Nadu (Coromandel Coast)
  • Important textile trading center.
  • Became headquarters of the Dutch VOC in India for a period (Fort Geldria).
  • Major site for slave trade by the Dutch to Southeast Asia.
  • Declined after Dutch shifted focus to Nagapattinam/Ceylon.
 Coromandel Coast routes Vijayanagara Empire, Nayakas, Dutch VOC
Other Notable Ports Medieval Period Various Coasts
  • West Coast: Bharuch (continued but declined), Sopara (declined), Dabhol, Chaul (Bahmani/Nizam Shahi ports), Diu (Portuguese).
  • East Coast: Nagapattinam (Chola port, continued importance), Chittagong (Bengal), Madras (founded by English), Calcutta (founded by English), Pondicherry (founded by French).
 Coastal and Ocean routes Various Indian Dynasties, European Companies
Trade Routes of Medieval India
Overland Routes Medieval Period Across India, connecting to Central Asia
  • Continued use of ancient routes (e.g., variations of Uttarapatha). Grand Trunk Road improved by Sher Shah/Mughals linked North India.
  • Connected major production centers (Agra, Delhi, Lahore, Multan, Burhanpur, Vijayanagara) to ports (Surat, Cambay, Hooghly, Masulipatnam).
  • Routes through Khyber Pass linked to Central Asia/Persia (less dominant than sea for high value goods).
  • Caravanserais provided facilities along routes.
 Linked major cities to key ports like Surat, Hooghly Delhi Sultanate, Mughals, Regional Kingdoms, Banjaras (transport communities)
Indian Ocean Maritime Routes Medieval Period (esp. post-10th C) Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal
  • Dominant mode for high-value, long-distance trade. Utilized monsoon winds.
  • Connected India to:
    • West: Red Sea (Egypt), Persian Gulf (Persia, Arabia), East Africa (Swahili Coast).
    • East: Southeast Asia (Malacca, Sumatra, Java), China.
  • Initially dominated by Indian, Arab, Persian merchants; later challenged and transformed by Europeans.
 Surat, Calicut, Goa, Cambay, Masulipatnam, Hooghly Cholas (earlier), Various Sultanates, Mughals, Vijayanagara, European Companies
European Maritime Routes (Cape Route) Late 15th C onwards Around Africa, connecting Europe directly to India
  • Established by Vasco da Gama (1498). Bypassed traditional land/Red Sea routes controlled by Ottomans/Venetians.
  • Led to direct European involvement and eventual dominance in Indian Ocean trade.
  • Facilitated bulk transport of goods between India and Europe.
 Linked European ports (Lisbon, Amsterdam, London, etc.) to Indian ports (Goa, Calicut, Surat, Madras, Calcutta) Portuguese, Dutch, English, French
Major Trade Goods
Textiles Medieval Period Pan-India (esp. Gujarat, Bengal, Coromandel)
  • India's single largest export. Cotton goods (calico, muslin, chintz) and Silk fabrics.
  • High demand in Southeast Asia, Middle East, Europe.
  • Key Centers: Gujarat (Cambay, Surat), Bengal (Hooghly), Coromandel (Masulipatnam, Pulicat).
 All major routes All major Indian states, European Companies
Spices Medieval Period Malabar Coast (pepper); SE Asia (cloves, nutmeg - traded via India)
  • Pepper remained a key export from Malabar. India also acted as an entrepôt for spices from Southeast Asia.
  • Initial driver for European exploration.
  • Key Ports: Calicut, Cochin, Goa (later controlled by Portuguese/Dutch).
 Indian Ocean & European Maritime Routes Zamorins, Portuguese, Dutch VOC
Indigo Medieval Period North India (Bayana near Agra), Gujarat
  • Blue dye highly valued in Europe for textiles.
  • Major export commodity, especially demanded by European companies.
 Land routes to ports (Surat), Maritime Routes Mughal Empire, English EIC, Dutch VOC
Saltpeter 17th - 18th C Bihar, Bengal
  • Potassium nitrate, essential ingredient for gunpowder.
  • Massive demand from Europe due to frequent wars.
  • Became a strategic bulk commodity export.
 River/Land routes to Hooghly/Calcutta, Maritime Routes Mughal Empire, English EIC, Dutch VOC
Bullion (Silver & Gold) Medieval Period (esp. 16th C onwards) Imported from Americas (via Europe), Japan, Middle East
  • India had a large trade surplus, absorbing vast quantities of world's silver (and some gold) in payment for its exports.
  • Crucial for Mughal coinage (silver Rupiya) and economy.
  • Imported primarily by European companies.
 European Maritime Routes, Indian Ocean Routes Mughal Empire, European Companies
Horses Medieval Period Imported from Arabia, Persia, Central Asia
  • Vital military import for cavalry-dependent Indian armies.
  • High demand from Sultanates, Vijayanagara, Mughals.
  • Controlled largely by Arabs, Persians, and later Portuguese (at Goa).
 Indian Ocean Routes (to West Coast ports like Goa, Surat) Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara, Bahmanis, Mughals, Portuguese
Other Goods Medieval Period Various
  • Exports: Diamonds (Golconda), Sugar, Opium (increasingly), Rice, Iron/Steel, Lacquerware, Perfumes.
  • Imports: Metals (Copper, Tin, Lead), Wine, Coral, Glassware, Velvets, Brocades, Slaves (from Africa).
 Various routes Various Indian & Foreign entities
Key Merchant Groups & European Companies
Indian Merchant Groups Medieval Period Across India
  • Baniyas: Predominantly Hindu/Jain trading communities, strong in Gujarat/North India (e.g., Surat). Involved in trade, banking, brokerage. Notable figures like Virji Vora.
  • Chettis/Chettiars: Trading communities dominant on the Coromandel Coast, involved in maritime trade with SE Asia, banking.
  • Komatis: Trading community in Andhra/Golconda region.
  • Khatris: Trading community prominent in North India/Punjab.
  • Muslim Merchants: Included Bohras (Gujarat - maritime), Khojas, Persians, Arabs settled in coastal towns.
  • Armenian Merchants: Played significant role as intermediaries in overland and maritime trade, esp. with Persia/Mughal India.
  • Banjaras: Nomadic trading communities specializing in bulk overland transport using pack animals.
 Operated along all major trade routes and ports Flourished under various Indian Dynasties, interacted/competed with Europeans
European Trading Companies Late 15th C onwards Coastal India (factories/settlements)
  • Portuguese (Estado da India): Early dominance (16th C), controlled key ports (Goa, Diu, Daman), used force/cartaz system. Focused on spice trade initially.
  • Dutch (VOC - Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie): Rose in 17th C, challenged Portuguese. Focused on spices (esp. from SE Asia), textiles, pepper, saltpeter. Major bases: Pulicat, Nagapattinam, Chinsurah, Cochin.
  • English (EIC - East India Company): Established factories (Surat, Madras, Bombay, Calcutta). Focused on textiles, indigo, saltpeter, later opium. Gradually gained political power, culminating in Battle of Plassey (1757).
  • French (Compagnie des Indes Orientales): Arrived later, competed with English. Main bases: Pondicherry, Chandernagore. Involved in Carnatic Wars.
  • Others: Danish, Swedish companies had minor presence.
 European Maritime Routes, Indian Ports Interacted/conflicted with Mughals, Marathas, regional rulers

Traveler/Observer Time Period (Approximate) Origin Core Observations & Contributions Key Works/Documents Associated Indian Dynasty/Region
Sulaiman al-Tajir ~9th Century CE (c. 851 CE) Arabia (Persian Gulf)
  • Arab merchant, one of the earliest Muslim travelers to India.
  • Described trade routes, ports (e.g., Kollam), and goods (spices, timber).
  • Noted interactions with local rulers and maritime commerce.
  • Early Islamic account of South Indian trade.
 Akhbar al-Sin wa’l-Hind Rashtrakutas (Deccan), Cheras (South India)
Al-Masudi ~10th Century CE Arabia
  • Arab historian and geographer.
  • Described India's wealth, trade, and military.
  • Detailed account of Gurjara-Pratihara rulers.
 Muruj-al-Dhahab (Meadows of Gold) Gurjara-Pratiharas (North India)
Al-Biruni ~11th Century CE Persia (Ghaznavid Empire)
  • Studied Indian culture, religion, science, and philosophy.
  • Compared Indian and Islamic knowledge systems.
  • Critically analyzed Hindu customs and caste system.
 Kitab al-Hind Ghaznavid Empire (North India)
Marco Polo ~13th Century CE (c. 1292–1294 CE) Italy (Venice)
  • Venetian merchant, visited South India en route from China.
  • Described Pandya kingdom’s pearl fisheries, trade (spices, gems), and Hindu customs.
  • Noted wealth of Malabar Coast and St. Thomas Christian communities.
 The Travels of Marco Polo Pandyas (South India), Cholas (declining)
Ibn Battuta ~14th Century CE (c. 1333–1341 CE) Morocco
  • Muslim traveler, served as qadi under the Tughlaq dynasty.
  • Described Delhi Sultanate’s cities (Delhi, Daulatabad), administration, and trade.
  • Noted cultural diversity, Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s policies, and social unrest.
 Rihla (The Journey) Tughlaq Dynasty (Delhi Sultanate)
Friar Jordanus ~14th Century CE (c. 1321–1328 CE) France/Italy (Dominican Order)
  • Catholic missionary, traveled to Gujarat and South India.
  • Described Indian flora, fauna, and Christian communities (Thana, Quilon).
  • Noted Hindu practices and trade wealth of the Malabar Coast.
 Mirabilia Descripta (Wonders Described) Yadavas (Deccan), Pandyas (South India)
Nicolo de’ Conti ~15th Century CE (c. 1419–1444 CE) Italy (Venice)
  • Venetian merchant, traveled across India via Hormuz.
  • Described Vijayanagara Empire’s wealth, cities (Vijayanagara), and Hindu customs.
  • Noted trade in Gujarat and Malabar, and practices like sati.
 Recorded in De Varietate Fortunae Vijayanagara Empire (South India)
Abdur Razzaq ~15th Century CE (c. 1443–1444 CE) Persia (Timurid Empire)
  • Ambassador of Shah Rukh to Vijayanagara.
  • Described Vijayanagara’s grandeur, king Deva Raya II, markets, and irrigation.
  • Noted cosmopolitan city life and military strength.
 Matla-us-Sadain wa Majma-ul-Bahrain Vijayanagara Empire (South India)
Athanasius Nikitin ~15th Century CE (c. 1468–1474 CE) Russia (Tver)
  • Russian merchant, traveled to the Bahmani Sultanate.
  • Described Deccan’s trade (horses, gems), cities (Bidar), and Hindu-Muslim interactions.
  • Noted wealth of rulers and his struggles as a Christian outsider.

- Important words -
Term Meaning
Amils Revenue officials in Mughal administration
Bargir Maratha cavalrymen who were provided horses by the state
Dam Small copper coin in Mughal India
Diwan Head of financial affairs
Diwan-i-Arz Department of Military Affairs
Diwan-i-Insha Ministry of Royal Correspondence
Diwan-i-Kul Chief Imperial Minister (Wazir)
Diwan-i-Risalat Department of Religious and Foreign Affairs
Faujdar Administrative officer in charge of a Sarkar
Ganj A grain market
Gomashta Commercial agent under British and Mughal rule
Hundis Bills of exchange or credit notes
Ibadat Khana House of Worship built by Akbar for religious discussions
Jagir Land grant given in return for administrative or military services
Jizya Tax on non-Muslims under Islamic rule
Khalisa Land revenue directly for the imperial treasury
Khutba Friday sermon in the mosque where rulers' names were read
Mansabdars Rank holders in Mughal administration
Misl Confederacy of Sikh regions
Nagaram Merchant guild or town assembly in South India
Pargana Administrative unit consisting of multiple villages
Qanungos Record keepers of revenue
Sabha Brahmin assembly in Chola administration
Sadr-us-Sudur Head of religious and judicial affairs
Sarkar Provincial unit of administration
Shaikhzadas Indian Muslim nobility
Sharia Islamic law
Subah Province under Mughal administration
Tankah Silver coin under Delhi Sultanate and Mughals
Umara Collective term for nobility
Ur Village assembly in Chola period
Vimanas Tower-like structures in South Indian temples
Waqf Land or property donated for religious purposes
Wilayat Spiritual territory of a Sufi saint
Zabt Revenue system based on land measurement
Zawabit State laws distinct from Sharia
Kulah-Daran Persian term meaning "wearers of the cap," used for officials or dignitaries in Mughal court culture.
Fanam Small gold or silver coin used in South India, particularly during Vijayanagara rule.
Aurang State-supervised workshop or manufactory in Mughal India for producing luxury goods like textiles, arms, or ornaments.
Banian Indian merchants and moneylenders, often agents of European trading companies.
Mirasidar Hereditary landholders in South India, particularly in Tamil regions, under Chola and Vijayanagara systems.
Shramana Wandering ascetics of non-Vedic traditions like Buddhism and Jainism, emphasizing renunciation and meditation.

Pattakila Head of a guild or trade association in South India; also local administrative officer under Cholas.
- Preface - Reassessing India’s Medieval Past - As a nation progresses, it reviews its history to determine: - Relevant legacies for growth - Inhibiting factors that may hinder progress - Medieval Indian history was traditionally seen as: - A period dominated by Turkish and Mughal rule - Primarily focused on political events rather than societal changes - This perspective has changed as historians now emphasize: - The evolution from tribe-based societies to territorial states - The gradual formation of classes and castes within this system - Emergence of a New Social Order - With the rise of land ownership and control over cultivators: - A feudal mode of society developed in India - However, key differences existed between: - Indian feudalism - European feudalism - Scope of This Book - This book traces key developments in India between the 8th and 17th centuries, covering: - Social trends - Economic growth - Political evolution - Cultural advancements - Brings together decades of historical research to offer: - A new orientation to medieval Indian history - Better context for debates on: - The nature of medieval Indian states - The level of religious freedom - Economic trends of the period - Debunking Historical Misconceptions - Challenges the notion that Indian history is simply the rise and fall of empires - Emphasizes the continuous institutional and cultural growth despite: - The breakdown of large empires into smaller states - The resurgence of centralized power later - Notes how economic and cultural exchange between regional and central states remained active - Final Thoughts - The Mughal era saw a triumph of growth over disintegration - The book does not cover: - The 18th-century decline of Mughal power - British rule and its consequences, which shaped India’s later history - India and the World - Changes in India and the World (8th–18th Century) - Global Transformations - The period from the 8th to the 18th century witnessed significant changes worldwide. - Both Europe and Asia saw the emergence of new: - Social structures - Political systems - These transformations influenced the thoughts and lifestyles of people. - Impact on India - India, with its long-standing trade and cultural ties, was affected by these global changes. - Key connections existed with regions around the Mediterranean Sea. - Various powerful empires, including the Roman and Persian Empires, played a role in shaping India’s interactions and influences. - Transformation of Europe (6th–15th Century) - Decline of the Roman Empire - By the sixth century, the Roman Empire had split into two parts: 1. Western Roman Empire (Capital: Rome) 2. Eastern Roman Empire (Capital: Byzantium/Constantinople) - Western Roman Empire - Collapsed under invasions from Slavic and Germanic tribes from Russia and Germany. - These tribes plundered the Roman territories but eventually settled, reshaping: - The population - Languages - Government structures - This period laid the foundation of many modern European nations through the blending of tribal and local cultures. - Byzantine Empire (Eastern Roman Empire) - Included Eastern Europe, Turkey, Syria, and North Africa (Egypt). - Maintained a strong monarchy and centralized administration. - Differed from the Catholic Church in Rome, forming the Greek Orthodox Church. - Played a crucial role in converting Russia to Christianity. - Cultural & Economic Influence - Acted as a link between Greco-Roman civilization and the Arab world. - Continued trade with Asia after the fall of Western Rome. - Many governance and cultural traditions were later adopted by the Arabs. - Contributed to the revival of Greek learning in the West. - Ultimately fell to the Turks in the 15th century. - Western Europe: The Dark Age & Revival - After the fall of the Western Roman Empire: - Cities declined due to economic collapse and loss of gold trade with Africa and the Orient. - The 6th to 10th centuries were termed the Dark Ages. - However, agriculture expanded, laying the groundwork for future recovery. - From the 10th century onward: - Cities revived, leading to economic and cultural growth. - 12th–14th centuries saw renewed prosperity in Western Europe. - Advances in science, technology, and trade fueled progress. - Universities were established (e.g., Padua, Milan), fostering learning and new ideas. - Legacy: Renaissance & New Europe - The intellectual revival in these universities helped spark the Renaissance. - This period reshaped Europe, leading to its modern transformation. - Europe - Growth of Feudalism in Europe - Rise of Feudalism - After the fall of the Roman Empire, a new system of society and governance emerged, known as feudalism. - The term comes from the Latin word “feudum”, which later became “fief” in English. - Power was concentrated in the hands of chiefs and their military followers, who controlled large tracts of land and played a key role in government. - The king was initially just one of the more powerful feudal chiefs. - To control the constant rivalry and conflict among the chiefs, kings required them to swear loyalty as vassals in exchange for recognition of their fiefs. - Chiefs could appoint sub-chiefs, who would receive a portion of land from their fiefs. - Though the king could theoretically reclaim land from disloyal vassals, this was rarely enforced. - Over time, the landed aristocracy became hereditary, restricting new entrants while still replacing disloyal nobles when necessary. - Serfdom & the Manor System - Serfdom was a key feature of feudal society: - Serfs were peasants who were tied to the land, unable to change professions, relocate, or marry without permission from their lord. - Manor System: - The lord of the manor lived in a house or castle and owned vast tracts of land. - A portion of the land was cultivated by the lord with the help of serfs. - Serfs split their time between tending their own fields and working on the lord’s land. - They also paid dues in cash and kind. - The lord was responsible for law enforcement, justice, and security. - Due to widespread lawlessness, even free peasants often accepted vassalage under a lord for protection. - Some historians argue that serfdom and the manor system were essential to feudalism. - Since India lacked both, some question whether it had feudalism. - However, samantas (local landed elites) held feudal-like power, and peasants remained dependent on them. - The manor system and serfdom began disappearing in Western Europe after the 14th century. - Military Organization in Feudalism - The Feudal Army: - The armored knight on horseback became the most iconic symbol of feudalism. - The shift to cavalry warfare in Europe began in the 8th century. - In the Roman era, the military was infantry-based, with heavy and light infantry armed with spears and short swords. - Horses were used mainly for drawing chariots for officers. - Arab Influence on European Warfare: - The arrival of the Arabs changed European warfare. - Arab armies used fast-moving cavalry and mounted archers, rendering traditional infantry ineffective. - This shift necessitated a new military structure, leading to feudalism’s expansion. - Kings lacked the resources to maintain large cavalry forces, so they delegated military responsibilities to fief-holders. - Technological Advancements: - The effectiveness of cavalry warfare was enhanced by two major inventions: 1. Iron Stirrup: Allowed heavily armored knights to remain stable on horseback and withstand the impact of a lance charge. 2.
