Kabul - Qandahar - Zabul (Zamindawar) - Were considered part of al-Hind (India). - These regions contained many Buddhist and Hindu shrines, including: - The 53.5-meter colossal Buddha statue at Bamiyan, surrounded by caves for monks. - The area up to the Oxus River was ruled by various dynasties, some claiming descent from Kanishka. - These kingdoms were supported by a mix of local tribes, including: - Hunas, Furks, Iranians, and Bhati Rajputs. - Resistance to Arab invasions: - These rulers put up stiff resistance to Arab raids for: - Tribute. - Plunder. - Slaves. - This resulted in continuous border skirmishes between the two sides. - The Ghaznavids - Rise of the Ghaznavids - Towards the end of the ninth century, Trans-Oxiana, Khurasan, and parts of Iran were ruled by the Samanids, who were of Iranian descent. - The Samanids had to continuously battle non-Muslim Turkish tribes on their northern and eastern frontiers. - This struggle led to the rise of a new type of soldier, the ghazi: - The ghazis fought for both religion and the state’s safety. - They acted as auxiliaries to the regular army and were sustained by plunder. - Their resourcefulness and endurance helped Muslim states survive against Turkish incursions. - Over time, many Turks converted to Islam, but conflicts with non-Muslim Turkish tribes continued. - The Islamized Turkish tribes later emerged as the greatest defenders and crusaders of Islam, though their pursuit of plunder remained central. - Foundation of the Ghaznavid Empire - Among the Samanid governors was a Turkish slave, Alp-Tigin, who: - Established an independent kingdom with its capital at Ghazni. - After the collapse of the Samanid kingdom, the Ghaznavids inherited the responsibility of defending Islamic lands from Central Asian tribes. - Mahmud of Ghazni (998–1030) - Mahmud ascended the throne in 998 and is considered a hero of Islam by medieval Muslim historians due to: - His defense against Central Asian Turkish tribal invaders, which further fueled the ghazi spirit. - His association with the Iranian cultural renaissance: - The Iranians resisted Arab cultural domination and maintained their language and traditions. - The Samanids had already encouraged Persian language and literature. - Firdausi’s Shah Namah, written in Mahmud’s court, glorified ancient Iranian heroes and the Iran-Turan conflict. - Persian language and culture became dominant in the Ghaznavid empire. - Mahmud himself claimed descent from the legendary Iranian king Afrasiyab. - The Turks thus became both Islamized and Persianized, and they carried this culture into India two centuries later. - Mahmud’s Invasions of India - While Mahmud was a defender of Islam against Turkish invaders, in India, he is remembered as a plunderer and temple destroyer. - He conducted seventeen raids into India, targeting: - The Hindushahi rulers, who controlled Peshawar and Punjab. - Their capital was at Udbhanda (Waihind, Peshawar). - The Hindushahi rulers recognized the threat from Mahmud and attempted to counter it: - Jayapala, the Hindushahi ruler, allied with: - The displaced Samanid governor of Ghazni. - The Bhati ruler of Multan. - The Amir of Multan. - However, their coalition failed, and Mahmud retaliated by devastating Kabul and Jalalabad. - Defeat of the Hindushahis - In 990–91, under Sabuk-Tigin (Mahmud’s father), the Shahis suffered a serious defeat, leading to the annexation of Kabul and Jalalabad. - Mahmud, after ascending the throne in 998, renewed attacks on the Shahis: - Jayapala had strengthened his rule by bringing Lahore under his control. - His rule now extended from Peshawar to Punjab. - In 1001, a decisive battle near Peshawar resulted in: - A devastating defeat for Jayapala. - The destruction of the Shahi capital. - The cession of territory west of the Indus to Mahmud. - Jayapala was succeeded by Anandpala, but in 1009, he too suffered defeat at the Indus. - Mahmud overran Nandana (Salt Range) and captured Nagarkot. - Anandpala ruled Lahore as a feudatory for some time but was eventually ousted in 1015. - Mahmud’s Further Raids in India - By 1015, the Ghaznavids controlled Punjab and Multan. - Mahmud then launched a series of plundering raids into northern India, alternating with campaigns in Central Asia. - His key plundering expeditions included: - 1018: Attacks on Mathura and Kanauj. - 1019: Attack on Kalinjar (Bundelkhand). - 1025: Raid on Somnath (Gujarat): - The Somnath temple was fabulously wealthy and attracted lakhs of pilgrims. - Mahmud led 30,000 cavalrymen through Multan and Jaisalmer. - The city commander fled, but local citizens put up strong resistance. - Mahmud broke the Sivalingam and took parts of it back to Ghazni. - On his return, he faced resistance from Jats in Sind, whom he later punished. - Impact of Mahmud’s Raids - Mahmud’s raids had two major consequences: 1. Political Impact: - The Ghaznavid conquest of Punjab and Multan transformed North India’s political landscape. - The northwestern frontier of India was now permanently breached. - Turkish forces could penetrate deeper into the Indo-Gangetic plains. 2. Economic and Religious Impact: - The plundered wealth financed Mahmud’s struggles in Central Asia. - Mahmud posed as a great destroyer of idols for the glory of Islam. - Decline of the Ghaznavids - After Mahmud’s death in 1030, the Seljuk Empire rose to prominence, controlling: - Syria - Iran - Trans-Oxiana - The Seljuks and Ghaznavids fought for control of Khurasan. - Masud, Mahmud’s son, was defeated and fled to Lahore. - As a result, the Ghaznavid Empire shrank to Ghazni and Punjab. - Though the Ghaznavids continued their plundering raids into India, they were no longer a serious military threat. - Emergence of New States in North India - Despite the Ghaznavid presence in Punjab, new kingdoms arose in North India that could counter their raids. - This prevented further Turkish expansion into India for the next 150 years. - The Rajput States - Rise of Rajput States - The emergence of the Rajputs and the debate about their origins have been previously mentioned. - With the decline of the Pratihara Empire, multiple Rajput states arose in North India. - Major Rajput dynasties included: - Gahadavalas of Kanauj - At its peak, the Gahadvala kingdom extended from Mongyr (Bihar) to Delhi. - Govind Chandra (early 12th century) was the greatest ruler. - Capital: Kanauj (with Banaras as a secondary capital). - Persian sources refer to him as the greatest ruler of Hindustan. - Known for resisting Ghaznavid raids into the doab. - Jai Chandra, his successor, struggled against the Chauhans. - Paramaras of Malwa - Chauhans of Ajmer - Originally served under the rulers of Gujarat. - Established their capital at Nadol (late 10th century). - Vigraharaj, their greatest ruler: - Captured Chittor, established Ajmer (Ajayameru) as the capital. - Built a Sanskrit college and the Anasagar lake at Ajmer. - Resisted Ghaznavid invasions. - Captured Delhi (Dhillika) from the Tomars (1151) but allowed them to rule as feudatories. - Came into conflict with Paramaras of Malwa, ruled by the legendary Bhoja. - Both Vigraharaj and Bhoja were patrons of poets and scholars. - Bhoja was known for works on philosophy, poetics, yoga, and medicine. - Other smaller dynasties: - Kalachuris (Jabalpur region) - Chandellas (Bundelkhand) - Chalukyas (Gujarat) - Tomars (Delhi) - Bengal remained under the Palas, later replaced by the Senas. - The Gahadavalas of Kanauj gradually pushed the Palas out of Bihar. - Prithviraj III and the Chauhan-Gahadavala Rivalry - Prithviraj III (Raja Prithviraj Chauhan): - Ascended the throne in 1177 at the age of 11. - Took full control of administration at 16. - Focused on expanding his empire, subjugating smaller Rajput states. - Struggled against the Chalukyan ruler of Gujarat. - Shifted focus to Ganga Valley after failures in Gujarat. - Led an expedition against Bundelkhand (Mahoba). - Famous warriors Alha and Udal perished in this conflict. - Jai Chandra of Kanauj supported Mahoba’s ruler against Prithviraj. - Rivalries between Chauhans and Gahadavalas weakened Rajput unity, preventing them from ousting Ghaznavids from Punjab. - Rajput Society and Governance - Clans were the foundation of Rajput society. - Each clan traced its lineage to a common ancestor, real or mythical. - Rajputs dominated compact territories, often organized in units of 12, 24, 48, or 84 villages. - Chiefs distributed land among sub-chiefs and warriors for sustenance. - Rajput society valued land, family, and honor (maan). - Rajput rulers governed with the help of chiefs (rana or rawat), often blood relatives. - Land tenure was considered sacred—lands were not taken away from subordinates unless in special cases (rebellion, lack of an heir, etc.). - Strengths and Weaknesses of Rajput Organization - Strengths: - Brotherhood and egalitarianism among Rajputs. - Weaknesses: - Lack of discipline due to egalitarianism. - Long-standing feuds between families. - Exclusive clan identity—refused to extend unity to non-Rajputs. - Disconnection from the common people—Rajputs formed only 10% of Rajasthan’s population and their proportion in other Rajput-dominated areas was also low. - Rajput Warfare and Military Culture - Rajputs treated war as a sport. - Land and cattle disputes led to constant inter-state conflicts. - Ideal rulers were expected to lead armies after Dussehra festival to invade neighbors. - Civilians suffered the most due to these wars. - Religious Patronage - Most Rajput rulers were staunch Hindus, with some also patronizing Jainism. - Brahmins and temples received generous land grants and donations. - Rajput rulers upheld Brahmin privileges and the caste system. - Lower land revenue rates for Brahmins continued in some Rajput states until Indian Union merger. - Brahmins legitimized Rajput claims as descendants of ancient Kshatriya dynasties. - Temple Architecture - 10th-12th century marked the climax (the most intense, exciting, or important part of something) of temple construction in North India. - Nagara style became prominent: - Tall curved spiral roofs (shikharas) over sanctum (garbhagriha). - Square main room with projections on sides. - Mandapa (anteroom) added in front. - Sometimes enclosed by high walls with lofty gates. - Major Temples and Centers - Khajuraho (Madhya Pradesh) – Built by Chandellas - Parsvanatha Temple - Visvanatha Temple - Kandarya Mahadeo Temple - Orissa – Notable temples: - Lingaraja Temple (11th century, Bhubaneshwar) - Sun Temple (13th century, Konark) - Jagannatha Temple (Puri) - Other important sites: - Mathura - Banaras - Dilwara (Abu, Rajasthan) - Temples became centers of social and cultural life. - Some, like Somnath, amassed great wealth and even engaged in business. - Rajputs also built forts, palaces, and public works (stepped wells, bunds, etc.). - Patronage of Arts and Literature - Rajput rulers supported Sanskrit scholars and poets. - Vastupala, minister of Chalukyan ruler Bhima (Gujarat): - Writer, patron of scholars. - Builder of Jain temple at Mt. Abu. - Ujjain and Dhara (Paramara capitals) were Sanskrit learning centers. - Literature in Apabhramsha and Prakrit flourished, particularly among Jain scholars. - Hemachandra (famous Jain scholar) wrote in Sanskrit and Apabhramsha. - Revival of Brahmanism led to Sanskrit replacing Apabhramsha/Prakrit among elites. - Emergence of modern North Indian languages (Hindi, Bengali, Marathi) from regional dialects. - The Turkish Conquest of North India - Patterns of Hindu-Muslim Relations Post-Ghaznavid Conquest - After the Ghaznavid conquest of Punjab, two distinct patterns of relations between Muslims and Hindus emerged: 1. Raids for Plunder – The successors of Mahmud of Ghazni carried out raids into the Gangetic valley and Rajputana, lured by wealth. The Rajput rulers put up strong resistance and won several victories against the Turks. However, the declining power of the Ghaznavid state and the Rajputs’ successes made them complacent. 2. Trade and Cultural Exchange – Muslim traders were welcomed as they facilitated trade between India and Central/West Asia, boosting the state’s income. As a result, Muslim colonies emerged in several towns of North India. Alongside traders, Sufi preachers arrived in Punjab, spreading their message of love, faith, and dedication to one God. Although their primary audience was Muslim settlers, they also influenced some Hindus. - Additionally, Lahore became a center of Arabic and Persian learning, and Hindu generals, such as Tilak (a barber by caste), served in the Ghaznavid armies, which also recruited Hindu (Jat) soldiers. - The Rise of the Ghurids - These interactions between Hindus and Muslims might have continued indefinitely, but a significant change in Central Asia’s political landscape altered the course of history. - By the mid-12th century, Turkish tribesmen (partly Buddhist, partly pagan) destroyed the power of the Seljuk Turks. - This led to the rise of two new powers: - The Khwarazmian Empire (based in Iran) - The Ghurid Empire (based in Ghur, northwest Afghanistan) - The Ghurids, initially vassals of the Ghaznavids, revolted and overthrew them. Under Sultan Alauddin, known as “Jahan-Soz” (the world burner), the Ghurids completely destroyed Ghazni in retaliation for past hostilities. - The Khwarazmians soon conquered Khurasan, restricting Ghurid expansion in Central Asia. - Left with no alternative, the Ghurids turned their focus towards India. - Muizzuddin Muhammad’s Early Conquests (1173–1190) - In 1173, Muizzuddin Muhammad bin Sam (also known as Shahabuddin Muhammad or Muhammad of Ghur) ascended the throne at Ghazni, while his elder brother ruled Ghur. - He launched his first campaigns into India via the Gomal Pass, capturing Multan and Uchch. - In 1178, he attempted to invade Gujarat but was defeated near Mount Abu. This defeat made him realize the importance of first securing Punjab before attempting deeper conquests in India. - By 1190, Muizzuddin Muhammad had successfully: - Conquered Peshawar, Lahore, and Sialkot - Established a stronghold in Punjab, preparing for an advance towards Delhi and the Gangetic Doab - The Rise of the Chauhans - Meanwhile, significant developments were taking place in North India: - The Chauhans had emerged as a dominant power. - They had defeated and killed several Turkish invaders attempting to enter Rajasthan from Punjab. - Around the mid-12th century, the Chauhans had also captured Delhi (Dhillika) from the Tomars. - Their expansion towards Punjab brought them into direct conflict with the Ghaznavid rulers of the region. - This growing power struggle set the stage for a decisive confrontation between the Ghurids and the Rajputs, which would soon unfold. - The Battle of Tarain - First Battle of Tarain (1191) - A conflict between Muizzuddin Muhammad and Prithviraj Chauhan was inevitable, as both had rival claims over Tabarhinda. - In 1191, the two forces clashed at Tarain, where Prithviraj’s army decisively defeated the Ghurids. - Muizzuddin Muhammad barely escaped with his life, thanks to a young Khalji horseman. - After this victory, Prithviraj captured Tabarhinda following a 12-month siege. - However, he made little effort to expel the Ghurids from Punjab, possibly believing it was just another temporary Turkish raid. - This miscalculation gave Muizzuddin Muhammad the time to regroup and plan another invasion the following year. He rejected Prithviraj’s proposal to let the Ghurids retain Punjab. - Second Battle of Tarain (1192): A Turning Point in Indian History - The Second Battle of Tarain (1192) proved decisive, as Muizzuddin Muhammad made meticulous preparations: - He reportedly marched with 1,206,000 men, including: - Heavy cavalry in full steel armor - 10,000 mounted archers - Prithviraj was not negligent; he recognized the Ghurid threat early and sought support from other northern Indian rajas. - Many rulers sent contingents, but Jaichandra of Kanauj refused to help, possibly due to old rivalries rather than the legendary tale of Prithviraj’s abduction of Jaichandra’s daughter, Sanyogita. - The Battle and its Aftermath - Prithviraj’s army reportedly had 300,000 troops, including a large cavalry force and 300 elephants. - Despite their numerical superiority, the Turkish army’s superior organization, discipline, and cavalry tactics proved decisive. - The Turkish cavalry, with their mounted archers and heavy cavalry, outmaneuvered and overwhelmed the Rajput forces. - Prithviraj attempted to escape but was captured near Saraswati (Sirsa). - Consolidation of Turkish Rule - After the victory, the Ghurids systematically expanded their control: - Hansi, Saraswati, and Samana were captured. - Ajmer was seized, though Prithviraj was briefly allowed to rule under Ghurid suzerainty—evident from coins bearing both his name and that of Muizzuddin Muhammad. - Prithviraj was eventually executed for “conspiracy”, and his son briefly succeeded him. - The Establishment of Turkish Power in Delhi and Rajasthan - Delhi was initially restored to the Tomars, but this policy was soon reversed. - Delhi became the base for further Turkish expansion into the Ganga Valley. - After a rebellion in Ajmer, a Turkish general was installed as the new ruler. - Prithviraj’s son fled to Ranthambor, where he founded a new Chauhan kingdom. - Thus, Delhi and eastern Rajasthan fell under Turkish rule, marking the beginning of Turkish dominance in northern India. - Expansion and Consolidation of Turkish Rule (1192–1206) - Conquest of the Ganga-Jamuna Doab and Kanauj - Between 1192 and 1206, the Turks extended their rule over the Ganga-Jamuna Doab, Bihar, and Bengal. However, to secure control over the Doab, they first had to defeat the Gahadavala kingdom of Kanauj, ruled by Jaichandra. - Jaichandra, though ruling peacefully for two decades, was not a strong warrior and had earlier suffered defeat against the Sena king of Bengal. - After the Battle of Tarain (1192), Muizzuddin Muhammad returned to Ghazni, entrusting Indian affairs to his slave and general, Qutbuddin Aibak. - Over the next two years, the Turks overran parts of the upper Doab without resistance from the Gahadavalas. - Battle of Chandawar (1194) and its Aftermath - In 1194, Muizzuddin returned to India, leading 50,000 cavalry across the Yamuna towards Kanauj. - A fierce battle was fought at Chandawar, where Jaichandra was killed by an arrow, and his army was defeated. - Muizzuddin then marched to Banaras, where he destroyed many temples. - The Turks established control over a vast territory, extending to the borders of Bihar. - These victories at Tarain (1192) and Chandawar (1194) laid the foundation of Turkish rule in northern India, though consolidating it took nearly fifty years. - Further Turkish Expansion - Muizzuddin Muhammad occupied the forts of Bayana and Gwalior, securing Delhi’s southern flank. Soon after, Aibak conquered Kalinjar, Mahoba, and Khajuraho from the Chandel rulers. - With a firm base in the Doab, the Turks launched raids into neighboring regions. - Aibak defeated Bhima III of Gujarat, plundering Anhilwara and other towns. However, the Turks were not strong enough to hold such distant territories. - Conquest of Bihar and Bengal - The Turks found greater success in the east under Bakhtiyar Khalji, a Khalji officer appointed to govern areas beyond Banaras. - Bakhtiyar Khalji was a parallel military commander, not a Sultan of Delhi. He fits between Ghori’s expansion and Aibak’s establishment of the Sultanate. - Bakhtiyar Khalji repeatedly raided Bihar, which was largely undefended. - During these attacks, he destroyed famous Buddhist monasteries, including Nalanda and Vikramasila, amassing wealth and followers. - He also gathered intelligence on Bengal, a rich land known for its resources and trade. - Conquest of Bengal (c. 1204) - After careful planning, Bakhtiyar Khalji marched towards Nadia, where Lakshmana Sena, the Sena ruler of Bengal, had built a palace. - Disguised as a horse merchant, Bakhtiyar launched a surprise attack on the palace, causing widespread confusion. - Taken off guard, Lakshmana Sena fled, allowing Bakhtiyar’s forces to capture the palace. - Soon after, Bakhtiyar occupied Lakhnauti (the Sena capital) without opposition, while Lakshmana Sena retreated to Sonargaon in southern Bengal, where he continued to rule. - Though Muizzuddin appointed Bakhtiyar as Bengal’s governor, he largely ruled independently. - Bakhtiyar’s Downfall - Bakhtiyar’s rule was short-lived: - He led a disastrous campaign into the Brahmaputra valley (Assam), where his army suffered from hunger, illness, and a total military defeat. - Trapped between a river and Assamese forces, the Turks were annihilated. - Bakhtiyar barely escaped with a handful of followers but was later stabbed by one of his own officers and died. - Muizzuddin Muhammad’s Final Years (1203–1206) - Meanwhile, Muizzuddin Muhammad and his brother attempted to expand the Ghurid empire into Central Asia. - In 1203, Muizzuddin suffered a crushing defeat against the Khwarizmi empire, forcing him to shift his focus entirely to India. - This defeat allowed the rise of a Turkish state centered in India. - In 1206, the Khokhars, a powerful tribe in western Punjab, revolted. Muizzuddin led a large campaign against them, massacring many and crushing the rebellion. - However, on his way back to Ghazni, Muizzuddin Muhammad was assassinated by a Muslim fanatic from a rival sect. - Comparison: Muizzuddin Muhammad vs. Mahmud of Ghazni - Muizzuddin is often compared to Mahmud of Ghazni, though their situations and achievements differed: - Mahmud of Ghazni had a larger empire and was more successful in Central Asia. - Muizzuddin Muhammad’s political achievements in India were greater, as he established a lasting Turkish state. - Mahmud’s conquest of Punjab paved the way for Muizzuddin’s success in northern India. - While both rulers used Islamic slogans to justify their conquests and plundering, neither was truly motivated by religious zeal. - They often allowed defeated rulers to retain power, annexing regions only when necessary. - Thus, Muizzuddin’s victories and policies led to the foundation of the Delhi Sultanate, marking the beginning of Turkish dominance in India. - Causes of the Defeat of the Rajputs - Basic info - The rapid conquest of the leading Rajput states in north India by the Turks within a short span of 15 years requires careful analysis. - A country is typically conquered when it suffers from social, political, economic, or military weaknesses compared to its neighbors. - In the case of the Rajputs, their defeat was not due to technological inferiority but rather organizational and strategic shortcomings. - Military Technology: No Clear Turkish Superiority - The Turks did not possess significantly superior weapons compared to the Indians. - The iron stirrup, which revolutionized warfare in Europe, had been in use in India since the 8th century. - The Turkish bows had a longer range, but Indian bows were considered more accurate and deadly, often with poisoned arrowheads. - In hand-to-hand combat, Indian swords were among the best in the world. - Elephants provided a key advantage for the Indian armies, while the Turkish cavalry likely had swifter and sturdier horses. - Organizational and Structural Weaknesses of the Rajputs - Rise of feudalism in India weakened administrative and military coordination. - Rajput rulers relied on regional chiefs, who rarely acted in coordination and dispersed after battles. - In contrast, the Turks maintained large standing armies through the Iqta and Ahalisa systems, allowing them to sustain prolonged campaigns. - The Turks excelled in mobility and coordination, while the Rajputs lacked: - Organized cavalry forces that could move quickly across long distances. - Large units of mounted archers or heavily armed cavalry, which were crucial in battle. - Despite possessing greater human and physical resources than the Ghaznavid and Ghurid empires, the Rajputs were unable to recover from their defeats due to their poor military organization. - Advantages of the Turkish Military System - The Iqta system ensured that Turkish chiefs had: - Land grants from which they collected revenue for the state. - An obligation to maintain troops for the Sultan. - Non-hereditary land tenure, which prevented local feudalism from developing. - The Sultan controlled revenues directly from Ahalisa lands, allowing him to maintain a large standing army. - The Turkish military was centralized, unlike the fragmented Rajput states. - Many Turkish officers were slaves who: - Were trained specifically for warfare. - Loyal to the Sultan, ensuring a stable and professional military command. - Role of Personal Bravery and Religious Motivation - The Rajputs were no less brave than the Turks in battle. - The Turks fought under the ‘Ghazi’ spirit, while the Rajputs considered retreat dishonorable. - Caste was not a barrier in Rajput armies—non-Rajputs and lower castes also participated in warfare, making Rajput forces numerically superior in many battles. - Lack of Strategic Vision Among the Rajputs - From the 10th century onward, the Turks had been infiltrating India. - The Rajputs fiercely resisted and won several battles, but they lacked long-term strategic vision. - Once outer defenses like Kabul and Lahore fell, the Rajputs failed to reclaim them, allowing the Turks a foothold in Punjab. - The Rajputs focused solely on internal Indian conflicts and ignored developments in Central Asia, which had historically influenced Indian history. - Conclusion - While the Turks did not have clear military superiority, their better organization, centralized administration, and strategic planning helped them defeat the divided and feudal Rajput states. - The Rajputs fought bravely but lacked coordination and long-term vision, ultimately leading to their defeat and the establishment of Turkish rule in north India. - The Delhi Sultanate—I (Circa 1200-1400) - - The Mamluk Sultans (13th Century) - After their conquest of Punjab and Multan, the Turks expanded into the Ganga Valley, Bihar, and parts of Bengal. However, for nearly a century after their initial success, the newly established Delhi Sultanate faced several challenges: - Challenges to the Delhi Sultanate - Foreign invasions threatened the stability of the Sultanate. - Internal conflicts among Turkish leaders weakened central authority. - Rajput resistance—dispossessed and subordinate Rajput rulers attempted to regain independence and expel the Turks. - Despite these difficulties, the Turkish rulers managed to consolidate their power. - Expansion of the Delhi Sultanate - By the end of the 13th century, the Sultanate was strong enough to: - Extend its rule over Malwa and Gujarat. - Begin penetrating into the Deccan and South India. - Impact of Turkish Rule in India - Within a hundred years, Turkish rule led to: - Significant social, administrative, and cultural changes across India. - The integration of new governance structures that shaped the future of Indian polity. - Thus, the establishment of the Mamluk dynasty not only secured Turkish rule in northern India but also set the stage for further expansion and lasting transformations in Indian society. - Struggle for the Establishment of a Strong Monarchy - Succession After Muizzuddin (Muhammad of Ghur) - After Muizzuddin’s death in 1206, his empire was divided among his generals. - Qutbuddin Aibak, a Turkish slave, took control of Delhi and became the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate. - Meanwhile, another slave of Muizzuddin, Yalduz, succeeded in Ghazni and claimed authority over Delhi. - Aibak’s Independence from Ghazni - Aibak refused to accept Yalduz’s claim and ruled independently from Lahore. - This marked a permanent break between Delhi and Ghazni, allowing the Delhi Sultanate to develop independently. - Significance of the Break from Central Asia - Severing ties with Ghazni protected India from being entangled in Central Asian politics. - The Delhi Sultanate evolved as a distinct political entity, focusing on Indian affairs rather than external influences. - This early assertion of independence laid the foundation for a strong and self-sufficient monarchy in India. - Iltutmish (1210-1236) – The Real Consolidator of Turkish Rule - Accession to the Throne - Aibak died in 1210 due to injuries from a fall while playing changan (polo). - He was succeeded by Iltutmish, his son-in-law. - However, Aibak’s son also claimed the throne, leading to a succession battle. - Iltutmish defeated Aibak’s son, preventing the principle of hereditary succession from taking root in the Delhi Sultanate. - Challenges to His Rule - Iltutmish faced opposition from multiple fronts: - Ali Mardan Khan declared himself ruler of Bengal and Bihar. - Qubacha, a fellow slave of Aibak, seized Lahore and parts of Punjab and declared independence. - Rajputs rebelled, reclaiming Kalinjar, Gwalior, and much of eastern Rajasthan (Ajmer, Bayana, etc.). - Even some of Iltutmish’s officers near Delhi were hesitant to accept his rule. - Securing the Northwest and the Mongol Threat - Iltutmish’s primary concern was the Khwarazm Shah’s conquest of Ghazni, bringing the powerful Khwarazm Empire to India’s doorstep. - To counter this, Iltutmish occupied Lahore to check the threat. - In 1218, the Mongols under Genghis Khan destroyed the Khwarazm Empire, creating one of the most powerful empires in history. - While the Mongols were distracted elsewhere, Iltutmish defeated Qubacha, reclaiming Multan and Uchch. - This extended the Delhi Sultanate’s frontier to the Indus once again. - Suppressing Rebellions in Bengal and Bihar - Iwaz, who took the title Sultan Ghiyasuddin, declared independence in Bengal and Bihar. - He was known for his public works and military raids, but Delhi’s authority remained weak in the region. - In 1226-27, Iltutmish’s son defeated and killed Iwaz near Lakhnauti, bringing Bengal and Bihar back under Delhi’s control. - However, Bengal and Bihar continued to challenge Delhi’s authority in the years to come. - Expanding Control Over Rajput Territories - Iltutmish recaptured Gwalior and Bayana. - Ajmer and Nagor were also brought under his rule. - He launched expeditions against Ranthambhor and Jalor to reassert Delhi’s dominance. - Nagda, the capital of Mewar (near Udaipur), was attacked, but Iltutmish had to retreat when the Gujarat armies arrived to support the Rana of Mewar. - In retaliation, Iltutmish sent an expedition against the Chalukyas of Gujarat, but it was defeated with losses. - Conclusion - Iltutmish not only defended Delhi Sultanate from internal rebellions and external threats but also strengthened Turkish rule in north India. His reign laid the foundation for a strong centralized state, making him the real consolidator of the Turkish conquests. - Raziya (1236-1239) – The First and Only Woman Ruler of the Delhi Sultanate - Iltutmish’s Unconventional Succession Choice - In his final years, Iltutmish faced a succession crisis, believing none of his surviving sons were fit to rule. - After much deliberation, he nominated his daughter, Raziya, as his successor. - He convinced the nobles and theologians (ulama) to accept her nomination, a bold and unprecedented decision in Indian history. - While women had ruled in Iran and Egypt, a woman being chosen over male heirs was a radical departure from tradition. - Raziya’s Struggles for Power - To secure her throne, Raziya had to fight: - Her brothers, who opposed her rule. - The powerful Turkish nobles, known as ‘Chahalgani’ (the Forty), who wanted a puppet ruler they could control. - Despite being a woman, Raziya was determined and independent: - She discarded female attire and held court unveiled. - She led armies in battle and actively participated in governance. - Iltutmish’s wazir, Nizam-ul-Mulk Junaidi, opposed her elevation and backed a noble rebellion against her. - Raziya defeated him, forcing him to flee. - She also sent an expedition against Ranthambhor, successfully establishing law and order. - Opposition from the Turkish Nobles - Raziya attempted to build a faction of nobles loyal to her, challenging the power of the Turkish aristocracy. - She appointed Yaqut Khan, an Abyssinian noble, as Superintendent of the Royal Stable, a position of trust and closeness to the ruler. - This led to accusations from the Turkish nobles, who: - Claimed Raziya was violating feminine modesty. - Spread false rumors of personal intimacy with Yaqut Khan. - However, contemporary writers do not confirm these allegations: - The claim that Yaqut lifted her onto her horse is false because Raziya always appeared in public on an elephant, not horseback. - Rebellions and Downfall - Revolts broke out in Lahore and Sirhind. - Raziya personally led an expedition against Lahore, forcing the governor to submit. - During the march to Sirhind, internal rebellion struck: - Yaqut Khan was killed. - Raziya was captured and imprisoned at Tabarhinda. - She managed to win over her captor, Altunia, and married him in a bid to regain power. - Together, they attempted to retake Delhi, but she was defeated. - While Razia was imprisoned, the nobles in Delhi did not keep the throne vacant. - They installed Bahram Shah (1240–1242 CE), another son of Iltutmish, as Sultan. - Bahram Shah became a puppet ruler of the powerful Turkish nobles. - While fleeing, Raziya was killed by bandits in a forest, marking the tragic end of her short but remarkable reign. - Conclusion - Raziya’s rule was brief but significant, as it marked: - The first open power struggle between the monarchy and Turkish nobles. - A bold challenge to gender norms, as she ruled with authority and military leadership. - The failure of the Turkish elite to accept a strong, independent female ruler, ultimately leading to her downfall. - Era of Balban (1246-1287) – The Architect of Strong Monarchy - Rise to Power - The struggle between the monarchy and the Turkish nobles continued after Iltutmish’s rule. - Ulugh Khan (later known as Balban) gradually consolidated power and ultimately ascended the throne in 1265. - Before becoming Sultan, he served as naib (deputy) to Nasiruddin Mahmud, a younger son of Iltutmish, whom Balban had helped secure the throne in 1246. - To strengthen his influence, Balban married his daughter to the young sultan. - His growing power alienated the Turkish nobles, who had hoped to control the government under the inexperienced Nasiruddin Mahmud. - Conflict with the Turkish Nobles - In 1253, the Turkish nobles conspired against Balban and removed him from power, replacing him with Izzuddin Raihan, an Indian Muslim. - The nobles accepted Raihan’s appointment as they could not agree among themselves on who should take Balban’s place. - Balban stepped aside but quietly built his own faction. - Within 1.5 years, he regained influence, preparing for a military showdown. - He may have established contact with the Mongols, who controlled much of Punjab. - Seeing Balban’s growing power, Sultan Mahmud dismissed Raihan; later, Raihan was defeated and killed. - Balban eliminated his rivals by any means necessary, even assuming the royal insignia (chaher) before formally ascending the throne. - Ascension to the Throne (1265) - Nasiruddin Mahmud died in 1265, possibly poisoned by Balban. - Some historians also suggest that Balban had Mahmud’s sons killed to clear his path to the throne. - Harsh as his methods were, his rule marked the beginning of strong, centralized government in the Delhi Sultanate. - Strengthening the Monarchy - Balban believed that only a strong monarchy could handle the internal and external threats to the empire. - He sought to increase the prestige and authority of the Sultanate by declaring himself a descendant of the legendary Iranian king Afrasiyab. - To prove his noble lineage, he became the self-proclaimed ‘champion of Turkish nobility’. - He excluded Indian Muslims from high offices, refusing to entertain anyone who lacked noble ancestry. - His elitism extended to ridiculous extremes: - He refused to grant an audience to an important trader because he was not high-born. - The historian Barani quoted Balban as saying: - “Whenever I see a base-born ignoble man, my eyes burn, and I reach in anger for my sword (to kill him).” - Suppression of the Turkish Nobles (Chahalgani) - Despite championing the Turkish nobility, Balban was not willing to share power. - He broke the power of the ‘Chahalgani’ (the Forty Turkish Nobles) and centralized authority under himself. - To achieve this, he even poisoned his cousin, Sher Khan. - Though a despot, he ensured impartial justice and punished even the highest-ranking officials if they defied him. - Military Reforms and Internal Stability - To maintain control, he: - Established a spy network in every department to stay informed. - Strengthened the army to suppress internal rebellions and defend against the Mongols. - Reorganized the military department (Diwan-i-Arz) and pensioned off unfit soldiers. - When retired soldiers (mainly Turks from Iltutmish’s time) protested, he had to partially withdraw this decision. - Law and Order: The ‘Blood and Iron’ Policy - The Ganga-Jamuna Doab and Awadh had become unsafe due to robbers, dacoits, and rebellious zamindars. - Near Delhi, the Mewatis plundered villages as far as the city’s outskirts. - To crush these elements, Balban enforced a ruthless policy of ‘Blood and Iron’: - The Meos were brutally hunted down and killed. - Forests around Delhi were cleared to prevent hideouts for criminals. - Numerous military outposts (thanas) were established. - His harsh methods restored order, impressing people with the strength of his government. - Court Etiquette and Royal Prestige - Balban projected an image of absolute power through elaborate ceremonies: - He maintained a grand court, surrounded by bodyguards with drawn swords. - He refused to laugh or joke in court and even gave up drinking wine to maintain his majestic demeanor. - He introduced Iranian customs, such as: - Sajada (prostration) - Paeos (kissing the monarch’s feet) - Though considered un-Islamic, these ceremonies were tolerated because the Delhi Sultanate stood as a symbol of Islamic power after the Mongol invasions destroyed many Muslim states. - Military Policy and the Mongol Threat - Despite having a strong army, Balban avoided distant military campaigns, fearing Mongol attacks on Delhi. - Instead, he: - Focused on defense and internal stability. - Led only one major expedition to Bengal. - Kept the army active through large-scale hunting expeditions. - Death and Legacy (1286-1287) - Balban died in 1286, marking the end of his strong, centralized rule. - He was one of the main architects of the Delhi Sultanate, particularly in: - Strengthening the monarchy’s authority. - Establishing a rigid administrative structure. - Defining the Sultanate’s institutions and governance model. - However, his narrow focus on Turkish nobles and exclusion of non-Turks created dissatisfaction, leading to instability after his death. - His failure to fully protect India from Mongol invasions remained a significant weakness of his rule. - The Mongols and the Problem of the Northwest Frontier - India’s Vulnerability in the Northwest - India’s natural boundaries largely protected it from external invasions, except in the northwest. - Invaders like the Huns, Scythians, and Turks entered India through the mountain passes in this region. - To prevent invasions into the fertile lands of Punjab and Sindh, control over the area extending from Kabul to Ghazni and Qandahar was crucial. - This region, flanked by the Hindukush, was the main route for reinforcements from Central Asia. - Due to political instability in West Asia, the Delhi Sultanate could not establish firm control over these frontiers, leaving India vulnerable. - The Khwarazmian Empire and the Rise of the Mongols - The Ghurids lost control over Kabul, Qandahar, and Ghazni when the Khwarazmian Empire emerged. - The Khwarazmians extended their boundary to the Indus, setting the stage for a struggle with the successors of Qutbuddin Aibak. - Before this struggle could unfold, a greater threat emerged: Chinggis Khan, the Mongol leader, who called himself “the scourge of God.” - In 1218, the Mongols attacked the Khwarazmian Empire, sacking cities from the Jaxartes to the Caspian Sea and from Ghazni to Iran. - The Mongols used terror as an instrument of war, massacring resisting cities and enslaving women and children. - Craftsmen were taken for the Mongol army, while others were drafted for labor. - The Mongol conquest devastated the region’s economy and cultural life, though eventual peace and trade revival led to slow recovery. - Many princes, scholars, theologians, and learned men fled to Delhi, making it a major center of Islam. - Turkish rulers, cut off from their homelands, had to adapt to Indian conditions. - Chinggis Khan and the Mongol Threat to India (1221) - After defeating the Khwarazmian ruler, Jalaluddin, Chinggis Khan pursued him to the Indus River. - Jalaluddin fought bravely but was defeated and escaped by crossing the Indus into India. - Chinggis Khan remained near the Indus for three months but did not invade India, focusing instead on Central Asia. - Had Chinggis invaded, India might have faced destruction greater than that caused by the Turks. - The Delhi Sultan Iltutmish diplomatically avoided conflict by refusing to grant asylum to Jalaluddin. - Jalaluddin stayed in the Cis-Sutlej region, leading to frequent Mongol raids. - Consequently, the Indus ceased to be India’s western boundary. - Defense of Lahore and Multan - Lahore and Multan were contested by Iltutmish, Yalduz, and Qubacha. - Their internal conflict weakened their positions, allowing Iltutmish to capture both cities. - This strengthened Delhi’s defense against Mongol incursions. - The Mongols after Chinggis Khan (1227–1240) - After Chinggis Khan’s death in 1227, his empire was divided among his sons. - Mongols under Batu Khan focused on conquering Russia, delaying further invasions into India. - This period allowed the Delhi Sultans to consolidate power and strengthen their army. - Mongol Raids and Balban’s Defense Strategy - In 1241, Tair Bahadur, the Mongol commander in Herat, Ghur, Ghazni, and Turkestan, sacked Lahore. - In 1245, Mongols attacked Multan, but Balban’s swift response saved it. - Balban faced Mongol pressure on the frontiers, especially when some Turkish nobles, including Sher Khan (Governor of Multan), sided with the Mongols. - The Delhi frontier shifted from the Jhelum to the Beas, with Multan constantly under Mongol pressure. - Balban’s Strategy: - Repaired forts at Tabarhinda, Sunam, and Samana to block Mongol advances. - Remained in Delhi for constant frontier vigilance. - Sent diplomatic envoys to Halaku Khan, the Mongol Il-Khan of Iran, maintaining peace. - Avoided war with the Mongols by allowing them to control much of Punjab. - Regular military campaigns kept Mongol incursions in check. - Placed his son, Prince Mahmud, in charge of Multan, who later died defending it. - Mongol Invasions during the Khalji Era (1292–1306) - After Balban’s death in 1286, his defensive strategies continued. - In 1292, Abdullah, a grandson of Halaku Khan, invaded with 150,000 troops but was defeated by Jalaluddin Khalji. - 4,000 Mongols converted to Islam and settled near Delhi. - Mongol invasions into Punjab increased due to political shifts in Central Asia. - Alauddin Khalji’s Mongol Campaigns - In 1297, Dawa Khan, Mongol ruler of Transoxiana, tried to conquer India. - In 1299, his son, Qutlugh Khwaja, led a 200,000-strong army to capture Delhi. - Mongols cut off Delhi’s communication lines and entered its streets. - Alauddin Khalji fought back, refusing to surrender. - Zafar Khan, a key general, was killed in battle. - The Mongols retreated without a decisive battle. - In 1303, Mongols returned with 120,000 troops while Alauddin was besieging Chittor. - He fortified Delhi at Siri and faced the Mongols for two months. - Daily skirmishes caused hardship to Delhi’s citizens. - Mongols retreated without success. - Impact of Mongol Invasions on the Delhi Sultanate - The Mongol invasions proved that the Delhi Sultans could defend against an enemy that had conquered Central and West Asia. - Alauddin Khalji took decisive steps: - Strengthened fortresses near the Beas River. - Expanded and modernized the Delhi army. - Successfully repelled later Mongol invasions with heavy Mongol casualties. - In 1306, after Dawa Khan’s death, civil war in Mongol territories reduced their threat to India. - Taking advantage of this, the Delhi rulers regained Lahore and extended control to the Indus. - Conclusion: A Century of Mongol Threat - Throughout the 13th century, the Delhi Sultanate faced a serious Mongol threat from the northwest. - The Mongols gained control over Punjab and Kashmir and repeatedly threatened Delhi. - However, due to the military strength, diplomacy, and resilience of the Turkish rulers, the Mongol threat was averted. - Eventually, the Punjab was reclaimed, ensuring India’s security until the rise of Timur in the 14th century. - The Mongol threat shaped the internal policies of the Delhi Sultanate, forcing rulers to centralize power and maintain a strong military. - Internal Rebellions and the Struggle for the Territorial Consolidation of the Delhi Sultanate - Challenges Faced by the Delhi Sultans - During the rule of the Bari Turks (also called the Mamluk or Slave rulers), the Sultans of Delhi had to contend with: - Internal dissensions - Foreign invasions - Internal rebellions - Nature of Internal Rebellions - Some rebellions were led by ambitious Muslim chiefs seeking independence. - Others were initiated by Rajput rajas and zamindars attempting to expel Turkish invaders or expand their own influence. - These rajas and zamindars not only fought against the Turks but also against each other. - The objectives of these rebellions varied, making it incorrect to classify them all as “Hindu resistance.” - India’s vast geography made centralized rule difficult. - Provincial governors were granted significant autonomy, encouraging them to assert independence. - Regional sentiments, which had strengthened between the seventh and twelfth centuries, further fueled opposition to Delhi’s rule. - Rebellions in Bengal and Bihar - The eastern regions, particularly Bengal and Bihar, persistently sought independence from Delhi. - Earlier, Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji expelled the Sena king, Lakshmana Sena, from Lakhnauti. - Later, Iwaz (Ghiyasuddin Sultan) functioned as an independent ruler, expanding his control over Bihar and extracting tribute from Jajnagar (Orissa), Tirhut (North Bengal), Bang (East Bengal), and Kamrup (Assam). - Iltutmish’s Campaigns in Bengal - In 1225, Iltutmish marched against Iwaz, who initially submitted but later rebelled. - Iltutmish’s son, the governor of Awadh, defeated and killed Iwaz. - A second expedition in 1230 was needed to stabilize the region. - Continued Struggles for Control - After Iltutmish’s death, Bengal’s governors frequently switched between asserting independence and submitting to Delhi. - Bihar largely remained under Lakhnauti’s control. - These independent rulers attempted, with limited success, to expand into Radha (South Bengal), Orissa, and Kamrup (Assam). - The rulers of Orissa and Assam successfully resisted Delhi’s expansion: - In 1244, Orissa’s ruler defeated the Muslim forces near Lakhnauti. - Subsequent attacks on Jajnagar (Orissa’s capital) also failed, proving that the Lakhnauti rulers lacked the strength to conquer neighboring Hindu territories. - Balban’s Reassertion of Control - Balban, a strong ruler, sought to bring Bengal and Bihar back under Delhi’s authority. - Tughril, a governor who initially submitted but later declared independence, was hunted down in 1280. - Balban punished Tughril’s family and followers severely. - This three-year campaign was Balban’s only distant military expedition. - Bengal’s Final Break from Delhi - After Balban’s death, his son Bughra Khan, the governor of Bengal, chose to rule independently rather than fight for Delhi’s throne. - He established a dynasty that ruled Bengal for forty years. - The Mongol Threat and Rajput Resistance in the North - During the 13th century, Delhi lost control over: - Bengal and Bihar - Most of Punjab, which fell under Mongol rule - Parts of the Ganga Doab, where Katehar Rajputs were a significant force - The Katehar Rajputs, based in Ahichchatra, frequently raided Badaun. - After becoming Sultan, Balban retaliated with large-scale massacres and plunder, clearing jungles and building roads to secure the region. - According to historian Barani, Balban’s campaign permanently secured the iqtas of Baran, Amroha, Sambhal, and Katehar (modern western Uttar Pradesh). - Challenges in Rajasthan and the Western Frontier - The Delhi Sultanate’s control over its southern and western frontiers was unstable. - Turkish Expansion into Eastern Rajasthan - Under Aibak, the Turks captured a chain of forts: - Tijara (Alwar), Bayana, Gwalior, Kalinjar - They extended into Ranthambhor, Nagaur, Ajmer, and Nadol (near Jalor) - These regions were previously part of the Chauhan empire, ruled by Chauhan families. - Rajput Resistance and Iltutmish’s Counterattack - Taking advantage of Iltutmish’s focus on the northwest, Rajput rulers recaptured Kalinjar, Gwalior, and Bayana. - Several other principalities, including Ranthambhor and Jalor, rejected Turkish rule. - In 1226, Iltutmish launched military campaigns to regain control: - He forced Ranthambhor to accept Turkish suzerainty. - He captured Jalor, which was strategically important on the Gujarat route. - However, he failed to extend his control over Gujarat and Malwa. - The Chalukyas of Gujarat repelled his attack. - The Paramaras of Malwa were too strong for Turkish forces. - Iltutmish did manage to raid Malwa, plundering Ujjain and Raisina. - Post-Iltutmish Turmoil and Rajput Gains - After Iltutmish’s death, many Rajput rulers rebelled, reclaiming their territories. - The Bhatti Rajputs of Mewat: - Encircled Bayana - Raided up to Delhi’s outskirts - The fort of Gwalior was recovered by the Rajputs. - Balban’s Rajput Campaigns - Failed to capture Ranthambhor and Gwalior. - Ruthlessly subdued Mewat, ensuring Delhi’s safety from Mewati raids for a century. - Maintained control over Ajmer and Nagaur. - Secured Turkish rule in eastern Rajasthan, taking advantage of continued Rajput infighting. - Impact of These Struggles - The territorial consolidation of the Delhi Sultanate during this period laid the groundwork for future expansions. - Key achievements: - Established a strong monarchy - Repelled Mongol invasions - Secured the Ganga Doab - Maintained control over Eastern Rajasthan - These developments set the stage for the next phase in Delhi Sultanate history—its expansion into Western India and the Deccan. - The Delhi Sultanate—II (Circa 1200-1400) The Khaljis and the Tughlaqs - - Political Confusion After Balban’s Death (1286) - Succession Crisis in Delhi - Balban’s chosen successor, Prince Mahmud, had died earlier in a battle with the Mongols. - His second son, Bughra Khan, was invited by the nobles to assume the throne but preferred to rule over Bengal and Bihar. - A grandson of Baibars was installed as Sultan, but he was too young and inexperienced to manage the situation. - Resentment Against Turkish Nobility - Turkish nobles attempted to monopolize high offices, leading to considerable resentment. - Many non-Turks, particularly the Khaljis, had arrived in India during the Ghurid invasion but were not given recognition in Delhi. - As a result, they sought opportunities in Bengal and Bihar or served as soldiers in the northwest to counter Mongol threats. - Rise of Indian Muslims in the Nobility - Over time, Indian Muslims were admitted into the nobility but were denied high offices. - Dissatisfaction among them was evident, as seen in the support for Imaduddin Raihan against Balban. - Balban’s Precedent for Power Struggles - Balban himself had sidelined the sons of Nasiruddin Mahmud. - His example demonstrated that a successful general, with sufficient support from the nobility and the army, could seize the throne by ousting the heirs of an established dynasty. - The Khaljis (1290-1320) - Rise of the Khalji Dynasty - Led by Jalaluddin Khalji, a group of Khalji nobles overthrew the incompetent successors of Balban in 1290. - The Khaljis were of mixed Turkish-Afghan origin and did not exclude Turks from high offices but ended the Turkish monopoly. - Their rebellion was welcomed by the non-Turkish sections of the nobility. - Jalaluddin Khalji (1290-1296) - Ruled for six years and attempted to soften the harsh policies of Balban. - Advocated that the state should be based on the willing support of the governed. - Acknowledged that since most Indians were Hindus, the Delhi Sultanate could not be a purely Islamic state. - Practiced a policy of tolerance, avoiding harsh punishments. - His policies were viewed as weak and unsuitable for the times. - His rule ended when he was treacherously murdered by his nephew and son-in-law, Alauddin Khalji, in 1296. - Alauddin Khalji (1296-1316) – Ruthless Consolidation of Power - Came to power by murdering Jalaluddin Khalji after accumulating vast wealth from his invasion of Deogiri (in the Deccan). - Faced several rebellions, both from nobles and his own relations. - To suppress opposition, he adopted extreme measures: - Mass execution of defected nobles and confiscation of their properties. - Elimination of rebellious family members. - Massacre of Mongol converts who had settled in Delhi and rebelled after campaigning in Gujarat. - Harsh punishments extended even to wives and children of rebels, a practice continued by his successors. - Measures to Control the Nobility - Introduced strict regulations to prevent conspiracies: - Nobles were forbidden from holding banquets or forming marriage alliances without the Sultan’s approval. - Ban on wine and intoxicants to discourage gatherings. - Established a spy service to monitor nobles’ activities. - These methods successfully subjugated the nobles, ensuring no further rebellions during his lifetime. - However, his policies weakened the dynasty in the long run. - Decline of the Khaljis (1316-1320) - After Alauddin Khalji’s death in 1316, his trusted general Malik Kafur took control. - Malik Kafur: - Placed a minor son of Alauddin on the throne. - Imprisoned or blinded Alauddin’s other sons. - Was soon assassinated by palace guards. - Khusrau Khan, a Hindu convert, took the throne. - Accused by historians of violating Islam, but he was no worse than previous monarchs. - No opposition from Muslim nobles or the Delhi population. - Even Nizamuddin Auliya, the famous Sufi saint, accepted his rule. - Indicated that Muslims of Delhi were no longer swayed by racial considerations and accepted rulers based on ability rather than lineage. - In 1320, a group of officers led by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq revolted. - Khusrau was defeated and killed, marking the end of the Khalji dynasty and the rise of the Tughlaq dynasty. - The Tughlaqs (1320-1412) - Establishment of the Tughlaq Dynasty - Founded by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq in 1320. - The dynasty ruled Delhi until 1412. - Key Rulers of the Tughlaq Dynasty - Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq (1320-1324): Established the dynasty. - Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1324-1351): Expanded the empire extensively. - Firuz Shah Tughlaq (1351-1388): Ruled over a smaller but still vast empire. - Extent of the Tughlaq Empire - Under Ghiyasuddin and Muhammad bin Tughlaq, the empire encompassed almost the entire Indian subcontinent. - Firuz Shah Tughlaq’s empire was slightly smaller but comparable to that of Alauddin Khalji. - Disintegration of the Tughlaq Empire - After Firuz Shah’s death (1388), the Delhi Sultanate weakened and North India fragmented into several small states. - Though the Tughlaqs ruled until 1412, the invasion of Delhi by Timur in 1398 effectively marked the end of their empire. - Overview of the Tughlaq Era - The expansion of the Delhi Sultanate from Alauddin Khalji’s time. - The internal reforms introduced during the period. - The factors leading to the decline and disintegration of the Sultanate. - Expansion of the Delhi Sultanate - Delhi Sultanate’s Initial Control Over Rajasthan - Eastern Rajasthan, including Ajmer, had come under Delhi Sultanate’s control. - Ranthambhor, the most powerful Rajput state, had gone out of Delhi’s control since Balban’s reign. - Jalaluddin Khalji attempted to invade Ranthambhor but failed, leaving southern and western Rajasthan outside the Sultanate’s rule. - Expansion Under Alauddin Khalji (1290-1320) - Within 25 years, the Delhi Sultanate’s armies: - Brought Gujarat and Malwa under control. - Subdued most Rajput princes in Rajasthan. - Overran the Deccan and South India, reaching Madurai. - Attempted to bring the entire region under direct Delhi administration. - This phase of expansion began with Alauddin Khalji and reached its peak under Muhammad bin Tughlaq. - Political Conditions Favoring Expansion - Malwa, Gujarat, and Deogir were ruled by Rajput dynasties that emerged in the 12th-13th century. - These kingdoms remained largely unchanged in governance, despite Turkish rule in the Ganga Valley. - Inter-kingdom rivalries made the conquest of Malwa and Gujarat easier and pushed the invaders further south: - The Malwa and Deogir rulers opposed Turkish expansion into Gujarat. - Deogir was constantly at war with Warangal (Telangana) and Hoysala (Karnataka). - The Hoysalas were in conflict with their neighbors, the Pandyas (Tamil region/Mabar). - Importance of Malwa and Gujarat for the Delhi Sultanate - These regions were fertile and populous. - They controlled western seaports and trade routes connecting them to the Ganga Valley. - Gujarat’s overseas trade brought in gold and silver from abroad. - Delhi’s supply of war horses had been disrupted due to Mongol activity in Central and West Asia. - Gujarat’s ports were crucial for importing Arabian, Iraqi, and Turkish horses, which were vital for the Sultanate’s army. - Alauddin Khalji’s Conquest of Gujarat (1299) - In early 1299, an army under two of Alauddin’s generals marched towards Gujarat via Rajasthan. - On the way, they raided and captured Jaisalmer. - Gujarat ruler Rai Karan fled without resistance, leaving major cities vulnerable. - Anhilwara, the capital of Gujarat, along with many temples and buildings, was sacked. - The Somnath temple, rebuilt in the 12th century, was plundered. - Wealthy Muslim merchants of Cambay were not spared. - Malik Kafur, later a key figure in the South Indian invasions, was captured and taken to Alauddin Khalji. - In 1299 CE, during Alauddin’s conquest of Gujarat, his generals captured Malik Kafur, who was then a Hindu slave of a wealthy Khwaja (merchant) in Cambay. - Kafur was converted to Islam, brought to Delhi, and impressed Alauddin with his loyalty, intelligence, and military skills. - He quickly rose in rank, eventually becoming Alauddin’s trusted commander and playing a decisive role in the Deccan campaigns. - Aftermath of Gujarat’s Conquest - Gujarat came under Delhi Sultanate’s control. - The ease of conquest suggests: - Rai Karan was unpopular among his subjects. - A discontented minister of Rai Karan possibly invited Alauddin’s invasion. - The Gujarat army was weak, and the administration was inefficient. - Rai Karan fled to southern Gujarat with Ramachandra of Deogir’s help. - This later led to war between Delhi and the Yadavas of Deogir. - Alauddin Khalji’s Conquest of Rajasthan - The Conquest of Ranthambhor (1301) - After subjugating Gujarat, Alauddin Khalji focused on Rajasthan, beginning with Ranthambhor. - Ranthambhor was ruled by Hamirdeva, a Chauhan successor of Prithviraj Chauhan. - Hamirdeva had won victories against Raja Bhoj of Dhar and the Rana of Mewar, but these conquests ultimately led to his downfall. - During the return from the Gujarat campaign, some Mongol soldiers rebelled over the division of loot. - The rebellion was crushed, and a massacre of the Mongols followed. - Two Mongol nobles fled to Ranthambhor seeking asylum. - Alauddin ordered Hamirdeva to expel or kill the Mongol nobles, but Hamirdeva refused. - Confident in the strength of his fort, which had previously resisted Jalaluddin Khalji, Hamirdeva sent defiant replies to Alauddin. - Alauddin’s first army was repulsed, forcing him to lead the campaign himself. - Poet Amir Khusrau, who accompanied the campaign, gave a detailed account of the siege. - After three months, the Rajputs performed ‘jashar’ (jauhar): - Women self-immolated on a funeral pyre. - Rajput warriors and Mongols fought to the last. - This is the first Persian account of ‘jashar’. - Ranthambhor fell in 1301. - The Siege of Chittor (1303) - After Ranthambhor, Alauddin moved against Chittor, the second most powerful state in Rajasthan. - Ruler Ratan Singh had angered Alauddin by: - Refusing passage to the Sultanate’s army for the Gujarat invasion. - Controlling the Ajmer-Malwa route, a strategic corridor. - The Legend of Padmini: - Some later accounts claim Alauddin attacked Chittor due to his desire for Ratan Singh’s queen, Padmini. - However, modern historians dismiss this as a later myth, first recorded over a century later by Malik Muhammad Jaisi in his epic Padmavat. - The legend’s fantastical elements (Padmini being from Singhaldvipa and Ratan Singh crossing seven seas to marry her) make it historically doubtful. - The idea that Alauddin could demand to see another ruler’s wife—or that Ratan Singh would agree to such an insult—contradicts Rajput customs and Islamic court protocol. - The Siege and Fall of Chittor (1303): - Alauddin laid a close siege to the fort. - After months of resistance, the fort was stormed. - Jashar (jauhar) was performed: - Rajput warriors died fighting. - Padmini and other queens committed self-immolation. - Ratan Singh was captured alive and held prisoner for some time. - Alauddin assigned Chittor to his son, Khizr Khan, and placed a Muslim garrison there. - Later, the fort was handed back to Ratan Singh’s cousin. - Subjugation of Other Rajput States - Jalor, on the route to Gujarat, was also conquered. - Almost all major Rajput states submitted to Alauddin Khalji. - However, he did not establish direct rule over Rajasthan: - Rajput rulers continued to govern but had to: - Pay tribute regularly. - Follow Delhi’s orders. - Muslim garrisons were placed in strategic towns like Ajmer and Nagaur. - Rajasthan was thoroughly subdued, securing Alauddin’s dominance over North and Central India. - Expansion into the Deccan and South India - Conquest of Malwa (Before 1306-07) - Even before completing the conquest of Rajasthan, Alauddin Khalji had annexed Malwa. - According to Amir Khusrau, Malwa was so vast that even wise geographers could not determine its frontiers. - Unlike Rajasthan, Malwa was brought under direct administration, and a governor was appointed. - Alauddin Khalji’s Campaigns in the Deccan (1306-07) - Expedition Against Rai Karan (Baglana) - In 1306-07, Alauddin launched two campaigns. - The first was against Rai Karan, the expelled ruler of Gujarat, who had taken refuge in Baglana (on the Malwa border). - Rai Karan resisted but was ultimately defeated. - Campaign Against Rai Ramachandra (Deogir) - The second campaign targeted Rai Ramachandra of Deogir, an ally of Rai Karan. - Rai Ramachandra had earlier agreed to pay annual tribute to Delhi but had fallen into arrears. - Alauddin’s slave-general Malik Kafur led the expedition. - Rai Ramachandra surrendered, was taken to Delhi, and treated with honor: - Granted the title “Rai Rayan” (King of Kings). - Gifted one lakh tankas and a golden canopy (symbolizing rulership). - Given a district in Gujarat. - His daughter was married to Alauddin. - This alliance proved crucial for further Delhi Sultanate expansion into the Deccan. - Malik Kafur’s Southern Expeditions (1309-1311) - Between 1309-1311, Malik Kafur led two major campaigns into South India: - Warangal (1309, Telangana) - Warangal, ruled by Prataparudra, was attacked. - Prataparudra was forced to surrender treasures, elephants, and promise an annual tribute. - Dwar Samudra, Mabar & Madurai (1311, Karnataka & Tamil Nadu) - The second campaign targeted Dwar Samudra (Karnataka), Mabar, and Madurai (Tamil Nadu). - Key highlights: - Amir Khusrau, the court poet, glorified these campaigns in a book. - First time Muslim armies penetrated as far south as Madurai. - Brought back immense wealth but no new geographical knowledge. - Muslim merchants and soldiers were already present in the region. - Kafur plundered temples (e.g., Chidambaram) but failed to defeat the Tamil armies. - As a reward, Alauddin appointed Kafur as “mulk-nai” (vice-regent) of the empire. - Direct Administration & Rebellions (1315-1316) - After Alauddin’s death in 1316, his policies started shifting towards direct control of the south. - In 1315, Rai Ramachandra died, and his sons revolted. - Malik Kafur crushed the rebellion and took direct control. - However, some outlying areas declared independence, and some remained under Ramachandra’s descendants. - Mubarak Shah’s Campaigns (Post-Alauddin, 1316-1320) - Mubarak Shah, Alauddin’s successor, reconquered Deogir and installed a Muslim governor. - He also raided Warangal, forcing the ruler to: - Cede a district. - Pay an annual tribute of 40 gold bricks. - Khusrau Khan, a slave of Mubarak Shah, raided Mabar and sacked Masulipatnam. - Expansion Under Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1320-1328) - Conquest of Warangal (1320-1323) - Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq (1320) adopted an aggressive expansion policy. - His son, Muhammad bin Tughlaq, was posted in Deogir. - Warangal was attacked again (1320-23): - Initially, Muhammad bin Tughlaq suffered a setback. - A rumor of the Sultan’s death caused panic among Delhi forces. - He reorganized and attacked again, defeating the Rai. - Warangal was annexed. - Conquest of Mabar & Orissa (1323-1324) - Mabar was annexed, and Muhammad bin Tughlaq raided Orissa, bringing back rich plunder. - The following year, he subdued Bengal (independent since Balban’s death). - Conquest of Kampili (1328, Karnataka) - The last Hindu principality in the region, Kampili (South Karnataka), was annexed in 1328. - A rebel cousin of Muhammad bin Tughlaq had taken refuge there, providing an excuse for conquest. - Challenges of Overexpansion - By 1324, the Delhi Sultanate stretched as far south as Madurai and east to Orissa. - This rapid expansion created huge administrative & financial challenges. - The next section examines Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s attempts to manage these problems. - Chronology of Delhi sultanate -
Dynasty Period Notable Rulers Key Contributions
Mamluk (Slave) Dynasty 1206–1290 Qutb-ud-din Aibak (1206–1210), Aram Shah (1210–1211), Iltutmish (1211–1236), Razia Sultana (1236–1240), Nasir-ud-din Mahmud (1246–1266), Ghiyas-ud-din Balban (1266–1287), Muiz-ud-din Qaiqabad (1287–1290) Foundation of Delhi Sultanate, Qutb Minar, Iqta system, Centralized administration, Concept of divine kingship
Khalji Dynasty 1290–1320 Jalal-ud-din Khalji (1290–1296), Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316), Mubarak Shah Khalji (1316–1320) Market reforms, Military expansion, Mongol resistance, Control over Deccan
Tughlaq Dynasty 1320–1414 Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq (1320–1325), Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325–1351), Firuz Shah Tughlaq (1351–1388), Successors (1388–1414) Administrative experiments, Transfer of capital, Expansion, Irrigation projects, Delhi sacked by Timur (1398)
Sayyid Dynasty 1414–1451 Khizr Khan (1414–1421), Mubarak Shah (1421–1434), Muhammad Shah (1434–1445), Ala-ud-din Alam Shah (1445–1451) Weak rule, Dependency on nobles, Political instability
Lodi Dynasty 1451–1526 Bahlul Lodi (1451–1489), Sikandar Lodi (1489–1517), Ibrahim Lodi (1517–1526) Strengthening of Delhi, Agricultural reforms, Defeated by Babur in the First Battle of Panipat (1526)
- Succession related data of delhi sultanates -

- Internal Reforms and Experiments - Consolidation and Reforms under Alauddin Khalji - By the time Alauddin Khalji ascended the throne, the Delhi Sultanate was well consolidated in its central region, covering: - Upper Ganga Valley - Eastern Rajasthan - This stability enabled the sultans to undertake internal reforms and experiments aimed at: - Improving administration - Strengthening the army - Enhancing land revenue administration - Expanding and improving cultivation - Ensuring the welfare of citizens in rapidly growing towns - While some measures were successful and marked new developments, others failed due to: - Lack of experience - Poor planning - Opposition from vested interests - Despite the setbacks, these reforms reflected the growing stability of the Turkish state, which was no longer solely focused on warfare and maintaining law and order. - Market Control and Agrarian Policy of Alauddin - Market Control Measures - Alauddin’s market control measures were considered one of the great wonders of the world. - After returning from the Chittor campaign, he issued orders to fix prices of all commodities, including food grains, sugar, cooking oil, clothing, horses, cattle, and slaves. - To implement this, he established three regulated markets in Delhi: - One for food grains - One for costly cloth - One for horses, slaves, and cattle - Each market was overseen by a high officer (stahna), who maintained merchant registers and strictly controlled prices and shopkeepers. - Regulating food grain prices was essential because cheap food supply was necessary to maintain citizen and army support. - Reasons for Market Control - The Mongol invasions highlighted the need for a large army, which required reducing prices and lowering salaries to sustain expenses. - Land revenue in the Doab region (Meerut to Kara near Allahabad) was now paid directly to the state rather than being assigned as iqta. - The land revenue rate was raised to 50% of the produce, forcing peasants to sell grains at low prices to banjaras (grain traders) who then sold it at fixed prices in cities. - The banjaras were registered, and their families were held collectively responsible for violations to prevent hoarding. - The state set up warehouses to store food grains, releasing them during famines or shortages. - Alauddin strictly monitored the market and imposed harsh punishments on shopkeepers who charged higher prices or used false weights. - Fixed Prices and Economic Impact - Fixed prices of grains (as per Barani): - Wheat → 7½ jitals per man - A man (or maund, in Persian “mann”) was a fixed weight unit. - In Alauddin Khalji’s time it varied regionally, but roughly about 15–20 kg. - Barley → 4 jitals per man - Good quality rice → 5 jitals per man - Horse price regulation was crucial for maintaining a strong army: - First-grade horse → 100-120 tankas - Inferior pony (tata) → 10-25 tankas - Prices of cattle and slaves were strictly regulated, and detailed price lists exist in Barani’s records. - Luxury goods (cloth, perfumes, etc.) were also price-fixed, though this was likely done to stabilize overall prices or to please the nobility. - Large sums were given to Multani traders to bring fine cloth to Delhi, making it the largest cloth market. - Impact on Salaries and Army - The state’s direct control over land revenue allowed salaries to be paid in cash, a first in the Sultanate. - Cavalry soldiers’ salary: - 238 tankas per year (20 tankas per month) - Covered personal expenses, horse maintenance, and equipment - Even in Akbar’s time, when prices were higher, a Mughal cavalryman earned only 20 rupees a month—showing Alauddin’s salary was not low. - Religious and Trade Implications - Historian Barani claims the market policy was aimed at punishing Hindus, as most traders were Hindus engaged in profiteering. - However, trade with Central Asia was controlled by Muslims (Khurasanis, Multanis), who also benefited from price regulations—something Barani ignores. - It is unclear if price control applied only to Delhi or the entire empire, but since army garrisons were spread across towns, other cities likely benefited as well. - Agrarian Reforms of Alauddin - Land Revenue Administration - Alauddin was the first Sultan to insist on land revenue being assessed by measuring cultivated land in the Doab region. - This prevented landlords (pahuts and mugaddams) from shifting their tax burdens onto poorer peasants. - New policies for landlords: - They had to pay taxes on cattle and houses, like regular peasants. - Illegal cesses they had imposed on villagers were abolished. - Barani’s account: They became so impoverished that they could no longer ride caparisoned horses or chew betel leaves, and their wives had to work in Muslim households. - Administration and Corruption Control - Revenue collection was directly handled by state officials (amils) rather than landlords. - Officials were given sufficient salaries, but Alauddin imposed strict audits on their accounts. - Corrupt officials faced severe punishments, including beatings and imprisonment. - Barani’s exaggeration: Officials were so terrified that no one would marry their daughters to them! However, government service remained prestigious, and this claim seems unlikely. - Motives Behind Agrarian Reforms - Though Barani claims the policies targeted Hindus, they were mainly aimed at rural elites rather than common peasants. - The reforms were not socialistic; they were pragmatic measures taken to: - Counter Mongol threats - Strengthen state control over resources - Maintain a strong standing army - Barani states Alauddin regulated everything, from food grains to socks, from combs to chapatis, leading to harsh punishments and resentment among traders. - Despite strict measures, his policies did not cause major rebellions or mass migration of peasants. - Legacy of Agrarian and Market Reforms - Alauddin’s regulations ended after his death, but they had long-lasting effects: - Strengthened the Delhi Sultanate’s military - Successfully repelled Mongol invasions beyond the Indus - Provided a blueprint for later agrarian policies of Sher Shah Suri and Akbar - Muhammad Tughlaq’s Experiments and Policies - Introduction - Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1324-51) is remembered as one of the most remarkable rulers of his time. - He was deeply read in religion and philosophy and had an open and critical mind. - Engaged with Muslim mystics, Hindu yogis, and Jain saints like Jinaprabha Suri. - Orthodox theologians criticized him as a ‘rationalist.’ - He appointed officials based on merit, disregarding noble lineage. - However, his hasty and impatient nature led to many failures, earning him the title of an ‘ill-starred idealist.’ - Accession to the Throne - Succeeded his father, Sultan Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, under suspicious circumstances. - A hastily erected wooden pavilion collapsed during a reception, killing the Sultan. - Rumors spread that Muhammad Tughlaq had orchestrated his father’s death. - Major Experiments and Policies - Transfer of Capital to Daulatabad - Deogir (renamed Daulatabad) was an important military base for Turkish rule in the south. - The Sultan wanted better control over the region, which was prone to rebellion. - Many officials, nobles, and Sufi saints were forced to migrate to Daulatabad. - A road was built with rest houses to facilitate travel. - However, harsh weather and distance led to many deaths. - Discontent arose as people longed for Delhi, leading to abandonment of the plan. - Impact - Strengthened cultural ties between North and South India. - Many settlers remained in Daulatabad, leading to the spread of Indo-Islamic culture in the Deccan. - Introduction of Token Currency - Introduced bronze coins with the same value as silver tankas due to a silver shortage. - Inspired by Chinese (Qublai Khan) and Mongol (Ghazan Khan of Iran) experiments. - Traders and common people resisted accepting the new currency. - Widespread forgery devalued the coins. - Sultan was forced to withdraw the currency, exchanging silver for legitimate bronze coins. - Massive financial loss and administrative failure. - Military Campaigns and Expansionist Policies - Defense Against Mongols - Faced Mongol invasions under Tarmashrin in Punjab and Sindh. - Successfully repelled Mongols and extended power beyond the Indus. - The Khurasan Project - Recruited a large army to invade Khurasan and Iraq but later disbanded it. - Unclear objective, possibly to restore the Hindukush-Qandahar frontier. - The Qarachil Expedition - Military campaign in the Kumaon Hills (Himalayas). - Some historians suggest it was aimed at controlling horse trade from China (Sinkiang). - Expedition suffered a disaster—out of 10,000 soldiers, only 10 returned. - Resulted in Delhi Sultanate’s control over hill regions like Kangra. - Agrarian Reforms and Revenue Policies - Peasant Rebellion in the Doab - Muhammad Tughlaq sought to improve agriculture but over-assessed revenue. - Fixed state share at half of the produce, but arbitrarily determined the rate. - Prices were artificially fixed, worsening the crisis. - A six-year famine devastated the region. - Peasants fled, prompting harsh measures to force compliance. - Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi: Agricultural Development Scheme - Established a new department to promote better farming. - Divided the region into development blocks led by officials. - Provided loans for high-yield crops like wheat, sugarcane, grapes, and dates. - Scheme failed due to corruption and misuse of funds. - Loans remained unrecovered, but later Sultan Firuz Tughlaq wrote them off. - Despite failure, the policy influenced future rulers like Akbar. - Nobility and Administrative Policies - Changes in Nobility Structure - Included commoners from professions like barbers, cooks, weavers, and wine-makers in administration. - Many were Muslim converts, and some Hindus were also given positions. - Old noble families resented the rise of these new officials. - Inclusion of Foreigners in Nobility - Welcomed nobles from various ethnic backgrounds, leading to a diverse but divided nobility. - This fragmentation weakened central authority and fostered rebellion. - Conclusion: The Paradox of Muhammad Tughlaq’s Rule - His reign marked both the zenith and beginning of disintegration of the Delhi Sultanate. - Many of his policies had long-term impacts, despite short-term failures. - His hasty nature and harsh punishments led to administrative instability. - The Delhi Sultanate never fully recovered from the setbacks of his reign. - Decline and Disintegration of the Delhi Sultanate: Firuz and His Successors - Rebellions During Muhammad Tughlaq’s Reign - The latter half of Muhammad Tughlaq’s reign saw repeated rebellions across the empire. - Rebellions by ambitious nobles in the outlying areas were common, but most were suppressed with the help of the central army and loyal nobles. - Major revolts occurred in Bengal, Mabar (Tamil Nadu), Warangal, Kampili (Karnataka), West Bengal, Awadh, Gujarat, and Sindh. - Muhammad Tughlaq, distrustful of everyone, moved constantly to suppress uprisings, exhausting his armies. - The most serious revolts were in South India, where local governors initiated rebellions. - A plague in his army during a campaign in the South killed two-thirds of his forces, dealing him a severe blow. - After returning from the South, a rebellion by brothers Harihara and Bukka led to the formation of the Vijayanagara Empire in South India. -
