In the Deccan, foreign nobles established a principality near Daulatabad, which grew into the Bahmani Empire. - Bengal also became independent, though Muhammad Tughlaq managed to quell revolts in Awadh, Gujarat, and Sindh. - He died in Sindh and was succeeded by his cousin, Firuz Tughlaq. - Challenges and Policies of Firuz Tughlaq - Upon accession, Firuz sought to prevent the disintegration of the Delhi Sultanate. - He appeased the nobles, army, and theologians while only asserting control over manageable regions. - Unlike his predecessors, he made no attempt to reassert control over South India and the Deccan. - Military Campaigns - Led two unsuccessful campaigns into Bengal, resulting in its permanent loss. - Campaigned against Jajnagar (Orissa), looted temples but did not annex the region. - Attacked Kangra in the Punjab hills. - Longest campaigns involved rebellions in Gujarat and Thatta, where the army suffered greatly in the Rann of Kutch. - Administrative and Military Reforms - Firuz was not a strong military leader but ensured a peaceful and stable reign. - Introduced hereditary succession for nobles: - A noble’s son inherited his office and estate. - If no son existed, the son-in-law or slave took over. - Abolished the torture of nobles and officials during audits. - Extended hereditary succession to the army: - Soldiers could pass their positions to their sons or sons-in-law, or even slaves. - Payments were made through land assignments instead of cash. - Led to corruption, as soldiers often bribed clerks to pass off useless horses. - Relations with Theologians and Religious Policies - Presented himself as a devout Islamic ruler to win the support of theologians. - Banned practices deemed un-Islamic, such as Muslim women visiting saints’ graves. - Persecuted heretical Muslim sects and made jizya a separate tax, exempting only women, children, the disabled, and the indigent. - Ordered the public execution of a Brahman for preaching against the Sharia. - Despite his religious orthodoxy, he patronized music and had a fondness for wine. - Social and Economic Policies - Banned cruel punishments like amputation for theft. - Established hospitals for free treatment of the poor. - Provided dowries for poor girls. - However, these benefits mainly helped Muslims from good families who had fallen on hard times. - Created a Public Works Department to manage infrastructure projects: - Repaired and dug irrigation canals (e.g., a 200-km canal from Sutlej to Hansi). - Established new towns like Hissar-Firuzah (Haryana) and Firuzabad (Uttar Pradesh), many of which still exist. - Slave Policy - Ordered officials to capture young boys from conquered areas and send them as slaves to the Sultan. - Accumulated about 180,000 slaves: - Some were trained as artisans and placed in royal workshops (Karkhanas). - Others formed a special corps of soldiers directly dependent on the Sultan. - However, like earlier Turkish sultans, Firuz faced difficulties in maintaining loyalty among these slave soldiers. - Disintegration After Firuz’s Death (1388) - After Firuz’s death, administrative and political instability returned. - Power struggles emerged between: - The Sultan and the nobles. - Local zamindars and rajas, who began acting independently. - Firuzian slaves, who attempted to install their own ruler. - Sultan Muhammad, Firuz’s son, initially consolidated power with slave support. - However, he later suppressed the Firuzian slaves, imprisoning and scattering them. - His successor, Nasiruddin Mahmud (1394-1412), was unable to control rebellious nobles and defiant rajas. - Provincial governors became independent, confining the Sultan’s rule to a small area around Delhi. - A contemporary wit remarked: - “The dominion of the Lord of the Universe (title of the sultans of Delhi) extends from Delhi to Palam.” - Timur’s Invasion (1398) and Final Collapse - The weakness of the Delhi Sultanate invited Timur’s invasion in 1398. - Timur, a Turk claiming descent from Genghis Khan, had built a vast empire from Syria to the Indus. - His invasion of India was purely for plunder, targeting the wealth accumulated by Delhi’s sultans. - Timur’s army mercilessly sacked and plundered towns en route to Delhi. - Upon entering Delhi, his forces massacred Hindus, Muslims, women, and children alike. - The invasion drained India of enormous wealth, including gold, silver, and jewelry. - Timur also took skilled Indian artisans (masons, stone cutters, carpenters) to build monuments in Samarqand. - Impact of Timur’s Invasion - Though politically insignificant, the invasion marked: - The end of strong rule by the Delhi sultans. - The final decline of the Tughlaq dynasty, which lingered until 1412. - Long-Term Causes of Disintegration - The Delhi Sultanate’s decline was not due to a single ruler but a combination of factors: - Constant conflict between the monarch and nobles. - Struggles with local rulers and zamindars. - The pull of regional and geographical forces. - No ruler could fundamentally change society to overcome these persistent challenges. - The overextension of the empire under Ghiyasuddin and Muhammad Tughlaq set off a chain reaction of disintegration. - Firuz’s reforms—though stabilizing in the short term—weakened the central administration, leading to ultimate collapse. - Conclusion - The period from 1200 to 1400 brought significant transformations in Indian society: - Changes in the system of government. - Evolution of social and economic conditions. - Advancements in art and architecture. - These themes will be explored in the next chapter. - Government, and Economic and Social Life under the Delhi Sultanate - Introduction - The establishment and expansion of the Delhi Sultanate (1200–1400) brought significant changes to India: - Development of a highly centralized state under the Turks. - Expansion of territorial control, reaching as far south as Madurai. - Influence on the administrative systems of successor states and the later Mughal Empire. - The beginning of the 15th century marked the decline of the Delhi Sultanate: - Disintegration led to the rise of independent regional states. - Despite political fragmentation, the Sultanate’s administrative legacy endured. - The Sultan: Supreme Authority in the Sultanate - Symbolic Connection with the Caliph - Many Turkish sultans in India declared themselves as the “Lieutenant of the Faithful”, recognizing the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad. - However, this was a symbolic and moral recognition, not a legal subordination. - By doing so, the Delhi Sultans asserted their authority within the larger Islamic world. - Powers and Responsibilities of the Sultan - The Sultan was the most powerful figure in the Sultanate, holding supreme political, military, and legal authority. - His primary responsibilities included: - Administration – Ensuring the smooth governance of the state. - Military leadership – Serving as the commander-in-chief of the armed forces. - Law and justice – Appointing judges while also acting as the final court of appeal. - Direct appeals could be made to the Sultan against any unjust actions by his officials. - Justice as a key function: - Balban was known for stern and impartial justice, punishing even his relatives and top officials. - Muhammad Tughlaq extended this policy to the religious classes (ulama), who had previously been exempt from severe punishments. - Succession and the Struggle for the Throne - No clear law of succession existed among the Muslim rulers of India. - Islamic theory favored election, but in practice: - Any son of a ruler could claim the throne. - The concept of primogeniture (eldest son inheriting the throne) was not fully accepted by either Muslims or Hindus. - Some rulers nominated a preferred successor, not necessarily the eldest son. - Iltutmish even nominated his daughter (Razia Sultan) over his sons. - However, noble approval was necessary for any nomination to be accepted. - Military strength was the decisive factor in succession: - A successful military leader could usurp the throne. - Public opinion also played a role—for example, the Khaljis avoided entering Delhi immediately after overthrowing Balban’s successors, instead building a new city, Siri, to establish their rule. - Central Administration of the Delhi Sultanate - The Role of the Sultan and His Ministers - The Sultan was the supreme authority and was assisted by a council of ministers. - These ministers were appointed at the Sultan’s discretion and could be removed at any time. - The number, powers, and functions of the ministers varied over time. - A well-defined administrative system emerged by the late 13th century. - The Wazir: Chief Minister of the Sultanate - The wazir was the most important administrative official after the Sultan. - Early Period: - Initially, wazirs were primarily military leaders. - 14th Century Changes: - The wazir became an expert in revenue affairs and controlled both income and expenditure. - Muhammad Tughlaq focused heavily on revenue administration, appointing Khwaja Jahan as his respected wazir. - A separate Auditor General (for expenditure) and an Accountant General (for income) were introduced. - Wazirs under Firuz Tughlaq: - Khan-i-Jahan, a converted Tailang Brahman, was appointed as wazir and held office for 18 years—a period considered the peak of the wazir’s influence. - His son, Khan-i-Jahan II, succeeded him but lost power after trying to manipulate succession following Firuz’s death. - The position of the wazir weakened after this period but regained prominence under the Mughals. - The Military Administration (Diwan-i-Arz) - The Diwan-i-Arz was responsible for military affairs and was led by the Ariz-i-Mamalik. - Key Responsibilities: - Recruitment, equipping, and payment of the army. - Maintaining troop discipline and military organization. - The Sultan as Commander-in-Chief: - The Sultan himself commanded the army to prevent power struggles. - Notable Military Reforms: - Balban emphasized military discipline and had soldiers march long distances under the pretext of hunting. - Alauddin Khalji introduced: - Regular mustering of troops to prevent fraud. - Branding system (dagh) for horses to ensure quality. - Descriptive rolls of soldiers for better record-keeping. - Direct salary payments in cash, abolishing the previous system of land grants (jagirs) for soldiers. - Alauddin’s army (claimed to be 300,000 by Barani) was instrumental in defending against Mongol invasions and conquering the Deccan. - Military Composition and Structure - The standing army was stationed across the empire, with a strong force in the capital. - The military included: - Cavalry: Dominated by Turks and Afghans (considered the most prestigious). - Infantry: Included Hindus, continuing from the Ghaznavid period. - Elephants: Trained for warfare. - Sappers and Miners Corps: Cleared roads and removed obstacles during marches. - Other Key Administrative Departments - The Religious and Judicial Department (Diwan-i-Risalat) - Functions: - Managed religious affairs, pious foundations, and stipends for scholars and religious leaders. - Supervised by the Chief Sadr, often a leading gazi. - The Chief Gazi also headed the justice department. - Judicial System: - Qazis (judges) were appointed across the empire, particularly in regions with large Muslim populations. - Muslim law (Sharia) governed civil matters for Muslims. - Hindus followed their own personal laws, enforced by village panchayats and caste leaders. - Criminal law was based on regulations set by the Sultan. - The Communication & Correspondence Department (Diwan-i-Insha) - Handled state correspondence, including: - Communication between the Sultan and other rulers. - Correspondence with provincial and local officials. - Management of formal and confidential diplomatic exchanges. - Intelligence and Internal Security - The Sultan maintained a network of intelligence agents (barids) across the empire. - The Chief Barid was always a trusted noble of the ruler. - This system kept the Sultan informed of developments across the empire. - The Royal Household and State Affairs - The Royal Household Department - Managed by the Wakil-i-Dar, who was responsible for: - The Sultan’s personal comforts. - Overseeing the large royal harem. - Maintaining order and seating arrangements for nobles at royal receptions. - Managed a network of karkhanas (workshops) that: - Stored goods needed by the royal family. - Sometimes produced luxury items under royal supervision. - The Department of Public Works - Established by Firuz Tughlaq, it was responsible for: - Construction of canals for irrigation. - Building roads, mosques, and public buildings. - The Slave Department - Also introduced by Firuz Tughlaq to manage: - The employment of royal slaves. - Their work in state-run karkhanas and administrative offices. - Conclusion - The central administration of the Delhi Sultanate was highly structured, with clear divisions of responsibility. - The Sultan held absolute power, assisted by a strong bureaucracy led by the wazir, and supported by specialized departments for military, finance, justice, intelligence, and public works. - These institutions laid the foundation for later Mughal governance. - Local Administration of the Delhi Sultanate - Division of Territories - After their conquest, the Turks divided the country into administrative units called igtas. - These were granted to leading Turkish nobles, who were known as mugtis or walis. - Over time, these igtas evolved into provinces (subas). - During the reign of Muhammad Tughlaq, there were 24 provinces, extending as far as Mabar in the south. - Role of the Mugti (Provincial Governor) - Initially, mugtis had significant autonomy in their regions. - Their main responsibilities included: - Maintaining law and order. - Collecting land revenue on behalf of the government. - Paying salaries to soldiers from the revenue collected. - Retaining any surplus after expenses. - As the central government gained strength, it tightened control over the mugtis: - It started to assess the actual income of provinces. - Salaries of soldiers and mugtis were fixed in cash. - Mugtis were required to remit excess revenue to the central treasury. - Auditing of provincial accounts (done every few years) often involved: - Harsh measures, including torture and imprisonment of mugtis. - Firuz Tughlaq later relaxed these strict policies towards the end of the Sultanate period. - Hierarchical Structure of Local Administration - Administrative Divisions Below Provinces - Below the provinces, the empire was divided into: - Sarkars (Districts) - Parganas (Administrative Units) - Villages (basic unit of administration) - The Pargana Administration - Villages were grouped into parganas, which formed the core of local administration. - Ami (Administrator): Headed the pargana. - Important village officials included: - Zamindars (landowners) - Muqaddam (village headman) - Patwari (village accountant) - Village Administration - Villages retained their traditional self-governing structure under Turkish rule. - The Sultanate did not interfere in village affairs as long as land revenue was paid. - Villages were traditionally grouped into units of 100 to 84 households (chasrasi system). - No significant administrative changes were initially made at the village level. - Land revenue collection continued through local officials, aiding the smooth transition of power to the Turks. - Reforms and Peasant Resistance - Administrative changes began under Alauddin Khalji in the early 14th century. - He introduced stricter revenue policies to increase state control. - These measures led to tensions between the government and peasants, sometimes resulting in rebellions. - Conclusion - The local administration of the Delhi Sultanate was a multi-tiered system, with provinces, districts, and villages functioning under different levels of authority. - The mugtis initially had autonomy but were later brought under tighter central control. - The village administration remained largely unchanged, ensuring stability, but Alauddin Khalji’s revenue reforms led to conflicts. - Economic and Social Life under the Delhi Sultanate - Limited Historical Records - Information about the economic condition of people during the Delhi Sultanate is scarce. - Contemporary historians primarily focused on court events rather than the lives of ordinary people. - However, some sources mention commodity prices and agricultural products. - Despite limited historical records, accounts like those of Ibn Battutah provide valuable insights into agriculture, trade, and daily life during the Delhi Sultanate. - The economy was primarily agrarian, with village industries playing a crucial role in production and trade. - Ibn Battutah’s Observations - Ibn Battutah, a traveler from Tangier, North Africa, visited India in the 14th century. - He lived at the court of Muhammad Tughlaq for eight years and traveled widely across India. - His writings provide insights into: - Agricultural products (fruits, flowers, herbs, crops). - Condition of roads and trade routes. - Daily life of the people. - Agriculture and Crops - Agriculture was the backbone of the economy, with fertile soil allowing multiple harvests. - Key crops grown in different regions: - East and South: Rice, sugarcane (grown extensively). - North: Wheat, oilseeds. - Other major crops: - Rice: Sown three times a year. - Sesame: Used for oil production. - Indigo: Important for dyeing fabrics. - Cotton: Essential for the textile industry. - Village Industries and Economy - Agriculture supported small-scale village industries, including: - Oil pressing (from sesame and other seeds). - Jaggery (raw sugar) production. - Weaving and dyeing of cloth (linked to cotton and indigo cultivation). - These industries formed the economic backbone of villages, sustaining local economies. - Peasants and Rural Gentry under the Delhi Sultanate - The Peasant Majority - Peasants formed the overwhelming majority of the population. - They worked hard to sustain themselves but lived at a subsistence level. - Recurring famines and wars further worsened their hardships. - Prosperous Peasants and Rural Elites - Not all peasants lived in poverty; some were owner-cultivators with their own land. - These wealthier peasants were: - Original settlers of the village. - Dominant members of the village panchayat. - The village headmen (muqaddams) and smaller landlords (zaats): - Enjoyed a higher standard of living. - Held additional lands at concessional revenue rates. - Sometimes exploited ordinary peasants by forcing them to pay extra revenue. - Their prosperity was evident as they: - Rode costly Arabi and Iraqi horses. - Wore fine clothes. - Adopted upper-class lifestyles. - Alauddin Khalji’s Reforms - Alauddin Khalji took strict action against wealthy village elites: - Restricted their privileges. - Reduced their economic power. - However, after his death, these groups regained their dominance. - Hindu Rais and Autonomous Rajas - A distinct wealthy section included the Hindu rais (autonomous rajas). - Many retained their estates under Delhi Sultanate rule. - Evidence from Balban’s court suggests that: - Hindu rais frequently visited the sultan’s court. - They remained influential even in areas under direct Sultanate control. - Trade, Industry, and the Merchants - Growth of Trade and Urban Economy - The consolidation of the Delhi Sultanate, improved communications, and a sound currency system (silver tanka and copper dirham) led to the growth of trade. - Towns expanded, and urban life flourished. Ibn Battutah described Delhi as the largest city in the eastern Islamic world, with Daulatabad (Deogir) matching its size, reflecting strong trade between the north and south. - Other major trade centers: - Northwest – Lahore, Multan - East – Kara, Lakhnauti - West – Anhilwara (Patan), Cambay (Khambayat) - A historian describes the Sultanate as having a “flourishing urban economy,” implying large-scale commerce. - Industries and Handicrafts - Bengal and Gujarat towns were known for fine fabrics, with other cities also producing high-quality textiles. - Major industrial centers and products: - Cambay (Gujarat) – Textiles, gold, and silver work - Sonatgaon (Bengal) – Raw silk and fine cotton (later called muslin) - Other crafts: Leatherwork, metalwork, carpet weaving, woodwork (including furniture), and stone-cutting. - The Turks introduced new crafts such as paper-making, a technique originally discovered by the Chinese and spread via the Arab world. - Technological Advancements - Textile industry improvements: - Introduction of the spinning wheel, which improved efficiency. - Cotton cleaning was enhanced using the cotton carder’s bow (dunia). - Metallurgical advancements: - Use of iron stirrups. - Large-scale use of armor for cavalry. - Growth in metal crafts. - Water-lifting technology: - Improvement of the rakat (misnamed the Persian wheel) allowed deeper water extraction for irrigation. - Construction innovations: - Introduction of a superior mortar enabled the construction of grand buildings featuring arches and domes. - Foreign Trade and Commerce - Indian exports: - Textiles (high demand in Red Sea and Persian Gulf trade, later introduced to China). - Imports: - West Asia – Satin, glassware, horses - China – Raw silk, porcelain - Africa – Ivory - Southeast Asia – Spices - India had a favorable trade balance, bringing gold and silver into the country. - Merchant Communities - Overseas and coastal trade: - Arabs were dominant in Indian Ocean trade but did not displace Indian traders (Tamils, Kalingas, Gujaratis – both Hindu and Muslim). - Coastal and north Indian trade was largely controlled by Marwaris and Gujaratis (many were Jains). - Muslim Bohra merchants were also active. - Overland trade (Central & West Asia): - Controlled by Multanis (mostly Hindus, but also included Muslims like Khurasanis, Afghans, Iranians). - Many merchants had settled in Delhi. - Wealth of merchants: - The rich Gujarati and Marwari merchants, especially Jains, funded temple construction. - Cambay was home to wealthy merchants with grand stone houses, gardens, and tanks. - Hindu and Muslim merchants lived luxuriously, attended by sword-bearing pages. - Multani merchants were so wealthy that Delhi’s nobles often borrowed money from them for celebrations. - Transport, Communication, and Postal System - Travel was dangerous due to robbers and marauding tribes. However, royal roads were well maintained, with sarais for travelers. - Major roads built: - Peshawar to Sonargaon (built earlier). - Delhi to Daulatabad (built by Muhammad Tughlaq). - Postal system: - Relays of horses and runners ensured fast delivery. - Runners, posted at towers every few kilometers, rang bells to signal the next relay. - Efficiency examples: - Fresh fruits from Khurasan reached the Sultan quickly. - Ganga water was delivered to Muhammad Tughlaq in Daulatabad (40-day journey from Delhi). - Economic Growth and Prosperity - Improved communications and trade (both overland and by sea) accelerated economic activity. - The Turks introduced or popularized several crafts and techniques, strengthening industries. - The second half of the 14th century was marked by economic growth and relative affluence due to technological advancements and agricultural expansion. - The Sultan and the Nobles - The Sultan and his royal lifestyle - Palaces and Grandeur: - The Sultan and nobles lived luxuriously, comparable to the ruling elites of West and Central Asia. - Almost every Sultan built his own palace. - Balban had a magnificent court designed to instill awe. - Alauddin Khalji and successors continued this tradition. - Muhammad Tughlaq’s palace (as described by Ibn Battutah): - Visitors passed through three heavily guarded gates. - The ‘Court of Thousand Pillars’ was a vast hall supported by polished wooden pillars, lavishly decorated. - This hall served as the public court of the Sultan. - Royal Gifts and Honors: - Muhammad Tughlaq gifted two robes of honor (summer & winter) to each noble annually. - Estimated 200,000 robes were distributed each year. - Made of imported fabrics—velvet, damask, wool—with brocade and costly materials. - Nobles received lavish gifts on occasions like: - Sultan’s birthday - Navroz (Persian New Year) - Annual coronation day - Royal Treasury and Luxury Goods - Aarkhanas (Imperial Workshops): - Supplied silk, gold, silverware, and luxury goods. - Rare and exquisite items were sourced from across the empire. - Firuz Tughlaq ordered superintendents to buy finely crafted items at any price. - Extravagance was common: A single pair of shoes for the Sultan cost 70,000 tankas. - Gold, silver, and jewels adorned most royal items. - The royal treasury also provided luxuries for the Harem. - The Harem and Royal Household - Composition of the Harem: - Contained queens and numerous female slaves from various countries. - Included female relatives of the Sultan (mother, aunts, etc.). - Had a large staff of servants and guards. - Separate accommodations were provided for each member. - Nobles and Their Ostentatious Lifestyle - Control and Revival: - Alauddin Khalji suppressed the nobility, restricting their excesses. - Under the Tughlaqs, nobles regained their power and wealth. - Magnificent Palaces & Wealth: - Nobles imitated the Sultan’s extravagant lifestyle. - Lived in lavish palaces, wore costly apparel. - Surrounded by servants, slaves, and retainers. - Competed in hosting grand feasts and festivals. - Some nobles also patronized art and literature. - Salaries and Wealth of the Nobles - Under Muhammad Tughlaq: - Vizier’s (chief minister’s) income = As large as the province of Iraq. - Leading ministers: Earned 20,000–40,000 tankas/year. - Chief Sadr (religious head): Received 60,000 tankas/year. - Khan-i-Jahan (wazir of Firuz Tughlaq): Earned 15 lakh tankas annually. - Wealth Accumulation: - Bashir (Firuz’s Ariz-i-Mamalik) left 13 crore tankas at death. - Firuz confiscated most of it, distributing the rest to Bashir’s sons. - Generally, nobles’ wealth remained secure and was inherited by their heirs. - Economic Influence and Land Ownership - Investment in Land & Agriculture: - Many nobles purchased land and built gardens, orchards, and markets. - Nobles & Sultans improved fruit cultivation (especially melons and grapes). - Firuz Tughlaq planted 1,200 orchards near Delhi. - Decline of Nobility’s Power: - Breakup of the Delhi Sultanate (early 15th century) disrupted these trends. - Town Life: Slaves, Artisans, and Others - Composition of Town Population - Turkish ruling class favored urban life. - Many towns developed around military garrisons and later became cultural centers. - Towns had a diverse population, including: - Nobles - Government clerks & officials – Educated by ulama, shared similar views. - Shopkeepers & artisans – Engaged in trade and handicrafts. - Beggars & commoners – Some carried arms, causing law-and-order challenges. - Slavery and Domestic Servants - Origins & Trade of Slaves - Slavery existed in India, West Asia, and Europe. - Sources of slaves: - War captives – Most common method (practiced by Turks & Hindus). - Born in household, purchased, or inherited (as per Hindu Shastras). - Imported slaves from Africa (mainly Abyssinians). - Uses of Slaves - Domestic service and personal attendants. - Skilled labor (e.g., artisans, craftsmen). - Companionship. - Military service (e.g., Firuz Tughlaq employed 180,000 slaves). - Royal bodyguards and court duties. - Living Conditions of Slaves - Masters had to provide food & shelter. - Slaves could marry & own property. - Harsh treatment was common, but freeing slaves was considered meritorious (both among Hindus & Muslims). - Economic Conditions and Social Inequality - Food Prices & Cost of Living - Alauddin Khalji’s era (low prices): - Wheat – 7½ jitals per man (135 kg). - Barley – 4 jitals. - Rice – 5 jitals. - (48 jitals = 1 silver tanka). - Muhammad Tughlaq’s reign: - Prices rose sharply. - Firuz Tughlaq’s era: - Prices declined again (possibly due to expanded cultivation). - Wages & Standard of Living - Firuz Tughlaq’s period: - A family (man, wife, servant, 1-2 children) could live on 5 tankas/month. - Alauddin Khalji’s period: - Artisan wages – 2-3 jitals/day (14-20 tankas/month). - Household servants – Earned even less. - Under Akbar: - Unskilled laborer’s wages – 2-4 rupees/month. - Hard living conditions for artisans & workers. - Social Inequality & Urban Lifestyle - Nobles & wealthy merchants (Hindus & Muslims) led lavish lives. - Commoners faced hardships, but their lives were enriched by festivals & fairs. - Rural Hindu society had fewer inequalities than urban Muslim society. - Caste, Social Manners, and Customs - Structure of Hindu Society - No major changes in Hindu social structure. - Brahmans continued to hold high status but were criticized if found unworthy. - Smriti texts reaffirmed caste duties: - Brahmans could engage in agriculture, even in normal times. - Kshatriyas were the only caste allowed to wield weapons and protect society. - Shudras had limited rights: - Their highest duty was serving other castes. - Could work in any occupation, except liquor & meat trade. - Forbidden from studying & reciting the Vedas, but allowed to listen to Puranas. - Extreme caste restrictions: - Some texts forbade eating a Shudra’s food, living with them, sitting on the same cot, or even receiving religious instruction from a learned Shudra. - The harshest restrictions were imposed on Chandalas and ‘outcastes’. - Position of Women in Hindu Society - Early marriage for girls remained the norm. - Duties of a wife: - Complete service & devotion to her husband. - Marriage annulment was allowed in special cases (e.g., desertion, loathsome disease), but not universally accepted. - Widow remarriage was prohibited in the Kali Age, but mostly for upper castes. - Practice of Sati: - Some texts strongly approved it, while others set conditions. - Ibn Battuta reported that women burned themselves on their husband’s pyre with drum beating & official permission from the Sultan. - Women’s Property Rights - A widow had the right to inherit her husband’s property if it was not jointly owned. - She was not just a guardian of the property but had full disposal rights. - This marked a slight improvement in women’s property rights under Hindu law. - Rise of Purdah System - Purdah (seclusion of women) became widespread among upper-class Hindu women. - Origins & Influence: - Practiced in ancient Iran & Greece. - Arabs & Turks introduced it to India, influencing Hindu elites. - Fear of invasions led to increased female seclusion. - Social & Religious Impact: - Symbol of status among upper classes. - Found religious justifications. - Hindered women’s freedom, making them more dependent on men. - Social Divisions in Muslim Society - Muslims were divided into ethnic & racial groups: - Turks, Iranians, Afghans, Indian Muslims rarely intermarried. - Converts from lower Hindu castes faced discrimination. - Economic disparities were sharp, with some groups being wealthy nobles and others poor converts. - Hindu-Muslim Social Relations - Limited interaction between Hindu & Muslim upper classes: - Hindus restricted intermarriage & inter-dining with Muslims, applying Shudra-like rules to them. - Social & Administrative Cooperation: - Hindus and Muslims did not live in total isolation. - Hindus served in Muslim armies and as personal managers of nobles. - Local administration remained largely in Hindu hands. - Daily social & economic interactions were common despite caste restrictions. - Cultural Differences & Social Tensions: - Differences in customs, beliefs, and interests created tensions. - These differences slowed down mutual understanding and cultural assimilation. - Further developments in Hindu-Muslim relations will be discussed in a later section. - Nature of the State - Militaristic and Aristocratic Structure - The Turkish state in India was militaristic and aristocratic. - Turkish nobles initially monopolized high offices, excluding Tajiks, Afghans, and other non-Turkish groups. - Under the Tughlaqs, the nobility expanded, but noble birth remained crucial for high positions. - Muslims in towns had better chances for army enrollment and state jobs. - Hindus dominated trade and held positions in: - Rural aristocracy - Lower administrative offices - Their cooperation was essential for governance. - Power Struggles - A tacit power-sharing existed between: - Rural Hindu aristocracy - City-based Muslim administrators - Frequent conflicts arose over: - Power and land (rather than religious differences). - Control over surplus production from land. - Muslims also fought among themselves over power. - Islamic Character of the State - Formally, the Sultanate claimed to be Islamic. - Sultans emphasized the Muslim identity of the state by: - Following the Sharia as much as possible. - Preventing open violations of Islamic law. - Appointing Muslim theologians (ulama) to high offices. - Granting revenue-free lands to Muslim scholars. - Limits of Religious Authority - Sultans did not let theologians dictate state policies. - Example: - Under Iltutmish, a group of theologians demanded strict enforcement of Islamic law, forcing Hindus to convert or face death. - The wazir rejected this, stating that Muslims were too few to implement such policies. Zawabit (State Laws) - Since Sharia was not always practical, sultans framed their own state regulations (zawabit). - Example: - Alauddin Khalji openly stated that he framed laws based on state needs, not religious laws. - Historian Barani criticized the Delhi Sultanate as not truly Islamic but secular (Gehandart) in its considerations. - Status of Hindu Subjects - Hindus were given the status of zimmis (protected people). - In exchange for Muslim rule, they paid a tax called jizyah. - Jizyah Taxation - Purpose: - A tax in lieu of military service. - Levied on a graduated scale based on means. - Exemptions: - Women, children, the poor, and Brahmins (initially). - Collection: - Originally collected along with land revenue (as most cultivators were Hindus). - Firuz Tughlaq later made it a separate tax and imposed it on Brahmins. - Misuse: - Some theologians harassed Hindus using jizyah collection. - However, jizyah alone was not a tool for forced conversion. - Privileged Classes and Social Hierarchy - Medieval states were based on privilege, not equality. - Before the Turks: - Rajputs & Brahmins were privileged. - Under the Sultanate: - Turks replaced Rajputs in privileged status. - Later, the privileged group included: - Turks, Iranians, Afghans, and some Indian Muslims. - Muslim theologians also held special privileges. - For the majority of Hindus, these political shifts had little impact on daily life. - Conclusion - The Sultanate was militaristic and aristocratic, dominated by a narrow clique of military leaders under the Sultan’s authority. - While claiming to be Islamic, it was pragmatic and often secular in governance. - Religious Freedom Under the Sultanate - Early Conquests and Treatment of Temples - During the early phase of conquest, many cities were sacked, and temples were targeted. - Reasons for targeting temples: - Justification of conquest. - Seizing treasures believed to be stored in them. - Hindu temples were converted into mosques. - Example: Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque near Qutub Minar, Delhi. - Originally a Vishnu temple. - Inner sanctum (with deity) was demolished. - Arches with Quranic verses were added. - Temple pillars were reused to build a cloister. - Similar incidents occurred in Ajmer and other places. - Once the Turks were settled, they began constructing new mosques rather than converting temples. - Legal and Policy Aspects of Religious Freedom - Muslim law (Sharia) governed the policy towards Hindu and Jain places of worship. - Restrictions on non-Muslim places of worship: - New temples were not allowed in areas where Islam was practiced. - Existing temples could be repaired (“since buildings do not last forever”). - No restrictions in villages (where Islam was not practiced). - Private temples inside homes were permitted. - Exceptions during wartime: - Enemies of Islam (including their deities) were to be fought and destroyed. - Hindu Worship and Tolerance in Peacetime - During peace, Hindus practiced their religion openly and publicly, even in Muslim-ruled areas. - Example: - Jalaluddin Khalji observed that: - In Delhi and provincial centers, Hindus publicly worshipped idols and preached Hindu texts. - Hindus celebrated processions with singing, dancing, and drumbeats outside the royal palace. - He admitted feeling “helpless” to stop it. - Limitations and Occasional Religious Persecution - Some Sultans and orthodox theologians pressured rulers to enforce stricter religious policies. - Occasional instances of forced conversions: - Prisoners of war were sometimes converted. - Criminals could escape punishment by accepting Islam. - Firuz Tughlaq executed a Brahmin for allegedly abusing the Prophet of Islam. - Despite such instances, the overall policy remained one of “toleration within limits”, with occasional lapses. - Conversion to Islam: Causes and Patterns - Conversions were not primarily due to force. - If Islam had spread by the sword, the Delhi region’s Hindu population would have been the first to convert, which was not the case. - The Hindu faith proved too strong to be destroyed by force. - Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya noted that some Hindus believed Islam to be true but did not convert. - Barani described Hindus as discarding Islam from their hearts “like a hair from kneaded flour.” - Reasons for Conversion - Political and economic benefits: - Conversion often brought state patronage and career opportunities. - Social mobility: - Some converted to improve social status. - Rulers or tribal chiefs converted first, followed by their followers. - Agricultural expansion: - In Punjab, Kashmir, and East Bengal, tribal communities converted when they became cultivators. - Occupational influence: - Many artisans in towns converted, including: - Weavers - Ironworkers - Paper-makers - These groups depended on Turkish patronage. - Role of Sufi Saints: - Sufis generally did not force conversions. - They welcomed both Hindus and Muslims to their discourses. - Their spiritual reputation created a receptive environment for Islam. - However, there is no evidence that lower-caste Hindus converted in large numbers due to caste discrimination. - Influx of Foreign Muslims and Demographic Impact - The Mongol invasion of West Asia led to the migration of many prominent Muslim families to India. - A steady influx of Afghans into India took place: - Many joined Turkish armies. - Others engaged in trade. - Under the Lodi rule (15th century), another large wave of Afghans arrived. - Despite this, Muslims remained a minority in India, influencing Hindu-Muslim relations and cultural attitudes. - Conclusion - The Delhi Sultanate followed a policy of limited religious tolerance, allowing Hindus to practice their faith, but with restrictions. - Conversions to Islam were driven by practical and social factors rather than force. - Despite foreign Muslim migrations, Hindus remained the majority, shaping the nature of Hindu-Muslim relations. - The Age of Vijayanagara and the Bahmanids, and the Coming of the Portuguese (Circa 1350-1565) - The Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdoms: Stability and Transformation - Dominance in Southern India - The Vijayanagara and Bahmani kingdoms ruled south of the Vindhyas for over 200 years. - They contributed significantly to: - Urban development: Built magnificent capitals and cities. - Architecture and culture: Constructed splendid buildings and promoted arts and literature. - Administration and economy: Ensured law and order, encouraged commerce and handicrafts. - During this period, while northern India faced political disintegration, the Deccan and southern India remained stable under their rule. - Decline of the Southern Kingdoms - Stability in the south ended with: - The disintegration of the Bahmani empire (late 15th century). - The fall of Vijayanagara after its defeat in the Battle of Bannihatti (1565). - Major Transformations in Indian History - Two significant events reshaped Indian history during this period: (a) Arrival of the Portuguese - The Portuguese arrived in southern India and sought to dominate the Indian seas. - This marked the beginning of European involvement in India. (b) Rise of the Mughals in Northern India - The advent of the Mughals initiated a new period of political integration in northern India. - Impact of These Developments - The arrival of the Portuguese led to a long era of conflict between: - Land-based Asian powers. - European naval powers dominating the seas. - The Vijayanagara Empire: Its Foundation and Conflict with the Bahmani Kingdom - Foundation of the Vijayanagara Kingdom - Founded by Harihara and Bukka, members of a family of five brothers. - Initially feudatories of the Kakatiyas of Warangal, later became ministers in Kampili (modern Karnataka). - When Kampili was overrun by Muhammad Tughlaq for sheltering a Muslim rebel, Harihara and Bukka were: - Imprisoned and converted to Islam. - Appointed to deal with rebellions in the region. - The Muslim governor of Madurai had already declared independence, while the rulers of Mysore and Warangal were asserting their autonomy. - Return to Hinduism: - On the advice of their guru Vidyaranya, they abandoned their new faith and founded Vijayanagara. - Some modern scholars dispute their conversion to Islam, considering them Karnataka nayaks rebelling against Turkish rule. - Harihara’s Coronation: - Took place in 1336. - Faced initial conflicts with the Hoysala ruler of Mysore and the Sultan of Madurai. - Expansion Under Harihara and Bukka - The Hoysala kingdom dissolved, allowing Harihara and Bukka to expand. - By 1346, the entire Hoysala kingdom came under Vijayanagara rule. - The administration was initially a cooperative commonwealth, with brothers and relatives managing newly conquered areas. - Bukka succeeded Harihara in 1356 and ruled until 1377. - Conflicts with the Sultanate of Madurai and the Bahmani Kingdom - Struggle Against the Sultanate of Madurai (1336-1377) - The Vijayanagara Empire clashed with the Sultan of Madurai, who: - Defeated and executed the Hoysala ruler. - Was eventually overthrown by Vijayanagara in 1377. - By this time, Vijayanagara ruled all of South India up to Rameshwaram, including Tamil Nadu and Kerala. - Conflict with the Bahmani Kingdom - The Bahmani Kingdom was founded in 1347 by Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah, also known as Hasan Gangu. - The Bahmani rulers and Vijayanagara clashed over three key regions: 1. Tungabhadra Doab (between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers). 2. Krishna-Godavari Delta (fertile region controlling foreign trade). 3. Marathwada and the Konkan (included Goa, an important port for horse imports from Iran and Iraq). - Military Conflicts Between Vijayanagara and Bahmani - The wars between the two kingdoms resulted in widespread devastation: - Towns and villages were burned and plundered. - Men, women, and children were captured and sold into slavery. - Brutal massacres were common. - 1367: - Bukka of Vijayanagara attacked the Mudkal fortress in the Tungabhadra doab, slaughtering its entire garrison except one man. - The Bahmani Sultan, enraged, vowed to slaughter 100,000 Hindus in revenge. - The Bahmani forces crossed the Tungabhadra River and defeated Vijayanagara. - Use of artillery was recorded for the first time in this battle in deccan. - The war ended in a treaty, restoring the doab to joint control and agreeing to humane treatment in future wars. - Expansion Under Harihara II (1377-1404) - After securing South India, Vijayanagara expanded towards the eastern seacoast. - Major rivals in the east: - Reddis in the Krishna-Godavari delta. - Rulers of Warangal. - Bahmani Sultans and Orissa. - Warangal and the Bahmanis formed an alliance, preventing Vijayanagara from gaining control of the Tungabhadra doab. - Harihara II’s Achievements: - Captured Belgaum and Goa from the Bahmanis. - Sent an expedition to Sri Lanka. - Reign of Deva Raya I (1404-1422) - Renewed war over the Tungabhadra doab with Firuz Shah Bahmani. - Deva Raya I’s Defeat: - Forced to pay 10 lakh gold coins, pearls, and elephants. - Married his daughter to the Bahmani Sultan, giving Bankapur as dowry. - Infrastructure Development: - Built a dam across the Tungabhadra for irrigation. - Constructed another dam on the Haridra River. - Rise of Deva Raya II (1425-1446) - Considered the greatest ruler of the Vijayanagara dynasty. - Military Reforms: - Realized the Bahmani superiority in cavalry and archery. - Enlisted 2,000 Muslim cavalrymen and ordered his Hindu soldiers to learn archery from them. - Increased the army to 80,000 cavalry, 200,000 infantry, and 60,000 archers. - Campaigns Against the Bahmanis (1443): - Attempted to reclaim Mudkal and Bankapur. - Three major battles were fought, but borders remained unchanged. - Foreign Relations: - Nuniz (Portuguese writer) claims Quilon, Sri Lanka, Pulicat, Pegu, and Tenasserim paid tribute to Vijayanagara. - Sri Lanka was invaded multiple times. - Vijayanagara as a Prosperous Empire - Nicolo Conti (Italian Traveler, 1420) - Described Vijayanagara as a massive and powerful city: - 90,000 men fit for war. - City walls stretched 60 miles. - Abdur Razzaq (Persian Traveler, 1440s) - Praised the empire’s wealth: - Had 300 ports comparable to Calicut. - The army numbered 1.1 million. - The city had seven citadels and magnificent markets. - Muslim quarters were provided in the city. - Ferishta (Historian) - Compared Vijayanagara’s power and wealth to the Bahmani kingdom: - Vijayanagara had greater economic strength but relied on superior military tactics. - Wealth and Trade - Gold and bullion were hoarded by the Vijayanagara rulers. - This stockpiling of wealth sometimes invited foreign invasions. - Conclusion - The Vijayanagara Empire emerged as South India’s most dominant power in the 15th century. - Its rulers balanced warfare and economic prosperity, while maintaining diplomatic ties with regional and foreign powers. - The constant struggle with the Bahmani kingdom shaped the political and military landscape of the Deccan region. - The Bahmani Kingdom—Its Expansion and Disintegration - Reign of Firuz Shah Bahmani (1397-1422) - Scholarship & Cultural Patronage: - Well-versed in religious sciences (Quranic commentaries, jurisprudence) and natural sciences (botany, geometry, logic). - Skilled calligrapher and poet, composed extempore verses. - Multilingual: Fluent in Persian, Arabic, Turkish, Telugu, Kannada, and Marathi. - Encouraged migration of scholars from Delhi, Iran, and Iraq to the Deccan. - Respected all religions, read the Old and New Testaments. - Ferishta describes him as an orthodox (strictly following established rules) Muslim, though fond of wine and music. - Administrative Reforms: - Inducted Hindus into administration on a large scale. - Deccani Brahmins became dominant, especially in revenue administration. - Balanced the influence of foreign nobles. - Economic & Scientific Advancements: - Encouraged astronomy, built an observatory near Daulatabad. - Developed major ports—Chaul and Dabhol—to boost maritime trade. - Ports attracted ships from the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, bringing luxury goods. - Military Campaigns: - Expansion towards Berar: - Defeated Gond Raja Narsing Rai of Kherla. - Received 40 elephants, 5 maunds of gold, and 50 maunds of silver as tribute. - Married the Rai’s daughter, later reinstated Narsing Rai as an Amir. - Conflict with Vijayanagara: - Married Deva Raya I’s daughter. - Continued struggle for Krishna-Godavari basin. - 1419: Defeated by Deva Raya II, weakening his position. - Forced to abdicate in favor of his brother, Ahmad Shah I. - Reign of Ahmad Shah I (1422-1436) - Religious Influence: - Known as a saint (wali) due to association with Sufi saint Gesu Daraz. - Military Conquests: - Warangal Campaign: - Aimed to punish Warangal ruler for aiding Vijayanagara. - Invaded Warangal, defeated and killed the ruler. - Annexed most of its territories. - Capital Shift: - Moved capital from Gulbarga to Bidar to consolidate newly acquired regions. - Further Expansion: - Turned attention towards Malwa, Gondwana, and the Konkan. - Mahmud Gawan and the Expansion of the Bahmani Kingdom - Early Life and Rise to Power - Iranian by birth; originally a trader. - Introduced to the Sultan, became a favorite, and received the title Malik-ud-Tujar. - Rose to the position of Prime Minister (Peshwa) and dominated state affairs for nearly 20 years. - Military Campaigns and Expansion - Eastern Expansion: - Led a deep raid into Vijayanagara territories, reaching Kanchi. - Overran the western coastal regions, including Dabhol and Goa. - Loss of Goa and Dabhol was a severe blow to Vijayanagara, boosting Bahmani overseas trade with Iran and Iraq. - Northern Frontiers: - Malwa (ruled by the Khalji dynasty) and Bahmani sultans vied for control over Gondwana, Berar, and the Konkan. - Bahmani sultans sought help from Gujarat to counter Malwa’s ambitions. - After a prolonged struggle, it was agreed that Kherla would go to Malwa and Berar to Bahmani. - Despite this, Malwa continued attempting to seize Berar, leading to further battles. - Interconnected Conflicts: - Struggles in North and South India were interconnected. - Western India: Malwa and Gujarat were drawn into Deccan affairs. - Eastern India: Orissa engaged in conflicts with Bengal and sought control over the Coromandel coast. - Orissa’s expansion southward weakened Vijayanagara further, especially after Deva Raya I’s death. - Administrative and Economic Reforms - Division of the Kingdom: - The Bahmani kingdom was reorganized into eight provinces (tarafs). - Each taraf was governed by a Tarafdar. - Salary and Military Administration: - Salaries and obligations of nobles were fixed. - Example: A noble maintaining 500 horses received 1,00,000 Awns per year (paid in cash or through jagir). - Those receiving a jagir were allowed expenses for revenue collection. - Revenue System: - Khalsa land was set aside in each province for the Sultan’s expenses. - Land measurement system was introduced to determine the cultivator’s dues to the state. - Patronage of Art and Education - Built a grand madrasa (college) in Bidar. - The building was three stories high, decorated with colored tiles, and accommodated 1,000 teachers and students. - Provided free clothing and food to students. - Attracted renowned scholars from Iran and Iraq. - Internal Struggles and Execution - Noble Rivalries: - The Bahmani nobility was divided into: - Deccanis (long-established local nobles). - Afranjis/Gharibs (newcomers, including Persians like Mahmud Gawan). - Mahmud Gawan faced opposition from Deccani nobles despite his conciliatory approach. - Downfall: - His enemies poisoned the Sultan’s mind against him. - Wrongfully accused, executed in 1482 at the age of 70. - Consequences: - Internal noble rivalries worsened. - Provincial governors became independent, leading to the fragmentation of the Bahmani kingdom into: - Golconda - Bijapur - Ahmadnagar - Berar - Bidar - Among them, Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, and Golconda played significant roles in Deccan politics until their eventual absorption into the Mughal Empire in the 17th century. - Cultural Significance of the Bahmani Kingdom - Acted as a cultural bridge between North and South India. - The unique Deccani culture that developed had distinct features, different from North India. - The successor states of the Bahmani kingdom continued these cultural traditions, influencing even the Mughal culture. - Climax of the Vijayanagara Empire and Its Disintegration - Internal Struggles After Deva Raya II (1446) - The death of Deva Raya II led to confusion and civil wars due to the absence of primogeniture. - Feudatories declared independence, and ministers became powerful, imposing heavy taxes. - The authority of the Raya shrank to Karnataka and parts of western Andhra. - The throne was usurped by the minister Saluva, ending the previous dynasty. - Saluva restored internal order and founded the Saluva dynasty, but it soon collapsed. - Eventually, the Tuluva dynasty was established by Krishna Deva Raya. - The Reign of Krishna Deva Raya (1509-1530) - Political and Military Challenges - Faced threats from: - Successor states of the Bahmani kingdom - The state of Orissa, which had seized Vijayanagara territories - The Portuguese, who were expanding their influence - The Portuguese tried to win Krishna Deva’s support by offering: - Assistance in recovering Goa from Bijapur - A monopoly in the supply of horses - Military Campaigns and Expansion - War with Orissa (Lasted 7 years) → Vijayanagara regained territories up to the Krishna River. - Conflict over the Tungabhadra Doab → Led to an alliance between Bijapur and Orissa against Vijayanagara. - 1520: Defeated Bijapur in the Battle of Raichur - Overran Raichur and Mudkal. - The Bijapur ruler fled across the Krishna River. - Vijayanagara armies reached Belgaum, occupied Bijapur, and sacked Gulbarga. - Vijayanagara emerged as the strongest military power in South India. - However, Krishna Deva paid little attention to naval power, ignoring the growing Portuguese influence over commerce. - Administration and Reforms - Attempted centralized administration by ousting the Nayaks from the Tungabhadra Doab and bringing it under direct rule. - Strengthened governance and law enforcement. - Cultural and Literary Contributions - A great builder → Constructed a new town near Vijayanagara and an enormous irrigation tank. - Scholar in Telugu and Sanskrit → Wrote: - A Telugu work on polity - A Sanskrit drama - Patron of Literature → Supported Telugu, Kannada, and Tamil poets. - Foreign travelers like Barbosa, Paes, and Nuniz praised his administration and the prosperity of Vijayanagara. - Religious Tolerance and Social Policies - Vijayanagara rulers were great patrons of Hinduism → Built temples, schools, and maths. - Temples were expanded with pillared halls, pavilions, and new structures. - Despite being a Hindu ruler, Krishna Deva allowed religious freedom. - Barbosa wrote: - “The king allows such freedom that every man may come and go and live according to his own creed, without suffering any annoyance, and without enquiry whether he is a Christian, Jew, Moor, or heathen.” - Justice and equity prevailed in his empire. - Decline After Krishna Deva Raya (1530-1565) - After Krishna Deva’s death, a succession struggle broke out since his sons were minors. - 1543: Sadashiva Raya ascended the throne (ruled until 1567) but was a puppet ruler. - Real power was held by a triumvirate, led by Rama Raja. - Wars and Conflicts Under Rama Raja - Diplomatic Manipulation → Played off the Muslim kingdoms (Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar) against each other. - Treaty with the Portuguese → Stopped supplying horses to Bijapur. - Series of Wars: - Defeated Bijapur and humiliated Golconda and Ahmadnagar. - However, Rama Raja lacked long-term strategy and merely maintained a balance of power. - The Battle of Talikota (1565) - The Muslim kingdoms (Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar) united against Vijayanagara. - Battle of Bannihatti (Talikota) → 1565 - Rama Raja was captured and executed. - 100,000 Hindus were slain. - Vijayanagara was thoroughly looted and destroyed. - The Final Decline of Vijayanagara - The Battle of Talikota marked the end of Vijayanagara’s golden age. - The kingdom survived for another 100 years but kept shrinking. - The Raya no longer played a major role in South Indian politics. - State and Economy under Vijayanagara - Kingship and Administration - The Vijayanagara rulers upheld an elevated concept of kingship. Krishna Deva Raya, in his book on polity, advised the king: - “With great care and according to your power, you should attend to the work of protecting (the good) and punishing (the wicked) without neglecting anything that you see or hear.” - He also emphasized levying taxes moderately. - The king was assisted by a council of ministers, consisting of great nobles. - The empire was administratively divided into: - Rafyes/Mandalam (Provinces) - Nadu (Districts) - Shale (Sub-districts) - Granza (Villages) - Provincial Governance and Nayak System - The tradition of village self-government, strong under the Cholas, weakened due to the rise of hereditary Nayakships. - Initially, provincial governors were royal princes, but later, nobles and vassal rulers were also appointed. - The governors: - Held independent courts - Appointed their own officers - Maintained their own armies - Issued small-denomination coins - Had no fixed tenure—ruled as long as they were capable - Could impose new taxes or remit old ones - Paid a fixed contribution of men and money to the central government - Some territories were controlled by subordinate rulers, who had been defeated but reinstated. - In centrally governed regions, Ameram (fixed revenue land grants) were given to military chiefs known as Palegars/Nayaks. - These Nayaks: - Maintained a fixed number of soldiers, horses, and elephants - Paid a sum to the central treasury - Grew powerful, sometimes resisting central control - This decentralization contributed to Vijayanagara’s defeat in the Battle of Bannihatti (1565) and eventual disintegration. - Some Nayaks, like those of Tanjore and Madurai, later declared independence. - Economic Conditions - Historians disagree on the condition of peasants, as foreign travellers had little knowledge of village life. - General observations: - Peasants: Lived in thatched houses with small doors, generally barefooted, and wore minimal clothing above the waist. - Upper Classes: Wore silk turbans and sometimes shoes but remained uncovered above the waist. - Ornaments: Worn by all classes, including earrings, necklaces, and armlets. - Taxation and Land Revenue - Land revenue rates varied based on crop type, soil, and irrigation method. - As per an inscription: - Winter crops (Aruvai rice): 1/3rd of the produce - Sesame, ragi, horse gram, etc.: 1/4th of the produce - Millet & dry land crops: 1/6th of the produce - Additional taxes included: - Property tax - Sales tax on agricultural produce - Professional tax - Military contributions (in times of distress) - Marriage tax - Nikitin (a 16th-century traveler) observed: - “The land is overstocked with people, but those in the country are very miserable, while the nobles are extremely affluent and delight in luxury.” - Urban Growth and Trade - Urbanization expanded significantly under Vijayanagara. - Many towns developed around temples, which played a crucial economic role. - Temples: - Needed foodstuffs and commodities for prasadam, priests, and devotees - Accumulated wealth and actively participated in both internal and overseas trade - Historians view the Vijayanagara period as a transitional phase from the old to a more organized economic structure. - The Advent of the Portuguese - Arrival of Vasco da Gama (1498) - Vasco da Gama landed at Calicut in 1498. - He was guided by Gujarati pilots from the African coast. - His arrival marked the beginning of European control over the oceans. - Impact: - Indian trade and traders suffered setbacks. - Eventually, European colonial rule expanded over India and neighboring countries. - However, modern historians (both Western and Indian) question the extent of Portuguese dominance. - Reasons for Portuguese Arrival - The 15th-century European economy was growing rapidly due to: - Expansion of agriculture (draining marshes, deforestation, better ploughs, scientific crop rotation). - Increased cattle production and meat supply. - Rise of towns and trade (internal and external). - High demand for Oriental goods (silk, spices, drugs) since Roman times. - Spices were especially important for preserving meat during winter. - Ottoman Expansion and Trade Monopoly - Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople (1453), Syria, and Egypt, controlling major trade routes. - Turkish monopoly on pepper hurt European traders. - Expansion of Turkish navy alarmed European nations. - Venice and Genoa, major traders, were too weak to resist Turkish control. - Spain and Portugal, supported by North Europeans and Genoese merchants, took the lead in finding a direct sea route to India. - Portuguese Maritime Expansion - Prince Henry the Navigator (1418 onwards): - Sent annual expeditions to explore Africa’s western coast. - Objectives: - Oust Arabs and Venetian rivals from Eastern trade. - Convert “heathens” in Africa and Asia to Christianity. - The Pope granted Portugal perpetual rights over any newly discovered lands in Africa and India. - Key Discoveries: - Bartholomew Diaz (1488) rounded the Cape of Good Hope, opening the sea route to India. - Technological Advancements: - Mariner’s compass & astrolabe enabled long voyages. - Gunpowder, printing, and metallurgy helped European naval supremacy. - Portuguese Trade Monopoly in India - Vasco da Gama’s return to Portugal: - Goods he brought were valued at 60 times the cost of the expedition. - However, direct trade between India and Europe remained slow. - Portuguese government imposed a monopoly, excluding: - Other European nations - Asian traders - Even private Portuguese merchants - Portuguese Naval Supremacy (1509) - The Sultan of Egypt, alarmed by Portuguese expansion, sent a fleet. - This fleet, supported by Gujarat’s ruler, was initially successful. - Portuguese, however, defeated them in 1509, making their navy supreme in the Indian Ocean. - This victory allowed Portuguese expansion into the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea. - Governorship of Albuquerque - Alfonso de Albuquerque (1510), new Portuguese governor, followed a fort-based expansion policy: - Established strategic forts in Asia and Africa. - Believed forts were essential for trade and political dominance. - Key Conquests: - Goa (1510): Captured from Bijapur. - Became the Portuguese commercial and political center in the East. - Allowed the Portuguese to dominate Gujarat’s seaports. - Colombo (Sri Lanka), Achin (Sumatra), Malacca (Malay Peninsula), and Socotra (Red Sea): - Strengthened Portuguese control over trade routes. - Failed attempts: - Could not capture Aden but forced Ormuz’s ruler (Persian Gulf) to allow a Portuguese fort. - Challenges to Portuguese Rule - Opposition from Turks and Indian Powers: - Ottoman Empire’s rise led to conflicts over Indian Ocean control. - The Turks advanced into Eastern Europe (1529), threatening Vienna. - Gujarat’s Sultan sought Ottoman support against the Portuguese. - Portuguese Concessions to Gujarat (1531-1536): - Built a fort at Chaul after failing to take Daman and Diu. - Formed a defensive alliance with Bahadur Shah (Gujarat’s ruler) against the Mughals. - Bahadur Shah granted Bassein (Vasai) Island to the Portuguese. - Portuguese Betrayal and Bahadur Shah’s Death (1536): - Bahadur Shah later regretted his concessions. - While negotiating with the Portuguese, a scuffle (a short, sudden, and disorderly fight or struggle, usually without weapons) broke out. - Bahadur Shah drowned while trying to escape. - Turkish Naval Campaigns (1536-1554) - Ottoman Empire challenged the Portuguese in Indian waters: - 1536: - Ottoman fleet (45 galleons, 20,000 men) besieged Diu, but failed. - 1551: - Peri Rais (Turkish admiral) attacked Portuguese forts in Muscat and Ormuz. - 1554: - Final Ottoman expedition under Ali Rais failed. - Portuguese-Ottoman Agreement (1566): - Both empires agreed to divide Indian trade, avoiding further conflict. - Ottomans shifted focus to Europe, abandoning Mughal alliance against the Portuguese. - Conclusion - Despite initial dominance, Portuguese power declined due to: - Rising Indian and European rivals. - Limited resources to maintain vast trade networks. - Growing strength of the Mughals, Marathas, and Dutch. - The Portuguese legacy continued in Goa, Daman, and Diu, which they controlled until 1961. - Portuguese Impact on Indian Trade, Society, and Politics - Limited Control Over Indian Ocean Trade - The Portuguese lacked the resources to police the vast Indian Ocean or fully control trade. - Their strategy focused on monopolizing certain goods and taxing others: - Royal monopoly: - Pepper, arms and ammunition, and warhorses. - Permit system: - Ships trading other commodities had to obtain permits from Portuguese officials. - Customs duty: - All ships traveling to the East or Africa were required to pass through Goa and pay duties. - To enforce these rules: - The Portuguese searched ships suspected of contraband trade. - Ships refusing inspection were seized or sunk, with passengers often enslaved. - This created continuous friction with traders accustomed to open trade practices. - However, their aggressive tactics were counterproductive: - Arab and Indian traders armed their ships, but primarily against pirates, not the Portuguese. - The Portuguese navy struggled to dominate long-established Asian trade networks. - Resistance and Adaptation of Indian and Arab Traders - Gujarat and Arab traders continued to dominate major trade routes: - Indian textiles, rice, and sugar were exchanged for Southeast Asian spices, West Asian gold and horses, and Chinese silk and porcelain. - Despite early Portuguese successes, they could not sustain a monopoly on the pepper and spice trade. - By the late 16th century, alternative trade routes emerged: - Mughal and Safavid empires promoted and safeguarded overland trade. - Gujarati merchants established a new supply route via Achin (Sumatra) → Lakshadweep → Egypt → Red Sea, beyond the reach of the Portuguese navy. - Limited Success in Establishing Goa as a Trade Hub - The Portuguese attempted to make Goa the dominant Asian trade center, surpassing Cambay and Surat (Gujarat). - However, they failed to achieve this goal. - Their influence was mostly negative, as they: - Weakened the Malabar trade by aggressive interference. - Disrupted sea trade from Bengal by raiding ships from Chittagong. - Expansion of New Trade Routes - The Portuguese expanded India’s trade with Japan (exporting Indian textiles and importing copper and silver). - They also opened Indian trade with the Philippines: - Indian textiles were exported to South America via the Philippines. - Silver was imported from South America in exchange. - Their naval power both disrupted traditional trade and created new opportunities. - Limited Contribution to Science and Technology - Unlike other European nations, the Portuguese did not transfer Renaissance science and technology to India. - Reasons: - Portugal was less influenced by the Renaissance than Italy or Northern Europe. - Later, the Jesuit-led (members of the Society of Jesus) Catholic reaction opposed scientific advancements. - However, they introduced new crops from Central America, including: - Chilies, potatoes, tomatoes, tobacco, tapioca, maize, sweet potatoes, pineapple, papaya, cashew nut, guava, avocado and, peanuts, which gradually became widespread. - Alphonso mango: - The Portuguese developed this premium variety of mango through advanced grafting techniques. The fruit was named after a Portuguese general, Afonso de Albuquerque. - Military Conflicts and Survival in the Deccan - The defeat of Vijayanagara (1565) at the Battle of Banihatti changed power dynamics in South India. - Previously, Vijayanagara relied on the Portuguese for warhorses, preventing direct conflict. - In 1570, an anti-Portuguese alliance formed: - Ali Adil Shah (Bijapur) - Nizam Shah (Ahmadnagar) - Zamorin (Calicut) - Their goal: - Expel the Portuguese from the Deccan coast. - Attack strategy: - Adil Shah led an assault on Goa. - Nizam Shah besieged Chaul. - However, Portuguese naval and military strength proved decisive. - Result: - The Portuguese retained their dominance over the Indian seas and Deccan coast. - Struggle for Empire in North India—I (Circa 1400-1525) - - The Fragmentation of the Delhi Sultanate and the Struggle for Power in North India - The Collapse of the Delhi Sultanate - The weakening of the Delhi Sultanate and Timur’s invasion of Delhi (1398) led to a major political crisis. - After Timur’s attack, the Tughlaq king fled, creating a power vacuum. - This emboldened several provincial governors and autonomous rulers to declare their independence. - Emergence of Independent States - First breakaway regions: - Bengal (East) - Sindh and Multan (West) - Deccan states (South) - Further disintegration: - Gujarat, Malwa, and Jaunpur (Eastern Uttar Pradesh) also declared independence. - In Rajputana, after the Muslim governor was expelled from Ajmer, various Rajput states asserted independence. - Balance of Power Among Regional States - Over time, a power balance emerged among these independent states: - West: Gujarat, Malwa, and Mewar checked each other’s expansion. - East: Bengal faced resistance from the Gajapati rulers of Orissa and Jaunpur. - North: The Lodi dynasty, which rose to power in Delhi (mid-15th century), engaged in a prolonged struggle with Jaunpur for control of the Ganga-Yamuna valley. - Key turning point: - The Lodis absorbed Jaunpur (late 15th century), shifting the balance of power. - This allowed them to expand into eastern Rajasthan and Malwa. - The Struggle for the Domination of North India - As Malwa began to disintegrate, tensions increased between: - Gujarat - Mewar - The Lodis (Delhi) - The victor in this contest would dominate all of North India. - Malwa became the focal point of this power struggle. - This intense rivalry motivated Rana Sanga to invite Babur, believing that the Lodi defeat would leave Mewar as the dominant power in North India. - Eastern India: Bengal, Assam, and Orissa - Bengal’s Independence from Delhi - Reasons for frequent independence from Delhi: - Distance from Delhi and unfamiliar waterways hindered Turkish rulers. - Muhammad Tughlaq’s preoccupation with rebellions led Bengal to break away in 1338. - Ilyas Khan’s Rise to Power (1342): - Captured Lakhnauti and Sonargaon, declaring himself Sultan Shamsuddin Ilyas Khan. - Expanded westward to Tirhut, Champaran, Gorakhpur, and Banaras. - Firuz Tughlaq’s Bengal Campaign: - Marched through Champaran and Gorakhpur, capturing Pandua. - Ilyas sought shelter in Ekdala Fort. - After two months, Firuz attempted a trick retreat, but Ilyas re-entered Ekdala. - A treaty established the river Kosi (Bihar) as the boundary. - Ilyas maintained independence while exchanging gifts with Delhi. - Ilyas Shah’s Legacy and Successors - Ilyas Shah’s popularity helped resist Firuz’s attempts to sway the people. - Firuz Tughlaq invaded again after Ilyas’ death, but his son Sikandar used the same tactics and defended Bengal. - Bengal remained independent for 200 years until Sher Shah’s conquest in 1538. - Notable Rulers and Developments - Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah (1389–1409): - Known for justice; humbly accepted a court ruling when he accidentally killed a widow’s son. - Maintained close relations with Persian poet Hafiz of Shiraz. - Revived diplomatic and trade ties with China. - Buddhist monks were sent to China upon the emperor’s request, proving Buddhism’s survival in Bengal. - Chittagong port flourished as a trade hub. - Hindu Rule Under Raja Ganesh: - Brief period, but his sons ruled as Muslims. - Cultural Achievements: - Capitals Pandua and Gaur adorned with unique Bengali-Islamic architecture. - Patronage of Bengali literature: - Maladhar Basu, author of Sri-Krishna-Vijaya, was titled Gunaraja Khan. - His son received the title Satyaraja Khan. - Alauddin Hussain Shah (1493–1519) oversaw significant literary growth. - Alauddin Hussain Shah’s Policies: - Restored law and order. - Liberal administration, offering high offices to Hindus (wazir, chief physician, mint master). - Vaishnavite saint Chaitanya was highly respected. - Bengal’s Expansion and Conflict with Assam - Attempts to control Brahmaputra valley: - Muslim rulers since Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji faced disastrous defeats. - Ilyas Shah invaded Kamta (Western Assam) but withdrew after reaching Gauliati. - Successors attempted plundering raids, but the river Karatoya remained Bengal’s boundary. - Ahoms and Kamta’s Conflict: - Kamta (West) and Ahoms (East) were rivals. - Ahoms, a Mongoloid tribe from Burma, became Hinduized, giving rise to the name Assam. - Alauddin Hussain Shah allied with Ahoms and destroyed Kamta’s capital, Kamtapur. - His son Nusrat Shah’s attack on the Ahoms failed. - Suhungmung (Svarga Narayana), the greatest Ahom ruler, expanded his kingdom and resisted Muslim invasions. - Vaishnavite reformer Shankaradeva flourished under Suhungmung’s rule, spreading Vaishnavism. - Bengal’s Expansion Towards Arakan and Chittagong - Sultan Hussain Shah conquered Chittagong from Arakan. - Also annexed Tipperah (modern Tripura). - Bengal’s Conflict with Orissa - Early skirmishes: - The Ganga dynasty of Orissa assisted Radha (South Bengal) in resisting Delhi’s rule. - Tried to conquer Lakhnauti, but failed. - Orissa’s Flourishing Under the Ganga Dynasty: - Built the Jagannatha temple (Puri) and Sun temple (Konark). - Ilyas Shah raided Orissa (1338), reaching Chilka Lake and looting elephants. - Firuz Tughlaq (1360) raided Orissa, massacring people and desecrating Jagannatha temple. - These raids weakened the Ganga dynasty, leading to the rise of the Gajapati dynasty. - The Gajapati Dynasty’s Rise (15th Century): - Expanded southward into Karnataka, clashing with Vijayanagara, Reddis, and Bahmani sultans. - Bengal’s strength prevented Orissa from expanding northward. - Bengal-Orissa Border Conflicts: - Frontier at river Saraswati (Midnapore and Hugli districts). - Orissa attempted to advance up to Bhagirathi but failed. - Alauddin Hussain Shah led raids into Orissa, reaching Puri and Cuttack. - Despite frequent battles, Orissa held its territory beyond Saraswati. - Conclusion: A Region of Dynamic Power Struggles - Bengal, Assam, and Orissa were highly contested regions during this period. - Bengal’s political stability, economic prosperity, and cultural vibrancy made it a dominant power. - Assam’s Ahom rulers resisted external invasions, strengthening their rule. - Orissa’s powerful Gajapati rulers expanded into the south but faced resistance from Bengal and Vijayanagara. - The constant rivalries shaped the political landscape of Eastern India. - Western India - Gujarat: A Wealthy Province - Gujarat was one of the wealthiest provinces of the Delhi Sultanate due to: - Flourishing seaports - Excellence in handicrafts - Fertile soil - Under Firuz Tughlaq: - Gujarat had a benevolent governor who encouraged Hindu worship (Ferishta’s account). - Zafar Khan, son of a Rajput convert, succeeded as governor. - After Timur’s invasion of Delhi: - Gujarat and Malwa became independent in all but name. - In 1407, Zafar Khan formally declared himself ruler as Muzaffar Shah. - Ahmad Shah I (1411–1443): Founder of the Gujarat Kingdom - Grandson of Muzaffar Shah. - Brought the nobility under control and strengthened administration. - Moved the capital from Patan to Ahmedabad (1413). - Expanded and consolidated the kingdom. - Ahmad Shah’s Architectural Contributions - Patronized a distinctive architectural style influenced by Jain traditions: - Slender turrets - Exquisite stone carvings - Highly ornate brackets - Major constructions: - Jama Masjid, Ahmedabad - Tin Darwaza - Ahmad Shah’s Military Campaigns and Policies - Conquest of Saurashtra: - Captured Girnar Fort, later restored it to the raja in exchange for tribute. - Religious Policies: - Imposed jizyah tax on Hindus (first time in Gujarat). - Attacked Sidhpur, destroying Hindu temples. - Administrative Inclusivity: - Despite religious policies, he appointed Hindus to key positions. - Ministers Manik Chand and Motichand (Bania community) served under him. - Strict Justice: - Executed his own son-in-law in the marketplace for murder. - Expansion in Rajasthan: - Subjugated Idar Fort, Jhalawar, Bundi, and Dungarpur. - Gujarat-Malwa Rivalry - Constant conflict between Gujarat and Malwa: - Muzaffar Shah defeated and imprisoned Hushang Shah of Malwa, but later reinstated him. - Malwa’s rulers tried to weaken Gujarat by supporting rebels and Hindu rajas. - Gujarat retaliated by attempting to install its own candidate as Malwa’s ruler. - Impact of the rivalry: - Weakened both kingdoms. - Prevented them from playing a larger role in North Indian politics. - Mahmud Begarha (1459–1511) - Expansion and Military Campaigns - Most famous Sultan of Gujarat, known for expansion and consolidation. - Called Begarha for capturing two powerful forts: - Girnar (Saurashtra, now Junagadh) - Champaner (Southern Gujarat) - Conquest of Girnar (Saurashtra) - The ruler of Girnar had been regularly paying tribute, but Mahmud decided to annex the kingdom to control Saurashtra, a rich region with: - Fertile land - Flourishing ports - Robbers and pirates disrupting trade - Siege of Girnar: - The raja resisted despite having few guns. - Allegedly fell due to treason—his kamdar (minister), whose wife had been taken by the raja, conspired against him. - The raja converted to Islam and joined Mahmud’s service. - Mahmud founded Mustafabad at the base of Girnar as Gujarat’s second capital. - Attack on Dwarka - Mahmud sacked Dwarka, claiming it harbored pirates attacking Mecca-bound pilgrims. - The campaign also resulted in the destruction of Hindu temples. - Conquest of Champaner (1454) - Strategic importance: - Key location for controlling Khandesh and Malwa. - The ruler had ties with the Sultan of Malwa despite being a feudatory of Gujarat. - Siege of Champaner: - The raja and his warriors, left without aid, performed jausar (ritual sacrifice) and fought to death. - Mahmud built Muhammadabad near Champaner, making it his principal residence with gardens and architectural marvels. - Architecture and Legacy - Jama Masjid in Champaner still stands, featuring: - Covered courtyard - Jain architectural influences - Finely crafted stonework, comparable to goldsmith artistry - Conflict with the Portuguese - The Portuguese disrupted Gujarat’s trade with West Asia. - Mahmud allied with Egypt’s ruler to counter them but failed. - Economic and Cultural Contributions - Long and peaceful reign fostered trade and commerce. - Built caravanserais and inns to ensure safe travel for merchants. - Encouraged translation of Arabic works into Persian. - Court poet Udayaraja composed in Sanskrit. - Personal Traits and Unique Characteristics - Appearance: - Long waist-length beard and mustache tied over his head. - Strange legend: - According to traveler Barbosa, he was fed poison since childhood, making his touch deadly to flies. - Enormous appetite: - Breakfast: Cup of honey, cup of butter, 100–150 bananas. - Daily intake: 10–15 kg of food. - Kept meat samosas by his pillow in case of midnight hunger. - Gujarat at its Peak - Under Mahmud Begarha, Gujarat reached its largest territorial extent. - Became one of the most powerful and well-administered states in India. - Later posed a serious challenge to Mughal Emperor Humayun. - Malwa: A Strategic Kingdom - Geographical and Political Importance -
