Located on the high plateau between the Narmada and Tapti rivers. - Controlled key trade routes between: - Gujarat and northern India. - North and south India. - Served as a buffer state against the ambitions of Gujarat, Mewar, the Bahmanis, and the Lodi Sultans of Delhi. - Any powerful state that controlled Malwa had a strategic advantage in dominating northern India. - Rise of Malwa (15th Century) - Reached its peak during the 15th century. - Capital shifted from Dhar to Mandu, a highly defensible and scenic location. - Mandu’s Architecture: - Unlike Gujarat’s architectural style, Mandu’s structures were massive and built on lofty plinths. - Extensive use of colored and glazed tiles added variety. - Famous monuments: - Jama Masjid - Hindola Mahal - Jahaz Mahal (Ship Palace) - Ruins still remain impressive today. - Internal Struggles and External Threats - Malwa was plagued by internal conflicts: - Frequent succession struggles. - Factional fights among noble groups for power and wealth. - Neighboring states Gujarat and Mewar often exploited Malwa’s instability for their own gains. - Hushang Shah (Early Malwa Ruler, Tolerant Policies) - Practiced religious toleration and encouraged Rajput settlement. - Granted jagirs to two elder brothers of Rana Mokal of Mewar. - Hindu temple construction was unrestricted (e.g., Lalitpur temple inscription). - Patronized Jains, the dominant merchants and bankers of the region. - Nardeva Soni, a Jain merchant, became treasurer and advisor to the Sultan. - Mahmud Khalji (1436–69): Malwa’s Most Powerful Ruler - Less tolerant than Hushang Shah. - Destroyed many temples during wars with Rana Kumbha of Mewar and neighboring Hindu rajas. - However, not part of a general policy of temple destruction. - A restless and ambitious ruler, constantly at war. - Fought against almost all neighbors, including: - Gujarat - Rajas of Gondwana and Orissa - Bahmani Sultans - Sultan of Delhi - Focused on overrunning South Rajputana and subduing Mewar. - Mewar: Rise and Dominance in Northern India - Early History and Background - Mewar’s rise in the 15th century significantly influenced northern India’s political landscape. - The Chauhans, after being ousted from Ajmer, shifted to Ranthambhor and established a powerful state. - Their power ended when Alauddin Khalji conquered Ranthambhor. - From its ruins, new states emerged: - Marwar (capital: Jodhpur, founded in 1465). - Nagaur, a Muslim principality. - Ajmer, once ruled by Muslim governors, changed hands frequently and became a point of contention among Rajput states. - Eastern Rajputana remained disputed, with Delhi’s rulers maintaining interest in the region. - Formation of Mewar - The early history of Mewar is obscure. - Bapa Rawal of the Guhilot clan is considered its virtual founder. - Migrated from Gujarat in the 7th century and dominated southwestern Rajasthan. - Guhilots ruled from Chittor until Ratan Singh was ousted by Alauddin Khalji. - Chittor then passed to the Sisodiyas, former feudatories of the Guhilots. - Rao Lakha and Mokal strengthened Mewar, making it the most powerful state in Rajasthan by the late 14th and early 15th centuries. - Rana Kumbha (1433–1468): The Greatest Mewar Ruler - Consolidated his rule by defeating internal rivals. - Expanded Mewar by conquering Bundi, Kotah, and Daungarpur (on the Gujarat border). - Kotah had been aligned with Malwa, and Daungarpur with Gujarat. - This led to conflicts with Gujarat and Malwa: - Khan of Nagaur, attacked by Rana Kumbha, sought Gujarat’s help. - Kumbha supported a rival of Mahmud Khalji of Malwa in an attempt to install him as ruler. - In retaliation, Mahmud Khalji gave refuge to Kumbha’s rivals, including his brother Mokal. - Mewar’s Struggles and Resistance - Wars with Gujarat and Malwa lasted throughout Kumbha’s reign. - Conflict with Rathors of Marwar: - Marwar had been under Mewar but gained independence under Rao Jodha. - Despite external threats, Rana Kumbha maintained Mewar’s position: - Kumbhalgarh was besieged multiple times by Gujarat. - Mahmud Khalji raided as far as Ajmer and placed his own governor there. - Despite these attacks, Kumbha retained most of his conquests (except outlying areas like Ranthambhor). - Rana Kumbha’s Contributions - Scholar and Patron of Learning: - Composed several books, some of which still exist. - Architectural Legacy: - Built the Victory Tower (Kirtistambha) at Chittor. - His palace ruins reflect his enthusiasm for architecture. - Developed irrigation projects by constructing lakes and reservoirs. - Mewar’s stone-cutting and sculpture remained at a high level during his reign. - Rana Sanga and Mewar’s Expansion - Kumbha was murdered by his son Uda in a bid for the throne. - Rana Sanga (Kumbha’s grandson) took the throne in 1508 after a long fratricidal conflict. - Key events before Sanga’s rise: - Malwa weakened internally. - Mahmud II of Malwa sought Gujarat’s help against Medini Rai, a powerful Rajput leader. - Medini Rai turned to Rana Sanga for support. - In 1517, Rana Sanga defeated Mahmud II and took him prisoner. - Eastern Malwa, including Chanderi, came under Mewar’s control. - Mewar vs. Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals - The Lodi rulers of Delhi saw Mewar’s expansion as a threat. - Ibrahim Lodi invaded Mewar but was defeated by Rana Sanga at Khatoli. - Lodi withdrew to focus on internal matters. - Meanwhile, Babur was approaching India (1525), setting the stage for a decisive conflict for supremacy. - Northwest and North India - The Political Landscape After Timur’s Invasion - Collapse of the Tughlaq Dynasty - Following Timur’s invasion, Sultan Mahmud Tughlaq fled Delhi, seeking refuge first in Gujarat and then in Malwa. - By the time he attempted to return, the throne of Delhi had lost its prestige. - In the Delhi region, ambitious nobles and zamindars began asserting their independence. - The Sharqi Sultanate (Jaunpur Sultanate) - Rise of the Sharqis - Malik Sarwar, a noble under Firuz Tughlaq, was one of the first to assert independence in the Ganga valley. - Initially appointed as the governor of the eastern region with the title Malik-us-Sharq (Lord of the East), his successors were called the Sharqis. - The Sharqi sultans established their capital at Jaunpur (eastern Uttar Pradesh) and adorned it with magnificent palaces, mosques, and mausoleums. - The Sharqi rulers developed a unique architectural style distinct from the Delhi Sultanate, marked by lofty gates and huge arches. - Cultural Patronage - Jaunpur became a center of learning and culture, earning the title “Shiraz of the East.” - Scholars, poets, and saints thrived under the patronage of the Sharqi rulers. - Malik Muhammad Jaisi, the famous poet and author of Padmavat, lived in Jaunpur. - Decline and Fall - At its peak, the Sharqi Sultanate extended from Aligarh (western Uttar Pradesh) to Darbhanga (north Bihar), and from Nepal’s boundary to Bundelkhand. - The Sharqis aspired to conquer Delhi but faced resistance from the Lodi dynasty. - After a series of conflicts, Bahlul Lodi of Delhi annexed Jaunpur in 1484. - The last Sharqi ruler died in exile, marking the end of the dynasty. - Despite their fall, the Sharqis maintained law and order and prevented Bengal’s expansion into eastern Uttar Pradesh. - Their cultural contributions continued to influence the region long after their demise. - Rise of the Lodi Dynasty - Bahlul Lodi (1451–1489) - Following Timur’s invasion, the Saiyid dynasty emerged in Delhi, but its rule was weak. - In Punjab, Afghan warlords gained power, with Bahlul Lodi emerging as the most significant. - Initially, he was granted the iqta (land grant) of Sirhind and checked the growing power of the warlike Khokhars in the Salt Range. - Called in to assist Delhi’s ruler against an attack from Malwa, Bahlul Lodi took control of Delhi. - In 1451, he formally ascended the throne, ending the Saiyid dynasty. - Expansion and Afghan Influence - The Lodis, unlike earlier Delhi rulers who were Turks, were Afghans. - Although Afghans had long served in the Delhi Sultanate’s army, few held high-ranking positions. - Their rising influence was evident in both Malwa and the Bahmani kingdom in the south. - Bahlul Lodi focused on consolidating his rule by inviting Afghan warriors from Roh (Afghanistan), promising them wealth and power. - This influx of Afghans strengthened his army, allowing him to defeat the Sharqis and change the demographic composition of Muslim society in India. - Sikandar Lodi (1489–1517) - Governance and Administration - Sikandar Lodi, the most capable Lodi ruler, ruled alongside Mahmud Begarha (Gujarat) and Rana Sanga (Mewar). - Unlike the tribal Afghan sardars, who viewed the sultan as primus inter pares (first among equals), Sikandar emphasized royal authority. - He introduced strict court protocols and enforced regular financial audits for nobles. - Corrupt officials were punished severely. - Though he managed to centralize power, the Afghan tradition of dividing the kingdom among the ruler’s sons persisted. - Economic and Agricultural Reforms - Sikandar Lodi ensured efficient governance, emphasizing law and order. - Roads and highways were made secure from bandits. - Prices of essential goods remained low. - To encourage agriculture, he abolished the octroi duty on grains. - He introduced the gaz-i-Sikandari (a new yard measurement) for standardized land assessment, later adopted by Sher Shah Suri. - Religious Policies - Sikandar Lodi was an orthodox ruler who strictly followed Islamic law (Sharia). - He prohibited certain practices among Muslims, such as women visiting saintly graves. - He re-imposed the jizya tax on Hindus and executed a Brahman for equating Hindu and Muslim scriptures. - Hindu temples, such as the one at Nagarkot, were demolished during his campaigns. - Patronage of Arts and Learning - Despite his orthodoxy, Sikandar Lodi was a patron of scholars, poets, and philosophers. - He invited intellectuals from Arabia and Iran to his court. - Many Sanskrit works were translated into Persian, including texts on music. - His reign saw an increase in Hindu participation in administration due to their Persian language skills. - Expansion and Strategic Developments - Sikandar Lodi expanded the Lodi territory by conquering Dholpur and Gwalior. - In 1506, he carefully selected the site for Agra, intending it to serve as a strategic center for eastern Rajasthan and routes to Malwa and Gujarat. - Sikandar Lodi (1488–1517) is credited with founding modern Agra as a capital city in 1504 CE. - Over time, Agra became the second capital of the Lodi dynasty. - The Looming Conflict: Lodi vs. Mewar - Sikandar Lodi sought to extend influence over Malwa and Rajasthan. - He took the Khan of Nagaur under his protection and tried to shift Ranthambhor’s allegiance from Malwa to Delhi. - His successor, Ibrahim Lodi, continued this expansionist policy but faced resistance from Mewar. - The growing power of Rana Sanga in Malwa and his expansion toward Agra and Bayana signaled an inevitable confrontation. - However, before this struggle could reach its climax (the most intense, exciting, or important part of something), Babur arrived in India, altering the course of history. - Kashmir in the Fifteenth Century - Isolation and Early Turmoil - For a long time, the beautiful valley of Kashmir remained a forbidden land to outsiders. According to al-Biruni, even Hindus who were not personally known to nobles were denied entry. - During this period, Kashmir was a center of Shaivism. However, the situation changed with the fall of Hindu rule in the mid-fourteenth century. - A major turning point was the devastating Mongol invasion of 1320, led by Dalucha. He ordered: - Massacre of men, while women and children were enslaved and sold to Central Asian merchants. - Plundering and burning of towns and villages. - The Kashmir government failed to resist this onslaught, leading to widespread discontent among the people. - Rise of Islam and Persecution of Hindus - Following the Mongol invasion, Kashmir underwent significant changes: - Muslim saints and refugees from Central Asia entered Kashmir, facilitated by the Baramulla route. - A unique group of Sufi saints, called Rishis, emerged, blending elements of Hinduism and Islam. - Conversion of lower-class Hindus to Islam took place, partly through preaching and partly by force. - During the reign of Sikandar Shah (1389–1413), Hindu persecution peaked: - Brahmins and learned Hindus were forced to either convert or flee. - Temples were destroyed, and gold and silver idols were melted for currency. - The harsh policies were influenced by his minister Suha Bhatt, a former Hindu who had converted to Islam. - Reign of Zainul Abidin (1420–1470) – The Great Sultan - The accession of Zainul Abidin, regarded as Kashmir’s greatest Muslim ruler, marked a reversal of these policies. - Reconciliation with Hindus: - Cancelled orders against Hindus and invited exiles to return. - Allowed those who had converted under pressure to revert to Hinduism. - Restored temples, land grants, and revived Hindu scholarship. - More than a century later, Abul Fazl recorded that Kashmir had 150 majestic temples, likely restored under Zainul Abidin. - Policies of Toleration: - Abolished the jizya (tax on non-Muslims) and banned cow slaughter. - Lifted the ban on sati out of respect for Hindu customs. - Appointed Hindus to high offices, including Suha Bhatt, his former minister. - His first two queens were Hindu princesses from Jammu, and they bore all his sons. - Contributions to Literature and Learning: - A scholar himself, fluent in Persian, Kashmiri, Sanskrit, and Tibetan. - Encouraged translations of Sanskrit texts (e.g., Mahabharata, Rajatarangini). - Patronized Persian and Sanskrit scholars. - Music enthusiast—received rare Sanskrit works on music from the Raja of Gwalior. - Economic and Cultural Development: - Sent artisans to Samarkand to learn papermaking and bookbinding. - Encouraged crafts like stone-cutting, bottle-making, gold-beating, and shawl-weaving. - Advanced musket-making and fireworks manufacturing. - Developed agriculture through the construction of dams, canals, and bridges. - Greatest engineering feat: Zaina Lanka, an artificial island in Wular Lake, where he built his palace and a mosque. - Military and Political Achievements - Though not a great warrior, Zainul Abidin successfully: - Defeated Mongol invasions in Ladakh. - Conquered Baltistan (Tibbat-i-Buzurg). - Maintained control over Jammu and Rajouri. - Unified the Kashmiri kingdom. - His fame spread across India and Asia, and he maintained diplomatic ties with major rulers of his time. - Conclusion: Cultural Impact of Regional Kingdoms - The fifteenth-century political landscape remained unstable, but the regional kingdoms made lasting cultural contributions: - Unique architectural styles emerged, incorporating local traditions. - Local languages and literature flourished. - While some rulers engaged in religious persecution, the broader trend was one of mutual accommodation and cultural integration. - Zainul Abidin’s rule anticipated Akbar’s policies in many ways, fostering a spirit of tolerance and cultural exchange that shaped Kashmir’s history. - Cultural Development in India (1300–1500) - Cultural Impact of the Delhi Sultanate - The establishment of the Delhi Sultanate in the early thirteenth century marked a new phase in India’s cultural development. - The Turkish invaders who arrived in India were not mere barbarians. - Turks and Their Cultural Background - The Turks originated from Central Asia and migrated to West Asia in the ninth and tenth centuries. - Unlike earlier Central Asian invaders who embraced Buddhism or Hinduism, the Turks adopted Islam and quickly assimilated into Arabo-Persian culture. - By the time they reached India, they had been influenced by a flourishing Islamic civilization that spanned from Morocco and Spain to Iran. - The region had made significant contributions in areas such as science, navigation, literature, and governance. - The Turks brought with them: - A well-defined faith in Islam to which they were deeply committed. - Advanced ideas in government, art, architecture, and administration. - Interaction Between Turks and Indians - Indian society had its own strong religious traditions and developed cultural expressions in art, architecture, and literature. - The interaction between these two civilizations led, over time, to the emergence of a new, enriched culture. - However, this process was long and complex, often marked by: - Destruction, followed or accompanied by periods of reconstruction. - Mutual misunderstandings and conflicts, as both cultures held deeply entrenched beliefs. - Assimilation and Cultural Exchange - Despite the challenges, the two cultures gradually influenced each other in various fields: - Art and architecture - Music and literature - Customs, ceremonies, and rituals - Religious beliefs - Science and technology - However, elements of confrontation and conflict remained strong within both communities. - A Process of Ups and Downs - The process of assimilation and convergence was not uniform. - It varied across different regions, fields, and historical periods. - While cultural integration did take place, it was accompanied by periods of resistance and discord. - Ultimately, the Delhi Sultanate played a crucial role in shaping India’s cultural landscape, fostering both conflict and synthesis between Turkish and Indian traditions. - Architecture During the Delhi Sultanate - The arrival of the Turks in India led to significant developments in architecture, blending indigenous and Islamic styles. - Their architectural contributions were shaped by their religious beliefs, technological advancements, and artistic preferences. - Early Turkish Constructions - The first requirement of the new rulers was houses to live in and places of worship. - Initially, existing temples and buildings were converted into mosques, while many others were destroyed, and their materials reused. - Examples: - Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque (near Qutub Minar, Delhi) – Originally a temple. - Arhai Din ka Jhonpra (Ajmer) – Originally a monastery. - The only new construction in Delhi was a façade of three elaborately carved arches in front of the garbhagriha, which was demolished. - Decorative Features: - Human and animal figures were avoided, as they were considered un-Islamic. - Instead, floral scrolls and Quranic verses were used in intricate designs. - Introduction of New Architectural Elements - The Turks soon began constructing their own buildings, employing both indigenous Indian craftsmen and architects from West Asia. - Key Features Introduced: - Arches and domes were widely used. - The arch and dome were not Turkish inventions; they were borrowed from Rome (via the Byzantine Empire) and refined by the Arabs. - Advantages of Arches and Domes: - Domes created an impressive skyline and were gradually built higher. - Large halls could be constructed without the need for numerous supporting pillars, making them useful for mosques and palaces. - Fine quality mortar was used for strong construction. - Comparison with Indigenous Architecture: - Indians had known arches and domes earlier but had not used them extensively. - Indian methods relied on placing stones over one another or using beams, whereas the Turks introduced the scientific method of constructing arches. - Both methods—arch and dome as well as slab and beam—were used in their buildings. - Decorative Styles and Artistic Influences - The Turks avoided human and animal figures in their architecture. - Instead, they used: - Geometrical and floral designs (Arabesque). - Calligraphy – Quranic verses carved into walls. - Indigenous motifs such as the bell, leaf, swastika, and lotus were also incorporated. - Indian stone-cutters’ expertise was fully utilized, as seen in: - Tomb of Iltutmish (Delhi) – Highly intricate carvings, with hardly any blank space. - The Turks introduced colored stone architecture, using: - Red sandstone as the primary material. - Yellow sandstone and marble for decoration and contrast. - Significant Architectural Achievements - Qutub Minar (13th Century) - The most magnificent Turkish construction of the 13th century. - Height: Originally 71.4 meters. - Builders: Begun by Aibak, completed by Iltutmish. - Common Misconception: It was not dedicated to Sufi saint Qutb-ud-Din Bakhtiyar Kaki; it was part of the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque. - Unique Features: - Skillfully projected balconies linked to the main tower. - Use of red and white sandstone, and marble. - Ribbed design, enhancing visual appeal. - Khalji Period (Late 13th – Early 14th Century) - Alauddin Khalji’s Architectural Contributions: - Built his capital at Siri (remains largely destroyed). - Planned a tower twice the height of Qutub Minar but did not complete it. - Constructed the Alai Darwaza, an entrance to the Qutub complex, featuring: - Well-proportioned arches. - First dome built using correct scientific principles. - By this time, Indian craftsmen had mastered the art of arches and domes. - Tughlaq Period (14th Century) - Marked both the climax (the most intense, exciting, or important part of something) of the Delhi Sultanate and the beginning of its decline. - Key Constructions: - Tughlaqabad Fort (Ghiyasuddin and Muhammad Tughlaq): - A huge palace-fortress complex. - A massive artificial lake was created by blocking the Yamuna. - Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq’s Tomb: - Built on a high platform, enhancing its skyline. - Marble dome, adding elegance. - Architectural Innovations: - Sloping Walls (Batter Technique): - Created an impression of strength and solidity. - Common in early Tughlaq buildings but absent in Firuz Tughlaq’s constructions. - Combination of Arch and Lintel-Beam Systems: - Visible in Firuz Tughlaq’s buildings. - Hauz Khas Complex: - A pleasure resort with a large lake and madrasa. - Kotla (Firuz Shah’s Fort): - Continued using indigenous Rajasthani and Gujarati architectural elements. - Material Choices: - Avoided expensive red sandstone. - Used cheaper grey stone, leading to minimal decoration. - Lotus motif became a standard decorative feature. - Lodi Period (15th – Early 16th Century) - Further developed the architectural traditions of the Delhi Sultanate. - Key Features: - Both arch-based and lintel-beam structures were used. - Balconies, kiosks, and eaves inspired by Rajasthani and Gujarati styles. - Buildings were placed on high platforms to enhance grandeur. - Many tombs were built in lush gardens (e.g., Lodi Garden, Delhi). - Octagonal tomb structures became common. - Legacy: - Many Lodi-era features were later adopted by the Mughals, culminating in masterpieces like the Taj Mahal. - Regional Variations and Later Developments - As the Delhi Sultanate fragmented, distinct architectural styles emerged in different regions: - Bengal - Gujarat - Malwa - Deccan - These styles retained local influences while incorporating Turkish innovations. - The Tughlaq-era style evolved and was modified in regional kingdoms, leading to an architectural renaissance in India. - Conclusion - The architectural legacy of the Delhi Sultanate was a blend of Indian and Islamic influences, introducing arches, domes, calligraphy, and intricate ornamentation while utilizing local craftsmanship. - Over time, this synthesis led to the emergence of an independent Indo-Islamic architectural style, which significantly influenced later Mughal and regional constructions. - Religious Traditions and Beliefs - Islamic Influence and Cultural Exchange in Early India - Islam’s Early Presence in India: - Established in Sindh (8th century) and Punjab (10th century). - Arab travelers settled in Kerala (8th–10th century). - Cultural and Religious Exchanges: - Arab travelers and Sufi saints spread ideas across India. - Al-Biruni’s Kitab-ul-Hind introduced Hindu ideas to West Asia. - Buddhist texts, Indian fables, astronomy, and medicine books were translated into Arabic. - Indian yogis frequently visited West Asia. - Influence of Indian Philosophy on Islam: - Scholars debate the impact of Buddhism and Vedanta on Islamic thought. - Buddhist monasteries, stupas, and images of the Buddha found in Afghanistan and Central Asia indicate strong Buddhist influence in these regions. - Both Greek and Indian philosophies contributed to Islamic philosophical development. - Rise of Sufism in India (12th century): - Influenced both Muslims and Hindus, creating a shared spiritual platform. - Early Sufis adopted Hindu rituals and yogic practices. - Despite assimilation, their core ideology remained fundamentally Islamic. - The Sufi Movement - Background and Development - 10th century: A turning point in Islamic history due to: - The rise of the Turks after the decline of the Abbasid Caliphate. - Changes in religious ideas and beliefs: - Decline of Mutazila (rationalist philosophy). - Rise of orthodox schools based on the Quran and Hadith. - Growth of Sufi mystic orders. - Rationalists were accused of skepticism and atheism due to their monistic belief that God and the world were one, which was seen as heretical. - Formation of Islamic Law Schools: - Orthodox traditions led to four major schools of Islamic law. - Hanafi School - Founder: - Imam Abu Hanifa (699–767 CE), Kufa (Iraq) - Flexible, relied on reasoning (qiyās) and consensus (ijmā‘) - Most widely followed: - Central Asia, South Asia (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh), Turkey - Adopted by Delhi Sultans, Mughals, and Ottomans - Maliki School - Founder: - Imam Malik ibn Anas (711–795 CE), Medina - Gave weight to the practice of people of Medina as law - Predominant in North Africa (Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya), parts of West Africa - Shafi‘i School - Founder: - Imam al-Shafi‘i (767–820 CE) - Tried to balance Hadith, reasoning, and systematic principles - Spread to East Africa, Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia), Egypt - Hanbali School - Founder: - Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (780–855 CE) - Literalist, strict reliance on Qur’an and Hadith, limited analogy - Dominant in Arabia, especially Saudi Arabia - Hanafi school (most liberal) was adopted by the eastern Turks, who later brought it to India. - Early Sufism and Key Figures - Origins and Motivations: - Early Sufis were mystics who emphasized deep devotion to God. - Rejected the extravagance and moral decay of the Islamic empire. - Maintained distance from state affairs. - Notable Early Sufis: - Rabia (8th century): - Emphasized love as the bond between God and the soul. - Mansur bin Hallaj (10th century): - Advocated pantheism (belief that God and the universe are one and the same) but was executed for heresy (beliefs or opinions that go against the established doctrines of a religion). - Al-Ghazzali (d. 1112): - Reconciled mysticism with Islamic orthodoxy. - Rejected rationalist philosophy, arguing that true knowledge of God comes only through revelation (Quran). - Organization of Sufism - Formation of Sufi Orders (Silsilahs): - 12 Sufi orders emerged. - Each order was led by a prominent mystic (pir). - Pirs lived in khangahs (hospices) with their disciples (murids). - Every pir appointed a successor (wali) to continue their work. - Hindu and Buddhist Influences on Sufism - Shared Practices and Rituals: - Penance, fasting, breath control—similar to Buddhist and Hindu yogic traditions. - Buddhism was prevalent in Central Asia before Islam’s arrival, influencing Islamic mysticism. - Hindu yogis visited West Asia, and texts like Amrit-kund were translated into Persian. - Debate exists on whether Buddhist and Vedantic philosophies significantly shaped Sufism. - Common Spiritual Ideas: - Similar beliefs on God’s nature, the soul, and the material world created a shared platform between Sufis and Hindu mystics. - This mutual understanding fostered religious tolerance. - Classification of Sufi Orders - Two broad divisions: - Ba-shara Sufis: Followed Islamic law (shara). - Be-shara Sufis: Did not strictly follow Islamic law. - Both orders existed in India, with Be-shara Sufis (wandering saints) gaining a broader following, often revered by both Muslims and Hindus. - The Essence of Sufism - Sufi teachings emphasized spiritual unity. - Persian poet Sanai expressed this spirit in his poetry: “Faith and infidelity, both are galloping on the way towards Him; And are exclaiming (together): He is one and none share His kingdom.” - The Chishti and Suharwardi Silsilahs - Chishti Order: - Established in India by Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti around 1192, shortly after Prithvi Raj Chauhan’s defeat. - Settled in Ajmer, an important political center with a significant Muslim population. - Left no written records, but his influence grew through his successors. - Prominent Chishti Saints: - Shaikh Muinuddin Chishti’s disciples: - Bakhtiyar Kaki and his disciple Farid-ud-Din Ganj-i-Shakar (confined activities to Hansi and Ajodhan). - Farid-ud-Din was deeply respected in Delhi, and some of his verses were later included in the Adi-Granth of the Sikhs. - Nizamuddin Auliya and Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Delhi were the most famous Chishti saints. - Mingled freely with the lower classes, including Hindus. - Lived a simple, austere life and spoke Hindawi to connect with the masses. - Did not actively seek conversions, but many later attributed their conversion to their blessings. - Popularized sama (musical recitations) to foster devotion, often using Hindi verses. - Nizamuddin Auliya adopted yogic breathing techniques, earning the title of sidh (‘perfect’) from yogis. - Chishti Expansion: - After Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Delhi’s death in the mid-14th century, the order lost a central figure in Delhi. - Chishti saints dispersed, spreading their influence to eastern and southern India. - Suharwardi Order: - Entered India around the same time as the Chishtis but remained largely confined to Punjab and Multan. - Prominent figures: Shaikh Shihabuddin Suharwardi and Hamid-ud-Din Nagori. - Unlike the Chishtis, they: - Did not embrace poverty and accepted state service. - Held important positions in the ecclesiastical department. - Key Differences: - Chishtis preferred to stay aloof from state politics and avoided rulers and nobles. - Suharwardis actively participated in state affairs. - Despite differences, both orders fostered a spirit of peace and harmony among different religious and sectarian groups. - Impact: - Mecca remained the holiest site, but the rise of popular saints provided a local spiritual focus for the masses. - The Bhakti Movement - Origins and Early Development - Stressed mystical union of the individual with God. - Though its roots lie in the Vedas, Bhakti was not emphasized in the early period. - Gained prominence with the rise of Buddhism, particularly Mahayana Buddhism, where Buddha was worshipped in his Avalokiteshvara (gracious) form. - Around the same time, the worship of Vishnu developed. - By the Gupta period, Bhakti was accepted as one of the three recognized paths to salvation (along with Jnana and Karma). - Bhakti in South India (7th–12th Century) - Saiva Nayanmars and Vaishnavite Alvars disregarded Jain and Buddhist austerities and preached personal devotion to God as a means of salvation. - Opposed the rigid caste system and spread their message in local languages. - Bhakti’s Spread to North India - Despite connections between North and South India, Bhakti ideas spread slowly to the North. - Challenge: - Nayanmars and Alvars used regional languages, while Sanskrit remained the dominant intellectual language in the North. - Bhakti was carried to the North by scholars and saints, including: - Namadeva (early 14th century) – A Maharashtrian saint, originally a tailor and former bandit, wrote devotional poetry in Marathi and engaged with Sufi saints in Delhi. - Ramananda (14th–15th century) – A follower of Ramanuja, substituted Rama worship for Vishnu worship and rejected caste-based restrictions. - Enrolled disciples from all castes, including: - Ravidas (cobbler) - Kabir (weaver) - Sena (barber) - Sadhana (butcher) - Why Bhakti Gained Popularity in the North: - Decline of Brahman prestige after Rajput defeats and the Turkish Sultanate’s establishment. - Nath Panthi movement questioned caste hierarchy and Brahman supremacy. - Sufi saints promoted equality and brotherhood, resonating with Bhakti ideas. - People sought a spiritual, emotional, and rational religion beyond rituals and ceremonies. - By the 15th–16th centuries, the Bhakti movement became widely accepted in North India. - Key Figures of the Bhakti Movement - Kabir (15th Century) - Uncertainty about his birth; legend says he was the son of a Brahman widow, raised by a Muslim weaver in Kashi. - His teachings combined Hindu and Islamic elements: - Emphasized one universal God (Allah, Sain, Sahib, etc.). - Rejected idol worship, pilgrimages, and ritualistic practices (including namaz). - Opposed asceticism and book knowledge as means of true wisdom. - Denounced the caste system and untouchability, advocating human equality. - Supported the poor and marginalized, though he was not a social reformer—focused on individual transformation. - Dr. Tara Chand’s View: - “Kabir’s mission was to preach a religion of love uniting all castes and creeds.” - Rejected ritualistic Hinduism and Islam in favor of spiritual unity. - Guru Nanak (1469–1538) - Founder of Sikhism; born into a Khatri family in Talwandi (now Nankana Sahib, Pakistan). - Initially trained in Persian and accountancy, but was drawn towards spiritual contemplation. - Had a mystical vision, renounced worldly life, and composed hymns. - Sang them with rabab accompaniment by Mardana. - Undertook extensive travels across India, Sri Lanka, and even Mecca and Medina. - Core Teachings: - Emphasized one God and devotion as the path to salvation, beyond caste, creed, or sect. - Advocated purity of character and the need for a guru for spiritual guidance. - Rejected idol worship, pilgrimages, and external rituals. - Promoted a middle path, balancing spirituality with household responsibilities. - Did not intend to create a new religion but sought to bridge Hindu-Muslim divides. - His teachings later evolved into Sikhism, while Kabir’s followers formed the Kabir Panth sect. - Impact and Resistance - Bhakti saints challenged orthodox Hinduism and Islam, advocating spiritual unity and equality. - Their influence extended to political and religious policies, notably influencing Akbar’s religious outlook. - However, orthodox factions within both Hinduism and Islam resisted change. - The 16th–18th centuries saw ongoing struggles between: - Liberal, non-sectarian forces (Bhakti, Sufi influences). - Traditional, orthodox elements reinforcing existing religious structures. - Long-term Impact: - Though caste and orthodox practices persisted, Bhakti created a lasting shift in religious thought. - Fostered an inclusive spiritual environment influencing future reform movements. - The Vaishnavite Movement - Bhakti Movement and Vaishnavism - Developed around the worship of Rama and Krishna, incarnations of Vishnu. - Krishna’s childhood escapades and love for Radha became central themes. - Used allegorically to depict the relationship between the individual soul and the supreme soul. - Chaitanya and Kirtan Tradition - Chaitanya popularized kirtans (musical gatherings) for mystic experience. - Worship emphasized love, devotion, song, and dance, leading to ecstasy. - Open to all, irrespective of caste or creed. - Saint-Poets of Vaishnavism - Their writings transcended caste and religious barriers. - Prominent figures: - Narsinha Mehta (Gujarat) - Meera (Rajasthan) - Surdas (Western Uttar Pradesh) - Chaitanya (Bengal and Orissa) - Inclusivity: Welcomed all devotees, regardless of caste or background. - Chaitanya’s Influence and Journey - Born in Nadia, a Vedantic rationalism center. - At 22, initiated into the Krishna cult in Gaya. - Traveled across India, including Vrindavan, reviving Krishna worship. - Attracted Muslims and lower castes but did not reject scriptures or idol worship. - Philosophical Approach - Rooted in Vedantic monism, emphasizing unity of God and creation. - Influenced by Vallabha, a Tailang Brahmin from the 15th–16th century. - Humanistic approach: Focused on love and beauty in all forms. - While they did not abolish caste, they softened its rigidity. - Connection Between Bhakti and Sufism - Bhakti concepts resembled those of Sufi saints and poets. - 15th century: Ibn-i-Arabi’s monistic ideas gained traction. - Unity of Being (Tauhid-i-Wajudi): All beings are manifestations of the divine. - Influence of Hindu traditions: Sufis engaged with yogis and saints. - Use of Hindi and Sanskrit: Some Sufis, like Malik Muhammad Jaisi, composed in Hindi. - Hindi Bhakti songs were more impactful on Sufis than Persian poetry. - Abdul Wahid Bilgrami: Wrote Haqa’iq-i-Hind, interpreting Bhakti terms in Sufi mysticism. - Common Platform for Religious Unity - By the 15th–16th centuries, Bhakti and Sufi movements had created a shared spiritual space. - Provided a foundation for Akbar’s concept of Tauhid (unity of all religions). - Literature and Fine Arts - Sanskrit Literature - Continued Prominence - Remained a vehicle for higher thought and literary expression. - Production of works was immense, possibly surpassing the previous period. - Flourished in various fields, including: - Philosophy (e.g., Ramanuja, Madhava, Vallabha). - Poetry, drama, fiction, medicine, astronomy, music. - Hindu law (Dharmashastras): Numerous commentaries and digests. - Role in Dissemination of Knowledge - Ideas spread rapidly across the country. - Network of specialized schools and academies existed, even under Muslim rule. - Benefited from the introduction of paper, aiding in: - Reproduction and distribution of texts. - Preservation of Ramayana and Mahabharata texts (11th–12th century). - Major Legal Works - Mitakshara of Vijayaneshwar (one of two principal Hindu law schools) – 12th century. - Chandeshwar of Bihar – Notable 14th-century commentator. - Most legal works produced in South India, Bengal, Mithila, and Western India. - Jain Contributions - The Jains actively contributed to Sanskrit literature. - Hemachandra Suri was the most prominent Jain scholar. - Limited Interaction with Islamic Culture - Sanskrit literature largely ignored the Muslim presence. - Minimal efforts to translate Islamic or Persian works. - Exceptions: - Yusuf and Zulaikha (Persian love story by Jami) translated. - Some works on the astrolabe (used in navigation and astrology) translated. - Arabic and Persian Literature - Arabic Literature - Arabic remained the primary language for: - Islamic scholarship and philosophy. - Scientific works, including some translations into Persian. - Digests of Islamic law, prepared in both Arabic and Persian. - Famous Persian digests: Compiled during Firuz Tughlaq’s reign. - Famous Arabic digest: Fatawa-z-Alamgiri (prepared under Aurangzeb). - Introduction of Persian in India - Turks introduced Persian in India during the 10th century. - Persian had already become the literary and administrative language of Central Asia and Iran. - Persian poets like Firdausi and Sadi flourished between the 10th and 14th centuries. - Lahore became the first centre for Persian literary cultivation in India. - Amir Khusrau: The Pioneer of Indo-Persian Literature - Born in 1252 (Patiali, near Badayun, Western UP). - Took pride in being Indian and praised the land: - “Hindustan is like heaven… greener and more beautiful than Khurasan.” - Developed a unique Persian style called Sabaq-i-Hindi (Style of India). - Wrote historical romances and poetry in multiple forms. - Praised Indian languages, including Hindi (Hindavi). - Participated in Sufi musical gatherings (Sama) with Nizamuddin Auliya. - Died in 1325, soon after Nizamuddin Auliya’s death, and was buried in the same compound. - Growth of Persian Historiography - A strong tradition of history writing in Persian emerged. - Notable historians: - Ziauddin Barani - Aff - Isami - Persian as a Cultural Link - Persian facilitated India’s cultural ties with Central Asia and Iran. - Became the language of administration and diplomacy. - Spread beyond North India as the Delhi Sultanate expanded south. - Sanskrit-Persian Interchange - Initially, minimal interaction between Sanskrit and Persian. - Zia Nakhshabi (d. 1350) pioneered translations from Sanskrit to Persian: - Taz Nama (Book of the Parrot): Popular Sanskrit tale translated into Persian. - Kok Shastra (Indian treatise on sexology). - Under Firuz Shah: - Sanskrit texts on medicine and music were translated into Persian. - Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin of Kashmir: - Commissioned translations of Rajatarangini and Mahabharata into Persian. - Sponsored translations of Sanskrit medical and musical texts. - Some scientific works (mathematics, astronomy, medicine) were also translated into Sanskrit during this period. - Regional Languages - Development of Regional Languages - Several regional languages, such as Hindi, Bengali, and Marathi, originated around the 8th century, while Tamil was much older. - By the 14th century, Amir Khusrau acknowledged their significance, stating: - “These languages have, from ancient times, been applied in every way to the common purposes of life.” - The maturity of these languages and their use in literature became a striking feature of the medieval period. - Factors Behind Their Growth - Decline in Brahminical influence led to a decrease in Sanskrit’s prestige. - Bhakti saints played a crucial role by using these languages in their teachings. - Many early saints helped shape regional languages for literary purposes. - Pre-Turkish regional kingdoms (e.g., Tamil, Kannada, Marathi regions) used local languages alongside Sanskrit for administration. - Even under the Delhi Sultanate, Hindi-knowing accountants were appointed in revenue departments. - Patronage and Administrative Use - After the Delhi Sultanate’s decline, regional languages gained prominence alongside Persian in local administrations. - South India: - Telugu literature thrived under Vijayanagara rulers’ patronage. - Deccan: - Marathi was an administrative language in the Bahmani kingdom and later at Bijapur’s court. - Bengal: - Nusrat Shah commissioned Mahabharata and Ramayana translations into Bengali. - Maladhar Basu translated the Bhagavata into Bengali under royal patronage. - Role of Sufis in Regional Literature - Sufi saints used Hindi Bhakti poetry in their musical gatherings. - In Jaunpur, Sufi poets like Malik Muhammad Jaisi: - Wrote in Hindi, making Sufi concepts accessible to the common people. - Helped popularize Persian poetic forms, such as the masnavi. - Fine Arts: Music and Cultural Integration - Introduction of Persian and Central Asian Musical Traditions - The Turks inherited a rich Arab musical tradition, further refined in Iran and Central Asia. - They introduced several new musical instruments to India, including: - Rabab - Sarangi - They also brought new musical modes and regulations. - Indian music had earlier influenced musical developments at the Caliphs’ court in Baghdad, but systematic interaction began under the Delhi Sultanate. - Amir Khusrau’s Contributions - Amir Khusrau, a master of both music theory and practice, played a key role in musical integration. - He introduced Perso-Arabic ragas, such as: - Aman - Ghora - Senam - He is sometimes credited with inventing the sitar, though there is no concrete evidence. - The tabla, often attributed to him, likely developed much later (late 17th or early 18th century). - Music During the Sultanate Period - Firuz Shah Tughlaq: - Regularly listened to music every Friday after namaz. - Under his reign, the Indian classical work Regadarpan was translated into Persian. - Spread of Music: - Musical gatherings expanded from Sufi abodes to noble courts. - Sultan Husain Sharqi of Jaunpur: - A great patron of music. - Pir Bodhan, a Sufi saint, was the second most renowned musician of the era. - Gwalior as a Musical Hub: - Raja Man Singh of Gwalior was a notable patron. - His court produced the work Mar Kautihal, which documented new musical modes introduced by Muslims. - Differentiation of North and South Indian Music - It is unclear when North and South Indian music diverged. - However, the distinction likely arose due to the incorporation of Perso-Arabic musical elements in North India. - A unique musical style, significantly influenced by Persian music, developed in Kashmir. - Later Patronage and Mughal Influence - After conquering Jaunpur, Sikandar Lodi continued its musical traditions, lavishly supporting musicians. - This patronage of music was later carried forward by the Mughals. - Struggle for Empire in North India—The Mughals and Afghans (1525-1555) - The Political Landscape of Central and West Asia in the Fifteenth Century - The Rise of Timur and His Empire - Following the disintegration of the Mongol Empire in the 14th century, Timur reunited Iran and Turan under a single rule. - His empire stretched from: - The lower Volga to the Indus River - Included Asia Minor (modern Turkey), Iran, Trans-Oxiana, Afghanistan, and part of Punjab - Timur died in 1405, but his grandson Shahrukh Mirza (d. 1448) managed to preserve a large part of the empire. - Under his patronage, Samarkand and Herat became major cultural centers of West Asia. - The ruler of Samarkand held great prestige in the Islamic world. - Decline of the Timurid Empire and the Rise of New Powers - The Timurid tradition of partitioning the empire led to internal conflicts. - As the Timurids weakened, two new forces emerged: 1. The Uzbeks: - A Turko-Mongol tribe that moved into Trans-Oxiana. - Though Muslims, they were looked down upon by the Timurids, who saw them as uncultured barbarians. 2. The Safavids of Iran: - A new Shiite dynasty descended from an order of saints tracing their ancestry to the Prophet. - They persecuted Sunnis, leading to religious conflicts with the Sunni Uzbeks. - Meanwhile, further west, the Ottoman Turks were rising in power, seeking to dominate Eastern Europe, Iraq, and Iran. - This set the stage for the sixteenth-century conflict between the three mighty empires: - Uzbeks - Safavids - Ottomans - Babur’s Struggles and the Uzbek Threat - In 1494, Babur inherited Farghana, a small state in Trans-Oxiana, at just twelve years old. - While the Timurid princes were engaged in internal battles, Babur attempted to capture Samarkand from his uncle. - He briefly occupied the city twice but lost it both times. - In his second attempt, the Uzbek chief Shaibani Khan was called in to remove Babur. - Shaibani defeated Babur, conquered Samarkand, and then overran other Timurid kingdoms. - Babur was forced to retreat to Kabul, which he conquered in 1504. - Babur’s Attempts to Reclaim Samarkand and the Safavid-Uzbek Conflict - For the next 14 years, Babur sought allies to reclaim his homeland from the Uzbeks. - He sought help from his uncle, the ruler of Herat, but was unsuccessful. - Ultimately, Herat also fell to Shaibani Khan, leading to direct conflict between: - The Uzbeks, who controlled Trans-Oxiana. - The Safavids, who claimed Herat and Khurasan. - In 1510, in a famous battle near Merv, Shah Ismail of Iran defeated and killed Shaibani Khan. - Babur’s Brief Rule in Samarkand and Final Uzbek Victory - With Iranian support, Babur recaptured Samarkand. - However, he struggled under Iranian control, as the Safavids treated him as a mere governor of an Iranian province, not an independent ruler. - The Uzbeks quickly recovered, and Babur was once again ousted from Samarkand, forcing him to return to Kabul. - Meanwhile, in 1514, Shah Ismail of Iran was defeated by the Ottoman Sultan, solidifying Uzbek dominance over Trans-Oxiana. - Babur’s Shift Toward India - With no hope of reclaiming Samarkand, Babur was ultimately forced to look toward India as his next conquest. - Babur’s Motivations and Early Attempts to Conquer India - Babur’s Long-Standing Desire to Conquer India - Babur himself stated that from the time he obtained Kabul (1504) until his victory at Panipat (1526), he had never stopped thinking about conquering Hindustan. - However, his plans were delayed due to: - Apprehensions of his degs (loyal followers and soldiers) - Disagreements between his brothers - Like earlier Central Asian invaders, Babur was drawn to India’s immense wealth. - His ancestor, Timur, had: - Plundered a vast treasure from India. - Taken skilled artisans who helped develop his empire and beautify his capital. - Annexed parts of Punjab, which remained under Timur’s successors for generations. - After conquering Afghanistan, Babur considered himself the rightful heir to these areas. - Economic and Strategic Reasons for Babur’s Invasion - Babur’s empire in Badakhshan, Qandhar, and Kabul was not wealthy enough to sustain his army and administration. - Abul Fazl noted that in some territories, military and administrative costs exceeded revenue. - With limited resources, Babur struggled to provide for his followers and feared an Uzbek attack on Kabul. - India was seen as: - A potential place of refuge. - A strategic base for launching operations against the Uzbeks. - Political Situation in Northwest India (Ideal Conditions for Babur’s Invasion) - Sikandar Lodi had died in 1517, and his son Ibrahim Lodi had succeeded him. - Ibrahim Lodi’s attempts to centralize power alienated: - Afghan chiefs - Rajputs - One of the most powerful Afghan chiefs, Daulat Khan Lodi, was the governor of Punjab and nearly independent. - He tried to maintain favor with Ibrahim Lodi by sending his son to court but also expanded his own power by annexing frontier regions like Bhira. - Babur’s Early Campaigns in Punjab - First Expedition (1518-19) - Babur captured the powerful fort of Bhira. - He then sent envoys to both Daulat Khan and Ibrahim Lodi, demanding the return of Turk-controlled territories. - However, Daulat Khan detained Babur’s envoy in Lahore, refusing to either: - Grant an audience - Forward the message to Ibrahim Lodi - After Babur returned to Kabul, Daulat Khan took advantage of his absence, occupied Bhira, and expelled Babur’s men. - Second Expedition (1520-21) - Babur crossed the Indus again and swiftly recaptured Bhira and Sialkot—both key gateways to India. - Lahore also fell to him. - He considered advancing further but was forced to retreat due to: - A revolt in Qandhar - A prolonged siege of Qandhar (lasting 1.5 years), which he successfully ended - With Qandhar secured, Babur was once again free to focus on India. - Invitation from Indian Nobles and Final Preparations - Around this time, Babur received an embassy from Daulat Khan Lodi, led by his son Dilawar Khan. - They invited Babur to invade India, arguing that: - Ibrahim Lodi was a tyrant. - He had lost the support of nobles. - Additionally, it is believed that Rana Sanga of Mewar also sent a separate invitation urging Babur to invade. - These appeals convinced Babur that the time was ripe to seize Punjab—if not all of India. - Final Conquest of Punjab (1525) - In 1525, while Babur was at Peshawar, he received news that: - Daulat Khan had switched sides again. - He had gathered 30,000-40,000 troops. - He had ousted Babur’s men from Sialkot and was advancing toward Lahore. - However, when Babur marched toward Lahore, Daulat Khan’s army quickly disbanded. - Daulat Khan surrendered and was pardoned. - Within three weeks of crossing the Indus, Babur became the undisputed master of Punjab. - The Battle of Panipat (20 April 1526) - Prelude to the Battle - A conflict between Babur and Ibrahim Lodi was inevitable. - Babur marched towards Delhi, and Ibrahim Lodi met him at Panipat with: - 100,000 men (though the actual number of fighting men was lower due to servants). - 1,000 elephants. - Babur had crossed the Indus with 12,000 men, but his forces increased due to: - Reinforcements from his army in India. - Support from Hindustani nobles and soldiers in Punjab. - Despite this, Babur’s army was still numerically inferior. - Babur’s Battle Preparations - To strengthen his position, Babur: - Anchored one wing of his army against Panipat’s buildings. - Protected the other wing with a ditch filled with tree branches. - Constructed a defensive wall using lashed-together carts. - Built breastworks between carts for resting guns and firing. - This setup was called the Ottoman (Rumi) device, inspired by the Ottoman victory over Shah Ismail of Iran. - Babur had two Ottoman master-gunners, Ustad Ali and Mustafa, which gave him a significant advantage. - Although gunpowder was known in India, its widespread use in artillery only became common with Babur. - The Battle Begins - Ibrahim Lodi was unaware of Babur’s strongly fortified position. - He had expected Babur to engage in mobile warfare, characteristic of Central Asians, involving rapid advances and retreats. - After seven or eight days of skirmishing, Ibrahim Lodi finally mobilized for battle. - His forces hesitated upon seeing Babur’s strong defenses. - While Ibrahim was still reorganizing his troops, Babur’s flanking forces attacked from the side and rear. - Babur’s Tactical Superiority - Babur’s gunners effectively used firearms from the front. - However, Babur credited much of his victory to his bowmen. - Interestingly, he made little mention of Ibrahim Lodi’s elephants, suggesting they played a minor role in the battle. - The Battle’s Climax - Despite early setbacks, Ibrahim Lodi’s army fought bravely. - The battle lasted two to three hours. - Ibrahim Lodi fought to the end, surrounded by 5,900–6,000 men. - More than 15,000 of Ibrahim Lodi’s soldiers were killed in the battle. - Impact of the Battle - Decisive Consequences - The Battle of Panipat is considered one of the most decisive battles in Indian history. - It: - Destroyed Lodi power. - Gave Babur control over Delhi and Agra. - Secured immense treasures stored by Ibrahim Lodi in Agra, solving Babur’s financial problems. - Left rich territories up to Jaipur open for Babur’s expansion. - Challenges After the Victory - Despite his success, Babur still had to fight two major battles to consolidate his rule: 1. Against Rana Sanga of Mewar. 2. Against the eastern Afghans. - Thus, Panipat was not politically decisive, as further conflicts were necessary to secure Babur’s empire. - Its real significance lay in: - Introducing modern warfare techniques (gunpowder and artillery) in India. - Opening a new phase in North India’s power struggle. - Post-Battle Difficulties - Babur faced multiple challenges after his victory: - Many of his begs (nobles) were unwilling to stay in India for long. - The hot climate and unfamiliar conditions increased their reluctance. - The Indian population showed hostility, abandoning villages in fear of Mughal armies—a reaction to Timur’s past plundering. - Babur’s Firm Stand - Babur understood that India’s wealth was necessary to build a strong empire and satisfy his followers. - He declared: - “Not for us the poverty of Kabul again!” - He firmly proclaimed his intention to stay in India. - Allowed those who wished to return to Kabul to leave, clearing internal tensions. - However, Babur’s presence in India alarmed Rana Sanga, who began preparing for a confrontation. - The Battle of Khanwa (1527) - Background and Causes - Conflict over Eastern Rajasthan and Malwa: - Rana Sanga and Ibrahim Lodi had been competing for dominance in this region. - After defeating Mahmud Khalji of Malwa, Rana Sanga’s influence extended up to Piliya Khar, near Agra. - Babur’s establishment of an Indo-Gangetic empire threatened Rana Sanga’s ambitions. - Sanga began preparations to either expel Babur or confine him to Punjab. - Babur’s Accusation of Betrayal: - Babur claimed Rana Sanga had invited him to India, promising to join him against Ibrahim Lodi. - However, Sanga made no move while Babur conquered Delhi and Agra. - It is unclear what precise promises Sanga made: - He may have hoped for prolonged warfare, allowing him to seize desired territories. - He may have assumed Babur, like Timur, would plunder Delhi and retreat. - Babur’s decision to stay in India changed the political situation completely. - Formation of the Anti-Babur Alliance - Many Afghans, including Mahmud Lodi (Ibrahim Lodi’s younger brother), joined Sanga, hoping to restore Afghan rule in Delhi. - Hasan Khan Mewati, the ruler of Mewat, also allied with Sanga. - Almost all prominent Rajput rulers sent troops to fight under Sanga. - Babur’s Response and Preparations - Morale Crisis in Babur’s Army: - Rana Sanga’s reputation and early victories against outlying Mughal posts (e.g., Bayana) demoralized Babur’s soldiers. - To rally his troops, Babur: - Declared the war against Sanga a jihad. - On the eve of battle, smashed all wine jars and flasks to prove his religious commitment. - Banned the sale and consumption of wine across his domains. - Abolished customs taxes for Muslims. - Strategic Fortifications at Khanwa: - Babur chose a defensive site at Khanwa, 40 km from Agra. - His defensive setup resembled Panipat’s strategy: - Wagons lashed together as an outer bastion. - A trench dug in front for added protection. - Gaps left for musketeers to fire and advance behind wheeled tripods. - The Battle - Sanga’s Forces and Initial Attacks: - Babur estimated Sanga’s army at over 200,000, including: - 10,000 Afghan cavalry. - A force of equal size from Hasan Khan Mewati. - While these figures may be exaggerated, Babur’s army was definitely outnumbered. - Sanga launched a fierce attack on Babur’s right, nearly breaching his defenses. - Babur’s Counterattack and Victory: - Mughal artillery inflicted heavy casualties on Sanga’s forces. - As Sanga’s forces began to weaken, Babur: - Ordered a central charge, with troops advancing from behind their tripods. - Pushed forward artillery, supported by chained wagons. - Used his flanking parties to attack from the side and rear, similar to his tactics at Panipat. - Sanga’s army was surrounded and suffered massive losses. - Rana Sanga escaped but later died—poisoned by his own nobles, who feared continuing the war would be disastrous. - Consequences of the Battle - End of Sanga’s Dream of a Rajput Empire - Rana Sanga was one of the bravest warriors of Rajasthan, but his death shattered the vision of a united Rajputana extending up to Agra. - Babur’s Consolidation of Power - Secured Mughal control over the Delhi-Agra region. - Strengthened his hold by capturing Gwalior, Dholpur, and other forts east of Agra. - Annexed large parts of Alwar, previously ruled by Hasan Khan Mewati. - Further Campaigns and Setbacks - Led a campaign against Medini Rai of Chanderi in Malwa. - Chanderi fell after a fierce battle—the Rajput defenders fought to the last man, while their women committed jauhar. - Babur’s plans for further expansion were cut short due to rising Afghan activities in eastern Uttar Pradesh. - Consequences of the Afghan Resistance and Babur’s Final Campaign - Afghan Resistance and Threats - Despite their defeat, the Afghans in eastern Uttar Pradesh had not accepted Mughal rule. - Afghan chiefs, initially loyal to Babur, were ready to revolt when given the opportunity. - Nusrat Shah, the ruler of Bengal and son-in-law of Ibrahim Lodi, supported the Afghan resurgence. - The Afghans expelled Mughal officials and advanced as far as Kanauj. - Their primary weakness was the absence of a strong, unifying leader. - Mahmud Lodi’s Leadership and Babur’s Response - Mahmud Lodi, Ibrahim Lodi’s brother and a former commander at Khanwa, arrived in Bihar. - The Afghans hailed him as their ruler, rallying behind him for another challenge to Mughal rule. - Recognizing the growing threat, Babur marched east from Agra in early 1529. - Battle of Ghagra (1529) and Its Aftermath - Babur crossed the Ganga near Banaras and confronted the combined forces of the Afghans and Nusrat Shah of Bengal at the river Ghagra. - Despite crossing the river and forcing the enemy to retreat, Babur could not secure a decisive victory. - His declining health and concerns about Central Asia led him to negotiate peace. - Peace Settlements and Babur’s Final Days - Babur made a nominal claim of suzerainty over Bihar but left most of it under Afghan control. - He signed a treaty with Nusrat Shah of Bengal, avoiding further conflict. - Shortly after, Babur fell seriously ill and died near Lahore while on his way to Kabul. - Significance of Babur’s Advent into India - Strategic and Economic Impact - Integrated Kabul and Qandhar into the Indian empire for the first time since the Kushan era. - Secured India from external invasions for nearly 200 years by controlling key entry points. - Strengthened India’s foreign trade, as Kabul and Qandhar served as caravan hubs for China and Mediterranean trade routes. - Political and Military Contributions - Destroyed the balance of power in north India by defeating the Lodis and the Rajput confederacy led by Rana Sanga. - Took a major step toward establishing an all-India empire, though further consolidation was needed. - Introduced advanced warfare by demonstrating the effectiveness of artillery and cavalry. - Led to the rapid popularization of gunpowder and artillery in India, favoring rulers with strong resources and marking the decline of small kingdoms. - Reinforcement of the Crown’s Prestige - Re-established the authority of the Crown, which had weakened since the death of Firuz Tughlaq. - Unlike the Lodis, Babur’s authority was unquestioned due to his lineage from Changez Khan and Timur. - None of his nobles could claim an equal status, ensuring a stable monarchy. - Personal Leadership and Character - Earned the loyalty of his begs through personal courage and shared hardships. - Led by example—once personally helped soldiers clear deep snow for passage during a harsh winter. - Balanced a love for wine and camaraderie with strict discipline and high expectations from his nobles. - Showed instances of extreme cruelty, such as making towers of skulls from enemies, though reflective of his era. - Religious and Cultural Policies - Though an orthodox Sunni, Babur was not a bigot and avoided religious conflicts in his court. - His declaration of jihad against Rana Sanga was politically motivated rather than religious. - No widespread evidence of temple destruction under his rule—mosques built at Sambhal and Ayodhya may have only been repairs. - Patronage of Literature and Arts - A prolific writer in Persian, Arabic, and Turkish, with the Tuzuk-i-Baburi being a literary classic. - Translated Sufi works and wrote poetry (masnavi). - Maintained connections with leading poets and artists of the time. - Passionate about nature, documenting India’s flora and fauna in detail. - Established the tradition of Mughal gardens with running water. - Legacy and Concept of the Mughal State - Defined the Mughal state as one based on a strong monarchy, free from religious bigotry. - Emphasized cultural and artistic patronage alongside military and administrative strength. - Set a precedent for his successors, shaping the future of Mughal rule in India. - Humayun’s Conquest of Gujarat and Struggle with Sher Shah - Challenges Faced by Humayun - Succeeded Babur in December 1530 at the age of 23. - Faced multiple problems: - Unstable administration and precarious finances. - The Afghans were not subdued and still hoped to expel the Mughals. - The Timurid tradition of partitioning the empire among brothers threatened unity. - Babur had advised kindness towards brothers but opposed partitioning the empire. - Kamran’s Expansion and Its Impact - At the time of Humayun’s accession, the empire included Kabul, Qandhar, and Badakhshan. - Kamran, Humayun’s younger brother, controlled Kabul and Qandhar but sought more territory. - He marched on Lahore and Multan, occupying them. - Humayun, to avoid civil war, accepted this and formally granted Punjab and Multan to Kamran. - This allowed Humayun to focus on the eastern threats without worrying about the western frontier. - Conflict with the Afghans and Sher Khan - The Afghan power was growing rapidly in the east. - In 1532, at Dadrah, Humayun defeated the Afghans, who had conquered Bihar and overrun Jaunpur. - Besieged Chunar, a key fort controlling routes to eastern India. - Sher Khan, an Afghan leader, held Chunar and negotiated peace by: - Retaining the fort while pledging loyalty to the Mughals. - Sending his son as a hostage. - Humayun, anxious about Bahadur Shah’s rising power, accepted the deal. - Bahadur Shah of Gujarat – A Rising Threat - Bahadur Shah, nearly the same age as Humayun, was ambitious and capable. - Came to power in 1526, conquered Malwa, and then besieged Chittor. - Fear of Mughal intervention forced him to sign a treaty with the Rajputs. - Humayun, meanwhile, spent time building Dinpanah in Delhi, which was criticized as a distraction. - However, Dinpanah was meant to: - Serve as a second capital if Agra was threatened. - Impress both friends and enemies. - In the meantime, Bahadur Shah conquered Ajmer and overran eastern Rajasthan. - Battle Against Bahadur Shah - Bahadur Shah gave refuge to Mughal enemies and supplied arms to Tatar Khan, cousin of Ibrahim Lodi. - Tatar Khan planned an invasion of Agra with 40,000 troops, but Humayun easily defeated him. - Determined to eliminate the threat from Gujarat, Humayun invaded Malwa. - Bahadur Shah avoided battle, abandoning Chittor and fortifying Mandsor. - Humayun’s cautious tactics forced Bahadur Shah to flee to Mandu, leaving behind: - Spiked guns (rendering them useless). - Wealth and military equipment. - Humayun captured Mandu, then pursued Bahadur Shah to Champaner, scaling its fort walls himself. - Bahadur Shah fled to Ahmedabad and finally to Kathiawar. - As a result, Malwa and Gujarat, along with their rich treasures, fell under Mughal control. - Loss of Gujarat and Malwa - Gujarat was placed under Askari, Humayun’s younger brother. - Humayun retired to Mandu, considering it a central and favorable location. - Problems arose: - People’s deep loyalty to Gujarati rule. - Askari’s inexperience and divided Mughal nobility. - Popular uprisings and military counterattacks. - Bahadur Shah’s power quickly revived, and Askari was forced to retreat to Champaner. - Fear arose that Askari might attempt to seize Agra or form his own empire. - To prevent this, Humayun: - Abandoned Malwa and pursued Askari. - Overtook him in Rajasthan, reconciled, and returned to Agra together. - Meanwhile, both Gujarat and Malwa were lost. - Outcome of the Gujarat Campaign - The campaign did not expand Mughal territory but neutralized Bahadur Shah as a threat. - Allowed Humayun to focus on Sher Khan and the Afghans. - Bahadur Shah later drowned in a scuffle with the Portuguese, permanently ending the threat from Gujarat. - Humayun’s Struggle Against Sher Shah and His Downfall - Strengthening of Sher Khan’s Position (1535–1537) - During Humayun’s Malwa campaign (Feb 1535 – Feb 1537), Sher Khan consolidated his power. - He became the undisputed ruler of Bihar, attracting Afghan support from across India. - Though he continued to profess loyalty to the Mughals, he systematically planned their expulsion. - He maintained close ties with Bahadur Shah of Gujarat, receiving heavy subsidies. - With these resources, he built a large, efficient army, including 1,200 elephants. - Shortly after Humayun’s return to Agra, Sher Khan used his strengthened army to defeat the Bengal king and force him to pay an indemnity of 1,300,000 dinars. - Humayun’s Chunar Campaign and Sher Khan’s Bengal Conquest - Humayun, realizing the strategic importance of Chunar, besieged the fort towards the end of the year. - The fort, strongly defended by Afghans, took six months to capture despite master-gunner Rumi Khan’s efforts. - Meanwhile, Sher Khan seized the powerful Rohtas Fort through treachery, ensuring his family’s safety. - He then invaded Bengal a second time and captured its capital, Gaur. - By this maneuvering, Sher Khan completely outwitted Humayun. - Humayun’s Miscalculation and the Bengal Expedition - Humayun failed to recognize that he lacked the necessary strength to confront Sher Khan. - Sher Khan offered a deal: he would surrender Bihar and pay an annual tribute of 10 lakh dinars if allowed to retain Bengal. - Humayun rejected this offer, unwilling to concede Bengal’s wealth, trade significance, and strategic position. - The wounded Bengal king, seeking refuge with Humayun, encouraged resistance but soon succumbed to his injuries. - Humayun thus undertook the Bengal campaign alone, leading to a disastrous sequence of events. - Disaster at Chausa (March 1539) - Sher Khan strategically allowed Humayun to advance into Bengal unopposed, intending to cut off his communications. - Humayun reached Gaur and established order but remained unaware of Sher Khan’s movements. - Meanwhile, his younger brother Hindal Mirza (Babur's youngest son) attempted to seize the Mughal throne at Agra, isolating Humayun further. - After a stay of 3–4 months, Humayun began his return journey. - Despite monsoon challenges, discontent among nobles, and constant Afghan attacks, Humayun managed to reach Chausa near Buxar. - His brother Kamran, who had marched from Lahore to Agra to suppress Hindal’s rebellion, refused to send reinforcements. - Sher Khan’s Deception and Humayun’s Tactical Mistake - Misled by a false peace offer from Sher Khan, Humayun crossed to the eastern bank of the Karamasa River. - The Afghan horsemen took advantage of this mistake and launched a surprise attack. - The battle turned into a catastrophe for the Mughals. - Humayun barely escaped, swimming across the river with the help of a water carrier. - Sher Khan captured immense booty, and around 7,000 Mughal soldiers, including prominent nobles, perished. - Final Defeat at Kanauj (May 1540) and Humayun’s Exile - After Chausa, Humayun’s only hope lay in unity among the Timurid princes. - Kamran commanded a seasoned army of 10,000 troops in Agra but refused to aid Humayun, doubting his leadership. - Humayun, in turn, refused to entrust Kamran with military command, fearing a power grab. - The growing distrust led Kamran to withdraw to Lahore with most of his troops. - The weakened Mughal army faced Sher Khan at Kanauj in May 1540. - Despite fierce resistance from Humayun’s brothers, Askari and Hindal, the Mughals suffered a decisive defeat. - This battle sealed Sher Khan’s victory and left Humayun without a kingdom. - Wandering and Seeking Support (1540–1545) - With Kabul and Qandhar under Kamran’s control, Humayun wandered across Sindh and neighboring regions for over two years. - He sought assistance from various rulers, including Maldeo of Marwar, but was unsuccessful. - His brothers turned against him, even attempting to imprison or kill him. - Despite these hardships, Humayun displayed remarkable resilience and fortitude. - Eventually, he sought refuge in Iran, where he gained the support of the Persian ruler. - With Persian aid, he recaptured Qandhar and Kabul in 1545. - Causes of Humayun’s Defeat - Underestimation of Afghan Strength: - Humayun failed to grasp the resilience of Afghan power in North India. - Lack of Local Support: - Unlike the Afghans, the Mughals did not win over local rulers and zamindars, leaving them numerically weak. - Disunity Among the Timurids: - Though initially loyal, Humayun’s brothers turned against him after Sher Khan’s victories. - Strategic and Tactical Mistakes: - His ill-planned Bengal campaign and misjudgment at Chausa exposed his military weaknesses. - Superiority of Sher Khan: - Sher Khan proved to be a more capable general and strategist than Humayun. - Humayun’s Later Years and Death - Humayun’s life was marked by extreme reversals—falling from power and later regaining it. - In 1555, following the collapse of the Sur empire, he managed to recover Delhi. - However, his return to power was short-lived. - In 1556, he died after falling from the first floor of his library in Delhi. - His favorite wife commissioned a magnificent mausoleum for him near the Delhi fort. - The tomb, known as Humayun’s Tomb, introduced a new architectural style in North India, particularly its grand marble dome. - Sher Shah and the Sur Empire (1540-1555) - Early Life and Rise to Power - Sher Shah was born as Farid, son of a small jagirdar in Jaunpur. - He gained administrative experience by managing his father’s jagir. - After the defeat and death of Ibrahim Lodi, he emerged as an important Afghan sardar. - The title “Sher Khan” was given to him for either killing a tiger or for his services. - Before Babur’s death, he became the de facto ruler of Bihar and played a key role in Afghan politics. - Expansion of the Sur Empire - Sher Shah’s empire was the largest in North India since Muhammad bin Tughlaq, stretching from Bengal to the Indus (excluding Kashmir). - In the west, he conquered Malwa and most of Rajasthan. - Malwa Campaign and the Puran Mal Incident - Malwa was in a weak state and could not resist Sher Shah. - Puran Mal, the Rajput ruler of Chanderi, vacated his fort under a promise of safe conduct. - However, he and 1,000 Rajput followers were treacherously attacked and killed along with their families. - Contemporary theologians justified this act, claiming no faith was needed with infidels. - Conflict with Maldeo of Marwar - Maldeo (ruler of Marwar, since 1532) expanded his control over western and northern Rajasthan. - He clashed with Mewar and other neighboring rulers. - His conquest of Bikaner forced Kalyan Das, Bhim, and Biram Deo to seek refuge at Sher Shah’s court. - Maldeo’s centralizing ambitions were seen as a threat by Delhi and Agra. - Battle of Samel (1544) - Rajput and Afghan forces clashed at Samel (between Ajmer and Jodhpur). - Maldeo withdrew after suspecting disloyalty among his sardars, influenced by Sher Shah’s ruse of dropping fake letters near his camp. - Some Rajput sardars refused to retreat and attacked Sher Shah’s center. - Despite early Rajput success, superior Afghan numbers and gunfire led to their defeat. - Aftermath and Rajasthan’s Conquest - The battle sealed Rajasthan’s fate. - Sher Shah besieged and captured Ajmer and Jodhpur. - Maldeo took refuge in Siwana and died shortly afterward. - The Rana of Mewar surrendered, sending the keys of Chittor to Sher Shah, who established outposts up to Mount Abu. - Within ten months, Sher Shah overran nearly all of Rajasthan. - Final Campaign and Death (1545) - Sher Shah’s last campaign was against Kalinjar, a crucial Bundelkhand fort. - During the siege, a gun explosion severely injured him. - He died in 1545, shortly after hearing of the fort’s capture. - Succession and Fall of the Sur Empire - Islam Shah (Sher Shah’s second son) ruled until 1553. - He was capable, but his reign was troubled by rebellions and Afghan tribal conflicts. - Fear of a Mughal invasion further weakened his rule. - His premature death led to a civil war among his successors. - This allowed Humayun to reclaim his empire in 1555 after defeating the Afghans in two major battles. - Sher Shah’s Legacy - Architecture and City Building - He was a great builder: - His tomb at Sasaram is regarded as a masterpiece of architecture. - He built a new city near Delhi, of which only Purana Qila (Old Fort) and its mosque survive. - Patronage of Literature - Sher Shah patronized scholars and poets. - Notable works during his reign include Padmavat by Malik Muhammad Jaisi. - Religious Policies - Sher Shah was not a bigot, as reflected in his social and economic policies. - Neither he nor Islam Shah depended on the ulama, though they respected them. - However, religious justifications were used for political actions, as seen in: - The treacherous killing of Puran Mal after he vacated Raisen Fort on the promise of safety. - He did not introduce new liberal policies: - Jizyah continued to be collected from Hindus. - His nobility was almost exclusively Afghan. - Empire features and contribution to India: Governance, Economy, and Legacy - Continuity with the Delhi Sultanate - The Sur Empire can be seen as a continuation and culmination of the Delhi Sultanate, with the rule of Babur and Humayun acting as an interregnum. - Sher Shah centralized power, continuing the administrative machinery of the Sultanate period. - Law and Order - Sher Shah re-established law and order throughout his empire. - He sternly dealt with robbers, dacoits, and zamindars who refused to pay revenue or disobeyed government orders. - His historian Abbas Khan Sarwani noted that zamindars were so cowed down that no one dared to rebel or harass travelers. - Trade, Communication, and Infrastructure - Roads and Sarais - Sher Shah revived and extended the Grand Trunk Road from the Indus River to Bengal. - He built roads connecting Agra, Jodhpur, Chittor, and Gujarat’s seaports. - Another major road linked Lahore to Multan, serving as a gateway to West and Central Asia. - 1,700 sarais (inns) were built at 8 km intervals, providing: - Fortified lodging for travelers. - Separate accommodations for Hindus and Muslims. - Brahmins appointed to provide food for Hindus and grain for their horses. - Many sarais evolved into market towns and also served as dak-chowkis (news stations). - Customs Reforms - Sher Shah streamlined customs duties, allowing payments only at: - Sikrigali (Bengal) for goods from Bengal and Bihar. - The Indus for goods from West and Central Asia. - No additional levies were imposed on roads, ferries, or towns. - Merchants were respected, and if one died, his property was not confiscated. - Currency and Standardization - He introduced a uniform currency, including gold, silver, and copper coins. - The silver rupee became the standard currency for centuries. - Weights and measures were standardized, facilitating trade and commerce. - Administration - Administrative Divisions - Pargana (district level): Managed by a shiqdar (administrator) and a munsif (revenue officer). - Sarkar (province level): Managed by a shiqdar-i-shiqdaran and a munsif-i-munsifan. - These divisions were not new, only the titles changed. - Over-Centralization of Power - Sher Shah’s direct involvement in governance was both a strength and a weakness. - While he worked tirelessly and personally toured the empire, his over-centralization created difficulties after his death. - Land Revenue System - Sher Shah insisted on land measurement before fixing the state’s share, set at one-third of the produce. - Peasants could pay in cash or kind, though cash was preferred. - All records of land, crops, and payments were maintained in a document called “patea” for transparency. - A cess was collected to safeguard against famine and natural disasters. - He was concerned about the peasantry, believing that excessive oppression would lead to desertion of villages and economic decline. - Military Reforms - Sher Shah directly recruited soldiers and maintained proper records. - His army included: - 150,000 cavalry - 25,000 infantry - 5,000 elephants - A well-equipped artillery park - He established cantonments across the empire and maintained strong garrisons. - Justice System - Sher Shah believed that “Justice is the most excellent of religious rites”. - He punished oppressors regardless of their rank. - Village panchayats and zamindars handled local cases, while qaadis (judges) were appointed for judicial matters. -
