The Ottomans had a strong navy and were engaged in naval conflicts against European fleets in the Mediterranean. - The Mughals lacked a powerful navy, limiting potential cooperation. - More importantly, the Mughals were wary of acknowledging Ottoman superiority, as the Ottoman Sultan claimed to be the Caliph’s successor. - Conclusion: Key Factors Shaping Mughal Foreign Policy - Hostility toward the Uzbeks due to their historical conflicts. - Strategic alliance with the Safavids to counter the Uzbeks and facilitate trade. - Maintaining distance from the Ottomans, avoiding submission to their Caliphal authority. - Geopolitical balancing to prevent over-dependence on any single power. - These considerations defined the Mughal foreign policy and influenced their diplomatic and military strategies in the region. - Akbar and the Uzbeks - Early Mughal-Uzbek Rivalry and Safavid Influence - 1510: The Safavids defeated Uzbek chief Shaibani Khan, allowing Babur to briefly regain Samarkand. - However, the Uzbeks later defeated the Persians, forcing Babur to abandon Samarkand. - Despite this setback, Persian assistance to Babur established a tradition of friendship between the Mughals and the Safavids. - Later, Humayun also received help from Shah Tahmasp (Safavid ruler) when he sought refuge after losing India to Sher Shah Suri. - Rise of the Uzbeks under Abdullah Khan and Akbar’s Diplomatic Response - 1570s: Abdullah Khan Uzbek expanded his power rapidly. - 1572–73: He seized Balkh, which, along with Badakhshan, had served as a buffer between the Mughals and the Uzbeks. - 1577: He sent an embassy to Akbar, proposing to partition Iran following the death of Shah Tahmasp (1576), which had thrown Iran into disorder. - Abdullah Khan’s Proposal: - Urged Akbar to join a Sunni alliance to invade Iran and liberate Iraq, Khurasan, and Fars from the Safavid “innovators” (Shias). - Approached the Ottoman Sultan with a similar proposal. - Akbar’s Strategic Response - Refused to engage in sectarian conflicts, emphasizing that differences in law and religion were not sufficient grounds for conquest. - Rejected Abdullah Khan’s derogatory remarks against the Safavids, citing the long-standing Mughal-Safavid friendship. - Justified his stance by highlighting that after the conquest of Gujarat, a new route for Hajj pilgrims had been established, eliminating concerns about religious travel restrictions. - Sent an embassy to Abdullah Khan, making it clear that the Mughals had no interest in a war against Iran. - Akbar’s Growing Interest in Central Asia - Granted asylum to Timurid prince Mirza Sulaiman, who had been ousted from Badakhshan by his grandson. - To facilitate Mughal movements, the Khyber Pass was improved for wheeled traffic. - Fear of a Mughal invasion made the gates of Balkh remain closed most of the time. - Uzbeks Instigate Unrest on the Northwest Frontier - To forestall a Mughal invasion of Badakhshan, Abdullah Khan instigated unrest among frontier tribes through an agent named Jalal, a religious fanatic. - The situation worsened to the extent that Akbar had to personally move to Attock. - During these operations, Raja Birbal (Akbar’s close friend) was killed in a battle in the Khyber Pass. - Direct Mughal-Uzbek Border and the Hindukush Agreement - 1585: Abdullah Khan suddenly conquered Badakhshan, prompting both Mirza Sulaiman and his grandson to seek refuge at Akbar’s court. - In the same year, with the death of Mirza Hakim (Akbar’s half-brother), Kabul was annexed into the Mughal Empire. - This marked the first direct border between the Mughals and the Uzbeks. - Diplomatic Engagements Between Akbar and Abdullah Khan - Abdullah Khan sent another embassy to Akbar, who was stationed at Attock on the Indus River. - Akbar’s continued presence near the frontier unsettled Abdullah Khan. - Meanwhile, the Uzbeks successfully captured Khurasan from Iran, reducing the immediate Persian threat. - The Hindukush Agreement (1585–1595) - Akbar chose diplomacy over war and sent an envoy to Abdullah Khan with a letter and a verbal message. - A mutual agreement was reached: - The Hindukush Mountains were established as the boundary between the two empires. - Mughals relinquished claims over Badakhshan and Balkh (formerly ruled by Timurid princes until 1585). - In return, the Uzbeks agreed not to lay claim to Kabul and Qandhar. - Although neither side formally abandoned its claims, this agreement secured a defensible frontier for the Mughals. - 1595: Akbar further strengthened his hold on the frontier by acquiring Qandhar. - End of the Uzbek Threat and Akbar’s Return to Agra - 1586 onwards: Akbar remained in Lahore to monitor the frontier situation. - 1598: With the death of Abdullah Khan Uzbek, the Uzbek power fragmented into warring principalities. - This eliminated the Uzbek threat for a considerable period, allowing Akbar to return to Agra. - Relations with Iran and the Question of Qandhar - Mughal-Safavid Relations and the Uzbek Factor - The fear of Uzbek power was the primary reason for the alliance between the Mughals and the Safavids, despite: - Uzbek efforts to incite anti-Shia sentiments against Iran. - Mughal disapproval of the intolerant policies of the Safavids. - The only contentious issue between them was Qandhar, which both claimed on strategic, economic, sentimental, and prestige grounds. - Historically, Qandhar had been a part of the Timurid Empire, ruled by Babur’s cousins in Herat, until the Uzbeks ousted them in 1507. - Strategic and Economic Importance of Qandhar - Vital for the defense of Kabul: - The fort of Qandhar was one of the strongest in the region, with ample water supply. - Located at the junction of roads leading to Kabul and Herat, it dominated southern Afghanistan. - A modern commentator remarked: “The Kabul-Ghazni-Qandhar line represented a strategic and logical frontier; beyond Kabul and Khyber, there was no natural line of defense. Moreover, the possession of Qandhar made it easier to control the Afghan and Baluch tribes.” - Increasing Mughal Interest in Qandhar: - After Akbar conquered Sindh and Baluchistan, Qandhar’s strategic and economic importance grew further. - It was a fertile province and a key hub for trade between India and Central Asia. - The route through Qandhar to Multan and the Indus River gained significance as Iran’s internal conflicts frequently disrupted traditional trade routes. - Akbar also highlighted Qandhar’s importance as an alternative pilgrimage and trade route to Mecca in his discussions with Abdullah Uzbek. - For the Safavids, Qandhar was less crucial: - Though an important outpost, it was not a vital part of Persia’s defense system, unlike its significance for the Mughals. - Early Mughal-Safavid Control Over Qandhar - 1522: Babur captured Qandhar while Uzbeks threatened Khurasan. - Mid-16th century: Shah Tahmasp seized Qandhar after Humayun’s death. - Akbar did not initially attempt to retake it, as it did not impact Mughal security at the time. - The situation changed when Abdullah Uzbek’s expansion threatened both Iran and the Mughals. - Mughal Conquest of Qandhar (1595) and Aftermath - 1595: Akbar recaptured Qandhar, not as part of an anti-Persian agreement with the Uzbeks, but to: - Establish a defensible northwestern frontier. - Counter the Uzbek advance, since by then, Khurasan had fallen under Uzbek control, cutting off Qandhar from Persia. - Despite this conquest, Mughal-Safavid relations remained cordial. - Jahangir, Shah Abbas I, and the Persian Reconquest of Qandhar (1622) - Shah Abbas I (ruled 1588–1625), one of the greatest Safavid rulers, sought good relations with the Mughals. - Regular exchange of embassies and gifts occurred between him and Jahangir. - Established diplomatic and commercial ties with the Deccan Sultanates, which Jahangir did not object to. - Cultural relations between the two empires deepened, with Nur Jahan playing an active role. - A famous Mughal painting depicts Jahangir and Shah Abbas embracing, symbolizing their perceived friendship. - 1620: Shah Abbas demanded the return of Qandhar and prepared for an invasion. - Jahangir was caught off guard, as he was diplomatically isolated and militarily unprepared. - Though efforts were made to fortify Qandhar, Shah Jahan’s unrealistic demands for leading the campaign caused delays. - 1622: Persia recaptured Qandhar. - Aftermath of the Loss: - Shah Abbas attempted to smooth tensions by sending a lavish embassy and offering diplomatic justifications, which Jahangir formally accepted. - However, the cordiality in Mughal-Safavid relations ended after this event. - Shah Jahan’s Recapture of Qandhar (1638) - 1629: After Shah Abbas’ death, Iran faced internal disturbances. - 1638: - After resolving his Deccan campaigns, Shah Jahan persuaded Ali Mardan Khan (Persian governor of Qandhar) to defect to the Mughal side. - Thus, Qandhar was restored to the Mughals. - The Balkh Campaign and Mughal-Uzbek Relations - Background: Mughal Concerns and the Uzbek Threat - Shah Jahan’s conquest of Qandhar was only a step toward a larger goal: securing the northwestern frontier from recurrent Uzbek attacks. - The Uzbeks, under Nazr Muhammad (ruler of Bokhara and Balkh) and his son Abdul Aziz, were ambitious and frequently raided Kabul and Ghazni, aided by Afghan tribes. - The Mughal court viewed these incursions as a serious threat to stability in Kabul and the Khyber Pass region. - Mughal Intervention and Initial Advances (1646) - Nazr Muhammad’s appeal for help: - Following a rebellion by his son Abdul Aziz, Nazr Muhammad retained only Balkh and sought Mughal assistance. - Shah Jahan, now secure from Persian threats, accepted the appeal. - Deployment of Mughal forces: - Shah Jahan moved from Lahore to Kabul and sent a large Mughal army under Prince Murad (his son) to support Nazr Muhammad. - The army composition: - 50,000 cavalry, 10,000 infantry - Included musketeers, rocketeers, gunners, and a Rajput contingent - Departed from Kabul in mid-1646 - Shah Jahan’s strategy: - Murad was instructed to treat Nazr Muhammad with respect and restore Balkh to him if he remained submissive. - If Nazr Muhammad wished to reclaim Samarqand and Bokhara, the Mughals were to assist him. - The broader objective: Establish a Mughal-friendly ruler in Bokhara. - Setbacks: Prince Murad’s Miscalculations - Murad’s impatience led to diplomatic failure: - Instead of waiting for coordination with Nazr Muhammad, Murad marched on Balkh unilaterally. - Ordered his men to enter Nazr Muhammad’s fort, causing Nazr Muhammad to flee. - This forced the Mughals to occupy Balkh, but they faced a hostile and uncooperative local population. - Rising Uzbek resistance: - Abdul Aziz rallied Uzbek tribes in Transoxiana. - Raised an army of 120,000 men across the Oxus River to challenge the Mughals. - Mughal Victory under Prince Aurangzeb (1647) - Aurangzeb replaces Prince Murad: - Murad, eager to return home, was replaced by Prince Aurangzeb. - The Mughals did not defend the Oxus directly (as it was easily fordable) but instead: - Stationed pickets at strategic locations - Kept the main force together for rapid response - Battle of Balkh (1647): - Abdul Aziz’s forces crossed the Oxus and engaged the Mughals outside Balkh. - The Mughals decisively defeated the Uzbeks, forcing them to retreat. - Diplomatic Breakdown and Mughal Withdrawal - Nazr Muhammad, now in Persian refuge, sought Mughal help again. - Shah Jahan’s conditions for reinstating Nazr Muhammad: - Nazr Muhammad was required to personally apologize and submit to Prince Aurangzeb before being restored to power. - However, Nazr Muhammad refused to humble himself, knowing that the Mughals could not hold Balkh indefinitely. - Mughal evacuation of Balkh (October 1647): - As winter approached and supplies ran low, the Mughals retreated. - Uzbeks harassed the retreating forces, leading to heavy Mughal casualties. - Aurangzeb’s leadership prevented a disaster, ensuring some order during the withdrawal. - Assessment of the Balkh Campaign - Military Success - First major victory of Indian arms in Central Asia (Balkh conquest, Uzbek defeat). - Defeated a 120,000-strong Uzbek force at Balkh (1647). - Political and Strategic Failure - Mughals lacked resources to hold Balkh long-term. - Balkh’s hostile population and Persian hostility made Mughal influence unsustainable. - Nazr Muhammad refused submission, leading to Mughal withdrawal. - Long-term Impact - Prevented the formation of a united Uzbek state, which could have threatened Mughal control over Kabul. - Nazr Muhammad remained friendly toward the Mughals after being reinstated, maintaining diplomatic ties. - However, the campaign ultimately yielded little political gain and drained significant Mughal resources. - Conclusion: Shah Jahan’s Strategic Dilemma - Unlike some interpretations, Shah Jahan did not aim to fix the Mughal frontier along the Oxus River, as it was not defensible. - Nor was his goal to reclaim Samarqand and Farghana, despite nostalgic references. - His primary aim was to secure Balkh and Badakhshan as buffer regions against Uzbek threats. - Alternative strategy: - Perhaps sticking to the Kabul-Ghazni-Qandhar line (established by Akbar) would have been wiser. - This could have saved men and money while ensuring long-term stability. - Mughal-Persian Relations—The Last Phase - Persian Conquest of Qandhar (1649) and Mughal Response - The Mughal setback in Balkh led to: - Revival of Uzbek hostility in the Kabul region. - Afghan tribal unrest in the Khyber-Ghazni area. - Persian confidence to attack Qandhar, capturing it in 1649. - Shah Jahan’s Reaction: - The loss of Qandhar was a severe blow to Mughal prestige. - He launched three consecutive campaigns under royal princes to recover it. - Three Failed Mughal Campaigns to Recover Qandhar (1649–1653) - First Attempt (1649) – Led by Aurangzeb - Army size: 50,000 troops. - Battle outcome: - The Mughals defeated the Persians outside Qandhar, but failed to capture the fort due to strong Persian resistance. - Second Attempt (1652) – Led by Aurangzeb - Tried again after three years, but failed once more. - Third Attempt (1653) – Led by Dara Shikoh - Most ambitious effort, led by Shah Jahan’s favorite son. - Despite his claims, Dara failed to force the fort into surrender. - Use of heavy artillery: - Attempted to breach the fort with two of the empire’s largest cannons. - Proved ineffective against Qandhar’s strong fortifications. - Causes of Mughal Failure at Qandhar - Not due to weak artillery, as some historians suggest. - Key factors: - Strength of Qandhar’s fortifications. - Skill and determination of the Persian defenders. - Limitations of medieval artillery in siege warfare. - Comparable to the Mughal experience in the Deccan, where strong forts posed similar challenges. - Strategic Impact of the Loss of Qandhar - Shah Jahan’s attachment to Qandhar was more sentimental than strategic. - The declining power of both the Uzbeks and the Safavids had reduced Qandhar’s strategic importance. - More damaging than the loss itself was the repeated Mughal failures, which: - Hurt their military prestige. - Undermined their reputation in Central Asia. - However, the Mughal Empire remained powerful, as seen during Aurangzeb’s reign. - In 1680, even the Ottoman Sultan sent an embassy to Aurangzeb, seeking his support. - Aurangzeb’s Diplomatic Approach and the 1668 Crisis - Abandoning the Qandhar contest: - Aurangzeb chose not to pursue further military campaigns. - Quietly resumed diplomatic relations with Persia. - Crisis of 1668: - Shah Abbas II of Iran insulted the Mughal envoy, made disparaging remarks about Aurangzeb, and threatened invasion. - Mughal military activity increased in Punjab and Kabul, preparing for a possible Persian attack. - However, before war could break out, Shah Abbas II died. - His weak successors ensured that Persia ceased to be a threat to India until Nadir Shah emerged more than 50 years later. - Long-Term Mughal Foreign Policy and Strategic Frontier - The Mughals successfully maintained a scientific frontier in the northwest: - Hindukush served as the natural boundary, with Qandhar as its outer bastion. - Military and diplomatic measures together protected India from foreign invasions. - Diplomacy was central to Mughal foreign policy, reinforcing their military strategy. - Friendship with Persia remained a priority, despite the temporary setbacks over Qandhar. - The idea of reclaiming the Mughal homelands in Central Asia was more of a diplomatic ploy than a serious military objective. - The Mughal Empire’s Status Among Major Islamic Powers - The Mughals insisted on parity with the leading Asian powers: - Safavids (Persia): - The Safavids claimed superiority due to their lineage from the Prophet. - Ottoman Sultans (Turkey): - Held the title Padshah-i-Islam and claimed to be the successors of the Caliphs of Baghdad. - Mughal foreign policy also promoted India’s commercial interests: - Kabul and Qandhar served as twin gateways for India’s trade with Central Asia. - Growth of Administration: Mansabdari System and the Mughal Army - Continuity and Modifications in Administration - The administrative and revenue systems introduced by Akbar continued under Jahangir and Shah Jahan, with only minor modifications. - However, significant changes took place in the functioning of the mansabdari system, particularly in salary structures, military obligations, and land distribution. - Changes in Mansabdars’ Salaries and Military Composition - Under Akbar - Mansabdars’ salaries: - Paid at an average rate of Rs. 240 per annum per sawar for maintaining their contingents. - Under Jahangir - Salary Reduction: - Reduced to Rs. 200 per annum per sawar. - Additional Allowances: - Mansabdars were allowed to retain 5% of their salary to cover contingent expenses. - Ethnic Composition of the Military: - The Mughal military favored mixed contingents to prevent tribal or ethnic exclusivity. - Soldiers were drawn from: - Irani and Turani Mughals, Indian Afghans, and Rajputs in fixed proportions. - However, in special cases, Mughal or Rajput mansabdars were permitted to recruit exclusively from their ethnic groups. - Structural Modifications in the Mansabdari System - Jahangir’s Reforms: Du-aspah Sih-aspah System - Introduced to allow nobles to maintain larger numbers of troopers without increasing their sawar rank. - A mansabdar granted this distinction was required to maintain double the number of troopers indicated by his sawar rank. - Example: - A mansabdar with a zat rank of 3000 and a sawar rank of 3000 du-aspah sih-aspah had to maintain 6000 troopers. - Normally, a mansabdar’s sawar rank could not exceed his zat rank. - Shah Jahan’s Reforms: Reducing the Sawar Requirement - Further reduction in the number of sawars a noble was required to maintain. - A noble was expected to maintain only one-third of his sawar rank, and in some cases, only one-fourth. - Example: - A noble with a zat rank of 3000 and a sawar rank of 3000 had to maintain only 1000 troopers (one-third rule). - If he held the du-aspah sih-aspah distinction, he would maintain 2000 troopers instead of 6000. - Payment Methods: Jagirs vs. Cash Salaries - Mansabdars were theoretically paid in rupees, but their salaries were typically disbursed through jagirs. - Preference for jagirs: - Cash payments were often delayed and involved bureaucratic hurdles. - Control over land was a symbol of social prestige. - The Mughals bureaucratized the nobility by implementing a structured system of ranks and regulations. - However, they failed to eliminate the nobility’s feudal attachment to land, which remained a major challenge. - Allocation of Jagirs and the Revenue System - The revenue department maintained a register of assessed income (jama). - Income was recorded not in rupees but in dams (40 dams = 1 rupee). - This document, called jama-dami, provided income estimates for different regions. - Issues with Financial Constraints - As the number of mansabdars increased and financial pressures grew, even these modifications were insufficient. - Drastic salary cuts could have led to discontent among nobles, which the rulers could not afford. - To manage expenses, a new scaling system was introduced to further reduce the quota of troopers and horses a noble had to maintain. - The Month-Scale System - The salaries of mansabdars were adjusted based on a month-scale, reducing their financial obligations. - Salaries were calculated for 10 months, 8 months, 6 months, or even less. - Example: - A mansabdar with a zat rank of 3000 and a sawar rank of 3000 was initially required to maintain 1000 troopers under the one-third rule. - Under the 10-month scale, he had to maintain 1800 horses. - Under the 5-month scale, he had to maintain only 1000 horses. - Allowances rarely fell below 5 months or exceeded 10 months. - Effects on Jagirs and Cash Salaries - This system applied to both jagirs and cash salaries. - Under Shah Jahan, agricultural expansion and cash crop production led to increased jagir incomes (jama-dami). - However, this increase matched the overall price rise, reducing its financial benefit. - Many Marathas in Mughal service were given mansabs on a 5-monthly basis or even less, granting them high rank in name while reducing their actual cavalry obligations. - This weakened the efficiency of the Mughal cavalry, as the availability of remounts declined. - Challenges in the Mansabdari System - Importance of the Dagh (Branding) and Jagirdari System - The mansabdari system relied on the proper functioning of: - Dagh system (branding of horses and soldiers). - Jagirdari system (land allocation for salaries). - If the dagh system was poorly enforced, the state suffered financial losses. - If the jama-dami was exaggerated or jagirdars were not paid properly, it led to discontent and poor military upkeep. - Effectiveness Under Shah Jahan - Despite these challenges, the system functioned effectively under Shah Jahan due to: - Meticulous administration. - Careful selection of competent officials, particularly wazirs. - Strict discipline, clear promotion policies, and a well-structured rewards system. - This ensured that the Mughal nobility remained loyal and efficient in both administration and military affairs, securing and expanding the empire. - The Mughal Army - The Mughal army was primarily cavalry-based, with mansabdars providing the majority of the troops. - However, the Mughal emperors also maintained independent military units outside the mansabdari system. - These included the ahadis, the royal bodyguards (walashahis), the infantry (piyadgan), and the artillery corps. - Cavalry: The Backbone of the Army - The cavalry formed the principal arm of the Mughal army. - Apart from the mansabdars’ contingents, the emperors recruited ahadis, individual troopers who were personally selected and highly trusted. - Ahadis were known as “gentlemen-troopers” and received significantly higher salaries than regular soldiers. - Each ahadi mustered up to five horses, though some shared a horse. - Their duties were diverse: - Many worked in imperial offices as clerks, court painters, or foremen in royal karkhanas (workshops). - Some were adjutants and messengers, carrying imperial orders. - Others served as skilled musketeers (banduq-andaz) and bowmen (tir-andaz). - During Shah Jahan’s reign, the number of ahadis reached 7,000, and they were well-distributed across different army divisions. - In addition to the ahadis, the emperors maintained: - A corps of royal bodyguards (walashahis), responsible for protecting the emperor. - Armed palace guards, who served on foot within the citadel and palace. - Infantry (Piyadgan): A Miscellaneous Force - The infantry was a large but heterogeneous group. - It mainly consisted of matchlock-bearers (banduqchis), who received salaries of 3 to 7 rupees per month. - Other categories of foot soldiers included: - Porters, servants, news runners, swordsmen, wrestlers, and slaves. - Slaves were not as numerous as in the Delhi Sultanate period. - Occasionally, a slave could rise to become a gentleman-trooper, but infantrymen generally had low social status. - Artillery: Strengths and Weaknesses - The Mughal artillery was well-organized and consisted of: - Heavy guns, used for sieging forts and defending cities. - Light artillery, which was highly mobile and accompanied the emperor on campaigns. - The Mughals initially employed Ottoman and Portuguese gunners to improve their artillery. - By Aurangzeb’s time, Mughal artillery had significantly improved, making it difficult for foreigners to find employment in this sector. - However, there were limitations: - Some big guns were too large and impractical. - A modern writer noted that these huge cannons made more noise than impact, as they: - Could not be fired frequently. - Were prone to bursting, killing the operators. - Despite this, Shah Jahan’s field artillery was well-organized and effective. - French traveler Bernier described the Mughal “artillery of the stirrup”, which included: - 50 small brass field guns. - Each gun mounted on a painted carriage with two ammunition boxes. - Guns drawn by two horses, with a third horse in reserve. - Swivel guns were also mounted on elephants and camels for added mobility. - Strength of the Mughal Army - Under Shah Jahan, the Mughal army had: - 2,00,000 cavalry (excluding troops stationed in districts). - 40,000 infantry (excluding non-combatants). - Under Aurangzeb, the cavalry strength rose to 2,40,000. - Mughal Military Efficiency Compared to Other Powers - European travelers, like Bernier, often criticized the Mughal army’s efficiency. - A deeper analysis shows: - The Mughal infantry was poorly organized, lacked discipline, and was ineffective compared to European armies. - In Europe, infantry became a dominant force due to the flintlock gun, which outclassed cavalry. - Indian rulers only realized this weakness in the 18th century, when European-trained armies easily defeated them. - However, the Mughals were not inferior to other Asian armies: - The Mughal army defeated the Uzbeks in the Balkh campaigns, proving it could match Central Asian and Persian forces in open battle. - Compared to European armies, the Mughals lagged in: - Infantry training and organization. - Naval warfare, which was a key strength of European maritime powers. - The Mughal military system was deeply tied to the jagirdari system, which functioned like a feudal structure. - The army’s strength and efficiency depended on the stability of land revenue administration. - Ultimately, the inability to modernize the infantry and artillery, along with weaknesses in naval power, contributed to the Mughal Empire’s decline in later years. - Economic and Social Life under the Mughals - Economic and Social Conditions under the Mughals - Introduction - By the end of the seventeenth century, the Mughal Empire had reached its territorial peak but faced numerous political and administrative challenges. - In the economic and social spheres, the period from Akbar to the late seventeenth century saw no fundamental changes, though there were significant social and economic developments. - Standard of Living and Village Life - Living Conditions of the Masses - European travelers who visited India described its wealth, particularly the opulent lifestyle of the ruling elite, in contrast to the widespread poverty of peasants, artisans, and laborers. - Babur noted the scanty clothing of the lower classes, stating that “peasants and people of low standing go about naked.” - European travelers like Ralph Fitch (late sixteenth century) and De Laet observed that many commoners had inadequate clothing, especially during winters. - Footwear was a luxury. Nikitin recorded that people in the Deccan walked barefoot, and Moreland found little mention of shoes north of the Narmada, except in Bengal. - Housing and Furniture - Villagers lived in simple mud houses, similar to those still seen today. - Furniture was minimal—cots, bamboo mats, and earthen utensils made by the village potter were common. - Copper and bell-metal utensils were expensive and rarely used by the poor. - Diet and Food Availability - Staple foods: rice, millet, pulses, fish (in Bengal and coastal areas), and meat (in the southern peninsula). - In North India, chapatis made of wheat or coarse grains, along with pulses and vegetables, were common. - Ghee and oil were cheap, making them a staple part of the diet, whereas salt and sugar were expensive. - On balance, while clothing was scarce, people had access to relatively better food. - Economic Structure of Villages - Peasant Classes and Land Ownership - Peasant income is hard to assess as villages operated largely on barter, with village artisans receiving compensation in commodities rather than money. - Peasant classifications: - Khudkasht (resident cultivators): Owned their land, paid land revenue at customary rates, and often rented out plows and bullocks to poorer peasants. - Muzarian (tenant cultivators): Worked on rented land, paid higher land revenue, and had lesser economic stability. - Landless laborers: Often from the “untouchable” or lower castes, they worked under severe hardships and faced the greatest suffering during famines. - Village Hierarchy and Inequality - Villages were highly unequal, with dominant castes monopolizing land ownership and exploiting lower sections. - While khudkasht cultivators had relatively better conditions, they too were under the control of zamindars, who in turn faced heavy state demands. - Agriculture and Cash Crops - Agricultural Efficiency and Innovations - India had a diversified agricultural economy, growing wheat, rice, gram, barley, pulses, and bajra, alongside cash crops like cotton, indigo, chay (red dye), sugarcane, and oilseeds. - Cash crops paid higher land revenue and were often sold for cash. - Peasants adapted to price changes and were open to cultivating new crops. - New crops introduced during the seventeenth century: - Tobacco - Maize - Eighteenth-century additions: - Potatoes - Red chilies - Peasant Rights and Land Tenure - Peasants could not be dispossessed as long as they paid revenue. - Land could be sold with community approval, and children inherited land rights. - However, land revenue demands (sometimes as high as half the produce) left peasants with minimal surplus, preventing agricultural expansion. - Economic Conditions in Cities - Urban Workforce and Wages - Cities had a large population of poor artisans, servants, slaves, soldiers, and manual laborers. - Salaries: - Lowest-grade servants earned less than two rupees per month. - Common laborers and foot soldiers earned around three rupees per month. - It was estimated that a man could feed his family on two rupees a month. - Comparison with Later Periods - Moreland noted that real wages had remained unchanged since Mughal times, though food had been more affordable then. - Under British rule, India’s economic stagnation contrasted sharply with Europe’s wealth growth during the same period. - Conclusion - Despite hardships, Mughal-era peasants had relatively stable access to food and land. However, widespread inequality persisted, with peasants burdened by high taxation and exploitative village hierarchies. - In urban areas, low wages and economic stagnation prevented upward mobility. While agricultural output remained robust, limited technological advancements and heavy state taxation hindered long-term economic growth. - The Ruling Classes: The Nobles and Zamindars - Composition of the Mughal Nobility - The ruling class in medieval India included the nobility and zamindars. - The Mughal nobility formed a privileged class socially and economically. - Theoretically, entry into the nobility was open to all, but aristocratic families—both Indian and foreign—had a significant advantage. - Origins and Ethnic Diversity - Initially, most Mughal nobles were from Turan and neighboring regions like Tajikistan, Khurasan, and Iran. - Although Babur was a Turk, the Mughals did not adopt a narrow racial policy. - Babur attempted to ally with Afghan nobles, but their instability led to continued conflicts in Bihar and Bengal until Akbar’s reign. - Over time, more Afghans, Indian Muslims (Shaikhzadas or Hindustanis), and Hindus were recruited. - Inclusion of Hindus in the Nobility - Akbar began inducting Hindus, particularly Rajputs, into the nobility. - The Kachhwahas dominated initially, and by 1594, Hindus formed about 16% of the nobility. - Hindu nobles, including Raja Man Singh, Raja Birbal, and Raja Todar Mal, held influential positions. - The recruitment of Rajputs reinforced the aristocratic nature of the nobility. - Many Kayasthas and Khatris also served in administrative roles, with some rising to noble status. - Expansion and Stability Under Later Rulers - Under Jahangir and Shah Jahan, the nobility became more stable, regulated by the mansabdari system. - Rules ensured orderly promotions, discipline, and competent recruitment. - The high salaries and religious tolerance of the Mughal court attracted foreign talent, leading to a “reverse brain drain.” - While many nobles migrated to India, they permanently settled, assimilating into Indian culture while retaining some unique traits. - Increase in Indigenous Nobles and Maratha Integration - By Jahangir and Shah Jahan’s reigns, most nobles were India-born. - The number of Afghans, Indian Muslims, and Hindus in the nobility continued to grow. - The Marathas entered the nobility during this period, with Jahangir recognizing their importance in the Deccan. - Shah Jahan continued this policy, and Aurangzeb later recruited many Marathas and Deccani Muslims. - Under Aurangzeb, Hindus formed about 33% of the nobility, with Marathas comprising more than half of them. - Wealth and Extravagance of the Nobility - Nobles received extremely high salaries but had significant expenditures: - Maintaining large households, servants, stables, and harems. - Living in luxurious mansions with gardens and running water. - Wearing expensive clothing and indulging in lavish meals. - Spending heavily on imported fruits and luxury items like ice. - Wearing elaborate jewelry, including earrings introduced by Jahangir. - Presenting mandatory gifts to the emperor twice a year, though they received gifts in return. - Despite their wealth, few nobles remained debt-free or left substantial inheritances. - Economic Role of the Nobility - Nobles contributed to economic activity by: - Purchasing or receiving land grants, developing orchards, and building markets (mandis). - Lending money to traders and engaging in commerce, often through intermediaries. - Abul Fazl encouraged nobles to invest in business ventures, even though Islamic law condemned usury. - Some nobles misused their power to monopolize trade, but this did not significantly disrupt commerce. - Even royal family members engaged in trade, with some owning ships for foreign trade. - Mir Jumla, a noble under Aurangzeb, ran a vast trade network with Persia, Arabia, and Southeast Asia. - Cultural and Bureaucratic Aspects of the Nobility - The Mughal nobility, despite ethnic divisions, formed a composite ruling class. - It promoted shared cultural values by supporting painters, musicians, poets, and scholars in Persian and Hindawi. - Though primarily feudal, it also exhibited bureaucratic and commercial tendencies. - The ruling class did not obstruct economic growth but whether it could have led India toward capitalism remains debatable. - Challenges and Decline Under Aurangzeb - The nobility expanded rapidly in the 17th century, leading to tensions and factionalism. - Issues within the sagirdari system weakened discipline and efficiency under Aurangzeb. - These challenges contributed to the decline of the nobility, a topic explored in later sections. - Zamindars and the Rural Gentry - Ownership and Rights in Land - Land ownership in medieval India was primarily hereditary, but new rights were constantly created: - Anyone who first brought land under cultivation was considered its owner. - Large areas of cultivable wasteland (banjar) allowed new settlements and land ownership. - Many zamindars owned land they cultivated and had hereditary rights to collect land revenue (taluqa/zamindari). - For revenue collection, zamindars received a share of up to 25% in some regions. - However, peasants retained hereditary rights and could not be dispossessed if they paid revenue. - Hierarchy in Rural Society - Zamindars vs. Peasants - Zamindars had hereditary rights over land revenue collection but were not absolute landowners. - Peasants had the right to cultivate the land and could not be removed arbitrarily. - Rajas and Chiefs - Above zamindars were rajas, who controlled larger or smaller territories with varying autonomy. - Persian writers referred to rajas as zamindars to emphasize their subordinate status. - Despite this, rajas held a higher position than ordinary zamindars. - Medieval rural society was highly segmented and hierarchical. - Military and Fortifications - Zamindars, rajas, and chiefs maintained private armed forces: - Lived in forts (garhis), which served as refuges and status symbols. - Possessed significant military strength (as per Ain-i-Akbari under Akbar): - 3,84,558 cavalry - 42,77,057 foot soldiers - 1,863 elephants - 4,260 cannons - However, due to dispersion, they could not field all forces at one location. - Social and Economic Role - Zamindars had close ties with peasants, often through caste, clan, or tribal affiliations. - They were present throughout India under various names: - Deshmukh, Patil, Nayak, etc. - Their widespread influence made them indispensable to the central authority. - Living Standards - Wealth varied among zamindars: - Smaller zamindars may have lived like peasants. - Larger zamindars had lifestyles comparable to petty rajas or nobles. - Most formed a loosely organized rural gentry, living in the countryside. - Beyond Revenue Collection - Zamindars were more than just tax collectors: - Maintained caste and kinship ties with landowning agricultural communities. - Set social standards and influenced local society. - Provided capital and organization for: - Establishing new villages. - Expanding and improving agriculture. - The Middle Strata in Medieval India - Debate on the Existence of a Middle Class - French traveler Bernier claimed India had no “middle state”, stating people were either extremely rich or in misery. - However, this was not entirely accurate: - India had a large class of wealthy traders and merchants, some among the richest in the world at the time. - These merchants had traditional rights, including protection of life and property. - Unlike European merchants, they did not administer towns. - In Europe, such rights were acquired under special conditions but were later curtailed by strong territorial states (e.g., France and Britain). - Defining the Middle Strata - If the “middle state” refers to people between the rich and the poor, then such groups existed in Mughal India: - Small mansabdars - Petty shopkeepers - Master craftsmen - Professionals, including: - Hakims (physicians) - Leading musicians and artists - Historians and scholars - Qazis (judges) and theologians - Petty officials and clerks, managing Mughal administration. - Economic and Social Standing - Petty officials: - Paid in cash but often supplemented income through corruption. - Scholars and religious figures: - Given small land grants for sustenance: - Known as madad-i-maash in Mughal India. - Called sasan in Rajasthan. - Though grants were renewed by rulers, they often became hereditary in practice. - Role and Influence - Members of the middle strata often formed part of the rural gentry, serving as a link between villages and towns. - Writers, historians, and theologians frequently emerged from this class. - However, the middle strata were not a single, unified class: - Interests varied significantly. - Members belonged to different religious and caste groups, reflecting the diversity of medieval Indian society. - Organization of Trade and Commerce in Medieval India - Structure of Indian Trading Classes - The trading classes in India were large, well-organized, and highly professional. - Traders were divided based on their scale of operations: - Long-distance and inter-regional traders: Known as seth, bora, or modi. - Local and retail traders: Called deoparis or banik. - Baniks also acted as agents in villages and towns, purchasing food grains and cash crops. - Banjaras: Specialized in transporting bulk goods over long distances with thousands of oxen carrying food grains, pulses, ghee, and salt. - Luxury goods like textiles and silks were transported using camels, mules, or carts. - Bulk goods were more efficiently transported via rivers and boats. - Inter-Regional Trade and Major Trade Centers - Trade was not limited to luxury goods; foodstuffs and textiles were key components. - Major trade routes and centers: - Bengal: Exported sugar, rice, muslin, and silk. - Coromandel Coast: A hub for textile production with active trade links to Gujarat. - Gujarat: The gateway for foreign goods; exported fine textiles and silks (patola) to North India. - North India: Imported luxury items while exporting indigo and food grains. - Lahore: A handicraft production center and a distribution hub for Kashmiri shawls and carpets. - Punjab and Sindh: Products moved down the Indus River, linking trade to Kabul and Qandahar. - Trade Networks and Financial Systems - A complex trading network linked wholesalers, merchants, and local traders via agents (gumashtas) and commission agents (dalals). - European traders (Dutch and English) observed the activeness and efficiency of Indian merchants. - Financial mechanisms facilitated trade: - Hundi (letters of credit): Allowed easy transmission of money across the country. - Hundis often included insurance, with rates depending on value, destination, and mode of transport (land, river, or sea). - Sarrafs (shroffs): Money changers who also dealt in hundis, functioning as private bankers. - Rich traders like Virji Vohra established agency houses across India, West Asia, and Southeast Asia, reducing financial risk. - Diversity of Trading Communities - The trading community in India was not restricted to a single caste or religion: - Gujarati merchants: Included Hindus, Jains, and Bohras (Muslims). - Rajasthan: Oswals, Maheshwaris, and Agarwals, later known as Marwaris. - Central Asia trade: Dominated by Multanis, Afghans, and Khatris. - South India: Led by Chettis (Coromandel Coast) and Muslim traders from Malabar (both Indian and Arab). - Wealth and Influence of Merchants - Some Indian merchants were as wealthy and powerful as the merchant princes of Europe: - Virji Vohra: Dominated Surat trade, owned a large fleet of ships, and was among the wealthiest of his time. - Abdul Ghafur Bohra (died 1718): Left 55 lakh rupees and 17 sea-going ships. - Malay Chetti, Kashi Viranna, and Sunca Rama Chetti: Wealthy traders with extensive commercial dealings. - Agra, Delhi, Balasore, and Bengal had many rich merchants. - Merchants’ Lifestyle and Legal Protection - Wealthy merchants in port towns lived luxuriously, mimicking nobility. - European travelers noted their well-built houses, though ordinary merchants lived above their shops. - Bernier observed that merchants hid their wealth to avoid being taxed unfairly. - However, Mughal emperors protected merchant property: - Sher Shah and Jahangir enacted laws safeguarding merchant wealth. - Property of merchants without heirs was preserved for public works (e.g., mosques, wells, bridges). - Though local officials sometimes harassed merchants, their property was generally safe. - Trade Infrastructure and Security - Road safety and transportation: - Sarais (inns) were built every 5 kos on major highways. - Insurance covered road safety risks. - The transport system was as developed as in Europe at the time. - Despite their wealth, traders had a low social status. - Merchants’ political influence: - Each merchant community had a leader (nagarseth) to negotiate with officials. - Merchants sometimes organized strikes (hartal) to push their demands. - Some Mughal nobles and royals, like Mir Jumla, were directly involved in trade. - However, the Mughals did not actively promote trade interests like European states (Britain, France, Holland). - Factors Behind Trade Expansion in the Seventeenth Century - Mughal political integration and law and order facilitated trade. - The Mughals developed roads and sarais for easy movement. - Taxes were levied only at empire entry points; illegal road tolls (rahdari) were discouraged. - Mughal rupees (silver coins of high purity) became the standard currency in India and abroad, aiding trade. - Commercialization of the economy: - Salaries of soldiers and administrative staff were paid in cash. - Under the zabti system, land revenue was collected in cash, boosting the money economy. - Around 20% of rural produce was marketed, leading to the rise of small towns (qasbas). - Demand for luxury goods fueled the expansion of handicraft production and urban centers. - Growth of Major Towns and Manufacturing - Sixteenth-century urbanization: - Agra and Fatehpur Sikri were larger than London (as per Ralph Fitch). - Lahore was among the largest cities in Europe or Asia (Monserrate). - Bernier stated that Delhi was comparable to Paris, and Agra was even bigger. - Other major towns: Ahmadnagar, Burhanpur, Multan, Patna, Rajmahal, and Dacca. - Ahmedabad was as large as London, while Patna had 2 lakh residents. - State Involvement in Trade and Industry - The Mughals concentrated rural wealth in the hands of the nobility, stimulating demand for luxury goods. - Government directly supported industries like: - Arms manufacturing (guns, cannons, armor). - Shipbuilding: - Shah Jahan (1651) initiated a naval program for voyages to West Asia. - By 1652, six ships were commissioned annually. - Indian shipyards adopted European models, reducing freight costs. - Indian steel swords were in high demand worldwide. - Foreign Trade and the European Traders - India’s Foreign Trade and Its Impact - India maintained extensive trade with Southeast and West Asia, supplying foodstuffs like sugar and rice. - Indian textiles were in high demand across Asia, with an English agent observing, “From Aden to Achin, from head to foot, everyone was clothed in Indian textiles.” - India primarily imported metals like tin and copper, certain spices, warhorses, and luxury items. - Due to its trade surplus, India received significant imports of gold and silver, prompting Bernier to remark that India was the “sink of gold and silver.” - Arrival of European Traders - The Portuguese arrived in India towards the end of the fifteenth century. - By the seventeenth century, other European traders, including the Dutch, English, and later the French, came to India due to economic expansion in Europe. - Decline of Portuguese Power and Rise of the Dutch - Portuguese influence weakened in the second half of the sixteenth century. - The Dutch established themselves in Masulipatam in 1606 and later dominated the spice trade in Java and Sumatra. - Indian textiles became the primary medium of exchange for spices, leading the Dutch to expand southward to the Coromandel Coast, where they set up operations at Pulicat. - Establishment of English Trade in India - The English initially sought spices but faced hostility from the Dutch, forcing them to focus on India. - In 1612, after defeating a Portuguese fleet, they established a factory at Surat, confirmed by a farman from Jahangir in 1618. - The English recognized Gujarat’s significance in textile exports and captured Ormuz (a Portuguese base) in 1622 with Persian help, securing access to the Persian Gulf. - By the early seventeenth century, both the Dutch and English had firmly established themselves in Indian trade, effectively ending Portuguese dominance. - Indian Traders and Their Resilience - Despite European dominance at sea, Indian traders retained a strong position in Asian trade. - Indian traders had better market knowledge and accepted lower profit margins (10–15%) than the Dutch (40–50%), making them competitive. - The Dutch and English depended on Mughal support and Indian traders to sustain their factories and operations. - European companies reduced costs by freighting Indian merchants’ goods on their ships, benefiting both parties. - Indian shipping expanded significantly, with the number of ships at Surat increasing from 50 in the mid-seventeenth century to 112 by the century’s end. - Expansion of European Trade Beyond Asia - European traders sought Indian exports for Europe, initially focusing on pepper and indigo, the best of which was produced at Sarkhej (Gujarat) and Bayana (Agra). - By the mid-seventeenth century, English traders developed a strong textile export trade to Europe. - Gujarat initially supplied the cloth, but increasing demand led to expansion into Agra and later the Coromandel Coast. - By 1660, cloth exports from Coromandel tripled those from Gujarat, with Masulipatam and Fort St. George (later Madras) becoming major ports. - The Dutch also entered this textile trade alongside the English. - Expansion into Bengal and Other Regions - The English explored Lahri Bandar (Indus River mouth) for Multan and Lahore’s produce, but Gujarat trade remained dominant. - They focused on Bengal and Orissa, despite disruptions from Portuguese and Magh pirates. - By 1650, the English had established themselves at Hooghly and Balasore, exporting raw silk, sugar, textiles, and saltpeter (used for gunpowder and as ship ballast). - By the end of the century, exports from eastern India equaled those from Coromandel. - Indian Textiles and European Demand - By the late seventeenth century, Indian textiles became highly popular in England. - In 1701, English authorities banned printed calicoes from Persia, China, and India due to domestic agitation, but the demand remained strong. - White calico exports surged from 9.14 lakh pieces in 1701 to 20 lakh pieces in 1719. - Intra-Asian Trade and Indian Overland Trade - While European trade with India grew, intra-Asian trade remained more profitable. - Only 14% of spices produced were exported to Europe, with most consumed in India and China. - Indian textile exports to West Asia and East Africa increased, while coffee from Yemen emerged as a new trade item. - Overland trade flourished through major centers like Lahore and Multan, with Indian traders settling across Iran, Central Asia, and even Russia. - However, overland trade declined with the collapse of the Safavid and Mughal empires. - Economic Consequences of Growing Foreign Trade - The influx of gold and silver led to rapid economic growth, but prices doubled in the first half of the seventeenth century. - The social impact of this price rise is unclear but likely weakened traditional village ties and made the nobility more materialistic. - European Attempts to Reduce Gold and Silver Exports - European nations sought to reduce gold and silver exports by monopolizing the spice trade and capturing Indian textile markets, but with limited success. - They turned to empire-building, with the Dutch controlling Java and Sumatra. - The English and French competed for control over India but could not succeed while India remained politically strong under the Mughals and later under capable provincial rulers. - European conquest became possible only when internal and external pressures weakened these Indian states. - Cultural and Religious Developments - Cultural Development Under the Mughals - Mughal Period as a Second Classical Age - The Mughal era witnessed an outburst of cultural activity in architecture, painting, literature, and music. - Traditions established during this time set a norm and deeply influenced succeeding generations. - The period is often regarded as a “second classical age”, following the Gupta age in northern India. - Fusion of Indian and Turko-Iranian Traditions - Indian cultural traditions were amalgamated with the Turko-Iranian influences brought by the Mughals. - The Timurid court at Samarqand had been a major cultural center of West and Central Asia. - Babur was conscious of this cultural heritage, critical of many existing Indian cultural forms, and determined to set proper standards. - Foundation of Mughal Cultural Growth - The fourteenth and fifteenth centuries had already seen a rich cultural development across various regions of India. - The Mughals built upon this existing foundation, making their cultural achievements possible. - People from different regions, faiths, and races contributed to this cultural growth. - The resulting culture of the period exhibited a composite national character, blending diverse traditions. - Mughal Architecture - Distinctive Features of Mughal Architecture - The Mughals built forts, palaces, gates, mosques, baolis (step-wells), and public buildings. - Formal gardens with running water were a notable feature, even in palaces and pleasure resorts. - Mughal gardens, such as Nishat Bagh (Kashmir), Shalimar Bagh (Lahore), and Pinjore Garden (Punjab foothills), have survived to this day. - Pre-Mughal Contributions - Sher Shah gave a new impetus to architecture. - His mausoleum at Sasaram (Bihar) and mosque in the Old Fort (Delhi) are architectural marvels. - These structures mark the climax of pre-Mughal architecture and the beginning of the new Mughal style. - Akbar’s Architectural Innovations - Akbar, the first Mughal ruler with time and resources for large-scale construction, built a series of forts, the most famous being Agra Fort (red sandstone, massive gates). - Mughal forts drew upon the Indian tradition of fort-building seen at Gwalior and Jodhpur. - The climax of fort-building was Shah Jahan’s Red Fort in Delhi. - Fatehpur Sikri - In 1572, Akbar began a palace-cum-fort complex at Fatehpur Sikri, completed in eight years. - Built atop a hill with an artificial lake, it included buildings influenced by Gujarat and Bengal styles, with deep eaves, balconies, and ornate kiosks. - The Panch Mahal, designed for fresh air, used pillars similar to Indian temples. - The Gujarat style was prominent in a palace believed to be for Akbar’s Rajput wife or wives. - Persian and Central Asian Influences - Glazed blue tiles were used for wall decoration and roofing. - The Jama Masjid and its grand entrance, Buland Darwaza (“Lofty Gate”), were built to commemorate Akbar’s victory in Gujarat. - The half-dome portal style, borrowed from Iran, became a defining feature of later Mughal architecture. - Jahangir’s Contribution to Mughal Architecture - Builders shifted from sandstone to marble. - Pietra dura (floral designs with semi-precious stones) became prominent, especially under Shah Jahan. - Shah Jahan and the Climax of Mughal Architecture - The Taj Mahal, a masterpiece, incorporated all architectural elements developed by the Mughals. - Humayun’s Tomb, built in Delhi during Akbar’s reign, with its massive marble dome, is considered a precursor to the Taj Mahal. - The double-dome technique, allowing for a larger outer dome with a smaller inner dome, was an innovation of this period. - The Taj Mahal’s chief glory lies in its massive dome, four slender minarets, delicate marble screens, pietra dura work, and formal garden setting. - Mosque Architecture Under Shah Jahan - Moti Masjid (Agra Fort) – built entirely of marble, similar to the Taj Mahal. - Jama Masjid (Delhi) – built in red sandstone, featuring a lofty entrance gate, tall slender minarets, and a series of domes. - Mughal Architectural Influence Beyond Shah Jahan - Aurangzeb was more economy-minded and built fewer structures. - However, Mughal architectural traditions continued into the 18th and 19th centuries. - Provincial and local kingdoms adopted Mughal styles for their palaces and forts. - The Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple, Amritsar) was rebuilt multiple times during this period, incorporating the arch-and-dome principle and other Mughal architectural elements. - Mughal Painting - Distinctive Contributions - The Mughals made a significant impact on painting by introducing new themes such as: - Court life - Battle scenes - The chase (hunting expeditions) - They added new colors and forms, creating a living artistic tradition that continued even after Mughal power declined. - Indian Traditions and Early Influences - India had a long tradition of painting, with the Ajanta wall paintings as early evidence of its richness. - Although painting declined after the 8th century, it survived through: - Palm-leaf manuscripts - Illustrated Jain texts (from the 13th century onward) - The Jains and some provincial kingdoms (such as Malwa and Gujarat) patronized painting in the 15th century. - A vigorous revival began only under Akbar. - Development Under Akbar - Humayun, while at the court of the Shah of Iran, brought two master painters to India. - Under Akbar’s rule: - A painting workshop was set up in the imperial palace (havbhanas). - A large number of painters, including Hindus and Muslims, were drawn from different regions and castes. - Notable painters of Akbar’s court: Daswant and Basawan. - Initially, Mughal painters illustrated Persian fables, but later moved to Indian themes by illustrating: - The Persian translation of the Mahabharata - Akbar Nama (his historical biography) - This transition freed Mughal art from Persian dominance. - Indian colors (such as peacock blue and Indian red) were introduced. - The flat Persian style was replaced with a more three-dimensional effect, achieved through the rounded Indian brush technique. - Climax Under Jahangir - Jahangir had a keen eye for art and further refined Mughal painting. - Special techniques developed under Jahangir: - Different artists worked on a single painting (e.g., one painted the face, another the body, another the feet). - Jahangir could identify individual artists’ contributions within a painting. - Major themes under Jahangir: - Portrait painting became highly fashionable. - Animals and nature were widely depicted, with Mansur excelling in this genre. - European Influence - Portuguese priests introduced European painting to the Mughal court under Akbar. - The most significant adoption was foreshortening, a technique that enhanced depth and perspective, making images more realistic. - Decline and Influence Beyond the Mughals - Under Shah Jahan, the tradition of Mughal painting continued but showed less innovation. - Aurangzeb’s lack of interest led to the dispersal of Mughal artists to different regions, influencing: - Rajasthani painting – blended Western Indian (Jain school) themes with Mughal styles. - Pahari painting – continued Mughal artistic traditions. - Themes in Rajasthani painting included: - Hunting and court scenes - Mythological subjects (e.g., Krishna and Radha) - Barahmasa (paintings of the seasons) - Ragas (melodies depicted in visual form) - The Mughal tradition was revived in the 18th century under Aurangzeb’s successors. - Language and Literature - Persian and Sanskrit as Administrative and Literary Languages - Persian and Sanskrit played an important role as languages of thought and administration at the all-India level. - The Bhakti Movement and regional rulers’ patronage contributed to the growth of regional languages. - By Akbar’s reign, Persian became so widespread in North India that he discontinued the practice of maintaining revenue records in both Persian and Hindavi. - However, Deccani states continued to maintain records in local languages until the late 17th century. - Persian Literature and Its Growth - Persian prose and poetry peaked during Akbar’s reign. - Key Persian writers: - Abul Fazl (historian and stylist, set the prose-writing style for generations). - Faizi (Akbar’s court poet, supervised the Mahabharata translation). - Utbi and Naziri (Persian poets who migrated to India, contributing to Mughal court culture). - Many Persian scholars and poets came from Iran to India, making the Mughal court a major cultural hub of the Islamic world. - Hindus also contributed to Persian literature, writing historical works and dictionaries. - Sanskrit Literature and Its Centers - Sanskrit continued to flourish, with most works produced in South and East India under local rulers’ patronage. - Banaras remained the main center where scholars from across India gathered. - Some Brahmins employed in the Mughal translation department also contributed to Sanskrit literature. - Development of Regional Languages - Regional languages matured during this period, producing some of the finest lyrical poetry. - Popular themes in Bengali, Oriya, Hindi, Rajasthani, and Gujarati poetry: - Krishna’s dalliance with Radha. - Krishna’s childhood pranks. - Stories from the Bhagavata Purana. - Translations of Ramayana and Mahabharata into regional languages continued. - Hindus and Muslims both contributed to regional literature: - Alaol wrote in Bengali and translated works from Persian. - Malik Muhammad Jayasi’s Padmavat (written in Hindi) used Alauddin Khalji’s attack on Chittor as an allegory for Sufi philosophy. - Hindi Literature and Mughal Patronage - Medieval Hindi (Braj dialect), spoken around Agra, received Mughal patronage. - From Akbar’s reign onward, Hindi poets became attached to the Mughal court. - Prominent Hindi poets: - Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan (blended Bhakti poetry with Persian influences). - Tulsidas (most influential Hindi poet, venerated Rama as both god and hero). - Used Awadhi dialect (spoken in eastern Uttar Pradesh). - Advocated a modified caste system based on individual qualities, not birth. - Promoted family values and complete devotion to Rama as a path to salvation. - Development of Regional Literature in South India - Malayalam emerged as an independent literary language. - Marathi literature peaked under Eknath and Tukaram. - Eknath defended Marathi’s literary value, stating: “If Sanskrit was made by God, was Prakrit born of thieves and knaves? Let these errings be of vanity alone. God is no partisan of tongues. To Him, Prakrit and Sanskrit are alike. - My language, Marathi, is worthy of expressing the highest sentiments and is rich, laden with the fruits of divine knowledge.” - Punjabi gained new life due to the writings of Sikh Gurus. - Music in Mughal period - Fusion of Hindu and Muslim Musical Traditions - Music was a cultural field where Hindus and Muslims cooperated. - Akbar was a great patron of music and supported Tansen of Gwalior, credited with composing many new ragas (melodies). - Jahangir and Shah Jahan continued Akbar’s tradition, and many Mughal nobles were also patrons of music. - Music Under Aurangzeb - Aurangzeb is often said to have banned music, but recent research shows: - He banned singing at the court but allowed musical instruments. - He was personally skilled in playing the veena. - Music thrived under the patronage of Aurangzeb’s queens, princes, and nobles. - The largest number of books on classical Indian music in Persian were written during his reign. - Music in the 18th Century - The greatest developments in Indian music came later during the reign of Muhammad Shah (1719–1748). - Muhammad Shah was a major patron of musicians, leading to significant musical advancements. - Religious Ideas, Beliefs, and Problems of Integration - The Bhakti Movement and Emerging Religious Trends - The Bhakti Movement continued to flourish during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Among the significant developments were: - The Sikh Movement in Punjab, originating from Guru Nanak’s preachings. - Maharashtra Dharma, a movement centered in Maharashtra. - The Sikh Movement and Its Evolution - The growth of Sikhism was closely linked to the institution of Guruship: - The first four gurus followed a tradition of meditation and scholarship. - Guru Arjan (5th Guru) played a crucial role in compiling the Adi Granth (Granth Sahib), the Sikh scriptures. - Guru Arjan adopted an aristocratic lifestyle to emphasize the combination of spiritual and worldly leadership. - He also introduced Dasvandh, a system of collecting one-tenth of Sikh earnings for community welfare. - Sikh-Mughal Relations and Conflicts - Akbar respected the Sikh gurus and is believed to have visited them. - Jahangir’s Conflict with Guru Arjan: - Guru Arjan was imprisoned and executed for allegedly aiding Prince Khusrau. - Guru Hargobind’s Struggles: - Briefly imprisoned by Jahangir, later released. - Clashed with Shah Jahan over a hunting incident. - Further conflicts arose over: - Building a new city near Jalandhar (objected to by Mughal authorities). - Seizure of two prized horses by royal officials (later retrieved by Bidhi Chand, a Sikh follower). - He successfully defended himself in battles but later retired peacefully. - Religious Conflicts vs. Political Struggles - Historian R.S. Tripathi argues that these conflicts were more political than religious. - The rich lifestyle of the gurus and the title Sachcha Padshah (True Sovereign) did not trouble the Mughal rulers. - Similar practices were seen among Sufi saints, who also received grand titles from their followers. - Mughal Policies and Religious Tolerance - There was no systematic persecution of Hindus under Mughal rule. - Shah Jahan initially displayed orthodox tendencies, such as demolishing newly built temples, but later softened his stance under the influence of his liberal son Dara Shikoh. - Dara Shikoh: - Translated the Bhagavad Gita into Persian. - Wrote an anthology of the Vedas, emphasizing their harmony with Islam. - The Bhakti and Non-Sectarian Movements - Dadu (Gujarat-Rajasthan) preached a non-sectarian path (Nirpaksha), rejecting both Hindu and Muslim labels. - Tukaram (Maharashtra): - Supreme exponent of Bhakti. - Lived in Pandharpur, a center for Vithoba (Vishnu worship). - Though a Shudra by birth, he personally performed puja, challenging orthodox norms. - Orthodox Hindu Reactions - Orthodox Hindus opposed these liberal ideas. - Raghunandan (Bengal), a leading Dharmashastra writer, asserted: - Only Brahmins had the right to read and preach scriptures. - In Kali Yuga, only two varnas remained: Brahmins and Shudras. - Ramdas (Maharashtra), later Shivaji’s spiritual guru, also upheld Brahminical privileges. - Orthodox Muslim Resistance and Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi - Sufism and religious harmony continued among Muslims, but some ulama opposed Akbar’s liberal policies. - Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi, a Naqshbandi Sufi, led a revivalist movement: - Opposed pantheistic mysticism (Wahdat al-Wujud), calling it un-Islamic. - Denounced Hindu-influenced practices, such as: - Music in religious gatherings (sama). - Excessive meditation. - Visiting saints’ tombs. - Advocated for: - Reimposition of jizya (tax on non-Muslims). - Minimal interaction between Hindus and Muslims. - Impact: - His ideas gained little traction. - Jahangir imprisoned him for claiming a higher spiritual status than the Prophet. - Aurangzeb also ignored his successors. - Liberalism vs. Orthodoxy: A Recurrent Struggle - The battle between entrenched privilege and egalitarianism was a recurring theme in Indian history. - Orthodox elements resisted reconciliation, obstructing Hindu-Muslim harmony. - The struggle culminated during Aurangzeb’s reign. - However, Akbar’s liberal policies were revived in the 18th century and became the norm once again. - Climax and Disintegration of the Mughal Empire—I - Problems of Succession - Lack of a Clear Succession Tradition - The final years of Shah Jahan’s reign were marked by a bitter war of succession among his sons. - There was no clear tradition of succession among the Muslims or the Timurids. - Some Muslim political thinkers accepted the ruler’s right to nominate a successor, but this was rarely enforced. - The Timurid tradition of partitioning the empire had failed and was never implemented in India. - Hindu traditions were also unclear. According to Tulsidas, a ruler could choose any of his sons as his successor, but this often led to disputes. - For instance, Rajput ruler Sanga had to fight his brothers to secure his throne. - Shah Jahan’s Illness and Dara’s Nomination - In late 1657, Shah Jahan fell seriously ill in Delhi, leading to rumors of his death. - His sons—Shuja in Bengal, Murad in Gujarat, and Aurangzeb in the Deccan—believed or pretended to believe these rumors and prepared for war. - Hoping to avoid conflict, Shah Jahan nominated his eldest son, Dara, as his successor (tvadi-ahd). - Dara’s mansab was raised to 60,000, and nobles were instructed to obey him. - Instead of ensuring a smooth transition, this move confirmed the other princes’ suspicions of Shah Jahan’s bias toward Dara, intensifying their ambitions. - Military Campaigns and the Battle of Dharmat (15 April 1658) - As the princes advanced toward Agra, Shah Jahan dispatched forces to counter them: - Sulaiman Shikoh (Dara’s son) and Mirza Raja Jai Singh led an army to confront Shuja in the east. - Raja Jaswant Singh of Jodhpur led another army to Malwa against Aurangzeb and Murad. - In Malwa, Aurangzeb and Murad invited Jaswant to step aside, but he chose to fight. - The Battle of Dharmat (15 April 1658) ended in Aurangzeb’s victory, boosting his confidence and demoralizing Dara’s allies. - Dara’s Strategic Mistakes - Overconfident, Dara had sent some of his best troops to fight Shuja, weakening Agra’s defense. - Sulaiman Shikoh defeated Shuja near Banaras (February 1658) and pursued him into Bihar. - After Dharmat, Dara recalled these troops, but they were too far to return in time. - Search for Allies and the Battle of Samugarh (29 May 1658) - Dara sought alliances with Rajput rulers Jaswant Singh and the Rana of Udaipur, but Aurangzeb won them over with promises of rank and religious freedom. - The Battle of Samugarh (29 May 1658) was a decisive contest of military skill. - Both armies had around 50,000 to 60,000 troops, but Aurangzeb’s forces were better trained and led. - Dara’s hastily assembled army, dependent on the Hada Rajputs and Saiyids of Barha, could not match Aurangzeb’s seasoned warriors. - Aurangzeb’s Capture of Agra and Shah Jahan’s Imprisonment - Aurangzeb justified his campaign as an effort to “free” Shah Jahan from the “heretical” Dara. - However, the war was not a conflict between religious orthodoxy and liberalism—both Hindu and Muslim nobles were divided in their loyalties. - After Dara’s defeat, Shah Jahan was besieged in the Agra Fort. Aurangzeb forced his surrender by cutting off the fort’s water supply. - Shah Jahan was confined to the female apartments of the fort but was not mistreated. - His daughter Jahanara Begum voluntarily stayed with him and cared for him until his death. - After Shah Jahan’s death, Aurangzeb honored Jahanara, increasing her pension from 12 lakh to 17 lakh rupees. - Elimination of Rivals - Aurangzeb had agreed to divide the empire with Murad, but he betrayed him, imprisoned him, and had him executed two years later. - Dara’s Final Struggles and Death - After Samugarh, Dara fled to Lahore but abandoned it upon Aurangzeb’s arrival. - He fled to Sindh, then Gujarat, and finally Ajmer, where he sought Jaswant Singh’s help. - Jaswant betrayed him, leading to the Battle of Deorai (March 1659)—Dara’s last stand. - Captured by a treacherous Afghan chief, Dara was handed over to Aurangzeb. - A jury of scholars ruled that Dara must be executed “to protect the faith and the state.” - Two years later, Dara’s son, Sulaiman Shikoh, was handed over by the ruler of Garhwal and met the same fate. - Defeat of Shuja and His Death - Aurangzeb defeated Shuja at Khajwah (December 1658) and entrusted the campaign against him to Mir Jumla. - Shuja fled to Arakan (April 1660), where he and his family were killed by the Arakanese on charges of rebellion. - Aftermath and Aurangzeb’s Rule - The civil war, lasting over two years, demonstrated that: - Nomination by the ruler or partition of the empire was never accepted. - Military strength was the only way to secure the throne. - Each successive war of succession became more destructive. - After consolidating power, Aurangzeb sought to mend relations with the families of his defeated brothers: - 1673: Dara’s son Siphir Shikoh was released, given a mansab, and married to Aurangzeb’s daughter. - Murad’s son, Izzat Bakhsh, was also freed and given a mansab. - 1669: Dara’s daughter, Jani Begum, was married to Aurangzeb’s son Muhammad Azam. - Several marriages between Aurangzeb’s family and the descendants of his defeated brothers helped unite the dynasty in the third generation. - Aurangzeb’s Reign and Religious Policy - Aurangzeb’s Rule and Governance - Aurangzeb ruled for nearly 50 years, during which the Mughal Empire reached its territorial zenith, spanning from Kashmir in the north to Jinji in the south, and from the Hindukush in the west to Chittagong in the east. - He was a hardworking ruler, paying close attention to all affairs of the state, as reflected in his letters. - A strict disciplinarian, he did not spare even his sons—Prince Muazzam was imprisoned for 12 years for alleged intrigue with the ruler of Golconda. - Unlike his predecessors, he lived simply and rejected ostentation. He was considered an orthodox, God-fearing Muslim and came to be regarded as a zinda pir (a living saint). - Aurangzeb’s Early Rule and Consolidation Efforts - Reassertion of Imperial Authority - Aurangzeb’s primary focus after ascending the throne was consolidating Mughal authority rather than aggressive territorial expansion. - His initial efforts were directed at recovering areas lost during the war of succession and those to which the Mughals had a legal claim. - Local Resistance and Rebellions - During the war of succession, many local zamindars and rajas: - Withheld revenue from the Mughal administration. - Plundered neighboring regions, including Mughal territories and royal highways. - To reestablish control, Aurangzeb took military action against several rebellious rulers. - Policy on Conquest and Annexation - Non-annexation approach: - Sent an army to Bikaner to enforce obedience but did not annex it. - Bundela chief Champat Rai, who had initially allied with Aurangzeb but later turned to plundering, was relentlessly pursued, but Bundela lands were not annexed. - Selective annexation: - In cases where rulers were accused of disloyalty, such as Palamau in Bihar, their territories were annexed. - Territorial Expansion - While Aurangzeb generally did not follow a forward policy, the imperial frontier expanded in: - The northeast. - The Deccan. - Historiographical Debates on Aurangzeb - Historians are divided on his rule: - Some believe he reversed Akbar’s policy of religious tolerance, leading to Hindu discontent and uprisings that weakened the empire. - Others argue that his predecessors’ laxity had already caused Hindu disloyalty, forcing Aurangzeb to adopt harsh measures to rally Muslim support. - Modern research places his policies in the context of social, economic, and institutional factors. - Aurangzeb’s Religious Beliefs and Policies - Aurangzeb followed the Hanafi school of Islamic law but issued zawabit (secular decrees) to adapt to India’s conditions. - His religious policies had to account for the fact that the majority of the Indian population was Hindu. - His early regulations included: - Prohibiting the Kalma from being inscribed on coins to prevent desecration. - Discontinuing Nauroz, a festival linked to Zoroastrian traditions. - Appointing muhtasibs (moral enforcers) to ensure public adherence to the sharia. - Banning public consumption of intoxicants and gambling. - Ensuring proper trade practices by regulating weights and measures. - Puritanical Measures and Courtly Restrictions - In 1669, he imposed further religious restrictions: - Banned singing in court, though instrumental music and the royal band (naubat) continued. - Court musicians were pensioned off, yet classical Indian music thrived under Persian scholars, and Aurangzeb himself played the veena. - Abolished jharokha darshan, considering it a superstitious practice. - Prohibited the weighing ceremony of the emperor against gold and silver. - Discouraged astrology, but his ban on almanacs was ignored even by his family. - Introduced austerity measures, such as: - Simplifying court decor. - Replacing silver inkstands with porcelain ones. - Replacing gold railings in the Diwan-i-Am with lapis lazuli. - Discontinuing the official department of history-writing to cut costs. - Economic and Administrative Policies Favoring Muslims - Initially exempted Muslim traders from taxes to boost their commerce but reinstated them after finding abuses in the system. - Attempted to reserve peshkar and karori posts (petty revenue officials) for Muslims but faced resistance and had to relax the rule. - Temple Policy and Jizyah - Temple Regulations: - At the beginning of his reign, he reaffirmed that old temples should not be demolished, but new ones should not be built. - Old temples could be repaired, as stated in farmans issued to temples in Banaras and Vrindavan. - However, officials had discretion in interpreting “long-standing temples,” leading to selective enforcement. - Destruction of Temples as a Political Tool: - As governor of Gujarat, he had ordered temple destruction, and upon becoming emperor, he reiterated these orders in 1665. - In 1669, learning that Hindus and Muslims studied together in Banaras, Multan, and Thatta temples, he ordered their destruction. - Prominent temples destroyed included: - Keshava Rai Temple (Mathura) - Vishwanath Temple (Banaras) - Somnath Temple - Temple destruction was used as punishment for rebellion, such as during wars with the Rathors of Marwar and the Rana of Udaipur (1679–80). - Despite this, grants to some Hindu temples and religious institutions continued. - Reintroduction of Jizyah (1679) - Jizyah was a poll tax on non-Muslims, abolished by Akbar but reinstated by Aurangzeb under pressure from theologians. - Contrary to some claims, he did not aim to convert India into Dar-ul-Islam, as Islamic law already recognized the Mughal state as such. - His religious convictions and political ambitions often conflicted, leading to contradictory policies. - Conclusion - Aurangzeb’s religious policies were deeply influenced by his personal beliefs, but political considerations also played a significant role. - His strict adherence to Islamic law and intolerance of perceived un-Islamic practices alienated large sections of society. - His temple destruction policies and re-imposition of jizyah created resentment among Hindus and weakened the empire’s internal stability. - Despite his administrative competence and military achievements, his religious intolerance undermined Mughal unity, contributing to the empire’s eventual decline. - Mughal Conflicts and Expansion in the Northeast and Bengal - Conflict with the Ahoms and Expansion in Assam - The Ahoms controlled the Assam Valley and were engaged in conflicts with: - The rulers of Kamata (Kamrup) - The Afghan rulers of Bengal - By the late 15th century, the Kingdom of Kamata declined and was replaced by the Kuch (Cooch Bihar) kingdom, which controlled North Bengal and Western Assam. -
