The Kuch kingdom continued its conflicts with the Ahoms but later split due to internal disputes in the early 17th century, leading to Mughal intervention. - Mughal Entry into Assam (1612–1638) - The Mughals, at the request of the Kuch ruler, defeated a breakaway faction and occupied Western Assam (up to the Bar Nadi) in 1612. - The Kuch ruler became a Mughal vassal, bringing them into direct contact with the Ahoms. - A long war followed, ending in a 1638 treaty, which: - Fixed Bar Nadi as the boundary between the Ahoms and the Mughals. - Brought Guwahati under Mughal control. - Aurangzeb’s Assam Campaign (1662–1663) - The Ahoms attempted to expel the Mughals from Guwahati and surrounding areas. - Mir Jumla, Aurangzeb’s governor of Bengal, launched a campaign to annex Assam and Cooch Bihar: - 1662: First, he attacked Cooch Bihar, annexing it to the Mughal Empire. - 1663: He invaded the Ahom kingdom, captured Garhgaon, and held it for six months. - The Ahoms were forced into a humiliating treaty, which required them to: - Send their princess to the Mughal harem. - Pay a heavy war indemnity. - Provide 20 elephants annually as tribute. - The Mughal boundary extended from Bar Nadi to the Bharali River. - Ahom Resistance and Mughal Retreat (1667–1680s) - Mir Jumla died soon after his victory, and the Mughal hold on Assam weakened. - 1667: The Ahoms resumed their struggle, recovering lost territories and recapturing Guwahati. - The Mughals also lost control of Cooch Bihar. - A prolonged Mughal-Ahom war continued for over 15 years. - Raja Ram Singh of Amber, leading the Mughal forces, lacked the necessary resources. - Ultimately, the Mughals abandoned Guwahati, retreating further west. - Impact of the Assam War - Exposed the limits of Mughal power in distant regions. - Highlighted Ahom military skill, especially in guerrilla warfare. - The prolonged Mughal invasion weakened the Ahom monarchy, eventually leading to internal decline and fragmentation. - Mughal Expansion in Bengal and Orissa - Shaista Khan’s Campaign in Bengal (1664–1666) - Mir Jumla’s aggressive policy was modified by Shaista Khan, who: - Secured a settlement with Cooch Bihar. - Focused on eliminating the Arakanese (Magh) pirates, who had terrorized Bengal from Chittagong. - Arakanese (Magh) Pirates and the Chittagong Campaign - The Arakanese pirates disrupted trade and depopulated areas up to Dacca. - Shaista Khan built a Mughal navy and: - Captured Sondip Island as a base. - Won over Portuguese mercenaries (Firingis) with financial incentives. - Defeated the Arakanese navy near Chittagong, capturing many ships. - 1666: Chittagong was stormed and captured. - Effects of the Chittagong Victory - Ended Arakanese piracy, allowing: - Expansion of trade and commerce. - Revival of agriculture in Eastern Bengal. - Mughal Control Over Orissa - The rebellion of Afghan Pathans in Orissa was crushed. - Balasore was reopened for commerce. - Aurangzeb’s Internal Challenges: Regional and Political Movements - Introduction - Aurangzeb faced multiple political challenges within the empire, including: - The Marathas in the Deccan – fighting for local independence. - The Jats and Rajputs in North India – with Rajput conflicts centered on succession and Jat uprisings having a peasant-agrarian background. - The Afghans and Sikhs in the Northwest – with the Afghan struggle being tribal and the Sikh movement being deeply influenced by religion. - Nature of the Conflicts - Rajputs: Primarily a succession dispute. - Marathas: Fought for local autonomy. - Jats: Uprising had economic and agrarian roots. - Sikhs: Religion played a dominant role in their movement. - Afghans: Their struggle was tribal in nature but also carried aspirations for a separate Afghan state. - Key Factors Behind These Movements - Economic and social factors played a significant role. - Regional independence remained a powerful sentiment. - Religion also had an undeniable influence. - While some argue that most of these movements (except the Afghan one) were a Hindu reaction to Aurangzeb’s religious policies, this perspective is debated. - Any resistance against the Muslim central government could be perceived as a challenge to Islam. - Rebel leaders often used religious slogans and symbols to gain wider support. - Thus, these movements were shaped by a mix of economic, social, regional, and religious factors rather than being purely religious conflicts. - Jat Rebellions Against the Mughal Government - Early Conflicts with the Mughals - The Jats of the Agra-Delhi region, primarily peasant cultivators, were the first to come into conflict with the Mughal government. - Though mostly peasants, some Jats were zamindars and had a strong sense of brotherhood and justice. - Conflicts with the Mughals dated back to Jahangir and Shah Jahan’s reigns, mainly over land revenue collection. - The imperial road to the Deccan and western seaports passed through Jat territory, making their revolts a significant concern for the Mughals. - Jat Revolt of 1669 - Led by Gokla, a local zamindar from Mathura, the Jats launched a rebellion. - The movement spread quickly among peasants, growing to 20,000 fighters. - Aurangzeb personally marched from Delhi to suppress the uprising. - Despite their large numbers, the Jats were defeated, Gokla was captured and executed. - The revolt was not completely crushed, and discontent continued. - Satnami Revolt of 1672 - Another armed conflict arose in Narnaul, near Mathura, involving the Satnamis, a religious sect. - The Satnamis were mostly peasants, artisans, and lower-caste people, rejecting caste distinctions and following a strict code of conduct. - What started as a minor clash with a local official escalated into a rebellion. - Aurangzeb personally led the campaign against them. - Interestingly, local Hindu zamindars, including Rajputs, sided with the Mughals against the Satnamis. - Jat Revolt of 1685 - Under Rajaram, the Jats revolted again, this time with better organization and guerrilla tactics. - They combined plundering with warfare, making the Delhi-Agra road unsafe. - Aurangzeb enlisted Raja Bishan Singh of the Kachhwaha dynasty to suppress the uprising. - Bishan Singh was appointed faujdar of Mathura, and the entire region was granted to him as zamindari. - The conflict was further complicated by disputes between Jat primary zamindars (land-owning cultivators) and Rajput intermediary zamindars (revenue collectors). - Rise of the Jat State - By 1691, Rajaram and his successor Churaman were forced to submit. - However, Jat resistance and plundering activities continued. - In the 18th century, taking advantage of Mughal civil wars and declining central authority, Churaman carved out a separate Jat principality, ousting the Rajput zamindars. - What began as a peasant uprising gradually transformed into an independent Jat-ruled state. - Afghan Resistance Against Aurangzeb - Historical Background - Conflict with the Afghans was not new for the Mughals. - Akbar had to fight the Afghan tribes, during which his close friend Raja Birbal lost his life. - Shah Jahan also faced conflicts with the Afghan tribesmen. - These conflicts were driven by economic, political, and religious factors: - The rugged mountainous terrain between Punjab and Kabul offered little livelihood. - The Afghans relied on plundering caravans or joining the Mughal army. - Their love for freedom made Mughal service difficult. - The Mughals kept them content by paying subsidies, but unrest grew when the population increased or an ambitious leader emerged. - First Afghan Revolt (1667-1671) - A new stirring among the Pathans began under Bhagu, leader of the Yusufzai tribe. - Bhagu proclaimed Muhammad Shah as king and declared himself wazir, signaling the Afghan desire for a separate state. - A religious revivalist movement, Raushanai, emphasizing strict ethics and devotion to a pir, gave moral strength to the movement. - The rebellion spread, with Hazara, Attock, and Peshawar districts being plundered, bringing traffic through the Khyber Pass to a halt. - Aurangzeb sent Amir Khan, the chief bakhshi, with a Rajput contingent to suppress the revolt. - After several hard-fought battles, the resistance was broken. - To maintain control, Maharaja Jaswant Singh of Marwar was appointed thanedar of Jamrud in 1671. - Second Afghan Revolt (1672-1675) - In 1672, a second major Afghan uprising took place under Afridi chief Akmal Khan. - Akmal Khan proclaimed himself king, read the khutba, and struck coins in his name, calling all Afghans to war against the Mughals. - His army, described as “more numerous than ants and locusts,” blocked the Khyber Pass. - Amir Khan led an advance to clear the pass but was ambushed and disastrously defeated in a narrow defile. - He barely escaped, but 10,000 Mughal soldiers perished, and goods worth two crores were looted. - Encouraged by this, other Afghan leaders, including Khushhal Khan Khattak, a sworn enemy of Aurangzeb, joined the resistance. - In 1674, another Mughal noble, Shujaat Khan, was defeated but rescued by a Rathore force sent by Jaswant Singh. - Aurangzeb’s Direct Intervention (1674-1675) - In mid-1674, Aurangzeb himself marched to Peshawar to restore order. - Through a combination of force and diplomacy, the Afghan resistance was broken. - By the end of 1675, peace was gradually restored. - Significance of the Afghan Uprising - The Afghan resistance showed that Mughal opposition was not limited to Hindus like the Jats and Marathas. - The uprising diverted Mughal attention from the Deccan, helping Shivaji: - It reduced pressure on Shivaji at a crucial time. - It delayed Mughal expansion in the Deccan until 1676, by which time Shivaji had: - Crowned himself. - Allied with Bijapur and Golconda. - Conflict Between the Sikh Gurus and the Mughals under Aurangzeb - Early Relations and Initial Clashes - Though there were some clashes between the Sikh Gurus and the Mughals under Shah Jahan, no significant conflict occurred between the Sikhs and Aurangzeb until 1675. - Aurangzeb recognized the growing influence of the Sikhs and attempted to engage Ram Rai, the elder son of Guru Har Rai, at his court. - However, Guru Har Rai disapproved of Ram Rai and instead nominated his younger son, Guru Har Kishan, as his successor, despite his young age. - Guru Har Kishan died soon after, and in 1664, Guru Tegh Bahadur became the next Sikh Guru. - Intrigues Against Guru Tegh Bahadur - Ram Rai contested the succession, both before and after Guru Har Kishan’s death. - Aurangzeb did not interfere but granted land in Dehra Dun to Ram Rai for a gurudwara. - Ram Rai, however, stayed in Delhi and actively worked against Guru Tegh Bahadur, poisoning the emperor’s mind against him. - To escape Ram Rai’s schemes, Guru Tegh Bahadur moved to Bihar and later served alongside Raja Ram Singh of Amber in Assam until 1671. - Execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675) - In 1675, Guru Tegh Bahadur and five followers were arrested and taken to Delhi. - He was accused of various charges and asked to renounce his faith, which he refused. - As a result, he was beheaded. - Reasons Behind Aurangzeb’s Actions - Defense of Hindu Faith: - According to Guru Gobind Singh’s poetic account, Guru Tegh Bahadur sacrificed his life to protect Kashmiri Brahmins from forced conversion. However, historical records of this event are lacking. - Opposition to Mughal Oppression: - Some traditions claim he protested against the Mughal governor of Kashmir, but evidence of large-scale forced conversions is scarce. - Religious Rivalry: - Another view suggests that Ram Rai influenced Aurangzeb to test the Guru by demanding a miracle, and his refusal led to execution. However, Aurangzeb was away from Delhi at the time. - Political Concerns: - Persian sources allege that the Guru had a large following and collected money from villagers, causing the Mughal administration to perceive him as a threat. However, these accounts are questionable. - Impact of Guru Tegh Bahadur’s Execution - The event forced the Sikhs to retreat to the Punjab hills and transformed the Sikh movement into a military brotherhood. - Guru Gobind Singh played a crucial role in this transformation. - Rise of Guru Gobind Singh and the Formation of the Khalsa - Early Years and Conflict with Hill Rajas - Guru Gobind Singh established his headquarters at Makhowal (Anandpur) in Punjab’s foothills. - Initially, Hindu hill rajas tried to use the Sikhs in their internal conflicts, but as Guru Gobind Singh’s power grew, tensions escalated. - By 1704, a coalition of hill rajas attacked Anandpur, but they failed to defeat him and sought Mughal intervention. - Mughal-Sikh Conflict - The conflict was not purely religious but involved political rivalries between the Sikh movement and the hill rajas. - Aurangzeb, concerned about the Guru’s rising influence, instructed Mughal officials to take action. - Mughal forces, led by Wazir Khan, besieged Anandpur. After prolonged resistance, Guru Gobind Singh negotiated for safe passage, but Wazir Khan’s troops betrayed him and attacked while crossing a river. - Two of the Guru’s sons were captured and executed after refusing to convert to Islam, while two more died in battle. - Later Years of Guru Gobind Singh - Guru Gobind Singh withdrew to Talwandi and was left largely undisturbed. - It remains unclear if Wazir Khan acted on Aurangzeb’s direct orders in executing the Guru’s sons. - Aurangzeb later wrote to the governor of Lahore, urging reconciliation with the Guru. - In 1706, Guru Gobind Singh wrote to Aurangzeb, explaining the events, and the emperor invited him to meet in the Deccan. - The Guru set out, but Aurangzeb died before their meeting. - Legacy of Guru Gobind Singh - Though he could not establish a Sikh state, he laid the foundation for its future realization. - In 1699, he founded the Khalsa, a militarized Sikh order, demonstrating how a religious movement could evolve into a political and military force. - Mughal-Rajput Relations and Rebellions - Mughal-Rajput Relations Under Jahangir and Shah Jahan - Jahangir’s Policy Towards Mewar - In 1613, Jahangir settled the long-standing conflict with Mewar. - He continued Akbar’s policy of granting favors to leading Rajput rajas and forging matrimonial alliances with them. - Shah Jahan’s Rajput Alliance - Shah Jahan maintained close ties with the Rajputs, and their contingents served with distinction in the Deccan, Balkh (Central Asia), and Qandhar. - However, no Rajput raja was appointed governor of a province, and no further matrimonial alliances were made with leading Rajput rulers, despite Shah Jahan being the son of a Rathor princess. - The consolidation of the Rajput alliance likely led to the belief that further matrimonial ties were unnecessary. - Shah Jahan continued to honor the heads of the two leading Rajput houses, Jodhpur and Amber. - Raja Jaswant Singh of Marwar was highly favored and, along with Jai Singh, held a mansab of 7000/7000 at the time of Aurangzeb’s accession. - Aurangzeb’s Early Rajput Policy - Efforts to Maintain Rajput Loyalty - Aurangzeb valued the Rajput alliance and sought to secure Mewar’s support by raising the Maharana’s mansab from 5000/5000 to 6000/6000. - Despite Jaswant Singh’s earlier opposition—fighting against Aurangzeb at Dharmat, defecting during the campaign against Shuja, and inviting Dara to Marwar—Aurangzeb pardoned him, restored his previous mansab, and entrusted him with important commands, including the governorship of Gujarat. - Jai Singh remained a close ally and confidant of Aurangzeb until his death in 1667. - Crisis in Marwar (1678-1679) - Jaswant Singh’s Death and Succession Dispute - Jaswant Singh died in 1678 while handling Afghan affairs in the northwest, leaving no surviving male heir at the time. - The Mughal tradition dictated that in cases of disputed succession, the state would be placed under khalisa (Mughal administration) until a successor was determined. - A similar precedent had been set in 1650, when Shah Jahan took Jaisalmer under khalisa before appointing a successor. - Mughal Justification for Annexing Marwar - Jaswant Singh, like many Mughal nobles, owed large sums to the Mughal treasury. - Several Rajputs, whom he had offended or whose territories had been granted to him as jagirs, saw his death as an opportunity to create disturbances. - Anticipating resistance, Aurangzeb allotted two parganas in Marwar for Jaswant Singh’s family and supporters. - He assembled a strong army and marched to Ajmer to enforce his authority. - Mughal Occupation and Resistance - Rani Hadi, Jaswant Singh’s chief queen, objected to handing over Jodhpur to the Mughals, as it was the watan (homeland) of the Rathors, but she was forced to submit. - Mughal officials were deployed throughout Marwar, and a thorough search was conducted for Jaswant Singh’s hidden treasures. - Large numbers of temples, including old ones, were demolished or sealed, and the Mughals treated Marwar as hostile territory. - Aurangzeb’s Decision and Rathor Rebellion - Aurangzeb’s Choice of Inder Singh - In Lahore, two of Jaswant Singh’s queens gave birth to sons after his death, strengthening their claim to the throne. - However, Aurangzeb awarded the sikka (throne) of Jodhpur to Inder Singh, grandson of Jaswant Singh’s elder brother Amar Singh, in exchange for a succession fee of 36 lakh rupees. - Aurangzeb may have believed that Shah Jahan had been unjust in passing over Amar Singh in favor of Jaswant Singh. - Some historians claim that Aurangzeb offered the throne to Ajit Singh (Jaswant Singh’s posthumous son) on the condition that he convert to Islam, but contemporary sources provide no evidence for this. - The Hukumat-ni-Bahi, a contemporary Rajasthani record, states that Aurangzeb offered Ajit Singh a mansab and allotted him two parganas in Marwar as a jagir. - Rejection of the Mughal Decision - The Rathor sardars, led by Durgadas, rejected Aurangzeb’s compromise as detrimental to Marwar’s interests. - When Aurangzeb ordered the confinement of the Rathor princes and their mothers in the fort of Nurgarh, the Rathors staged a daring escape. - One of the princes was successfully smuggled out of Agra and crowned Ajit Singh at Jodhpur amidst great celebration. - Aurangzeb’s Response - Recognizing that Inder Singh had little support, Aurangzeb set him aside for incompetence but refused to recognize Ajit Singh. - Branding Ajit Singh a “pretender,” he summoned forces from across the empire and marched to Ajmer once again. - The Rathor resistance was crushed, and Jodhpur was occupied. - Durgadas fled with Ajit Singh to Mewar, where Rana Raj Singh provided him with a secret hideout. - Mewar’s Involvement in the War (1679-1681) - Mewar Joins the Conflict - Rana Raj Singh, initially an ally of Aurangzeb, turned against him due to: - Mughal interference in Rajput successions - Mughal efforts to detach vassal states like Dungarpur and Banswara from Mewar - The military occupation of Marwar and rejection of Ajit Singh’s claim - He sent 5,000 troops under a trusted commander to support Rani Hadi’s resistance in Jodhpur. - Aurangzeb’s Campaign Against Mewar - In November 1679, Aurangzeb launched an invasion of Mewar. - His forces raided Udaipur and attacked the Rana’s camp. - The Rana retreated into the hills, adopting guerrilla tactics, which the Mughals struggled to counter. - The war became highly unpopular, and Aurangzeb’s repeated admonitions had little effect on his commanders. - Prince Akbar’s Rebellion (1681) and Aftermath - Rebellion of Prince Akbar - Aurangzeb’s son, Prince Akbar, attempted to exploit Rajput discontent and rebelled against his father. - In January 1681, he allied with Rathor chief Durgadas and marched on Ajmer, where Aurangzeb was vulnerable. - However, delays and Aurangzeb’s counter-tactics caused dissension in Akbar’s camp, forcing him to flee to Maharashtra. - Settlement with Mewar and Marwar - With Akbar’s rebellion defeated, Mewar became a secondary concern for Aurangzeb. - In a treaty with Rana Jagat Singh (Rana Raj Singh’s successor): - Mewar surrendered some parganas in lieu of jizyah. - The Rana received a mansab of 5000 and pledged loyalty to the Mughals. - Aurangzeb promised that Ajit Singh would receive a mansab and Marwar upon reaching adulthood. - This agreement satisfied neither the Rajputs nor the Mughals. - Final Resolution - The Mughals retained control over Marwar, and sporadic conflict continued. - In 1698, Ajit Singh was finally recognized as Marwar’s ruler, but the Mughals refused to relinquish Jodhpur. - Tensions persisted until Aurangzeb’s death in 1707. - Conclusion: The Failure of Aurangzeb’s Rajput Policy - Aurangzeb’s handling of Marwar and Mewar was rigid and counterproductive. - It weakened the Mughal-Rajput alliance, damaged Mughal military prestige, and exposed his inflexible nature. - While it did not indicate a broader anti-Hindu agenda—given the rise of Maratha nobility—it contributed to the empire’s decline. - However, the real struggle for the Mughal Empire lay in the Deccan campaigns. - Climax and Disintegration of the Mughal Empire—II - - Rise of the Marathas in the Deccan - Marathas in the Administrative and Military Systems - The Marathas held important positions in the administrative and military systems of Ahmadnagar and Bijapur. - Their power and influence in governmental affairs increased as the Mughals advanced into the Deccan. - Both the Deccani sultans and the Mughals sought their support. - Malik Ambar extensively used Marathas as loose auxiliaries in his army. - Influence of Maratha Families - Several influential Maratha families exercised local authority in certain areas, including: - The Mores - The Ghatages - The Nimbalkars - Unlike the Rajputs, the Marathas did not have large, well-established states. - Shahji Bhonsale and Early Maratha State-Building - The credit for establishing a large Maratha state goes to Shahji Bhonsale and his son, Shivaji. - Shahji acted as a kingmaker in Ahmadnagar for some time and defied the Mughals. - However, after the Treaty of 1636, Shahji: - Yielded the territories he controlled. - Joined the service of Bijapur. - Shifted his focus to Karnataka. - Attempts to Establish Independent Principalities - Taking advantage of unsettled conditions, Shahji attempted to establish a semi-independent principality at Bangalore. - This was similar to how: - Mir Jumla, the leading noble of Golconda, sought to carve out a principality on the Coromandel coast. - The Abyssinian chiefs (Sidis) on the western coast acted in a similar manner. - Prelude to Shivaji’s Rise - These developments set the stage for Shivaji’s attempt to carve out a large principality around Poona. - Shivaji’s Rise and Early Conquests - Inheritance and Early Military Exploits (1645–1647) - Shahji left the Poona jagir to his neglected senior wife, Jija Bai, and his minor son, Shivaji. - At just 18 years old, Shivaji demonstrated his military prowess by capturing several hill forts near Poona: - Rajgarh - Kondana - Torna - In 1647, after the death of his guardian, Dadaji Kondadeo, Shivaji became his own master, gaining full control of his father’s jagir. - Conquest of Javli and Expansion in the Mavala Region (1656) - Shivaji’s true career of conquest began in 1656 when he defeated the Maratha chief Chandra Rao More and conquered Javli. - The Javli kingdom and the accumulated treasure of the Mores were significant, and Shivaji acquired them through treachery. - With the conquest of Javli: - Shivaji became the undisputed master of the Mavala region (highlands). - His path to Satara and the Konkan coastal strip was cleared. - The Mavali foot soldiers became a crucial component of his army. - He further strengthened his position by acquiring more hill forts near Poona. - Conflict with the Mughals and the Bijapur Sultanate (1657–1659) - In 1657, the Mughal invasion of Bijapur saved Shivaji from immediate conflict with Aurangzeb. - Taking advantage of the situation, Shivaji switched sides and made deep inroads into Mughal territory, looting wealth. - However, when Aurangzeb reached an agreement with Bijapur, he: - Pardoned Shivaji but remained distrustful of him. - Advised the Bijapur ruler to expel Shivaji from his conquered territories. - Suggested that if Bijapur employed Shivaji, he should be stationed in Karnataka, far from Mughal frontiers. - With Aurangzeb preoccupied in the north, Shivaji resumed conquests at Bijapur’s expense, expanding into: - Konkan (coastal strip between the Ghats and the sea). - Several hill forts in the region. - Confrontation with Afzal Khan (1659) - Alarmed by Shivaji’s rise, Bijapur sent Afzal Khan, a premier noble, with 10,000 troops to capture him. - Treachery was common in those days, and both Afzal Khan and Shivaji had used it before. - Shivaji’s forces, unaccustomed to open battle, hesitated to engage Afzal Khan’s superior army. - Afzal Khan invited Shivaji for a personal meeting, promising to secure his pardon from Bijapur’s court. - Aware of the trap, Shivaji arrived prepared and, in a cunning but daring act, murdered Afzal Khan (1659). - His forces then routed the leaderless Bijapuri army, capturing: - Goods - Equipment - Artillery - Flushed with victory, Shivaji’s troops: - Overran the fort of Panhala. - Advanced into South Konkan and Kolhapur, making extensive conquests. - Shivaji’s Growing Reputation and Aurangzeb’s Response - Shivaji’s daring exploits made him a legendary figure. - His reputation soared, and he was believed to have magical powers. - Many, including Maratha warriors and Afghan mercenaries, joined his army. - Aurangzeb, alarmed by Shivaji’s rise near the Mughal frontiers, ordered his governor of the Deccan, Shaista Khan, to launch an invasion. - War with Shaista Khan and Mughal Retaliation (1660–1663) - The conflict initially went badly for Shivaji: - In 1660, Shaista Khan occupied Poona and made it his headquarters. - Mughal forces seized North Konkan, despite facing stiff resistance from Maratha troops. - Shivaji, pushed into a corner, devised a bold counterattack: - In 1663, he infiltrated Shaista Khan’s camp in Poona under the cover of night. - He attacked Shaista Khan in his harem, killing: - His son - One of his captains - Shaista Khan was wounded but escaped. - This daring raid disgraced Shaista Khan, leading to: - Aurangzeb transferring him to Bengal. - Aurangzeb refusing him an audience, a significant humiliation at the time. - Attack on Surat (1664) - Shivaji followed up with another audacious move: - In 1664, he attacked Surat, the premier Mughal port. - His forces looted it extensively, returning with immense treasure. - Treaty of Purandar and Shivaji’s Visit to Agra - Appointment of Raja Jai Singh and the Siege of Purandar (1665) - After Shaista Khan’s failure, Aurangzeb assigned Raja Jai Singh of Amber, one of his most trusted advisers, to handle Shivaji. - Jai Singh was given full military and administrative authority, allowing him to bypass the Mughal viceroy in the Deccan and report directly to Aurangzeb. - Unlike his predecessors, Jai Singh: - Did not underestimate the Marathas. - Made careful diplomatic and military preparations. - Appealed to Shivaji’s rivals and opponents, including the Sultan of Bijapur, to isolate him. - Jai Singh marched to Poona and decided to strike at the heart of Shivaji’s domain—Fort Purandar, where Shivaji had lodged his family and treasure. - In 1665, Jai Singh besieged Purandar, successfully blocking all Maratha relief attempts. - With defeat imminent, Shivaji was forced to open negotiations, leading to the Treaty of Purandar. - Terms of the Treaty of Purandar (1665) - After intense negotiations, Shivaji and Jai Singh agreed to the following terms: - Surrender of Forts and Territory: - Out of 35 forts, 23 forts (along with surrounding lands yielding 4 lakh huns annually) were to be surrendered to the Mughals. - 12 forts (yielding 1 lakh huns annually) would remain under Shivaji’s control, provided he served and remained loyal to the Mughal throne. - Grant of Bijapuri Territory: - Shivaji retained 4 lakh huns worth of Bijapuri Konkan territory, which he already controlled. - The Mughals granted him additional 5 lakh huns worth of uplands (Balaghat), which Shivaji was expected to conquer himself. - In return, Shivaji was to pay 40 lakh huns to the Mughals in installments. - Mansab for Sambhaji and Shivaji’s Military Role: - Shivaji requested exemption from personal service. - Instead, a mansab of 5000 was granted to his minor son, Sambhaji. - Shivaji promised to join Mughal campaigns in the Deccan when required. - Mughal-Maratha Relations and the Failure of Jai Singh’s Strategy - Jai Singh’s strategy aimed to create a rift between Shivaji and Bijapur’s ruler, ensuring Shivaji remained loyal to the Mughals. - However, the success of this plan depended on Mughal support for Shivaji in reclaiming the lands surrendered to them from Bijapur. - This proved to be a fatal flaw: - Aurangzeb distrusted Shivaji and doubted the value of a joint Mughal-Maratha attack on Bijapur. - Jai Singh, on the other hand, had grander ambitions: - He envisioned the conquest of Bijapur and the entire Deccan. - He believed that once this was achieved, Shivaji would have no choice but to remain a Mughal ally. - He wrote to Aurangzeb: “We shall hem Shivaji in like the center of a circle.” - However, the Mughal-Maratha expedition against Bijapur failed. - Shivaji, who had been assigned to capture Fort Panhala, was also unsuccessful. - Seeing his plan collapse, Jai Singh persuaded Shivaji to visit Aurangzeb in Agra, hoping: - A reconciliation between Shivaji and Aurangzeb. - Increased Mughal support for a renewed attack on Bijapur. - Shivaji’s Visit to Agra and His Dramatic Escape (1666) - Shivaji’s visit to Agra turned out to be a disaster: - He felt insulted when he was ranked among mansabdars of 3000—a rank previously granted to his minor son, Sambhaji. - During Aurangzeb’s birthday celebrations, the emperor did not grant Shivaji an audience, further humiliating him. - Angered by this treatment, Shivaji: - Stormed out in protest. - Refused imperial service—a shocking act never before seen at the Mughal court. - A strong faction at court urged Aurangzeb to punish Shivaji severely to maintain imperial dignity. - Aurangzeb’s Dilemma and Shivaji’s Escape - Since Shivaji had come to Agra on Jai Singh’s assurance, Aurangzeb sought Jai Singh’s advice. - Jai Singh advocated leniency, but before a decision could be made: - Shivaji dramatically escaped from detention in 1666. - The details of his escape are well known and need not be repeated here. - Aurangzeb blamed himself for his carelessness in allowing Shivaji to escape. - Impact of Shivaji’s Visit to Agra - The Agra incident marked a turning point in Mughal-Maratha relations. - Though Shivaji remained inactive for two years after his escape, it was now clear that: - Unlike Jai Singh, Aurangzeb placed little value on an alliance with Shivaji. - To Aurangzeb, Shivaji was merely a petty zamindar (landholder). - As subsequent events proved, Aurangzeb’s failure to recognize Shivaji’s importance and refusal to forge an alliance with him were among the greatest political mistakes of his reign. - Shivaji: Conquests, Administration, and Legacy - Renewed Conflict with the Mughals and Bijapur - Aurangzeb’s rigid interpretation of the Treaty of Purandar, despite its practical failure following the unsuccessful expedition against Bijapur, provoked Shivaji into resuming his conquests. - The loss of 23 forts and territory worth four lakh hons annually to the Mughals, without compensation from Bijapur, was unacceptable to Shivaji. - In 1670, he sacked Surat for the second time. - Over the next four years, he reclaimed several forts, including Purandar, and made deep inroads into Mughal territories (especially Berar and Khandesh). - The Mughal preoccupation with the Afghan uprising in the northwest gave Shivaji an advantage. - He also resumed conflict with Bijapur, securing Panhala and Satara through bribes and raiding the Kanara region. - Coronation at Raigarh (1674) - Shivaji’s formal coronation at Raigarh in 1674 marked his transformation from a petty jagirdar of Poona to the most powerful Maratha chief. Given the extent of his dominions and the size of his army, he could claim status equal to that of the weakened Deccani sultans. - The coronation served multiple purposes: - Political Legitimacy: Elevated him above other Maratha chiefs, some of whom saw him as an upstart. - Social Status: Strengthened his position by marrying into powerful Maratha families like the Mohites and Shirkes. - Religious Validation: Gaga Bhatta, the presiding priest, declared him a high-class Kshatriya. - Diplomatic Recognition: Enabled him to sign treaties with Deccani sultans as an independent ruler rather than a rebel. - Maratha Nationalism: Strengthened Maratha identity and aspirations. - Karnataka Expedition (1676-1679) - Shivaji embarked on an ambitious Karnataka campaign in 1676, with the support of Madanna and Akhanna, ministers at Hyderabad. - Alliance with the Qutb Shah: - Shivaji was welcomed at Golconda, and a treaty was signed. - The Qutb Shah agreed to pay one lakh hons (₹5 lakh) annually and host a Maratha ambassador. - Joint sharing of territory and booty. - The Qutb Shah supplied troops, artillery, and financial aid. - Military Success: - Captured Jinji and Vellore from Bijapuri officials. - Conquered lands controlled by his half-brother Ekoji. - Breach of Trust: - Despite claiming the title of Haindava-Dharmoddharak (Protector of Hindu Faith), Shivaji plundered the local Hindu population. - Refused to share the loot with the Qutb Shah, leading to strained relations. - The Karnataka expedition was Shivaji’s last major campaign. The fort at Jinji, which he fortified, later served as a crucial refuge for his son Rajaram during Aurangzeb’s war on the Marathas. - Administrative System - Shivaji established a sound administrative system, largely inspired by the Deccani states. - Ashtapradhan Council (Ministers) - Although he appointed eight ministers (Ashtapradhan), they were directly responsible to the ruler, not functioning as a collective council. - Peshwa – Finance and general administration. - Sar-i-Naubat (Senapati) – Military commander (mostly honorary). - Majumdar – Accountant. - Waqia Navis – Intelligence, postal services, and household affairs. - Surunavis (Chitnis) – Official correspondence. - Dabir – Foreign affairs and ceremonial duties. - Nyayadhish – Judiciary. - Panditrao – Religious and charitable affairs. - Army Organization - Cash salaries were preferred, though revenue grants (saranjam) were sometimes awarded. - Strict discipline: - Women and dancing girls were not allowed in the army. - Plunder was strictly accounted for. - Regular cavalry (Paga): 30,000–40,000 troops, commanded by Havaldars (fixed salaries). - Forts were strategically supervised, guarded by Mavali foot soldiers and gunners. - Anti-treachery measures: Three officers of equal rank managed each fort. - Revenue System - Modeled after Malik Ambar’s reforms. - A new revenue assessment was completed by Annaji Datto in 1679. - Contrary to some beliefs, Shivaji did not abolish the zamindari (deshmukhi) system nor completely eliminate jagirs (mokasa). - Mirasdars (hereditary landowners) were strictly supervised: - Sabhasad, an 18th-century chronicler, noted that mirasdars paid the government only a fraction of their revenue. - Many had built forts, enlisted musketeers, and defied authority. - Shivaji demolished their strongholds and forced submission. - Additional Revenue: Chauth System - Imposed a one-fourth (chauth) tax on Mughal territories as a tribute. - Legacy and Final Years - Shivaji passed away in 1680, shortly after returning from the Karnataka campaign. However, his legacy was far-reaching: - Military Genius: - Master of guerrilla warfare and rapid troop movement. - His army was highly mobile and efficient. - Relied heavily on plunder for military funding. - State-Building: - Though war-driven, his kingdom was not merely a “war-state”. - His rule had a popular base and represented local resistance against Mughal encroachments. - By curbing the deshmukhs’ power, he laid the foundation for a strong Maratha state. - Shivaji’s leadership, diplomacy, and military acumen ensured that the Marathas remained a dominant force even after his death, influencing Indian history for centuries to come. - Aurangzeb and the Deccan States: Phases of Relations - The relations between Aurangzeb and the Deccan states can be divided into three distinct phases: 1. First Phase (Until 1668): - The primary objective was to recover from Bijapur the territories of the former Ahmadnagar state, which had been surrendered to it by the treaty of 1636. 2. Second Phase (1668–1684): - The main threat in the Deccan during this period was the Marathas. - The Mughals pressured Bijapur and Golconda to align with them against Shivaji and later his son, Sambhaji. - While doing so, the Mughals gradually encroached upon the territories of the Deccan states, aiming to bring them under complete Mughal control. 3. Final Phase (1684 Onwards): - Aurangzeb abandoned hopes of securing the cooperation of Bijapur and Golconda against the Marathas. - Convinced that the destruction of the Marathas required the conquest of these states first, he decided to subjugate Bijapur and Golconda entirely. - Mughal Expansion and Treaty Violations - The Treaty of 1636, under which Shah Jahan had ceded one-third of the Ahmadnagar territories to Bijapur and Golconda as a bribe to keep them from supporting the Marathas, included a Mughal promise “never ever” to conquer these states. However, Shah Jahan himself disregarded this agreement. - In 1657-58, both Golconda and Bijapur faced Mughal threats: - Golconda was forced to pay a hefty indemnity. - Bijapur had to surrender the Nizam Shahi territories granted to it in 1636. - Justification for Mughal Actions - The Mughals justified these aggressive moves by arguing that: - Both states had expanded significantly in Karnataka. - Since they were considered Mughal vassals, the Mughals were entitled to “compensation” for their conquests, which had been possible only due to Mughal neutrality. - However, the real reason was financial: - Maintaining Mughal armies in the Deccan was costly. - The revenue from Mughal-controlled territories was insufficient. - For a long time, the shortfall was covered by subsidies from Malwa and Gujarat treasuries. - Consequences of Mughal Expansion - The policy of limited expansion in the Deccan had far-reaching consequences, which neither Shah Jahan nor Aurangzeb fully grasped: - It permanently eroded trust in Mughal treaties and assurances. - A “union of hearts” against the Marathas became impossible. - Despite Aurangzeb’s relentless efforts for 25 years, the policy brought little success. - The First Phase of Aurangzeb’s Deccan Policy (1658–1668) - Upon ascending the throne, Aurangzeb faced two major challenges in the Deccan: 1. The rising power of Shivaji. 2. Persuading Bijapur to relinquish the territories it had acquired under the Treaty of 1636. - Initial Gains and the Mughal Strategy - Kalyani and Bidar had been secured in 1657. - Parenda was obtained through bribery in 1660. - However, Sholapur remained under Bijapur’s control. - After his accession, Aurangzeb ordered Jai Singh to take action against both Shivaji and Adil Shah of Bijapur. - This directive reflected Aurangzeb’s overconfidence in Mughal military superiority and his underestimation of his opponents. - However, Jai Singh, an astute politician, warned Aurangzeb: “It would be unwise to attack both these foes at the same time.” - Jai Singh was the only Mughal statesman of this period who advocated an aggressive forward policy in the Deccan. - He believed that the Maratha problem could not be resolved without Mughal expansion in the region—a conclusion Aurangzeb himself would reach two decades later. - The Plan to Invade Bijapur and Aurangzeb’s Reluctance - While planning his invasion of Bijapur, Jai Singh wrote to Aurangzeb: “The conquest of Bijapur is the preface to the conquest of all Deccan and Karnataka.” - However, Aurangzeb hesitated to commit to this bold strategy. His reluctance was due to: - The threat posed by the ruler of Iran in the northwest. - The long and arduous nature of a Deccan campaign, which would require the emperor’s personal presence. - The risk of leaving a large Mughal army under the command of an ambitious noble or prince, a lesson Shah Jahan had learned to his misfortune. - Shah Jahan’s continued existence, which restricted Aurangzeb from embarking on a distant military campaign. - Jai Singh’s Failed Bijapur Campaign (1665) - With limited resources at his disposal, Jai Singh’s Bijapur campaign was doomed to fail. - The Deccan states united against the Mughals, as the Qutb Shah of Golconda sent a large force to aid Bijapur. - The Deccanis employed guerrilla tactics: - They lured Jai Singh’s forces towards Bijapur. - They devastated the countryside, cutting off Mughal supplies. - Jai Singh’s campaign suffered from logistical shortcomings: - He lacked siege artillery. - A prolonged siege was impossible. - His eventual retreat proved costly, yielding neither money nor additional territory. - The failure of this campaign, coupled with Aurangzeb’s criticisms, led to Jai Singh’s death in 1667. - End of the First Phase (1668) - In 1668, the Mughals secured the surrender of Sholapur through bribery, marking the end of the first phase of Mughal expansion in the Deccan. - The Second Phase of Aurangzeb’s Deccan Policy (1668–1684) - Mughal Inactivity and the Rise of Golconda’s Leadership (1668–1676) - Between 1668 and 1676, the Mughals largely remained inactive in the Deccan. - During this period, a new political dynamic emerged with the rise of Madanna and Akhanna, two talented brothers who virtually controlled the administration of Golconda from 1672 until its annexation in 1687. - Their primary objective was to establish a tripartite alliance between: 1. Golconda 2. Bijapur 3. Shivaji’s Marathas - However, this alliance was frequently disrupted due to: - Factional conflicts within Bijapur - Shivaji’s growing ambitions, which led him to alternately loot Bijapur and then support it against the Mughals - Mughal Attempts to Influence Bijapur - The factions at Bijapur pursued inconsistent policies, aligning either with or against the Mughals based on their immediate interests. - Despite his concerns over the growing Maratha power, Aurangzeb was reluctant to expand Mughal territories in the Deccan. - Instead, he pursued a policy of manipulating Bijapur’s internal politics to: - Install a pro-Mughal faction - Weaken Shivaji’s influence - Ensure Bijapur remained independent of Golconda’s control - To achieve this, the Mughals launched several military interventions, but these efforts only strengthened the unity of the three Deccan states against the Mughals. - Diler Khan’s Failed Siege of Bijapur (1679–1680) - In a final, desperate attempt, Diler Khan, the Mughal viceroy, led a campaign to capture Bijapur in 1679–1680. However, the Mughals were outmatched by the combined strength of the Deccan states. - A new factor in the conflict was the Karnataki matchlock-armed foot soldiers. - 30,000 of these troops, sent by Berar chief Prem Naik, played a decisive role in repelling the Mughal siege of Bijapur. - Additionally, Shivaji dispatched a large force to aid Bijapur and launched raids into Mughal territories. - End of the Second Phase - Diler Khan’s campaign failed, exposing Mughal territories to repeated Maratha incursions. - As a result, he was recalled by Aurangzeb, marking the end of this phase of Mughal expansion in the Deccan. - The Final Phase of Aurangzeb’s Deccan Campaign (1681–1707) - Aurangzeb’s Renewed Efforts (1681–1684) - Between 1676 and 1680, the Mughals achieved little success in the Deccan. When Aurangzeb arrived in the region in 1681 while pursuing his rebel son, Prince Akbar, he initially focused on: - Targeting Sambhaji, the son and successor of Shivaji. - Attempting to detach Bijapur and Golconda from their alliance with the Marathas. - However, these efforts failed, much like before. The Deccan states viewed the Marathas as their only shield against Mughal expansion and refused to abandon them. - The Fall of Bijapur (1686) - Frustrated with diplomatic failures, Aurangzeb decided to force Bijapur into submission. He issued a set of demands to the Adil Shah, treating him as a Mughal vassal: - Supply provisions to the Mughal army. - Allow free passage for Mughal forces through Bijapur’s territory. - Provide 5,000–6,000 cavalry to assist the Mughals against the Marathas. - Expel Sharza Khan, a prominent anti-Mughal noble in Bijapur. - These demands led to open conflict. The Adil Shah sought military support from both Golconda and Sambhaji, who responded immediately. - However, even the combined strength of the Deccan states could not withstand the full might of Aurangzeb’s army, especially with the emperor himself leading the campaign. - Despite their resistance, Bijapur fell in 1686 after an 18-month siege, with Aurangzeb personally present in the final stages. - The length and difficulty of the siege justified the earlier failures of Jai Singh (1665) and Diler Khan (1679–1680) against Bijapur. - The Fall of Golconda (1687) - With Bijapur defeated, an attack on Golconda became inevitable. Aurangzeb saw multiple “offenses” in the Qutb Shah’s rule: - He had placed supreme power in the hands of two Hindus, Madanna and Akhanna. - He had supported Shivaji on multiple occasions. - He had openly defied Aurangzeb’s warnings. - In 1685, despite stiff resistance, the Mughals occupied Golconda, and the Qutb Shah offered peace, agreeing to: - Pay a large indemnity to Aurangzeb. - Cede certain territories. - Dismiss Madanna and Akhanna. - The Qutb Shah complied, and Madanna and Akhanna were brutally murdered in 1686. However, even this betrayal failed to save him. - The Mughals besieged Golconda again in early 1687, and after six months of fierce resistance, the fort fell due to treachery and bribery. - The Maratha Resistance (1689–1690) - With Bijapur and Golconda destroyed, Aurangzeb turned his full attention to crushing the Marathas. - In 1689, a Mughal force captured Sambhaji at his secret hideout in Sangameshwar. He was paraded before Aurangzeb and executed as a rebel and an infidel. - This decision proved to be a major political mistake. Instead of securing Mughal control, Sambhaji’s execution: - Eliminated a potential negotiating partner who might have submitted. - Turned the Marathas into an even more decentralized and resilient force. - Gave them a renewed cause for resistance. - The Maratha sardars, without a single central authority, began launching guerilla warfare—plundering Mughal territories, vanishing at the approach of Mughal forces, and regrouping elsewhere. - Rajaram, Sambhaji’s younger brother, was crowned king but had to flee to Jinji on the eastern coast when the Mughals attacked his capital. - The Maratha resistance now expanded from the western to the eastern coast. - Aurangzeb’s Stubborn Pursuit (1690–1703) - By 1690, Aurangzeb believed Maratha power had been crushed and shifted focus to annexing the rich Karnataka region into the Mughal Empire. - However, he overextended his supply lines, making them vulnerable to Maratha attacks. - Mughal control over Bijapur weakened as it became a hub of Maratha activities. From 1690 to 1703, Aurangzeb refused to negotiate, believing that total military conquest was the only solution. - The siege of Jinji (1690–1698) lasted nearly 8 years, but Rajaram escaped before it fell. - The Marathas intensified their attacks, recapturing many forts. - By 1700, Aurangzeb launched siege after siege, dragging his army across the Deccan for five and a half years (1700–1705). - Despite his victories, the Marathas never stopped fighting. Mughal forces suffered from floods, disease, and constant guerrilla attacks. - The nobles and soldiers became weary, and some even made secret pacts with the Marathas, paying them chauth (tribute) in exchange for safety. - Aurangzeb’s Last Years and Failed Negotiations (1703–1707) - By 1703, Aurangzeb finally considered negotiations. He offered to: - Release Shahu, the son of Sambhaji, who had been captured. - Grant him Shivaji’s swarajya and the right of sardeshmukhi over the Deccan. - Shahu, treated well in Mughal captivity, was given the title of Raja, a mansab of 2000/2000, and was married into respected Maratha families. - However, at the last moment, Aurangzeb canceled the agreement, uncertain about the Marathas’ true intentions. - By 1706, realizing the futility of his efforts, Aurangzeb slowly retreated to Aurangabad, harassed by Maratha forces. - When Aurangzeb died in 1707, he left behind: - A crumbling Mughal empire, weakened by decades of war. - A victorious Maratha force, now the dominant power in the Deccan. - Discontent and rebellion across North India, fueled by his aggressive policies. - Aurangzeb’s Deccan campaign, which had lasted over 25 years, had drained the Mughal treasury and shattered the empire’s military strength. - His obsession with total conquest had only strengthened the very enemies he sought to destroy. - Decline of the Mughal Empire - Introduction: The Aftermath of Aurangzeb’s Death - The Mughal Empire declined rapidly after Aurangzeb’s death. - The Mughal court became a battleground for factional conflicts among nobles. - Ambitious provincial governors asserted independence. - Maratha incursions expanded from the Deccan into the empire’s heartland. - The empire’s weakness was exposed when Nadir Shah imprisoned the Mughal emperor and looted Delhi in 1739. - Aurangzeb’s Role in the Decline - Debate on Aurangzeb’s Responsibility - Historians debate whether the empire’s downfall was due to Aurangzeb’s flawed policies or later developments. - Recent analyses consider economic, social, administrative, and intellectual trends of the time. - Economic and Social Context - The 17th century saw an expansion of trade and handicraft production. - Growth in cultivation was driven by population increase, economic forces, and Mughal policies. - Detailed records were maintained on agriculture, including ploughs, bullocks, wells, and cultivators. - Agriculture and Revenue System - Challenges in Agricultural Growth - Despite expansion, agricultural production stagnated. - No new techniques emerged to counter declining soil fertility. - The land revenue system was burdensome: - Under Akbar, the state’s share was one-third of the produce. - By the mid-17th century, it rose to nearly half, including zamindars’ portions. - Regional Variations in Revenue Demand - Revenue burden varied by region: - Lower in infertile areas like Rajasthan and Sindh. - Higher in fertile regions like Kashmir’s saffron lands. - Social Barriers to Land Expansion - Despite available surplus land, landless laborers existed in many villages. - Dalits and marginalized communities were kept in menial roles. - Dominant castes and zamindars had little incentive to allow them to acquire land. - Nobility, Jagirdari Crisis, and Administrative Decline - Expansion of the Nobility and Economic Strains - The number of mansabdars increased: - 2,069 in Jahangir’s reign (1605). - 8,000 under Shah Jahan (1637). - 11,456 in Aurangzeb’s later years. - Revenue increase did not match the rise in nobility. - Extravagant court expenditures under Shah Jahan worsened financial stress. Zamindars and Peasant Unrest - Zamindars resisted excessive revenue demands. - Peasants migrated between villages seeking better conditions. - Extracting more revenue from jagirs led to peasant unrest and zamindar revolts. - Jagirdari Crisis and Corruption - Jagirs in newly conquered regions like Karnataka yielded little revenue. - Corruption among officials led to nobles paying bribes for profitable jagirs. - Shah Jahan had reduced the cavalry requirements of mansabdars to address the jagir shortage. - Aurangzeb’s conquest of the Deccan failed to resolve the problem. - The jagirdari system, once a pillar of Mughal governance, became a source of instability: - Shortage of Jagirs: Productive lands were kept under khalisa (imperial control) for financing wars, leaving nobles with insufficient revenue. - Revenue Exploitation: Many nobles resorted to unauthorized means to extract more revenue, worsening rural unrest. - Peasant and Zamindar Resistance: The pressure to increase revenue led to widespread resistance, further weakening Mughal authority. - The crisis was worsened in the Deccan, where nobles struggled to collect revenue due to Maratha incursions. - Some entered private agreements with Maratha leaders, paying chauth in exchange for security. - Military Challenges and the Maratha Problem - The Mughal military, once dominant, struggled with new challenges: - Infantry Neglect: - The failure to modernize the infantry and mobile artillery reduced the empire’s effectiveness against guerrilla-style warfare, particularly in the Deccan. - Neglected infantry with flint guns and mobile field artillery. - Overextension: - The conquest of Bijapur and Golconda overstretched Mughal resources, leaving the empire vulnerable to Maratha attacks. - Declining Central Control: - As local nobles sought autonomy and engaged in private deals, the empire’s military structure weakened. - Nobles resisted changes that threatened their cavalry-dominated prestige. - Aurangzeb’s Strategic Mistakes - Miscalculated the Maratha movement. - Ignored Jai Singh’s advice to ally with Shivaji. - Executed Sambhaji, losing a leader he could have negotiated with. - Underestimated Maratha resilience after Bijapur and Golconda’s fall. - Failed Negotiations with the Marathas - Aurangzeb demanded a truncated Maratha swarajya and loyalty to the Mughal throne. - By 1703, an agreement was nearly reached, but Aurangzeb remained distrustful. - The Marathas were granted mansabs but were not given positions of real trust. - Maratha and Rajput Relations - Aurangzeb’s handling of the Marathas and Rajputs contributed to long-term instability: - Failure to Integrate Marathas: Unlike the Rajputs, who were given high mansabs and administrative roles, Maratha leaders were distrusted and not fully incorporated into the Mughal system. - Marwar Conflict: Aurangzeb’s interference in Marwar’s succession led to prolonged war with Rajput states, damaging Mughal prestige. However, the Rajputs did not actively contribute to the empire’s disintegration after Aurangzeb’s death. - Economic, Social, and Administrative Factors - The decline of the Mughal Empire was not solely due to Aurangzeb’s personal policies or military campaigns but was influenced by broader economic, social, and administrative forces. - Economic Weaknesses: - The burden of land revenue was excessive in many areas, reducing incentives for agricultural expansion. - The absence of new agricultural techniques and declining soil fertility further slowed growth. - Social Structure: - The rigidity of caste and class structures, particularly the marginalization of Dalits and landless laborers, prevented efficient land utilization and agricultural development. - Administrative Decay: - The Mughal administrative system required a strong and capable monarch to function effectively. - With the weakening of the central authority, factionalism among nobles grew, and the jagirdari system collapsed under financial strain. - Religious Policies and Their Impact - Aurangzeb’s religious orthodoxy played a role in alienating sections of society: - Temple Destruction and Jizya: - His policies, such as temple demolitions and the reimposition of jizya, created resentment among non-Muslims. - Lack of Unifying Vision: - Unlike Akbar’s inclusive policies, Aurangzeb’s focus on Islamic law failed to create unity among diverse communities. - Limited Long-Term Impact: - Despite these policies, the empire’s decline was more influenced by economic and administrative issues rather than religious conflicts alone. - Conclusion: The Mughal Empire’s Legacy - While Aurangzeb’s reign marked the beginning of the empire’s decline, its downfall was a gradual process influenced by multiple factors: - Economic Stagnation: - Agricultural and manufacturing growth failed to keep pace with rising demands. - Administrative Breakdown: - The centralization of power without efficient reforms led to instability. - Military Limitations: - The Mughal military, though once powerful, failed to adapt to changing warfare tactics, particularly against the Marathas’ guerrilla strategy. - Rise of Provincial Powers: - The weakening of central authority allowed regional powers like the Marathas, Rajputs, Sikhs, and later the British to assert their influence. - Thus, Aurangzeb was both a victim of circumstances and a contributor to the very circumstances that led to his downfall. - Victim of Circumstances: - He inherited an empire that was already vast and difficult to manage. - Over time, factors like economic strain, administrative inefficiency, and emerging regional powers weakened Mughal control. - Contributor to His Own Downfall: - His policies—such as religious intolerance, prolonged wars in the Deccan, and harsh treatment of Rajputs and Marathas—exacerbated the empire’s problems. - His military campaigns drained resources and alienated powerful groups, leading to widespread rebellion and instability. - Assessment and Review - Social Developments - Persistence of the Caste System: - Despite challenges from Islam and the decline of Rajput power, the caste system remained dominant. - Role of Bhakti and Sufi Movements: - Groups like the Nath Panthis, Jogis, and Bhakti saints criticized caste divisions but had limited impact. - A compromise emerged—saints generally restricted their critiques to spiritual matters, while Brahmins accepted Bhakti as a salvation path for all castes, especially Shudras. - Women and Social Mobility: - Bhakti saints, including Mirabai and Surdas, provided women with a platform to rise beyond their traditional roles. - However, Brahmins retained control over religious teaching and education. - Cultural and Religious Developments - Interfaith Harmony and Challenges: - Bhakti and Sufi saints emphasized shared values between Hinduism and Islam, fostering a spirit of mutual tolerance. - However, sectarian forces remained influential and occasionally impacted state policies. - Impact on Language and Literature: - Saints contributed to the growth of regional languages and literature. - Their focus on spiritual concerns led to neglect in the fields of science and technology. - Status of Women - Worsening Conditions: - The practice of purdah (seclusion) became more widespread. - Hindu women lacked rights to remarriage and inheritance, unlike Muslim women. - Even among Muslims, these rights were increasingly restricted. - Political and Economic Developments - Political and Administrative Integration: - The Turks initiated and the Mughals consolidated a unified administration, primarily in northern India. - Their influence extended indirectly to other regions. - Economic Growth and Trade: - A well-minted silver currency, improved roads, and urbanization facilitated trade. - Handicrafts and commerce peaked in the seventeenth century. - Aristocratic Nature of the Ruling Class: - The Mughal elite comprised both Muslims and Hindus but remained largely aristocratic, limiting upward mobility for lower-class individuals. - Aurangzeb’s efforts to integrate Marathas into the administration were largely unsuccessful due to regional, religious, and social barriers. - Feudal Structure: - The Mughal nobility depended on land revenue collected from peasant proprietors. - Zamindars played a crucial role in revenue collection, maintaining their privileges in return for state loyalty. - Military and Foreign Relations - Defense Against Foreign Invasions: - The Turks defended India against Mongol invasions in the 13th and 14th centuries. - The Mughals secured India’s northwest frontiers for 200 years, focusing on the Kabul-Ghazni line. - European Trade and Expansion: - India’s global reputation as a center for spices and textiles attracted European traders. - European powers sought control over Indian trade and territory but were largely unsuccessful while the Mughal empire remained strong. - The empire’s decline in the 18th century, coupled with economic and technological advancements in Europe, enabled colonial expansion. - Scientific and Technological Backwardness - Limited Maritime and Naval Development: - The Mughals understood the importance of trade but neglected naval power. - Stagnation in Science and Technology: - India failed to produce mechanical innovations like the European clock. - While Indian artisans could replicate European designs (e.g., shipbuilding), innovation remained minimal. - Role of Social Structures: - Caste restrictions and deference to traditional knowledge stifled scientific progress. - Akbar’s efforts to introduce science into education were resisted. - Cultural Integration and Legacy - Unified Cultural Identity: - Despite diversity in race, religion, and language, India developed a largely unified culture. - The seventeenth century was marked by a surge in artistic and cultural achievements, often called a second classical age. - Challenges to Cultural Integration: - Religious dogmatism and conflicts within the ruling class threatened this unity but did not completely dismantle it. - Regional Contributions: - The Vijayanagara kingdom continued Chola traditions in the south. - The Bahmani kingdom and its successor states contributed to cultural developments. - These regional influences merged into Mughal-era cultural forms. - Economic Prospects and European Influence - Industrial Growth and Limitations: - Trade and manufacturing expanded, but development was uneven across regions. - Gujarat, the Coromandel coast, and Bengal became economic hubs in the seventeenth century. - The Industrial Revolution Question: - Would India have had its own industrial revolution if the Mughal empire had survived? - Despite continued trade expansion in the eighteenth century, India lagged behind Europe in science, technology, and economic organization. - Limitations in Manufacturing: - Small-scale production and reliance on simple tools limited productivity. - Caste restrictions and lack of capital prevented artisans from evolving into entrepreneurs. - Emergence of European Dominance: - The dadni (putting-out) system increased production but made artisans dependent on merchants. - British and other European powers leveraged these economic conditions to establish colonial control. - Despite remarkable developments in political and cultural integration, India’s stagnation in science and technology, along with rigid social structures, ultimately made it vulnerable to European expansion. - -
- Medieval History PYQs - [1995] - Q1: The Mughal school of painting formed the spinal column of different schools of Indian miniature art. Which one of the following painting styles was not affected by Mughal painting? - Options: (a) Pahari (b) Rajasthani (c) Kangra (d) Kalighat - Answer: (d) Kalighat - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Mughal school of painting emerged in the 16th century CE under emperors like Akbar (r. 1556-1605 CE), blending Persian techniques with Indian themes. Flourishing in ateliers (e.g., Fatehpur Sikri), it influenced regional miniature styles through patronage, artist migration, and cultural exchange from the 16th to 18th centuries CE. Styles like Pahari, Rajasthani, and Kangra evolved in this milieu, while Kalighat emerged later with distinct roots. - Correct Option Explained: - (d) Kalighat: - Correct—Kalighat painting, originating in the 19th century CE around the Kalighat Temple in Kolkata, West Bengal, was a folk art form unaffected by Mughal painting. It developed as a bazaar art by patuas (scroll painters) for pilgrims, featuring bold lines, vibrant colors, and themes like Hindu deities (e.g., Kali) and social satire (e.g., British rule critiques). Its roots lie in Bengal’s indigenous pata tradition, not Mughal miniature techniques. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Pahari: - Incorrect—Pahari painting (c. 17th-19th centuries CE), from the Himalayan hill states (e.g., Guler, Kangra), was heavily influenced by Mughal art. Artists like Nainsukh (c. 1710-1778 CE) adopted Mughal realism and portraiture (e.g., Guler portraits), merging them with local devotional themes (e.g., Krishna-Radha). - (b) Rajasthani: - Incorrect—Rajasthani painting (c. 16th-19th centuries CE), from Rajasthan’s courts (e.g., Mewar, Marwar), evolved under Mughal influence. Akbar’s artists trained Rajput painters, leading to styles like the Ragamala series (e.g., Mewar, 1605 CE), blending Mughal finesse with Rajput vibrancy. - (c) Kangra: - Incorrect—Kangra painting (c. 18th-19th centuries CE), a Pahari sub-style from Himachal Pradesh, was shaped by Mughal techniques via refugee artists post-Mughal decline (e.g., 1739 CE, Nadir Shah’s invasion). Its delicate brushwork and romantic themes (e.g., Kangra Krishna Lila, 1780 CE) reflect Mughal naturalism. - Painting Style Details: - Mughal School: - Period: c. 16th-18th centuries CE. - Features: Realism, Persian motifs (a recurring theme, pattern, or design that appears in various forms), historical scenes (e.g., Akbarnama). - Kalighat: - Period: c. 19th century CE. - Features: Folk style, bold outlines, mass-produced pats. - Pahari: - Period: c. 17th-19th centuries CE. - Features: Miniatures, devotional themes, Mughal-influenced detailing. - Rajasthani: - Period: c. 16th-19th centuries CE. - Features: Bright colors, courtly themes, Mughal-trained artists. - Kangra: - Period: c. 18th-19th centuries CE. - Features: Soft hues, romantic narratives, Mughal finesse. - Other Related Painting Styles: - Deccani: - Context: c. 16th-17th centuries CE, Deccan sultanates. - Influence: Mughal techniques (e.g., Bijapur portraits). - Company School: - Context: c. 18th-19th centuries CE, British India. - Influence: European realism, not Mughal (e.g., botanical art). - Madhubani: - Context: Bihar, ancient to modern. - Influence: Folk tradition, no Mughal impact (e.g., Mithila ritual art). - Tanjore: - Context: c. 17th-19th centuries CE, Tamil Nadu. - Influence: South Indian temple art, minimal Mughal effect. - Bengal Pata: - Context: Pre-19th century CE, Bengal. - Influence: Indigenous scrolls, precursor to Kalighat. - Cultural Significance: - Mughal painting’s influence unified miniature traditions across northern India, while Kalighat’s independence reflects Bengal’s folk resilience, emerging in a colonial context distinct from Mughal courtly patronage. - Related Evidence: - Artifacts: - Akbarnama (c. 1590 CE): Mughal style exemplar. - Kalighat pats: British Museum collection (19th century CE). - Texts: - Ain-i-Akbari (c. 1590 CE): Mughal atelier details. - Archaeology: - Kangra paintings: Lahore Museum (18th century CE). - Related Figures: - Akbar: - Mughal emperor (r. 1556-1605 CE); painting patron. - Nainsukh: - Pahari artist (c. 1710-1778 CE); Mughal influence. - Kalighat Patuas: - Anonymous folk artists (19th century CE). - Broader Connection: - Links to Mughal culture (e.g., Q129 [Gupta ports]), regional art (e.g., Q133 [Yogini temple]), or colonial shifts (e.g., Q125 [Hundi]). - Key Takeaway: - Kalighat (d) was not affected by Mughal painting, unlike Pahari, Rajasthani, and Kangra, due to its later folk origins. - Q2: Who among the following were famous jurists (a person who is an expert in law) of medieval India? - Statements: 1. Vijnanesvara 2. Hemadri 3. Rajasekhara 4. Jimutavahana - Options: (a) 1, 2, and 3 (b) 2, 3, and 4 (c) 1, 2, and 4 (d) 1 and 4 - Answer: (c) 1, 2, and 4 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Medieval India (c. 8th-18th centuries CE) saw the development of Hindu legal traditions under regional kingdoms, building on the Dharmashastra framework (e.g., Manu Smriti, c. 200 BCE). Jurists like Vijnanesvara, Hemadri, and Jimutavahana produced influential commentaries on civil and ritual law, while figures like Rajasekhara excelled in other fields, reflecting the intellectual diversity of the period. - Evaluation of Individuals: - 1. Vijnanesvara: - Correct—Vijnanesvara (c. 11th century CE), a jurist under the Kalyani Chalukyas (Karnataka), authored the Mitakshara, a commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti (c. 2nd century CE). This work became a cornerstone of Hindu property law, defining coparcenary rights (e.g., Q137 [Mitakshara]), widely adopted across India except Bengal. - 2. Hemadri: - Correct—Hemadri (c. 13th century CE), a minister and jurist under the Yadava dynasty of Devagiri (Maharashtra), wrote the Chaturvarga Chintamani. This text covers dharma, rituals, and legal procedures (e.g., inheritance, penance), influencing medieval Hindu jurisprudence and practice in western India. - 3. Rajasekhara: - Incorrect—Rajasekhara (c. 9th-10th centuries CE), a poet and dramatist under the Pratihara court (e.g., Mahendrapala I), is known for literary works like Karpuramanjari (Prakrit play) and Kavyamimamsa (poetics). He was not a jurist, focusing on aesthetics, not law (e.g., Q131 [playwrights]). - 4. Jimutavahana: - Correct—Jimutavahana (c. 12th century CE), a Bengal-based jurist of the Navya Nyaya school, authored the Dayabhaga, a legal treatise on inheritance emphasizing succession over coparcenary (e.g., Q137 [Dayabhaga]). It became the dominant law in eastern India, particularly Bengal. - Why (c) 1, 2, and 4?: - Vijnanesvara (1): - Jurist via Mitakshara, foundational legal text. - Hemadri (2): - Jurist via Chaturvarga Chintamani, legal-ritual guide. - Rajasekhara (3): - Not a jurist; a literary figure, no legal works. - Jimutavahana (4): - Jurist via Dayabhaga, key inheritance law. - Jurist Details: - Vijnanesvara: - Period: c. 11th century CE; Kalyani Chalukya court. - Work: Mitakshara; coparcenary (joint inheritance system) focus. - Hemadri: - Period: c. 13th century CE; Yadava dynasty. - Work: Chaturvarga Chintamani; rituals, law. - Rajasekhara: - Period: c. 9th-10th centuries CE; Pratihara court. - Work: Karpuramanjari; poetry, drama. - Jimutavahana: - Period: c. 12th century CE; Bengal. - Work: Dayabhaga; succession focus. - Other Related Medieval Legal Figures: - Medhatithi: - Context: c. 9th century CE; Kashmir. - Work: Commentary on Manu Smriti. - Lakshmidhara: - Context: c. 12th century CE; Kannauj. - Work: Krityakalpataru; ritual-law digest. - Devanabhatta: - Context: c. 12th century CE; South India. - Work: Smritichandrika; southern legal text. - Apararka: - Context: c. 12th century CE; Konkan. - Work: Commentary on Yajnavalkya Smriti. - Kulluka Bhatta: - Context: c. 13th century CE; Bengal. - Work: Manusmriti commentary, post-Dayabhaga. - Historical Significance: - Jurists like Vijnanesvara, Hemadri, and Jimutavahana codified Hindu law, shaping property rights and social norms in medieval India, bridging ancient Smriti traditions with regional practices, unlike Rajasekhara’s literary contributions. - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Mitakshara (Vijnanesvara): Legal manuscript tradition. - Dayabhaga (Jimutavahana): Bengal legal codex. - Inscriptions: - Yadava grants (c. 13th century CE): Hemadri’s context. - Colonial Records: - British courts (19th century CE): Applied Mitakshara, Dayabhaga. - Related Figures: - Vikramaditya VI: - Chalukya king (r. 1076-1126 CE); Vijnanesvara’s patron. - Bhillama V: - Yadava king (r. c. 1187-1191 CE); Hemadri’s era. - Mahendrapala I: - Pratihara king (r. c. 885-910 CE); Rajasekhara’s patron. - Broader Connection: - Links to medieval law (e.g., Q137 [Mitakshara]), literature (e.g., Q131 [playwrights]), or dynasties (e.g., Q135 [Yadavas]). - Key Takeaway: - Vijnanesvara (1), Hemadri (2), and Jimutavahana (4) were famous jurists of medieval India, not Rajasekhara (3), making (c) correct. - Q3: Which one of the following monuments has a dome said to be one of the largest in the world? - Options: (a) Tomb of Sher Shah, Sasaram (b) Jama Masjid, Delhi (c) Tomb of Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq, Delhi (d) Gol Gumbaz, Bijapur - Answer: (d) Gol Gumbaz, Bijapur - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Monumental domes in India reflect architectural evolution from the Delhi Sultanate (c. 13th century CE) to the Mughal and Deccan periods (c. 16th-17th centuries CE). Influenced by Persian and Central Asian styles, these structures vary in size and engineering, with the Gol Gumbaz standing out for its scale during the Adil Shahi dynasty in the Deccan. - Correct Option Explained: - (d) Gol Gumbaz, Bijapur: - Correct—Gol Gumbaz, built in 1656 CE under Muhammad Adil Shah (r. 1627-1656 CE) in Bijapur (modern Karnataka), boasts a dome with an external diameter of 44 meters (144 feet) and an internal span of 37.9 meters (124 feet). Often cited as one of the world’s largest pre-modern domes, it rivals structures like the Pantheon (43.3 meters, Rome) and Hagia Sophia (31.8 meters, Istanbul), per Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) measurements and architectural studies (e.g., Percy Brown, 1942). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Tomb of Sher Shah, Sasaram: - Incorrect—Built in 1545 CE in Sasaram, Bihar, under Sher Shah Suri (r. 1540-1545 CE), this tomb’s dome measures about 22 meters (72 feet) in diameter. Though impressive and set on an artificial lake, it’s significantly smaller than Gol Gumbaz. - (b) Jama Masjid, Delhi: - Incorrect—Constructed in 1656 CE under Shah Jahan (r. 1628-1658 CE), the Jama Masjid’s central dome is approximately 25 meters (82 feet) in diameter. A Mughal masterpiece, it’s large but not among the world’s largest, dwarfed by Gol Gumbaz. - (c) Tomb of Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq, Delhi: - Incorrect—Erected c. 1325 CE in Delhi under Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq (r. 1320-1325 CE), this tomb’s dome is modest, around 8-10 meters (26-33 feet) in diameter. Its austere Tughlaq style prioritizes strength over scale, far smaller than Gol Gumbaz. - Monument Details: - Gol Gumbaz: - Location: Bijapur, Karnataka. - Features: 44m dome, whispering gallery, 37m height. - Period: Adil Shahi, 1656 CE. - Tomb of Sher Shah: - Location: Sasaram, Bihar. - Features: 22m dome, octagonal, lake setting. - Period: Sur dynasty, 1545 CE. - Jama Masjid: - Location: Delhi. - Features: 25m dome, red sandstone, three domes. - Period: Mughal, 1656 CE. - Tomb of Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq: - Location: Delhi. - Features: 8-10m dome, sloping walls, fortress-like. - Period: Tughlaq, c. 1325 CE. - Other Related Monumental Domes: - Taj Mahal: - Location: Agra, Uttar Pradesh. - Context: 35m dome (external), Mughal, 1632-1653 CE. - Humayun’s Tomb: - Location: Delhi. - Context: 22m dome, Mughal, 1565-1572 CE. - Bibi Ka Maqbara: - Location: Aurangabad, Maharashtra. - Context: 20m dome, Mughal-inspired, 1668 CE. - Qutb Shahi Tombs: - Location: Hyderabad, Telangana. - Context: Multiple domes, largest ~20m, 16th-17th centuries CE. - Ibrahim Rauza: - Location: Bijapur, Karnataka. - Context: 14m dome, Adil Shahi, 1627 CE. - Architectural Significance: - Gol Gumbaz’s dome exemplifies Deccan engineering, using pendentives and an acoustic “whispering gallery,” contrasting with Mughal elegance (Jama Masjid) and earlier Sultanate simplicity (Tughlaq), marking a peak in Indian Islamic architecture. - Related Evidence: - Archaeology: - Gol Gumbaz: ASI measurements (44m diameter). - Jama Masjid: Mughal records (Shahjahannama). - Texts: - Percy Brown (1942): Indian Architecture, dome comparisons. - Inscriptions: - Sher Shah Tomb: Construction date (1545 CE). - Related Figures: - Muhammad Adil Shah: - Adil Shahi ruler (r. 1627-1656 CE); Gol Gumbaz patron. - Shah Jahan: - Mughal emperor (r. 1628-1658 CE); Jama Masjid builder. - Sher Shah Suri: - Sur ruler (r. 1540-1545 CE); tomb architect. - Broader Connection: - Links to Mughal art (e.g., Q1 [painting]), medieval architecture (e.g., Q133 [Yogini]), or dynasties (e.g., Q135 [post-Gupta]). - Key Takeaway: - Gol Gumbaz (d) has a dome said to be one of the largest in the world, unlike the smaller domes of Sher Shah’s Tomb, Jama Masjid, or Tughlaq’s Tomb. - Q4: Ashtapradhan was a council of ministers: - Options: (a) In the Gupta administration (b) In the Chola administration (c) In the Vijayanagar administration (d) In the Maratha administration - Answer: (d) In the Maratha administration - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The term "Ashtapradhan" (meaning "eight chief ministers" in Sanskrit) refers to a council of eight ministers instituted by Shivaji (r. 1674-1680 CE), the founder of the Maratha Empire, during the late 17th century CE. This administrative innovation, rooted in Hindu governance traditions, was designed to streamline military and civil administration in the Maratha Swarajya (self-rule), contrasting with earlier Indian dynasties like the Guptas, Cholas, and Vijayanagar, which had different systems. - Correct Option Explained: - (d) In the Maratha administration: - Correct—The Ashtapradhan was a unique feature of the Maratha administration under Shivaji, established around 1674 CE during his coronation at Raigad (modern Maharashtra). It included roles like Peshwa (prime minister), Amatya (finance), and Sachiv (secretary), each with specific duties to support decentralized governance and military campaigns against Mughal rule (e.g., Aurangzeb, r. 1658-1707 CE). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) In the Gupta administration: - Incorrect—The Gupta Empire (c. 4th-6th centuries CE) had a centralized bureaucracy with officials like Mahadandanayaka (chief general) and Sandhivigrahika (foreign minister), as seen in inscriptions (e.g., Allahabad Pillar, c. 380 CE). There’s no evidence of an "Ashtapradhan" council; their system relied on feudatories and a king-centric model, not a fixed eight-minister structure. - (b) In the Chola administration: - Incorrect—The Chola dynasty (c. 9th-13th centuries CE) used a sophisticated administration with officials like Perundanam (higher officers) and Sirudanam (lower officers), alongside village assemblies (e.g., Uttaramerur inscriptions, c. 920 CE). While efficient, it lacked a council named "Ashtapradhan," focusing instead on regional governors and naval power. - (c) In the Vijayanagar administration: - Incorrect—The Vijayanagar Empire (c. 14th-16th centuries CE) had a council of ministers under kings like Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509-1529 CE), with titles like Pradhani (chief minister) and provincial governors (Nayakas). Foreign accounts (e.g., Domingo Paes, c. 1520 CE) describe a flexible advisory body, but it was not formalized as "Ashtapradhan" with eight specific roles. - Administration Details: - Maratha (Ashtapradhan): - Location: Western India, centered in Maharashtra. - Features: Eight ministers—e.g., Peshwa (PM), Pant Pratinidhi (advisor), Senapati (commander). - Period: Initiated 1674 CE, Shivaji’s reign. - Gupta: - Location: Northern India, Magadha base. - Features: Feudal hierarchy, no fixed council of eight. - Period: c. 4th-6th centuries CE. - Chola: - Location: Southern India, Tamil Nadu. - Features: Village councils, no "Ashtapradhan." - Period: c. 9th-13th centuries CE. - Vijayanagar: - Location: Southern India, Karnataka-Andhra. - Features: Flexible council, Nayaka system. - Period: c. 14th-16th centuries CE. - Other Related Administrative Systems: - Mughal Mantri Parishad: - Context: c. 16th-18th centuries CE;
