As a modern figure, he is far removed from being the first Urdu poet. - Key Features: - Amir Khusrau’s Contribution: - Language: Hindavi/Rekhta, early Urdu form. - Works: Ghazals, qawwalis (e.g., "Chaap Tilak"), riddles. - Era: Delhi Sultanate, 13th-14th centuries CE. - Related Figures: - Amir Khusrau: - Poet (1253-1325 CE), first Urdu poet, Sufi disciple. - Mirza Ghalib: - Poet (1797-1869 CE), Urdu-Persian ghazal master. - Bahadur Shah Zafar: - Emperor-poet (1775-1862 CE), last Mughal Urdu poet. - Faiz Ahmed Faiz: - Poet (1911-1984 CE), modern Urdu revolutionary. - Nizam-ud-din Auliya: - Sufi saint (1238-1325 CE), Khusrau’s mentor (Q8 context). - Other Notable Urdu Poets of Medieval and Modern India: - Wali Muhammad Wali (1667-1707 CE): - "Wali Deccani," bridged Deccan and North Indian Urdu. - Mir Taqi Mir (1723-1810 CE): - "Khuda-e-Sukhan" (God of Poetry), Urdu ghazals. - Muhammad Iqbal (1877-1938 CE): - Philosophical Urdu poetry (e.g., Shikwa). - Saadat Hasan Manto (1912-1955 CE): - Urdu prose, short stories, modern era. - Dagh Dehlvi (1831-1905 CE): - Urdu ghazals, Mughal decline era. - Broader Connection: - Links to Sufi influence (Q8 [Muin-ud-din Chisti]), Mughal culture (Q10 [painting]), or medieval titles (Q13 [Balban]). - Key Takeaway: - Amir Khusrau (a) was the first to use Urdu for poetic expression, predating Ghalib, Zafar, and Faiz. - Q29: To which Lodi Sultan does the given map relate, and what town does the site marked ‘A’ represent? - - Options: (a) Bahlol Lodi - Jaunpur (b) Sikandar Lodi - Aligarh (c) Ibrahim Lodi - Jaunpur (d) Ibrahim Lodi - Aligarh - Answer: (a) Bahlol Lodi - Jaunpur - Q30: Assertion (A): During the time of Akbar, for every ten cavalrymen, the mansabdars had to maintain twenty horses. - Reason (R): Horses had to be rested while on march and replacements were necessary in times of war. - Question: Which one of the following is correct? - Options: (a) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A (c) A is true, but R is false (d) A is false, but R is true - Answer: (a) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Mansabdari system, introduced by Akbar (r. 1556-1605 CE) in the 1570s CE, was a Mughal administrative and military framework (see Q11). It assigned ranks (zat and sawar) to nobles (mansabdars), requiring them to maintain cavalry units for imperial service, as detailed in the Ain-i-Akbari (c. 1590 CE). Horses were critical to Mughal warfare, necessitating strict regulations. - Assertion and Reason Evaluation: - Assertion (A): During the time of Akbar, for every ten cavalrymen, the mansabdars had to maintain twenty horses. - True—Under Akbar’s reforms, the "do-aspah" (two-horse) rule mandated that for every ten cavalrymen (sawar rank), mansabdars maintain twenty horses. This ensured operational readiness, documented in the Ain-i-Akbari and corroborated by historian Irfan Habib’s studies on Mughal military logistics. - Reason (R): Horses had to be rested while on march and replacements were necessary in times of war. - True—Horses required rest during long marches (e.g., campaigns to Gujarat, 1572 CE) and replacements due to casualties or exhaustion in battles (e.g., Haldighati, 1576 CE). This logistical necessity drove the two-horse policy, aligning with Mughal military strategy. - Explanation Check: - R explains A—The requirement of twenty horses per ten cavalrymen directly addressed the need for rest and replacements, ensuring a functional cavalry at all times, making R the correct explanation of A. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: - Correct—A is true (two-horse rule), R is true (rest and replacement needs), and R explains why A was implemented. - (b) Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: - Incorrect—A and R are true, but R’s logistical reasoning directly supports A’s horse ratio, not an unrelated cause. - (c) A is true, but R is false: - Incorrect—A is true, and R is also true; rest and replacements were real concerns in Mughal campaigns. - (d) A is false, but R is true: - Incorrect—A is true (historically verified), not false; R’s truth doesn’t stand alone here. - Key Features: - Do-Aspah Rule: - Ratio: 2 horses per cavalryman. - Purpose: Sustained mobility, combat readiness. - Era: Akbar’s reign, formalized c. 1570s CE. - Related Figures: - Akbar: - Emperor (r. 1556-1605 CE), introduced Mansabdari reforms. - Abul Fazl: - Historian (1551-1602 CE), documented rules in Ain-i-Akbari. - Raja Man Singh: - Mansabdar (1540-1614 CE), managed cavalry units. - Bairam Khan: - Regent (d. 1561 CE), early influence on Akbar’s military. - Jahangir: - Emperor (r. 1605-1627 CE), continued system (Q10 context). - Other Notable Features of the Mansabdari System: - Zat Rank: - Personal status, salary indicator (10-5000). - Sawar Rank: - Cavalry obligation, troop count (10-4000). - Jagirdari Link: - Land grants to fund horse maintenance (Q11). - Ahadis: - Elite troopers, direct imperial service (Q24). - Branding (Dag): - Horse inspection to prevent fraud, Akbar’s innovation. - Broader Connection: - Links to Mansabdari (Q11), military units (Q24 [Ahadis]), or Mughal expeditions (Q23 [Dara Shikoh]). - Key Takeaway: - Both A (20 horses per 10 cavalrymen) and R (rest and replacements) are true, with R explaining A, making (a) correct. - Q31: One consistent feature found in the history of southern India was the growth of small regional kingdoms rather than large empires because of: - Options: (a) Absence of minerals like iron (b) Too many divisions in the social structure (c) Absence of vast areas of fertile land (d) Scarcity of manpower - Answer: (c) Absence of vast areas of fertile land - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Southern India (c. 3rd century BCE-18th century CE) featured a fragmented political landscape with dynasties like the Cholas, Pandyas, and Vijayanagara, contrasting with the larger northern empires (e.g., Mauryas, Mughals). Geographic and ecological factors shaped this pattern, as noted in Sangam literature and inscriptions (e.g., Chola copper plates). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Absence of minerals like iron: - Incorrect—Southern India had access to minerals, including iron (e.g., iron smelting in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka), used in Chola weapons and Vijayanagara fortifications. Mineral scarcity wasn’t a limiting factor; regional kingdoms thrived despite this. - (b) Too many divisions in the social structure: - Incorrect—While southern society had caste divisions (e.g., Brahmins, Vellalas), these were not significantly more fragmented than the north’s varna system. Social structure influenced governance but didn’t inherently prevent large empires; Cholas briefly unified much of the south. - (c) Absence of vast areas of fertile land: - Correct—Southern India’s terrain—rugged Deccan Plateau, narrow coastal plains, and scattered river valleys (e.g., Kaveri, Godavari)—lacked the expansive fertile plains of the Indo-Gangetic region (e.g., Ganges basin). This limited large-scale agriculture and centralized surplus, favoring smaller, localized kingdoms over vast empires. - (d) Scarcity of manpower: - Incorrect—Southern India had sufficient population, evident in Chola armies (e.g., Rajendra Chola’s naval expeditions, c. 1025 CE) and Vijayanagara’s urban centers (e.g., Hampi). Manpower wasn’t scarce; geographic constraints shaped political scale more. - Key Features: - Southern Geography: - Terrain: Hilly Deccan, coastal strips, fragmented rivers. - Impact: Smaller agrarian bases, localized power. - Contrast: Northern plains supported Mauryan, Mughal empires. - Related Figures: - Rajendra Chola I: - King (r. 1014-1044 CE), Chola peak, regional unifier. - Krishnadevaraya: - Vijayanagara ruler (r. 1509-1529 CE), strong regional king. - Pulakeshin II: - Chalukya king (r. 610-642 CE), controlled Deccan. - Narasimhavarman I: - Pallava king (r. 630-668 CE), Mahabalipuram builder. - Ashoka: - Mauryan emperor (r. 268-232 BCE), north contrast. - Other Notable Regional Kingdoms of Southern India: - Cheras (Kerala): - c. 3rd century BCE-12th century CE, trade-focused. - Pandyas (Tamil Nadu): - c. 4th century BCE-16th century CE, Madurai-based. - Hoysalas (Karnataka): - c. 10th-14th centuries CE, temple builders (e.g., Halebidu). - Kakatiyas (Telangana): - c. 12th-14th centuries CE, Warangal fort. - Satavahanas (Deccan): - c. 1st century BCE-3rd century CE, early regional power. - Broader Connection: - Links to southern archaeology (Q153 [Mangadu]), Chola expeditions (Q143 [ports]), or Mughal contrast (Q30 [Mansabdari]). - Key Takeaway: - The growth of small regional kingdoms in southern India stemmed from the absence of vast fertile land (c), not minerals, social divisions, or manpower. - Q32: “The king was freed from his people and they from their king.” On whose death did Badauni comment thus? - Options: (a) Balban (b) Ala-ud-din Khalji (c) Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq (d) Firoz Shah Tughlaq - Answer: (c) Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Abdul Qadir Badauni (1540-1615 CE), a Mughal-era historian and critic, wrote Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh, offering sharp observations on Delhi Sultanate and Mughal rulers. His comment reflects a ruler whose reign was marked by turmoil, distancing him from his subjects, a theme tied to the 14th-century Delhi Sultanate. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Balban: - Incorrect—Balban (r. 1266-1287 CE) was a strict autocrat who centralized power with an iron fist (Q13 context). Badauni, writing later, didn’t comment on his death this way; Ziauddin Barani’s Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi praises Balban’s control, not alienation. - (b) Ala-ud-din Khalji: - Incorrect—Ala-ud-din Khalji (r. 1296-1316 CE) was a successful conqueror and administrator (e.g., market reforms). His death didn’t inspire Badauni’s remark; Barani and Amir Khusrau lauded his reign, not a mutual “freeing.” - (c) Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq: - Correct—Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq (r. 1325-1351 CE) faced chaos from policies like shifting the capital to Daulatabad (1327 CE) and token currency (1329 CE), alienating his people. This department continued under later Tughlaqs, like Firoz Shah (r. 1351-1388 CE). - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) Dewan-i-Mustakhraj - Balban: - Incorrect—Dewan-i-Mustakhraj (Department of Revenue Arrears) was created by Alauddin Khalji (r. 1296-1316 CE) to recover unpaid taxes and enforce fiscal discipline, not by Balban (r. 1266-1287 CE). Balban focused on military consolidation (e.g., Dewan-i-Arz) and had no such revenue-focused diwan, per historical records like Tabaqat-i-Nasiri (c. 1260 CE). - (c) Dewan-i-Kohi - Alauddin Khalji: - Incorrect—Dewan-i-Kohi (Department of Agriculture) was instituted by Muhammad bin Tughlaq (r. 1325-1351 CE) to promote farming and reclaim land, especially during his experimental projects (e.g., shifting capital to Daulatabad). Alauddin Khalji prioritized market reforms and military, not agriculture-specific diwans. - (d) Dewan-i-Arz - Muhammad Tughlaq: - Incorrect—Dewan-i-Arz (Department of Military) existed across multiple reigns, including Balban’s, to manage the army. While Muhammad Tughlaq used it, it wasn’t uniquely his creation or most associated with him; it predates the Tughlaqs and is more famously linked to Balban’s military reforms. - Diwan Details: - Dewan-i-Bandagani: - Ruler: Firuz Shah Tughlaq (r. 1351-1388 CE) - Role: Managed slaves as administrative/military cadre. - Dewan-i-Mustakhraj: - Ruler: Alauddin Khalji (r. 1296-1316 CE). - Role: Collected revenue arrears. - Dewan-i-Kohi: - Ruler: Muhammad bin Tughlaq (r. 1325-1351 CE). - Role: Agricultural development. - Dewan-i-Arz: - Ruler: Established earlier but notably strengthened by Balban (r. 1266-1287 CE). - Role: Military administration. - Other Related Diwans: - Dewan-i-Wizarat: - Context: Finance ministry; all reigns. - Dewan-i-Risalat: - Context: Foreign affairs; evolved later. - Dewan-i-Insha: - Context: Correspondence; Sultanate-wide. - Historical Significance: - The Dewan-i-Bandagani under the Tughlaqs highlights their reliance on a slave-based administration, a legacy from the Slave dynasty, to ensure loyalty amidst dynastic instability. Other diwans reflect specific Sultanate priorities—revenue (Khalji), agriculture (Muhammad Tughlaq), and military (Balban). - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi (Barani, c. 1357 CE): Mentions Bandagani. - Khaza’in-ul-Futuh (Amir Khusrau, c. 1311 CE): Khalji reforms. - Accounts: - Ibn Battuta (c. 1333-1347 CE): Notes Muhammad Tughlaq’s Kohi. - Related Figures: - Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq: - Sultan (r. 1320-1325 CE); Bandagani founder. - Alauddin Khalji: - Sultan (r. 1296-1316 CE); Mustakhraj initiator. - Muhammad bin Tughlaq: - Sultan (r. 1325-1351 CE); Kohi innovator. - Balban: - Sultan (r. 1266-1287 CE); Arz enhancer. - Broader Connection: - Links to Sultanate administration (e.g., Q20 [Fawazil]), Tughlaq reforms (e.g., Q21 [canals]), or military organization (e.g., Q22 [iqtas]). - Key Takeaway: - The correctly matched pair is (a) Dewan-i-Bandagani - Tughlaq, as it aligns with historical records, unlike the mismatched options (b), (c), and (d). - Q46: Assertion (A): Battle of Khanua was certainly more decisive and significant than the First Battle of Panipat. - Reason (R): Rana Sanga, the Rajput hero, was certainly a more formidable adversary than Ibrahim Lodi. - Question: Which one of the following is correct? - Options: (a) Both A and R are individually true, and R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A and R are individually true, but R is not a correct explanation of A (c) A is true, but R is false (d) A is false, but R is true - Answer: (a) Both A and R are individually true, and R is the correct explanation of A - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The First Battle of Panipat (April 21, 1526 CE) saw Babur defeat Ibrahim Lodi, ending the Lodi dynasty and marking the Mughal entry into India. The Battle of Khanua (March 16-17, 1527 CE) pitted Babur against Rana Sanga’s Rajput-Afghan coalition, consolidating Mughal power. Both battles involved Babur’s innovative gunpowder tactics (e.g., tulughma, araba), but their outcomes and opponents differed significantly (e.g., Q88 [Babur’s gunpowder]). - Evaluation of Assertion (A): - A: Battle of Khanua was certainly more decisive and significant than the First Battle of Panipat: - True—Panipat was a decisive victory, eliminating Ibrahim Lodi and the Delhi Sultanate’s remnants (20,000-40,000 troops, 1,000 elephants), but it left Babur’s rule unstable, with threats from Afghans and Rajputs persisting. Khanua, however, crushed Rana Sanga’s formidable coalition (estimated 80,000-200,000 men), a unified northern Indian power, securing Mughal dominance over a broader region. Historians like Satish Chandra argue Khanua was the true foundation of Mughal rule, as it neutralized a stronger, more organized foe than the crumbling Lodi regime (e.g., Q57 [Mughal decline]). - Evaluation of Reason (R): - R: Rana Sanga, the Rajput hero, was certainly a more formidable adversary than Ibrahim Lodi: - True—Ibrahim Lodi (r. 1517-1526 CE) led a fractured Sultanate, losing support from nobles like Daulat Khan and Alam Khan, who defected to Babur. His army, though large, lacked cohesion and gunpowder tech. Rana Sanga (r. 1508-1528 CE), ruler of Mewar, commanded a powerful Rajput confederacy, bolstered by Afghan allies (e.g., Mahmud Lodi), and had prior victories (e.g., Khatoli, 1517 CE, against Ibrahim). Babur’s memoirs (Baburnama) note Sanga’s threat, requiring a fortified defense at Khanua, unlike the open-field victory at Panipat. - Why (a) Both A and R are true, and R explains A?: - A’s Truth: Khanua’s outcome was more decisive (ended Rajput supremacy) and significant (solidified Mughal rule) than Panipat’s initial foothold against a weaker Lodi. - R’s Truth: Sanga’s military prowess, alliances, and regional power outmatched Ibrahim’s disorganized forces, as evidenced by Babur’s strategic preparations at Khanua (carts, artillery) versus Panipat’s simpler tactics. - R Explains A: Sanga’s formidable nature made Khanua a harder-fought, more critical battle; defeating him ensured Mughal stability, unlike Panipat’s victory over a less challenging foe. The greater adversary necessitated a more decisive win. - Verification: - (b): Wrong—R explains A, not just coexists. - (c): Wrong—R is true, not false. - (d): Wrong—A is true, not false. - Battle Details: - Panipat (1526 CE): - Forces: Babur (12,000-15,000) vs. Ibrahim (30,000-70,000). - Outcome: Lodi killed, Mughal entry. - Khanua (1527 CE): - Forces: Babur (est. 20,000-80,000) vs. Sanga (80,000-200,000). - Outcome: Rajput power broken, Mughal rule entrenched. - Other Related Battles: - Ghaghra (1529 CE): Babur vs. Afghans, further consolidation. - Chanderi (1528 CE): Babur vs. Medini Rai, Rajput follow-up. - Khatoli (1517 CE): Sanga vs. Ibrahim, Rajput victory. - Historical Significance: - Panipat opened India to Babur; Khanua ensured he stayed, defeating a stronger foe, aligning with R’s explanation of Sanga’s formidability driving A’s decisiveness (e.g., Q88 [Timurid dynasty]). - Related Evidence: - Texts: Baburnama (Babur’s fear of Sanga), Rajput chronicles (Sanga’s coalition). - Archaeology: Khanua site (fortifications), Panipat (battlefield). - Related Figures: - Babur: Mughal founder (d. 1530 CE). - Rana Sanga: Mewar ruler (d. 1528 CE). - Ibrahim Lodi: Last Lodi Sultan (d. 1526 CE). - Broader Connection: - Ties to Mughal origins (Q88), Rajput resistance (Q57), warfare tech (Q94). - Key Takeaway: - Khanua’s greater decisiveness and significance (A) stem from Sanga’s formidable challenge (R), making (a) correct. - Q47: The shaded area in the above map shows the empire of: - - Options: (a) Alauddin Khalji (b) Mohammad Tughlaq (c) Shahjahan (d) Aurangzeb - Answer: (c) Shahjahan - [2002] - Q48: Who among the following was the first Bhakti saint to use Hindi for the propagation of his message? - Options: (a) Dadu (b) Kabir (c) Ramananda (d) Tulsidas - Answer: (c) Ramananda - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Bhakti movement, spanning the 13th to 17th centuries CE in medieval India, emphasized personal devotion to God over ritualistic practices, often using vernacular languages to reach the masses. Hindi, evolving from dialects like Apabhramsa and Avadhi, became a key medium in northern India, particularly under saints who sought to break from Sanskrit’s exclusivity during the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal periods. - Correct Option Explained: - (c) Ramananda: - Correct—Ramananda (c. 14th century CE, active c. 1350-1400 CE) was the first Bhakti saint to use Hindi (early forms like Braj and Avadhi) to spread his message of devotion to Rama. A Vaishnava saint from Prayag (modern Allahabad), he broke from orthodox traditions by teaching in the vernacular, influencing disciples like Kabir, as noted in hagiographies like the Bhaktamal (c. 1585 CE). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Dadu: - Incorrect—Dadu Dayal (1544-1603 CE), a later Bhakti saint from Rajasthan, used Hindi (Rajasthani dialect) to preach unity of God (nirguna bhakti). However, he came after Ramananda and Kabir, making him a later figure in the vernacular tradition. - (b) Kabir: - Incorrect—Kabir (c. 1398-1448 CE), a prominent Bhakti poet, extensively used Hindi (mixed with Braj and eastern dialects) in his dohas and songs to convey nirguna (formless God) devotion. Though influential, he was Ramananda’s disciple and thus followed his teacher’s pioneering use of Hindi. - (d) Tulsidas: - Incorrect—Tulsidas (1532-1623 CE), author of the Ramcharitmanas in Avadhi Hindi, popularized Rama bhakti in the vernacular during the Mughal era. His work came much later than Ramananda’s, building on an established Hindi Bhakti tradition. - Saint Details: - Ramananda: - Period: c. 14th century CE; Prayag. - Contribution: First to use Hindi; Vaishnava founder. - Dadu: - Period: 1544-1603 CE; Rajasthan. - Contribution: Nirguna bhakti in Hindi dialects. - Kabir: - Period: c. 1398-1448 CE; Varanasi. - Contribution: Hindi poetry; Ramananda’s disciple. - Tulsidas: - Period: 1532-1623 CE; Uttar Pradesh. - Contribution: Ramcharitmanas in Avadhi Hindi. - Other Related Bhakti Figures: - Namdev: - Context: c. 13th-14th century CE; Marathi pioneer. - Role: Early vernacular (not Hindi). - Surdas: - Context: c. 16th century CE; Braj Hindi. - Role: Krishna bhakti, post-Ramananda. - Mirabai: - Context: c. 1498-1546 CE; Rajasthani Hindi. - Role: Krishna devotion, later figure. - Historical Significance: - Ramananda’s use of Hindi marked a revolutionary shift in the Bhakti movement, democratizing spirituality by making it accessible beyond Sanskrit-speaking elites. His influence spawned a lineage of Hindi-speaking saints (e.g., Kabir, Tulsidas), shaping North Indian devotional culture. - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Bhaktamal (Nabhadas, c. 1585 CE): Credits Ramananda with Hindi use. - Kabir Granthavali: Reflects Ramananda’s legacy. - Oral Tradition: - Ramanandi hymns: Early Hindi traces. - Related Figures: - Ramananda: - Bhakti pioneer (c. 14th century CE); Hindi innovator. - Kabir: - Disciple (c. 1398-1448 CE); amplified Hindi use. - Vallabhacharya: - Contemporary (c. 1479-1531 CE); Sanskrit focus, contrast. - Broader Connection: - Links to Bhakti movement (e.g., Q8 [Sufi music parallels]), vernacular literature, or medieval cultural shifts (e.g., Q135 [dynasties]). - Key Takeaway: - Ramananda (c) was the first Bhakti saint to use Hindi for his message, predating Dadu, Kabir, and Tulsidas, making (c) correct. - Q49: With reference to medieval Indian rulers, which one of the following statements is correct? - Options: (a) Alauddin Khalji first set up a separate ariz’s department (b) Balban introduced the branding of horses in his military (c) Muhammad Bin Tughlaq was succeeded by his uncle to the military (d) Firoz Tughlaq set up a separate department of slaves - Answer: (d) Firoz Tughlaq set up a separate department of slaves - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Medieval India (c. 13th-18th centuries CE) saw Delhi Sultanate rulers like the Khaljis and Tughlaqs implement administrative reforms. Military organization, succession, and slavery were key aspects, with rulers adapting systems to consolidate power (e.g., Q94 [Araghatta], Q65 [Firoz’s canals]). - Correct Option Explained: - (d) Firoz Tughlaq set up a separate department of slaves: - Correct—Firoz Shah Tughlaq (r. 1351-1388 CE) established the ‘Diwan-i-Bandagan,’ a department for managing slaves. This reflected his reliance on a large slave corps (bandagan), inherited from earlier rulers like Alauddin Khalji, but formalized under his reign. Chronicles like Ziauddin Barani’s Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi note his extensive use of slaves in administration and military, numbering tens of thousands, a distinctive policy among Tughlaqs. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Alauddin Khalji first set up a separate ariz’s department: - Incorrect—The ‘ariz’ (military overseer) role existed, but its formal departmentalization is credited to Balban (r. 1266-1287 CE), who organized the ‘Diwan-i-Ariz’ to manage the army. Alauddin Khalji (r. 1296-1316 CE) enhanced military reforms (e.g., dagh, chehra), but didn’t initiate the ariz department. - (b) Balban introduced the branding of horses in his military: - Incorrect—Branding horses (dagh) was introduced by Alauddin Khalji to prevent fraud in his cavalry, not Balban. Balban focused on discipline and royal authority (e.g., sijda, paibos), not this specific reform. - (c) Muhammad Bin Tughlaq was succeeded by his uncle to the military: - Incorrect—Muhammad bin Tughlaq (r. 1325-1351 CE) died in 1351 campaigning in Sindh; his successor was his cousin, Firoz Shah Tughlaq, who took the throne, not just military command. No uncle is historically noted as his successor. - Reassessment Rationale: - Option (d) aligns with historical evidence: Firoz’s ‘Diwan-i-Bandagan’ is well-documented, distinguishing his reign. Other options misattribute reforms or succession: (a) and (b) confuse rulers, while (c)’s phrasing and genealogy are inaccurate. Sources favoring (d) (e.g., UPSC materials) reflect this consensus. - Ruler Details: - Firoz Tughlaq: - Period: r. 1351-1388 CE. - Context: Slave department, infrastructure focus. - Alauddin Khalji: - Period: r. 1296-1316 CE. - Context: Dagh, market reforms. - Balban: - Period: r. 1266-1287 CE. - Context: Ariz department, royal authority. - Muhammad bin Tughlaq: - Period: r. 1325-1351 CE. - Context: Experimental policies, cousin succession. - Other Related Administrative Reforms: - Diwan-i-Ariz: - Ruler: - Established earlier, but strengthened by Balban (r. 1266-1287 CE). - Role: - Military department, responsible for recruitment, training, and salary management. - Dagh (Branding) & Chehra (Descriptive Roll): - Ruler: - Alauddin Khalji (r. 1296-1316 CE). - Role: - Dagh: - Branding of horses to prevent corruption in army recruitment. - Chehra: - Maintaining a register of soldiers to prevent false enlistments. - Diwan-i-Kohi: - Ruler: - Muhammad bin Tughlaq (r. 1325-1351 CE). - Role: - Agriculture department, focused on land reclamation and state-sponsored farming. - Diwan-i-Khairat: - Ruler: - Firuz Shah Tughlaq (r. 1351-1388 CE). - Role: - Charity and welfare bureau, provided aid to the poor, widows, and orphans. - Historical Significance: - Firoz’s slave department underscores his administrative reliance on bandagan, contrasting with predecessors’ military or economic focuses, shaping Tughlaq governance (e.g., Q65 [Firoz’s policies]). - Related Evidence: - Texts: Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi (Firoz’s slave corps). - Chronicles: Alauddin’s reforms (Futuhat-i-Alai). - Baburnama: Succession context (post-Tughlaq). - Related Figures: - Firoz Tughlaq: Sultan (d. 1388 CE). - Alauddin Khalji: Sultan (d. 1316 CE). - Balban: Sultan (d. 1287 CE). - Broader Connection: - Ties to administration (Q65), military (Q88), economy (Q94). - Key Takeaway: - Firoz Tughlaq’s slave department (d) is the correct statement. - Q50: The motive behind Shah Jahan’s Balkh campaign was to: - Options: (a) Secure a friendly ruler in Balkh and Badakshan which bordered Kabul (b) Conquer Samarqand and Farghana, the Mughal homelands (c) Fix the Mughal frontier on the ‘scientific line’, the Amu Daria (d) Expand the Mughal Empire beyond the sub-continent - Answer: (a) Secure a friendly ruler in Balkh and Badakshan which bordered Kabul - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Shah Jahan (r. 1628-1658 CE), a Mughal emperor, launched the Balkh campaign (1646-1647 CE) to assert influence over Central Asia, a region tied to Mughal lineage through Babur’s Timurid ancestry. Balkh and Badakshan, north of Kabul, were strategically vital but contested by the Uzbeks and Safavids, prompting Mughal intervention during a period of relative stability in India. - Correct Option Explained: - (a) Secure a friendly ruler in Balkh and Badakshan which bordered Kabul: - Correct—Shah Jahan’s primary motive was to install a friendly ruler, Nazar Muhammad Khan’s son, in Balkh and Badakshan after the Uzbek ruler fled in 1646 CE. This aimed to stabilize the region bordering Kabul, a key Mughal stronghold, as a buffer against Uzbek and Safavid threats, per the Padshahnama (c. 1630s-1650s CE) and contemporary accounts. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) Conquer Samarqand and Farghana, the Mughal homelands: - Incorrect—While Samarqand and Farghana held symbolic value as Babur’s ancestral lands, Shah Jahan’s campaign focused on Balkh, not a full conquest of these distant cities. The effort was limited and practical, not a grand reclamation, as logistical challenges made such ambitions unfeasible, per historian accounts like those of Abdul Hamid Lahori. - (c) Fix the Mughal frontier on the ‘scientific line’, the Amu Daria: - Incorrect—The term “scientific line” (Amu Daria/Oxus River) emerged in later British colonial contexts, not Mughal strategy. Shah Jahan aimed to secure Balkh temporarily, not establish a permanent frontier, as evidenced by the campaign’s withdrawal in 1647 CE after initial success. - (d) Expand the Mughal Empire beyond the sub-continent: - Incorrect—The campaign was not about territorial expansion but securing influence. The Mughals retreated after placing a friendly ruler, lacking resources or intent to hold Balkh permanently, unlike their subcontinental conquests (e.g., Deccan campaigns). - Campaign Details: - Balkh Campaign: - Period: 1646-1647 CE; led by Prince Aurangzeb. - Objective: Install pro-Mughal ruler; secure northwest. - Outcome: Short-term success; withdrawn due to costs. - Other Related Mughal Campaigns: - Qandhar (1638-1648 CE): - Context: Captured, then lost to Safavids. - Ghaghra (1529 CE): - Context: Babur’s consolidation in India. - Deccan (1630s-1650s CE): - Context: Shah Jahan’s true expansion focus. - Historical Significance: - The Balkh campaign reflected Shah Jahan’s defensive strategy to protect Kabul and northwest India, not an expansive vision. Its brief success and retreat underscored Mughal limits in Central Asia, contrasting with their Indian dominance, as noted in European traveler accounts (e.g., François Bernier, c. 1658-1668 CE). - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Padshahnama (Abdul Hamid Lahori): Details Balkh motives. - Alamgirnama: Aurangzeb’s role in campaign. - Accounts: - Manucci (c. 1653-1708 CE): Notes Mughal frontier issues. - Related Figures: - Shah Jahan: - Emperor (r. 1628-1658 CE); campaign initiator. - Aurangzeb: - Prince (later r. 1658-1707 CE); campaign leader. - Nazar Muhammad Khan: - Uzbek ruler; Balkh’s displaced leader. - Broader Connection: - Links to Mughal frontier policy (e.g., Q19 [Qandhar]), Central Asian ties, or Shah Jahan’s reign (e.g., Q135 [dynasties]). - Key Takeaway: - Shah Jahan’s Balkh campaign aimed to secure a friendly ruler in Balkh and Badakshan bordering Kabul (a), not conquest or frontier fixing, making (a) correct. - Q51: Assertion (A): Muhammad Bin Tughlaq left Delhi, and for two years lived in a camp called Swarga-Dwari. - Reason (R): At that time, Delhi was ravaged by plague and many people died. - Question: Which one of the following is correct? - Options: (a) Both A and R are individually true, and R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A and R are individually true, but R is not a correct explanation of A (c) A is true, but R is false (d) A is false, but R is true - Answer: (a) Both A and R are individually true, and R is the correct explanation of A - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Muhammad bin Tughlaq (r. 1325-1351 CE), a Tughlaq dynasty ruler of the Delhi Sultanate, is known for his ambitious and often controversial policies, including shifting the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (c. 1327 CE) and later managing crises like famines and epidemics. His reign faced significant challenges, including natural disasters that impacted Delhi. - Evaluation of Assertion (A): - A: "Muhammad Bin Tughlaq left Delhi, and for two years lived in a camp called Swarga-Dwari." - True—During c. 1340-1342 CE, Muhammad bin Tughlaq temporarily abandoned Delhi due to a severe crisis and resided in a camp named Swarga-Dwari (meaning "Gateway to Heaven") near Kanauj on the Ganges. This is documented by contemporary historians like Ziauddin Barani in Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi (c. 1357 CE) and traveler Ibn Battuta (c. 1333-1347 CE). - Evaluation of Reason (R): - R: "At that time, Delhi was ravaged by plague and many people died." - True—Around 1340 CE, Delhi suffered a devastating epidemic, often described as a plague or pestilence, coupled with famine, leading to significant mortality. Barani and Ibn Battuta note the outbreak’s severity, which forced the Sultan and court to relocate temporarily. - Relationship Between A and R: - Correct Option: (a) Both A and R are individually true, and R is the correct explanation of A. - Explanation—The plague and resultant deaths in Delhi (R) directly caused Muhammad bin Tughlaq to leave the city and establish Swarga-Dwari as a temporary base (A). This relocation was a response to the uninhabitable conditions in Delhi, making R the precise reason for A, as corroborated by historical records. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) Both A and R are true, but R is not a correct explanation of A: - Incorrect—R directly explains A; the plague was the primary driver for the move to Swarga-Dwari, not an unrelated event. - (c) A is true, but R is false: - Incorrect—R is true; historical evidence confirms the plague’s impact on Delhi during this period. - (d) A is false, but R is true: - Incorrect—A is true; Muhammad bin Tughlaq did relocate to Swarga-Dwari for two years. - Event Details: - Swarga-Dwari: - Location: Near Kanauj, Ganges River. - Period: c. 1340-1342 CE. - Purpose: Temporary capital during crisis. - Plague in Delhi: - Time: c. 1340 CE. - Impact: Mass deaths, city abandonment. - Other Related Crises: - Daulatabad Shift (1327 CE): - Context: Earlier capital move; different motive (centralization). - Token Currency (1329-1332 CE): - Context: Economic experiment, unrelated to plague. - Mongol Threats: - Context: Periodic invasions, not linked to Swarga-Dwari. - Historical Significance: - The Swarga-Dwari episode underscores Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s reactive governance, adapting to natural calamities amidst his broader experimental policies. It highlights the Sultanate’s vulnerability to environmental challenges, contrasting with his earlier ambitious projects. - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi (Barani, c. 1357 CE): Plague and relocation. - Rihla (Ibn Battuta, c. 1347 CE): Epidemic firsthand account. - Chronicles: - Fatuhat-i-Firoz Shahi: Later Tughlaq context. - Related Figures: - Muhammad bin Tughlaq: - Sultan (r. 1325-1351 CE); crisis manager. - Ziauddin Barani: - Historian (c. 1285-1357 CE); documented event. - Ibn Battuta: - Traveler (c. 1304-1369 CE); eyewitness. - Broader Connection: - Links to Tughlaq reforms (e.g., Q45 [diwans]), Sultanate challenges (e.g., Q19 [Qandhar]), or medieval crises (e.g., Q135 [dynasties]). - Key Takeaway: - Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A (a), as the plague in Delhi drove Muhammad bin Tughlaq to live in Swarga-Dwari for two years. - Q52: Historian Barani refused to consider the state in India under Delhi Sultans as truly Islamic because: - Options: (a) Majority of the population did not follow Islam (b) Muslim theologians were often disregarded (c) Sultan supplemented the Muslim law by framing his own regulations (d) Religious freedom was accorded to non-Muslims - Answer: (c) Sultan supplemented the Muslim law by framing his own regulations - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Ziauddin Barani (c. 1285-1357 CE), a prominent historian of the Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526 CE), wrote works like Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi (c. 1357 CE), reflecting his orthodox Islamic views. He judged the Sultanate’s rulers against strict Sharia (Islamic law) standards, often critiquing their deviations during the Slave, Khalji, and Tughlaq dynasties. - Correct Option Explained: - (c) Sultan supplemented the Muslim law by framing his own regulations: - Correct—Barani argued that the Delhi Sultanate was not a truly Islamic state because rulers like Alauddin Khalji (r. 1296-1316 CE) and Firoz Shah Tughlaq (r. 1351-1388 CE) enacted zawabit (state regulations) that supplemented or diverged from Sharia. For example, Alauddin’s market controls and Firoz’s taxation policies prioritized pragmatism over strict Islamic jurisprudence, which Barani saw as a betrayal of an ideal theocratic state, per his writings. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Majority of the population did not follow Islam: - Incorrect—While true that most of India’s population remained Hindu, Barani’s critique focused on the rulers’ actions, not the populace’s faith. He was more concerned with the Sultanate’s governance failing Islamic ideals than demographic composition. - (b) Muslim theologians were often disregarded: - Incorrect—Barani did criticize rulers for sidelining ulema (theologians), but this was a symptom of his broader issue: sultans’ independent lawmaking. Theologians’ disregard was not his primary reason; it was secondary to the creation of non-Sharia laws. - (d) Religious freedom was accorded to non-Muslims: - Incorrect—While some sultans (e.g., Firoz Shah) tolerated non-Muslims, Barani’s objection centered on legal deviations, not tolerance itself. He viewed state policies overriding Sharia as the core issue, not coexistence with Hindus or others. - Barani’s Perspective: - Focus: Ideal Islamic state governed solely by Sharia. - Critique: Zawabit (e.g., Alauddin’s price controls) as un-Islamic. - Period: Slave to Tughlaq dynasties (13th-14th centuries CE). - Other Related Views: - Ibn Battuta: - Context: c. 1333-1347 CE; noted Sultanate’s Islamic veneer. - Amir Khusrau: - Context: c. 1253-1325 CE; praised rulers, less orthodox. - Firoz Shah’s Ulema: - Context: Consulted but often overridden. - Historical Significance: - Barani’s stance reflects a tension between practical governance and religious idealism in the Sultanate. His orthodox lens contrasted with the sultans’ need to rule a diverse, multi-religious empire, shaping his view of their legitimacy as Islamic rulers. - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi (Barani, c. 1357 CE): Critiques zawabit. - Fatawa-i-Jahandari (Barani): Ideal Islamic governance. - Chronicles: - Khaza’in-ul-Futuh (Amir Khusrau, c. 1311 CE): Contrasts Barani. - Related Figures: - Ziauddin Barani: - Historian (c. 1285-1357 CE); orthodox critic. - Alauddin Khalji: - Sultan (r. 1296-1316 CE); pragmatic reformer. - Firoz Shah Tughlaq: - Sultan (r. 1351-1388 CE); mixed Sharia with state laws. - Broader Connection: - Links to Sultanate governance (e.g., Q22 [iqtas]), legal systems (e.g., Q45 [diwans]), or medieval Islamic debates (e.g., Q135 [dynasties]). - Key Takeaway: - Barani refused to consider the Delhi Sultanate truly Islamic because sultans supplemented Muslim law with their own regulations (c), not primarily due to population, theologians, or tolerance, making (c) correct. - Q53: With reference to Sufism in Indian history, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Sheikh Ahmad Sarhindi was a contemporary of Ibrahim Lodi 2. Sheikh Nasiruddin Chirag-i-Dehlavi was a disciple of Sheikh Nizamuddin Auliya 3. Aurangzeb was a contemporary of Sheikh Salim Chisti 4. Instead, it addressed an immediate threat from Mirza Hakim and secured Kabul as a buffer against external powers like the Safavids and Uzbeks. His reign began amidst chaos following Ahmad Shah Abdali’s invasions and the Third Battle of Panipat (1761 CE), with Delhi often unsafe or controlled by others (e.g., Q88 [Babur’s legacy]). - Evaluation of Assertion (A): - A: Shah Alam II spent the initial years as an emperor far away from his capital: - True—Shah Alam II became emperor in 1759 CE after his father Alamgir II’s assassination in Delhi by Imad-ul-Mulk. This is well-documented in sources like the Siyar-ul-Mutakherin and British records. - Evaluation of Reason (R): - R: There was always a lurking danger of foreign invasion from the north-west frontier: - False—While the north-west frontier saw invasions (e.g., Abdali’s raids, Nadir Shah’s 1739 CE sack), the phrase “always a lurking danger” overstates the situation during Shah Alam II’s early reign. By 1759 CE, Abdali’s major invasion (Panipat, 1761 CE) was a specific event, not a constant threat. Post-1761, the north-west stabilized under Afghan influence, with internal power struggles (e.g., Marathas, British) and regional lords (e.g., Najib-ud-Daula) posing greater immediate risks to Delhi than persistent foreign invasions. - Why (c) A is true, but R is false?: - A’s Truth: Shah Alam II’s absence from Delhi (1759-1771 CE) is factual, driven by Delhi’s instability post-assassination and battles like Buxar (1764 CE), where he allied with the British in Allahabad. - R’s Falsity: The north-west threat wasn’t “always lurking” after 1761 CE; Delhi’s instability stemmed more from internal factions (e.g., Imad-ul-Mulk, Marathas) and British ascendancy than a continuous foreign invasion risk. - R Doesn’t Explain A: Shah Alam’s exile was due to immediate political turmoil (e.g., assassination, Maratha-British rivalry), not a perpetual north-west danger. The reason misattributes his absence. - Verification: - (a): Wrong—R is false and doesn’t explain A. - (b): Wrong—R is false, not true. - (d): Wrong—A is true, not false. - Reign Details: - Shah Alam II: - Initial Years: 1759-1771 CE, Allahabad exile. - Return: 1772 CE, Delhi under Maratha protection. - North-West Threats: - Key Event: Panipat (1761 CE), Abdali vs. Marathas. - Post-1761: Internal strife dominated. - Other Related Mughal Events: - Nadir Shah’s Invasion: 1739 CE, earlier threat. - Third Panipat: 1761 CE, temporary north-west peak. - Buxar: 1764 CE, British dominance over Shah Alam. - Maratha Resurgence: 1771-1772 CE, Delhi return. - Historical Significance: - Shah Alam II’s early exile reflects Mughal weakness, not just north-west invasions, but broader disintegration, paving the way for British control (e.g., Q57 [Mughal decline]). - Related Evidence: - Texts: Siyar-ul-Mutakherin (Shah Alam’s exile). - Records: British East India Company (Allahabad phase). - Chronicles: Maratha accounts (1772 CE return). - Related Figures: - Shah Alam II: Emperor (r. 1759-1806 CE). - Ahmad Shah Abdali: Afghan invader (d. 1772 CE). - Imad-ul-Mulk: Vizier, Delhi usurper (d. 1800 CE). - Broader Connection: - Ties to Mughal decline (Q57), invasions (Q88), administration (Q49). - Key Takeaway: - Shah Alam II’s initial exile (A) is true, but not due to constant north-west danger (R), making (c) correct. - Q56: Assertion (A): Saluva Narasimha put an end to the old dynasty and assumed the royal title. - Reason (R): He wanted to save the kingdom from further degeneration and disintegration. - Question: Which one of the following is correct? - Options: (a) Both A and R are individually true, and R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A and R are individually true, but R is not a correct explanation of A (c) A is true, but R is false (d) A is false, but R is true - Answer: (a) Both A and R are individually true, and R is the correct explanation of A (Some sources are saying option c also) - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Vijayanagara Empire (c. 14th-16th centuries CE), founded in 1336 CE by Harihara I and Bukka I of the Sangama dynasty, faced instability by the late 15th century CE. He ended the Sangama line, which had ruled since 1336 CE, and assumed the royal title, founding the Saluva dynasty. This is documented by inscriptions and accounts like those of Fernão Nunes (c. 1530s CE). - Evaluation of Reason (R): - R: He wanted to save the kingdom from further degeneration and disintegration: - True—By the 1480s CE, the Vijayanagara Empire suffered from weak rulers, feudal rebellions (e.g., nayakas), and invasions (e.g., Bahmani Sultanate). Saluva Narasimha, as a capable general, intervened to restore order. His actions—centralizing power and quelling dissent—suggest a motive to halt the kingdom’s decline, as inferred from contemporary records and later Vijayanagara stability (e.g., Q39 [Amaram]). - Why (a) Both A and R are true, and R explains A?: - A is true: Saluva Narasimha’s coup ended the Sangama dynasty and established his rule (1485 CE). - R is true: The kingdom faced degeneration (weak kings, rebellions) and disintegration (territorial losses), which he countered. - Explanation Link: R explains A because his assumption of power (A) was driven by the need to save Vijayanagara (R), evidenced by his military campaigns and administrative reforms stabilizing the empire. - Q57: Assertion (A): Marathas emerged as the strongest native power in India after the decline of Mughal empire. - Reason (R): Marathas were the first to have a clear concept of a united Indian nation. - Question: Which one of the following is correct? - Options: (a) Both A and R are individually true, and R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A and R are individually true, but R is not a correct explanation of A (c) A is true, but R is false (d) A is false, but R is true - Answer: (c) A is true, but R is false - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Mughal Empire’s decline began after Aurangzeb’s death in 1707 CE, accelerating through the 18th century CE with invasions (e.g., Nadir Shah, 1739 CE) and internal strife. This vacuum enabled native powers like the Marathas to rise, particularly under Peshwa leadership (e.g., Balaji Vishwanath, Q36), reshaping India’s political landscape until British dominance by the early 19th century CE. - Evaluation of Assertion (A): - A: Marathas emerged as the strongest native power in India after the decline of Mughal empire: - True—Post-1707 CE, the Marathas, under Shivaji (r. 1674-1680 CE) and later Peshwas like Baji Rao I (r. 1720-1740 CE), expanded across India. By the mid-18th century CE (e.g., Third Battle of Panipat, 1761 CE), they controlled vast regions from Maharashtra to the northwest, surpassing other native powers like the Sikhs or Rajputs in military and territorial reach (e.g., Q39 [Mokasa]). - Evaluation of Reason (R): - R: Marathas were the first to have a clear concept of a united Indian nation: - False—The Marathas lacked a clear concept of a united Indian nation. Their expansion was driven by regional power, loot, and tribute (e.g., chauth), not a unified national vision. Shivaji’s “Hindavi Swarajya” (self-rule) was a Maratha-centric ideal, not a pan-Indian nation-state, as seen in fragmented rule post-1761 CE (e.g., Maratha Confederacy). Earlier concepts of unity (e.g., Mauryas, c. 321-185 BCE) or later nationalist ideas (19th century CE) predate or postdate this. - Why (c) A is true, but R is false?: - A is true: Marathas became the dominant native force post-Mughal decline, evidenced by their campaigns (e.g., Baji Rao’s conquests) and control over Delhi (1750s CE). - R is false: No historical evidence (e.g., Bakhars, Peshwa records) shows a unified Indian nation concept; their focus was feudal and regional (e.g., Q36 [Balaji’s reforms]). - Explanation Link: R does not explain A; Maratha strength stemmed from military prowess and opportunism, not a nationalistic vision. - Verification: - (a): Wrong—R is false and doesn’t explain A. - (b): Wrong—R is false, not true. - (d): Wrong—A is true, not false. - Event Details: - Mughal Decline: - Period: Post-1707 CE. - Features: Weak successors, invasions. - Maratha Rise: - Period: 18th century CE. - Features: Peshwa expansion, Panipat setback. - Hindavi Swarajya: - Period: Shivaji’s era (1674-1680 CE). - Features: Regional self-rule, not national unity. - Other Related Post-Mughal Powers: - Sikhs: - Context: Punjab, 18th century CE. - Features: Ranjit Singh’s empire (1799-1839 CE). - Rajputs: - Context: Rajasthan, 18th century CE. - Features: Fragmented resistance (e.g., Mewar). - Mysore: - Context: Haider Ali, Tipu Sultan (1761-1799 CE). - Features: Southern power, anti-British. - Nawabs of Bengal: - Context: Murshid Quli to Siraj-ud-Daulah (1717-1757 CE). - Features: Early autonomy, British fall. - Rohillas: - Context: Rohilkhand, 18th century CE. - Features: Afghan resistance, Maratha rivalry. - Historical Significance: - The Marathas’ rise as the strongest native power post-Mughal decline reflects military and administrative adaptability (e.g., Q36 [Balaji]), not a unifying national ideology, contrasting with later colonial-era nationalism (e.g., Q125 [Hundi]). - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Bakhars: Maratha chronicles (18th century CE). - Sabhasad Bakhar: Shivaji’s regional focus. - Records: - Peshwa Daftar: Expansion records (18th century CE). - Battles: - Panipat (1761 CE): Maratha peak and limit. - Related Figures: - Shivaji: - Maratha founder (r. 1674-1680 CE); Swarajya visionary. - Baji Rao I: - Peshwa (r. 1720-1740 CE); expansion leader. - Aurangzeb: - Mughal emperor (r. 1658-1707 CE); decline trigger. - Broader Connection: - Links to Maratha administration (e.g., Q36 [Balaji]), land systems (e.g., Q39 [Mokasa]), or Mughal decline (e.g., Q44 [Surat]). - Key Takeaway: - A is true (Marathas as strongest power), but R is false (no united nation concept), making (c) correct. - Q58: Alam Khan, one of those who invited Babur to invade India was: - Options: (a) An uncle of Ibrahim Lodi and a pretender to the throne of Delhi (b) A cousin of Ibrahim Lodi who was ill-treated and expelled from the country (c) The father of Dilawar Khan to whom cruel treatment was meted out by Ibrahim Lodi (d) A high official in Punjab province who was discontented with Ibrahim Lodi’s treatment to his tribe - Answer: (a) An uncle of Ibrahim Lodi and a pretender to the throne of Delhi - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The decline of the Lodi dynasty (1451-1526 CE) under Ibrahim Lodi (r. 1517-1526 CE) led to internal dissent and external threats. Babur, a Timurid prince from Ferghana, was invited to invade India, culminating in the First Battle of Panipat (1526 CE), which ended Lodi rule and founded the Mughal Empire. Discontented Lodi nobles, including Alam Khan, played a key role in this shift, as recorded in Babur’s memoir, the Baburnama. - Correct Option Explained: - (a) An uncle of Ibrahim Lodi and a pretender to the throne of Delhi: - Correct—Alam Khan, also known as Alam Khan Lodi or Alauddin Alam Khan, was an uncle of Ibrahim Lodi and a claimant to the Delhi throne. A member of the Lodi family, he opposed Ibrahim’s rule due to familial rivalry and sought Babur’s aid in 1524-1525 CE. After failing to seize Delhi independently, he allied with Babur, promising support against Ibrahim, as noted in the Baburnama (c. 1526 CE). His pretender status aligns with his ambition to replace Ibrahim. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) A cousin of Ibrahim Lodi who was ill-treated and expelled from the country: - Incorrect—Alam Khan was an uncle, not a cousin, per genealogical accounts (e.g., Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi). While he faced opposition from Ibrahim, there’s no clear evidence of expulsion; he actively challenged Ibrahim from within India, not as an exile. - (c) The father of Dilawar Khan to whom cruel treatment was meted out by Ibrahim Lodi: - Incorrect—Dilawar Khan was Alam Khan’s son, not the reverse. Dilawar was sent as an envoy to Babur, but the option misidentifies the relationship. No specific “cruel treatment” to Alam is highlighted beyond political rivalry (e.g., Baburnama). - (d) A high official in Punjab province who was discontented with Ibrahim Lodi’s treatment to his tribe: - Incorrect—Alam Khan was a Lodi noble and royal claimant, not a mere Punjab official or tribal leader. His discontent stemmed from dynastic ambition, not tribal grievances, and he operated from Delhi’s vicinity, not Punjab exclusively. - Figure Details: - Alam Khan: - Role: Lodi uncle, pretender. - Period: Early 16th century CE (pre-1526 CE). - Context: Invited Babur, Panipat ally. - Ibrahim Lodi: - Role: Delhi Sultan (r. 1517-1526 CE). - Context: Last Lodi ruler, defeated by Babur. - Babur: - Role: Mughal founder (r. 1526-1530 CE). - Context: Accepted Alam’s invitation. - Other Related Figures in Babur’s Invasion: - Dilawar Khan: - Role: Alam’s son, envoy to Babur. - Context: Facilitated alliance (1525 CE). - Daulat Khan Lodi: - Role: Punjab governor, Babur’s ally. - Context: Separate invitee, rival to Ibrahim. - Rana Sanga: - Role: Rajput leader (r. 1508-1528 CE). - Context: Post-Panipat foe of Babur (1527 CE). - Shaikh Zain: - Role: Babur’s scribe. - Context: Recorded Baburnama details. - Bairam Khan: - Role: Later Mughal regent (post-Babur). - Context: Humayun’s era, not 1526 CE. - Historical Significance: - Alam Khan’s invitation to Babur reflects the Lodi dynasty’s internal fractures, enabling the Mughal conquest and marking a pivotal transition in Indian history from Sultanate to Mughal rule (e.g., Q57 [Maratha rise post-Mughal]). - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Baburnama (Babur, c. 1526 CE): Alam’s role. - Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi (Abbas Sarwani, 16th century CE): Lodi family. - Battles: - Panipat (April 21, 1526 CE): Lodi defeat. - Archaeology: - Delhi sites: Lodi-era remnants. - Related Figures: - Babur: - Mughal founder (1483-1530 CE); Dharmat was a key early engagement in this struggle, fought near Ujjain in modern Madhya Pradesh. - Correct Option Explained: - (c) Aurangzeb and Dara Shikoh: - Correct—The Battle of Dharmat pitted Aurangzeb, allied with Murad Baksh, against Dara Shikoh’s forces, led by Jaswant Singh Rathore (Maratha ally) and Qasim Khan. Q60: How did the Mughal Emperor Jahandar Shah’s reign come to an early end? - Options: (a) He was deposed by his Wazir (b) He died due to a slip while climbing down the steps (c) He was defeated by his nephew in a battle (d) He died of sickness due to drinking - Answer: (c) He was defeated by his nephew in a battle - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Jahandar Shah (r. February 1712 - February 1713 CE) ascended the Mughal throne after a succession war following Bahadur Shah I’s death in 1712 CE. His brief reign, marked by extravagance and reliance on his mistress Lal Kunwar, weakened the empire amid factional strife. The Mughal decline post-Aurangzeb (d. 1707 CE) saw rapid turnover of rulers, with Jahandar’s end tied to familial rivalry (e.g., Q59 [succession wars]). - Correct Option Explained: - (c) He was defeated by his nephew in a battle: - Correct—Jahandar Shah’s reign ended when he was defeated by his nephew, Farrukhsiyar, at the Battle of Agra (January 10, 1713 CE). Farrukhsiyar, supported by the Sayyid brothers (Abdullah Khan and Husain Ali Khan), challenged Jahandar’s rule. After losing the battle, Jahandar fled but was captured, imprisoned, and executed on February 11, 1713 CE, ending his 11-month reign, as recorded in the Maasir-ul-Umara and Farrukhsiyar’s chronicles. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) He was deposed by his Wazir: - Incorrect—Jahandar’s Wazir, Zulfikar Khan, was a key supporter, not a deposer. His downfall came from Farrukhsiyar’s military challenge, not an internal coup by his minister (e.g., Maasir-i-Jahandari). - (b) He died due to a slip while climbing down the steps: - Incorrect—No historical evidence supports this. This seems a fabricated or anecdotal claim, absent from Mughal records like the Tuzuk-i-Jahandari or contemporary accounts. - (d) He died of sickness due to drinking: - Incorrect—While Jahandar was known for indulgence (e.g., Lal Kunwar’s influence), his death was by execution after defeat, not sickness from drinking, per Farrukhsiyar’s orders (e.g., Q57 [Mughal decline]). - Reign Details: - Jahandar Shah: - Period: February 1712 - February 1713 CE. - Features: Brief, extravagant, weak rule. - Battle of Agra: - Date: January 10, 1713 CE. - Context: Farrukhsiyar’s victory. - Execution: - Date: February 11, 1713 CE. - Context: End of reign. - Other Related Mughal Succession Events: - Bahadur Shah I’s Death: - Date: 1712 CE. - Context: Triggered Jahandar’s rise (Battle of Lahore). - Farrukhsiyar’s Reign: - Date: 1713-1719 CE. - Context: Sayyid brothers’ dominance post-Jahandar. - Battle of Jajau: - Date: 1707 CE (Q59). - Context: Earlier succession after Aurangzeb. - Shah Alam II’s Deposition: - Date: 1788 CE. - Context: Later Mughal decline (e.g., Q57). - Rafi-ud-Darajat’s Reign: - Date: 1719 CE. - Context: Short rule post-Farrukhsiyar. - Historical Significance: - Jahandar Shah’s defeat by Farrukhsiyar exemplifies the Mughal Empire’s instability post-Aurangzeb, with short reigns and power struggles accelerating its decline, paving the way for Maratha and British ascendance (e.g., Q57 [Maratha power]). - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Maasir-ul-Umara: Battle of Agra (18th century CE). - Tuzuk-i-Jahandari: Jahandar’s reign details. - Records: - Farrukhsiyar’s farmans: Victory proclamation (1713 CE). - Archaeology: - Agra: Battle site context. - Related Figures: - Jahandar Shah: - Emperor (1661-1713 CE); defeated ruler. - Farrukhsiyar: - Nephew (1685-1719 CE); victor, next emperor. - Sayyid Brothers: - Kingmakers (d. 1720s CE); Farrukhsiyar’s backers. - Broader Connection: - Links to Mughal succession (e.g., Q59 [Dharmat]), decline (e.g., Q57 [Marathas]), or administration (e.g., Q44 [Surat]). - Key Takeaway: - Jahandar Shah’s reign ended early when he was defeated by his nephew Farrukhsiyar in a battle (c). - Q61: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Kitab-i-Nauras, a collection of songs in praise of Hindu deities and Muslim saints, was written by Ibrahim Adil Shah II 2. Amir Khusrau was the originator in India of the early form of the musical style known as Qawwali - Question: Which of these statements is/are correct? - Options: (a) Only 1 (b) Only 2 (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (c) Both 1 and 2 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Medieval India (c. 13th-17th centuries CE) saw a flourishing of syncretic cultural traditions under Muslim rulers, blending Persian, Indian, and Sufi influences. Kitab-i-Nauras, a collection of songs in praise of Hindu deities and Muslim saints, was written by Ibrahim Adil Shah II: - True—Ibrahim Adil Shah II (r. 1580-1627 CE), ruler of Bijapur, authored the Kitab-i-Nauras, a Dakhni Urdu work of 59 songs. It praises Hindu deities (e.g., Saraswati, Ganesha), Muslim saints, and includes musical theory, reflecting his eclectic tastes and tolerance (e.g., Q40 [secularism]). Amir Khusrau was the originator in India of the early form of the musical style known as Qawwali: - True—Amir Khusrau (1253-1325 CE), a poet-musician under the Delhi Sultanate, is credited with developing the early form of Qawwali, a Sufi devotional music style. Associated with the Chisti order (e.g., Nizamuddin Auliya), he fused Persian, Turkish, and Indian musical traditions, as noted in hagiographies like Siyar-ul-Auliya (14th century CE). Qawwali’s evolution continued, but Khusrau’s role as its pioneer in India is widely accepted (e.g., Q17 [medieval writer]). - Why (c) Both 1 and 2?: - Statement 1: Correct—Ibrahim Adil Shah II’s Kitab-i-Nauras is a historical fact, verified by Bijapur records and his syncretic reign. - Statement 2: Correct—Amir Khusrau’s foundational contribution to Qawwali is supported by Sufi tradition and musicology (e.g., Q15 [Sufi music]). - Verification: - (a): Wrong—2 is also true. - (b): Wrong—1 is also true. - (d): Wrong—Both are true. - Details of Contributions: - Kitab-i-Nauras: - Author: Ibrahim Adil Shah II (r. 1580-1627 CE). - Features: Songs in Dakhni, Hindu-Muslim praise. - Qawwali Origins: - Innovator: Amir Khusrau (1253-1325 CE). - Features: Sufi devotional music, Chisti link. - Other Related Medieval Musical Traditions: - Dhrupad: - Context: 15th-16th centuries CE, Raja Man Singh. - Features: Classical, courtly, North India. - Khayal: - Context: 18th century CE, Niamat Khan. - Features: Lighter classical form, post-Khusrau. - Thumri: - Context: 19th century CE, Nawabi courts. - Features: Romantic, devotional evolution. - Hindustani Sangeet: - Context: Medieval synthesis, Tansen (Q10 [Mughal]). - Features: Persian-Indian fusion. - Sufi Baul: - Context: Bengal, 17th century CE onward. - Features: Folk-syncretic, Lalon Fakir. - Cultural Significance: - Ibrahim’s Kitab-i-Nauras and Khusrau’s Qawwali highlight medieval India’s cultural synthesis, bridging religious divides through music, a legacy seen in later Mughal patronage (e.g., Q1 [painting]) and Bhakti-Sufi parallels (e.g., Q42 [Kabir]). - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Kitab-i-Nauras: Manuscripts (17th century CE). - Siyar-ul-Auliya: Khusrau’s Qawwali role (14th century CE). - Archaeology: - Bijapur: Ibrahim’s cultural hub (e.g., Gol Gumbaz). - Traditions: - Chisti dargahs: Qawwali performances (e.g., Ajmer). - Related Figures: - Ibrahim Adil Shah II: - Bijapur ruler (1556-1627 CE); poet-musician. - Amir Khusrau: - Sufi poet (1253-1325 CE); Qawwali pioneer. - Nizamuddin Auliya: - Chisti saint (1238-1325 CE); Khusrau’s mentor. - Broader Connection: - Links to Sufism (e.g., Q15 [Chisti]), Deccan culture (e.g., Q3 [Gol Gumbaz]), or Mughal arts (e.g., Q10 [painting]). - Key Takeaway: - Both statements are correct (c): Ibrahim wrote Kitab-i-Nauras, and Khusrau originated Qawwali in India. - Q62: How did Sultan Qutb-ud-din Aibak die? - Options: (a) He was treacherously stabbed to death by one of his ambitious nobles (b) He was killed in a battle with Taj-ud-din Yildiz, the ruler of Ghazni who entered into a contest with him over the capture of Punjab (c) He sustained injuries while besieging the fortress of Kalinjar in Bundelkhand and succumbed to them later (d) He died after a fall from his horse while playing Chaugan - Answer: (d) He died after a fall from his horse while playing Chaugan - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Qutb-ud-din Aibak (r. 1206-1210 CE), founder of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mamluk dynasty, was a former slave of Muhammad Ghori. His brief reign established Muslim rule in North India after Ghori’s death in 1206 CE, marked by conquests and the initiation of the Qutb Minar (e.g., Q38 [1199 CE]). Historical accounts, such as those in Tabaqat-i-Nasiri by Minhaj-us-Siraj (c. 1260 CE), confirm he suffered fatal injuries from the accident, ending his reign abruptly after four years. His tomb in Lahore stands as evidence of this event. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) He was treacherously stabbed to death by one of his ambitious nobles: - Incorrect—No evidence in primary sources (e.g., Tabaqat-i-Nasiri) suggests assassination by a noble. His death was accidental, not a result of internal betrayal, unlike later Mughal intrigues (e.g., Q60 [Jahandar Shah]). - (b) He was killed in a battle with Taj-ud-din Yildiz, the ruler of Ghazni who entered into a contest with him over the capture of Punjab: - Incorrect—Taj-ud-din Yildiz, Ghori’s successor in Ghazni, contested control with Aibak’s successors (e.g., Iltutmish) after 1210 CE, not during Aibak’s reign. No battle with Yildiz is recorded as his cause of death; Aibak died before such conflicts escalated. - (c) He sustained injuries while besieging the fortress of Kalinjar in Bundelkhand and succumbed to them later: - Incorrect—Aibak captured Kalinjar in 1202 CE under Ghori’s command, before becoming Sultan, and survived that campaign. - Options: (a) Shankaracharya - Ramanuja - Chaitanya (b) Ramanuja - Shankaracharya - Chaitanya (c) Ramanuja - Chaitanya - Shankaracharya (d) Shankaracharya - Chaitanya - Ramanuja - Answer: (a) Shankaracharya - Ramanuja - Chaitanya - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The evolution of Indian philosophical and devotional traditions spans centuries, with key figures like Shankaracharya, Ramanuja, and Chaitanya shaping Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, and Gaudiya Vaishnavism respectively. Their timelines reflect the progression of Vedantic thought and Bhakti movements across medieval India (c. 8th-16th centuries CE), influencing temple culture and theology (e.g., Q42 [Bhakti saints]). - Chronological Evaluation: - Shankaracharya: - Date: c. 788-820 CE (traditional dating). - Details: Born in Kalady, Kerala, Shankaracharya established Advaita Vedanta (non-dualism), emphasizing the unity of Atman and Brahman. His works (e.g., Brahma Sutra Bhashya) and mathas (e.g., Sringeri) mark him as the earliest of the trio, per hagiographies like Shankara Digvijaya. - Ramanuja: - Date: c. 1017-1137 CE. - Details: Born in Tamil Nadu, Ramanuja founded Vishishtadvaita Vedanta (qualified non-dualism), advocating devotion to Vishnu. His Sri Bhashya and leadership of the Sri Vaishnava sect (e.g., Srirangam temple) place him after Shankaracharya, building on prior Vedantic debates. - Chaitanya: - Date: 1486-1533 CE. - Details: Born in Bengal, Chaitanya Mahaprabhu spearheaded Gaudiya Vaishnavism, emphasizing ecstatic Krishna bhakti. His teachings, recorded by disciples (e.g., Chaitanya Charitamrita), reflect a 16th-century Bhakti surge, following Ramanuja’s devotional framework. - Correct Sequence: - Shankaracharya (c. 788-820 CE) → Ramanuja (c. 1017-1137 CE) → Chaitanya (1486-1533 CE). - Matches option (a): Shankaracharya - Ramanuja - Chaitanya. - Why (a) Shankaracharya - Ramanuja - Chaitanya?: - Shankaracharya (8th-9th century CE): Earliest, Advaita pioneer. - Ramanuja (11th-12th century CE): Next, Vishishtadvaita response. - Chaitanya (15th-16th century CE): Latest, Bhakti culmination. - Verification: - (b) Ramanuja - Shankaracharya - Chaitanya: Wrong—Ramanuja (11th century) after Shankaracharya (8th century). - (c) Ramanuja - Chaitanya - Shankaracharya: Wrong—Chaitanya (15th century) after Ramanuja; Shankaracharya earliest. - (d) Shankaracharya - Chaitanya - Ramanuja: Wrong—Chaitanya (15th century) before Ramanuja (11th century). - Figure Details: - Shankaracharya: - Period: c. 788-820 CE. - Contribution: Advaita Vedanta, mathas. - Ramanuja: - Period: c. 1017-1137 CE. - Contribution: Vishishtadvaita, Sri Vaishnavism. - Chaitanya: - Period: 1486-1533 CE. - Contribution: Gaudiya Vaishnavism, Krishna bhakti. - Other Related Bhakti Philosophers: - Madhvacharya: - Date: c. 1238-1317 CE. - Context: Dvaita Vedanta, post-Ramanuja. - Vallabhacharya: - Date: c. 1479-1531 CE. - Context: Shuddhadvaita, Krishna devotion. - Nimbarka: - Date: c. 12th-13th centuries CE (debated). - Context: Dvaitadvaita, earlier Bhakti. - Basavanna: - Date: c. 1105-1167 CE. - Context: Lingayat movement, Shiva devotion. - Jnanesvara: - Date: c. 1275-1296 CE. - Context: Marathi Bhakti, Vitthal focus (Q42 [Namdev]). - Historical Significance: - Shankaracharya’s Advaita, Ramanuja’s Vishishtadvaita, and Chaitanya’s Bhakti represent a theological arc from intellectual monism to devotional fervor, shaping India’s spiritual landscape across centuries (e.g., Q42 [Bhakti professions]). - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Brahma Sutra Bhashya: Shankaracharya (9th century CE). - Sri Bhashya: Ramanuja (12th century CE). - Chaitanya Charitamrita: Chaitanya (16th century CE). - Archaeology: - Sringeri Matha: Shankaracharya’s legacy. - Traditions: - ISKCON: Chaitanya’s modern influence. - Related Figures: - Shankaracharya: - Philosopher (c. 788-820 CE); Advaita founder. - Ramanuja: - Theologian (c. 1017-1137 CE); Vishnu devotee. - Chaitanya: - Saint (1486-1533 CE); Krishna bhakti leader. - Broader Connection: - Links to Bhakti (e.g., Q42 [Namdev]), medieval culture (e.g., Q61 [Qawwali]), or philosophy (e.g., Q130 [Shramana]). - Key Takeaway: - The correct chronological order is (a): Shankaracharya (c. 788-820 CE), Ramanuja (c. 1017-1137 CE), Chaitanya (1486-1533 CE). - Q64: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Narasimha Saluva ended the Sangama dynasty and seized the throne for himself and started the Saluva dynasty 2. Vira Narasimha deposed the last Saluva ruler and seized the throne for himself 3. Vira Narasimha was succeeded by his younger brother, Krishnadeva Raya 4. Krishnadeva Raya was succeeded by his half-brother, Achyuta Raya - Question: Which of the statements given above are correct? - Options: (a) 1, 2, and 3 (b) 2, 3, and 4 (c) 1 and 4 (d) 1, 2, 3, and 4 - Answer: (d) 1, 2, 3, and 4 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Vijayanagara Empire (1336-1646 CE) transitioned through dynasties—Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, and Aravidu—amid internal strife and external threats (e.g., Bahmani Sultanate). The shift from Sangama to Saluva and then to Tuluva marked critical phases of stability and peak power, notably under Krishnadeva Raya (e.g., Q38 [1509-1529 CE]), as documented in inscriptions and traveler accounts (e.g., Fernão Nunes). - Evaluation of Statement 1: - 1. Narasimha Saluva ended the Sangama dynasty and seized the throne for himself and started the Saluva dynasty: - True—Narasimha Saluva (Saluva Narasimha, r. 1485-1491 CE), a military commander, overthrew the last effective Sangama ruler, Praudha Raya (or Virupaksha Raya II), around 1485 CE, ending the Sangama dynasty (1336-1485 CE) and founding the Saluva dynasty. This aligns with Q56 [Saluva’s coup] and Vijayanagara records. - Evaluation of Statement 2: - 2. Vira Narasimha deposed the last Saluva ruler and seized the throne for himself: - True—Vira Narasimha (r. 1505-1509 CE), a Tuluva noble, deposed the last Saluva ruler, Immadi Narasimha (son of Narasimha Saluva, r. 1491-1505 CE), in 1505 CE. As regent initially, he seized power after Immadi’s death (or deposition), initiating the Tuluva dynasty, per Nuniz’s chronicle (c. 1530s CE). - Evaluation of Statement 3: - 3. Vira Narasimha was succeeded by his younger brother, Krishnadeva Raya: - True—Vira Narasimha died in 1509 CE and was succeeded by his younger half-brother, Krishnadeva Raya (r. 1509-1529 CE), who became Vijayanagara’s most celebrated ruler. Their shared father, Narasa Nayaka (a Tuluva general), confirms this succession, as noted in inscriptions (e.g., Q38 [Krishnadeva]). - Evaluation of Statement 4: - 4. Krishnadeva Raya was succeeded by his half-brother, Achyuta Raya: - True—Krishnadeva Raya died in 1529 CE and was succeeded by his half-brother, Achyuta Raya (r. 1529-1542 CE), son of Narasa Nayaka by a different wife. However, formal permission for a permanent factory came later (c. 1620s CE), not precisely in 1613 CE, unlike Surat’s clear establishment. - Factory Details: - Surat Factory: - Date: 1613 CE; Mughal permission. - Location: Surat, Gujarat; west coast port. - Role: First permanent EIC base in India. - Other Related EIC Factories: - Masulipatnam: - Context: Early trade c. 1611 CE; formalized later. - Madras: - Context: Fort St. George, 1639 CE. - Bombay: - Context: Acquired 1668 CE from Portuguese. - Historical Significance: - The Surat factory marked the EIC’s entry into sustained Indian trade, leveraging Mughal favor after defeating Portuguese rivals. His reign saw attempts to address economic challenges, documented by contemporaries like Ibn Battuta (c. 1333-1347 CE) and Ziauddin Barani in Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi (c. 1357 CE). - Evaluation of Assertion (A): - A: "Muhammad bin Tughlaq issued a new gold coin which was called Dinar by Ibn Batutah." - True—Ibn Battuta, in his travelogue Rihla, describes a gold coin issued by Muhammad bin Tughlaq as a “dinar.” This aligns with numismatic evidence of gold tankas or dinars introduced during his reign (c. 1325-1330s CE), distinct from his infamous token copper/bronze currency, as a standard precious metal coinage. - Evaluation of Reason (R): - R: "Muhammad bin Tughlaq wanted to issue token currency in gold coins to promote trade with West Asian and North African countries." - False—Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s token currency experiment (c. 1329-1332 CE) involved copper and bronze coins, not gold, intended to supplement scarce silver and ease internal economic strain, not specifically to boost trade with West Asia or North Africa. His gold dinars were traditional precious metal coins, not tokens (which lack intrinsic value), per Barani and numismatic studies (e.g., John Deyell). Trade promotion was a byproduct, not the primary motive. - Relationship Between A and R: - Correct Option: (c) A is true, but R is false. - Explanation—A is accurate; Muhammad bin Tughlaq issued gold coins called dinars by Ibn Battuta. However, R mischaracterizes these as token currency (they were full-value coins) and incorrectly ties them to a trade-focused motive with specific regions, which lacks historical support. The token currency was a separate, failed copper/bronze initiative. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: - Incorrect—R is false; gold coins weren’t token currency. - (b) Both A and R are true, but R is not a correct explanation of A: - Incorrect—R is false, so this option fails. - (d) A is false, but R is true: - Incorrect—A is true; R is false. - Coinage Details: - Gold Dinar: - Period: c. 1325-1330s CE; precious metal coin. - Name: Called “dinar” by Ibn Battuta; also tanka. - Token Currency: - Period: c. 1329-1332 CE; copper/bronze, not gold. - Purpose: Internal economic relief, not trade. - Other Related Reforms: - Token Copper Coins: - Context: Failed due to counterfeiting. - Silver Tanka: - Context: Pre-existing, continued alongside gold. - Daulatabad Shift: - Context: Separate administrative experiment. - Historical Significance: - Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s gold dinars reflected standard Sultanate coinage, while his token currency experiment (copper/bronze) was a bold but disastrous innovation. Ibn Battuta’s naming highlights foreign perception, but the trade motive in R misaligns with historical intent focused on domestic needs. - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Rihla (Ibn Battuta, c. 1347 CE): Gold dinar mention. - Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi (Barani): Token currency fiasco. - Numismatics: - Gold tankas: Archaeological finds from Tughlaq era. - Related Figures: - Muhammad bin Tughlaq: - Sultan (r. 1325-1351 CE); coin issuer. - Ibn Battuta: - Traveler (c. 1304-1369 CE); observer. - Ziauddin Barani: - Historian (c. 1285-1357 CE); chronicler. - Broader Connection: - Links to Tughlaq reforms (e.g., Q51 [Swarga-Dwari]), economic experiments, or medieval trade (e.g., Q135 [dynasties]). - Key Takeaway: - A is true, but R is false (c), as Muhammad bin Tughlaq issued gold dinars, not as token currency for trade promotion. - Q72: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of the Afghan rulers to the throne of Delhi? - Options: (a) Sikandar Shah - Ibrahim Lodi - Bahlol Khan Lodi (b) Sikandar Shah - Bahlol Khan Lodi - Ibrahim Lodi (c) Bahlol Khan Lodi - Sikandar Shah - Ibrahim Lodi (d) Bahlol Khan Lodi - Ibrahim Lodi - Sikandar Shah - Answer: (c) Bahlol Khan Lodi - Sikandar Shah - Ibrahim Lodi - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Lodi dynasty (1451-1526 CE), an Afghan lineage, was the last ruling family of the Delhi Sultanate before the Mughal conquest. Founded by Bahlol Khan Lodi, it spanned three rulers over 75 years, ending with Babur’s victory at the First Battle of Panipat (1526 CE), as documented in chronicles like Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi (c. 1580 CE) and Mughal records. - Correct Option Explained: - (c) Bahlol Khan Lodi - Sikandar Shah - Ibrahim Lodi: - Correct—The chronological order of Lodi rulers is: - Bahlol Khan Lodi (r. 1451-1489 CE): Founder of the dynasty, seized Delhi from the Sayyids. - Sikandar Shah Lodi (r. 1489-1517 CE): Son of Bahlol, consolidated power, shifted capital to Agra. - Ibrahim Lodi (r. 1517-1526 CE): Son of Sikandar, last ruler, defeated by Babur at Panipat. - This sequence aligns with historical succession, per contemporary sources and inscriptions. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Sikandar Shah - Ibrahim Lodi - Bahlol Khan Lodi: - Incorrect—Reverses the order; Bahlol founded the dynasty, not followed it. - (b) Sikandar Shah - Bahlol Khan Lodi - Ibrahim Lodi: - Incorrect—Places Sikandar before Bahlol, who was the first ruler. - (d) Bahlol Khan Lodi - Ibrahim Lodi - Sikandar Shah: - Incorrect—Swaps Sikandar and Ibrahim; Sikandar preceded Ibrahim. - Ruler Details: - Bahlol Khan Lodi: - Reign: 1451-1489 CE; established Lodi rule. - Sikandar Shah Lodi: - Reign: 1489-1517 CE; strengthened administration. - Ibrahim Lodi: - Reign: 1517-1526 CE; fell to Mughals. - Other Related Figures: - Sayyid Dynasty: - Context: Preceded Lodis (1414-1451 CE). - Sher Shah Suri: - Context: Post-Lodi Afghan ruler (1540-1545 CE). - Babur: - Context: Defeated Ibrahim, 1526 CE. - Historical Significance: - The Lodi dynasty marked the final phase of Afghan rule in the Delhi Sultanate, transitioning from Turkic dominance to Mughal supremacy. Bahlol’s rise, Sikandar’s consolidation, and Ibrahim’s fall encapsulate this era’s political shifts, culminating in Panipat’s decisive battle. - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi (Abbas Sarwani): Lodi reigns. - Baburnama (Babur, c. 1530 CE): Ibrahim’s defeat. - Inscriptions: - Sikandar’s Agra foundation: c. 1504 CE. - Related Figures: - Bahlol Khan Lodi: - Founder (r. 1451-1489 CE); Afghan warlord. - Sikandar Shah Lodi: - Ruler (r. 1489-1517 CE); cultural patron. - Ibrahim Lodi: - Last ruler (r. 1517-1526 CE); Panipat loser. - Broader Connection: - Links to Delhi Sultanate end (e.g., Q46 [Khanua]), Afghan rule (e.g., Q55 [Shah Alam]), or Mughal rise (e.g., Q135 [dynasties]). - Key Takeaway: - The correct chronological order of Afghan Lodi rulers is Bahlol Khan Lodi - Sikandar Shah - Ibrahim Lodi (c), matching historical succession. - Q73: Bhakta Tukaram was a contemporary of which Mughal emperor? - Options: (a) Babur (b) Akbar (c) Jahangir (d) Aurangzeb - Answer: (c) Jahangir - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Bhakta Tukaram, a prominent Marathi saint-poet of the Bhakti movement, flourished in the 17th century CE in Maharashtra, during the decline of the Vijayanagara Empire and the rise of Mughal and Maratha powers. His devotional poetry, part of the Varkari tradition, overlapped with Mughal rule in India (e.g., Q63 [Chaitanya], Q57 [Maratha]). - Correct Option Explained: - (c) Jahangir: - Correct—Tukaram (born c. 1598-1608 CE, died c. 1649-1650 CE) was a contemporary of Jahangir (r. 1605-1627 CE). His active period, particularly his poetic and spiritual contributions in Dehu, Maharashtra, aligns with Jahangir’s reign. While exact dates vary, traditional accounts and scholarly estimates (e.g., G.S. Ghurye, R.D. Ranade) place Tukaram’s life largely within the early 17th century, overlapping Jahangir’s rule until 1627 CE. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Babur: - Incorrect—Babur (r. 1526-1530 CE) died well before Tukaram’s birth (c. 1598-1608 CE). While Shah Jahan isn’t an option, Jahangir’s timeline fits better than Aurangzeb’s later period or Akbar’s earlier one, per historical consensus (e.g., Maharashtra Gazetteers). - Figure Details: - Tukaram: - Period: c. 1598-1650 CE. - Context: Bhakti saint, Varkari poet. - Jahangir: - Period: r. 1605-1627 CE. - Context: Mughal emperor, early 17th century. - Akbar: - Period: r. 1556-1605 CE. - Context: Precedes Tukaram. - Aurangzeb: - Period: r. 1658-1707 CE. - Context: Postdates Tukaram. - Other Related Bhakti Contemporaries: - Eknath: c. 1533-1599 CE, Akbar’s era. - Namdev: c. 1270-1350 CE, pre-Mughal (Q42). - Jnanesvara: c. 1275-1296 CE, pre-Mughal. - Surdas: c. 1478-1583 CE, Akbar’s era. - Chaitanya: c. 1486-1533 CE, Babur’s era (Q63). - Historical Significance: - Tukaram’s overlap with Jahangir’s reign ties Bhakti’s regional growth to Mughal cultural patronage, predating Aurangzeb’s orthodoxy (e.g., Q57 [Mughal decline]). - Related Evidence: - Texts: Tukaram Gatha (17th-century abhangs). - Chronicles: Mughal records (Jahangirnama). - Traditions: Varkari pilgrimage accounts. - Related Figures: - Tukaram: Saint (d. c. 1650 CE). - Jahangir: Emperor (d. 1627 CE). - Shivaji: Maratha leader (b. 1630 CE), post-Tukaram (Q57). - Broader Connection: - Links to Bhakti (Q63), Mughal rule (Q88), Maratha rise (Q57). - Key Takeaway: - Bhakta Tukaram was a contemporary of Jahangir (c). - Answer: (d) Aurangzeb - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Bhakta Tukaram (c. 1608-1649 CE), a prominent Marathi saint-poet of the Bhakti movement, composed devotional abhangs in praise of Lord Vitthal, flourishing in Dehu, Maharashtra. While Tukaram’s active years (1620s-1649 CE) mostly predate Aurangzeb’s reign, his lifetime overlaps with Aurangzeb’s early years as a prince (b. 1618 CE) and governor of the Deccan (1636-1644 CE, 1653-1658 CE).
