His work reflects the Mughal tradition of commissioning official histories, akin to Abul Fazl’s role under Akbar, as preserved in manuscripts and later translations. - Correct Option Explained: - (b) An official historian of the reign of Shahjahan: - Correct—Abdul Hamid Lahori was the official historian of Shah Jahan (r. 1628-1658 CE), authoring the Padshahnama (completed c. 1640s CE), a detailed chronicle of Shah Jahan’s reign up to 1636 CE (later continued by others). Commissioned by the emperor, Lahori’s work covers events like the Deccan campaigns and Taj Mahal construction, per Mughal court records and his own text. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) An important military commander during Akbar’s reign: - Incorrect—Lahori lived in the 17th century (d. 1654 CE), well after Akbar’s reign (1556-1605 CE). He was a scholar, not a military figure, and there’s no evidence linking him to Akbar’s era or command roles. - (c) An important noble and confidant of Aurangzeb: - Incorrect—While Lahori’s lifetime overlapped with Aurangzeb’s early years (b. 1618 CE, r. 1658-1707 CE), he died in 1654 CE before Aurangzeb’s reign began. He served Shah Jahan, not Aurangzeb, and was a historian, not a noble or confidant. - (d) A chronicler and poet during the reign of Muhammad Shah: - Incorrect—Muhammad Shah (r. 1719-1748 CE) ruled decades after Lahori’s death (1654 CE). Lahori’s work predates this period, and while a chronicler, he’s not notably recognized as a poet, focusing instead on prose history under Shah Jahan. - Lahori’s Details: - Role: Official historian. - Period: Active c. 1628-1654 CE; Shah Jahan’s reign. - Work: Padshahnama, volumes I-II (up to 1636 CE). - Other Related Historians: - Abul Fazl: - Context: Akbar’s historian (Akbarnama, d. 1602 CE). - Inayat Khan: - Context: Later Shah Jahan historian (Shahjahannama). - Muhammad Kazim: - Context: Aurangzeb’s historian (Alamgirnama). - Historical Significance: - Lahori’s Padshahnama provides a primary source for Shah Jahan’s reign, detailing military campaigns (e.g., Balkh, 1646-1647 CE) and architectural feats, reflecting Mughal patronage of historiography. His work bridges earlier chroniclers like Abul Fazl and later ones under Aurangzeb. - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Padshahnama (Lahori): Shah Jahan’s reign chronicle. - Manuscripts: - British Library copies: Lahori’s original work. - Accounts: - European travelers (e.g., Bernier, c. 1658-1668 CE): Mughal court context. - Related Figures: - Shah Jahan: - Emperor (r. 1628-1658 CE); Lahori’s patron. - Abdul Hamid Lahori: - Historian (d. 1654 CE); Padshahnama author. - Aurangzeb: - Later emperor (r. 1658-1707 CE); post-Lahori. - Broader Connection: - Links to Mughal historiography (e.g., Q50 [Balkh]), Shah Jahan’s era (e.g., Q66 [Nizam Shahis]), or medieval records (e.g., Q135 [dynasties]). - Key Takeaway: - Abdul Hamid Lahori was an official historian of Shah Jahan’s reign (b), accurately identifying his role and era. - [2007] - Q75: Where is the famous Vijaya Vittala temple having its 56 carved pillars emitting musical notes located? - Options: (a) Belur (b) Bhadrachalam (c) Hampi (d) Srirangam - Answer: (c) Hampi - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Vijaya Vittala Temple, a masterpiece of Vijayanagar architecture, was constructed during the height of the Vijayanagar Empire (c. 1336-1646 CE), particularly under rulers like Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509-1529 CE). Hampi’s ruins, including this temple, draw global attention for their engineering marvels. - Related Evidence: - Inscriptions: - Hampi records: Vittala Temple patronage. - Accounts: - Domingo Paes (c. 1520 CE): Describes Hampi’s grandeur. - Archaeology: - ASI findings: Confirms musical pillars’ acoustics. - Related Figures: - Krishnadevaraya: - King (r. 1509-1529 CE); temple patron. - Harihara I: - Founder (r. 1336-1356 CE); early Vijayanagar. - Devaraya II: - King (r. 1422-1446 CE); architectural era. - Broader Connection: - Links to Vijayanagar history (e.g., Q69 [Wodeyar]), South Indian temples (e.g., Q68 [Angkor Wat parallels]), or medieval art (e.g., Q135 [dynasties]). - Key Takeaway: - The Vijaya Vittala Temple with its 56 musical pillars is located in Hampi (c), distinguishing it from other temple sites. - [2008] - Q76: During the time of which Mughal Emperor did the English East India Company establish its first factory in India? - Options: (a) Akbar (b) Jahangir (c) Shahjahan (d) Aurangzeb - Answer: (b) Jahangir - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The English East India Company (EIC), chartered by Queen Elizabeth I on December 31, 1600 CE (Q26 context), began trading in India during the Mughal Empire (16th-18th centuries CE). (c) Hampi: - Correct—Hampi (Karnataka), the Vijayanagara capital, is the location of the Virupaksha Temple, a UNESCO World Heritage site, active since the 7th century CE and expanded under rulers like Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509-1529 CE). - (d) Srikalahasti: - Incorrect—Srikalahasti (Andhra Pradesh) features the Srikalahasteeswara Temple, dedicated to Shiva, tied to a 5th-century CE legend, but it’s distinct from Virupaksha. - Key Features: - Virupaksha Temple: - Location: Hampi, Karnataka. - Period: 7th century CE, Vijayanagara peak (14th-16th CE). - Style: Dravidian, with gopuram, pillared halls. - Related Figures: - Krishnadevaraya: - Vijayanagara king (r. 1509-1529 CE), temple patron (Q31). - It flourished across regions, with poets and saints using vernacular languages to express bhakti, contrasting with earlier philosophical traditions like Buddhism (Q12 context for Bhakti poetry). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Nagarjuna: - Correct (Not a Bhakti proponent)—Nagarjuna (c. 150-250 CE), a Buddhist philosopher, founded the Madhyamaka school of Mahayana Buddhism, focusing on the concept of "shunyata" (emptiness). Q81: Why did Buddhism start declining in India in the early medieval times? - Statements: 1. Buddha was by that time considered as one of the incarnations of Vishnu and thus became a part of Vaishnavism 2. Invading tribes from Central Asia till the time of the last Gupta king adopted Hinduism and persecuted Buddhists 3. Kings of Gupta dynasty were strongly opposed to Buddhism - Question: Which of the statements given above is/are correct? - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 1 and 3 only (c) 2 and 3 only (d) 1, 2, and 3 - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Buddhism, flourishing in India from the Mauryan era (c. 3rd century BCE) under Ashoka, began declining in the early medieval period (c. 7th-13th centuries CE). This shift coincided with the rise of Hindu devotionalism (Bhakti, Q80 context), Gupta patronage, and later invasions, weakening Buddhist institutions like monasteries (viharas). - Statement Evaluation: - 1. Buddha was by that time considered as one of the incarnations of Vishnu and thus became a part of Vaishnavism: - Correct—By the early medieval period (c. 7th-8th centuries CE), Hindu texts like the Vishnu Purana and Bhagavata Purana listed Buddha as an avatar of Vishnu. This assimilation, evident in Gupta and post-Gupta art (e.g., Buddha icons with Vishnu traits), absorbed Buddhist followers into Vaishnavism, reducing its distinct identity. - 2. Invading tribes from Central Asia till the time of the last Gupta king adopted Hinduism and persecuted Buddhists: - Incorrect—The Gupta dynasty ended c. 550 CE with Vishnugupta, before major Central Asian invasions (e.g., Huns under Mihirakula, c. 5th-6th centuries CE). These invaders disrupted Buddhism (e.g., Nalanda attacks), but their adoption of Hinduism and systematic persecution of Buddhists occurred later (e.g., Turkic invasions, 12th-13th centuries CE), not "till the last Gupta king." - 3. Kings of Gupta dynasty were strongly opposed to Buddhism: - Incorrect—Gupta kings (c. 4th-6th centuries CE), like Chandragupta II and Kumaragupta I, were Hindu patrons but not strongly opposed to Buddhism. They supported Buddhist centers (e.g., Nalanda, funded by Kumaragupta I), showing tolerance, though their preference for Hinduism (e.g., Vaishnava temples) indirectly weakened Buddhist prominence. - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1 only: - Correct—Statement 1 is true (Buddha’s assimilation into Vaishnavism); 2 and 3 are false due to timeline errors and Gupta tolerance. - (b) 1 and 3 only: - Incorrect—1 is true, but 3 is false; Guptas weren’t strongly anti-Buddhist. - (c) 2 and 3 only: - Incorrect—Both 2 (invasion timeline) and 3 (Gupta opposition) are false. - (d) 1, 2, and 3: - Incorrect—Only 1 is true; 2 and 3 misalign with historical evidence. - Key Features: - Buddhist Decline: - Period: Early medieval (c. 7th-13th centuries CE). - Cause: Assimilation into Hinduism, loss of patronage. - Contrast: Gupta era (4th-6th centuries CE) coexistence. - Related Figures: - Kumaragupta I: - Gupta king (r. 415-455 CE), Nalanda patron. - Ashoka: - Mauryan emperor (r. 268-232 BCE), early Buddhist peak. - Harsha: - King (r. 606-647 CE), late Buddhist supporter. - Shankaracharya: - Philosopher (c. 8th century CE), Advaita rival to Buddhism. - Mihirakula: - Hun invader (fl. 6th century CE), early disruptor. - Other Notable Factors in the Decline of Buddhism in India: - Rise of Bhakti Movement: - c. 7th century CE onward, devotional shift (Q80). - Loss of Royal Patronage: - Post-Harsha (7th century CE), Hindu kings dominated. - Islamic Invasions: - c. 12th-13th centuries CE, sacked Nalanda, Bodh Gaya. - Monastic Isolation: - Viharas detached from lay society, weakened support. - Philosophical Challenges: - Advaita Vedanta (Shankara) outdebated Buddhist schools. - Broader Connection: - Links to Bhakti (Q80 [Tukaram]), southern kingdoms (Q31 [Cholas]), or medieval shifts (Q32 [Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq]). - Key Takeaway: - Only statement 1 (Buddha as Vishnu avatar) is correct for Buddhism’s decline, making (a) the answer. - [2012-I] - Q82: With reference to Dhrupad, one of the major traditions of India that has been kept alive for centuries, which of the following statements are correct? - Statements: 1. Dhrupad originated and developed in the Rajput kingdoms during the Mughal period 2. Dhrupad is primarily a devotional and spiritual music 3. Dhrupad Alap uses Sanskrit syllables from Mantras - Question: Select the correct answer using the codes given below: - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1, 2, and 3 (d) None of the above is correct - Answer: (b) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Dhrupad, one of India’s oldest classical music forms, traces its roots to ancient Vedic chants and evolved through medieval times. It flourished under royal patronage, particularly during the Mughal period (16th-19th centuries CE), but its origins predate this era, tied to temple traditions and later courtly refinement (Q10 context for Mughal arts). - Statement Evaluation: - 1. Dhrupad originated and developed in the Rajput kingdoms during the Mughal period: - Incorrect—Dhrupad’s origins are older, linked to the Samaveda (c. 1500 BCE) and medieval temple music (c. 13th-14th centuries CE). It was refined, not originated, during the Mughal period under figures like Raja Man Singh Tomar of Gwalior (r. 1486-1516 CE), a pre-Mughal Rajput king, and later Mughal courts (e.g., Akbar’s era). Rajput kingdoms contributed, but it didn’t originate there during Mughal times. - 2. Dhrupad is primarily a devotional and spiritual music: - Correct—Dhrupad’s essence is devotional, rooted in spiritual themes (e.g., praise of deities like Krishna, Shiva). Its slow, meditative structure, focusing on raga purity, reflects a spiritual intent, even when performed in courts, as noted in texts like Sangit Ratnakar (13th century CE). - 3. Dhrupad Alap uses Sanskrit syllables from Mantras: - Correct—In the Alap (introductory section), Dhrupad employs Sanskrit syllables like "re," "na," "ta," derived from Vedic mantras (e.g., "Om Anant Hari"), sung in a free-rhythm style to elaborate the raga, a practice preserved by traditions like the Dagar bani. - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1 and 2 only: - Incorrect—2 is true (devotional nature), but 1 is false (origin misattribution); excludes 3, which is true. - (b) 2 and 3 only: - Correct—2 (devotional music) and 3 (Sanskrit syllables) are accurate; 1 is incorrect. - (c) 1, 2, and 3: - Incorrect—1 is false (didn’t originate in Mughal-era Rajput kingdoms); 2 and 3 are true. - (d) None of the above is correct: - Incorrect—2 and 3 are correct, so this option doesn’t apply. - Key Features: - Dhrupad: - Structure: Alap, Jor, Jhala, Dhrupad composition. - Roots: Vedic chants, temple music. - Peak: Medieval courts (Gwalior, Mughal era). - Related Figures: - Raja Man Singh Tomar: - King (r. 1486-1516 CE), Gwalior, Dhrupad patron. - Tansen: - Musician (c. 1500-1586 CE), Akbar’s court, Dhrupad exponent. - Swami Haridas: - Saint (c. 15th-16th centuries CE), influenced Tansen. - Nayak Baiju: - Musician (c. 14th century CE), early Dhrupad figure. - Akbar: - Emperor (r. 1556-1605 CE), supported Dhrupad (Q30). - Other Notable Classical Music Traditions of India: - Khayal: - c. 14th-15th centuries CE, Amir Khusrau influence, flexible style. - Thumri: - c. 19th century CE, romantic, North Indian courts. - Carnatic Music: - South Indian, Tyagaraja (Q80), systematic ragas. - Qawwali: - Sufi devotional, Amir Khusrau (Q28), 13th century CE. - Tarana: - Fast-paced, rhythmic syllables, Mughal courts. - Broader Connection: - Links to Mughal arts (Q10 [painting]), Bhakti (Q80 [Tyagaraja]), or medieval culture (Q33 [Jama Masjid]). - Key Takeaway: - Statements 2 (devotional music) and 3 (Sanskrit syllables) are correct about Dhrupad, not 1, making (b) the answer. - Q83: With reference to the religious history of medieval India, the Sufi mystics were known to pursue which of the following practices? - Statements: 1. Meditation and control of breath 2. Severe ascetic exercises in a lonely place 3. Recitation of holy songs to arouse a state of ecstasy in their audience - Question: Select the correct answer using the codes given below: - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2, and 3 - Answer: (d) 1, 2, and 3 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Sufism, a mystical branch of Islam, arrived in India around the 12th-13th centuries CE with saints from Central Asia and Persia, flourishing under the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal Empire. Sufi mystics (e.g., Chishtis, Suhrawardis) blended Islamic spirituality with local traditions, using diverse practices to connect with the divine, as seen in hagiographies like Fawaid-ul-Fuad (Q8 context). - Statement Evaluation: - 1. Meditation and control of breath: - Correct—Sufis practiced "zikr" (remembrance of God), often involving rhythmic breathing and meditation to focus the mind and soul. Techniques like "pas-e-anfas" (breath control) were used by orders like the Chishtis to achieve spiritual concentration, noted in Sufi texts. - 2. Severe ascetic exercises in a lonely place: - Correct—Some Sufis, particularly from the Qalandar and early Chishti orders, engaged in "chilla" (40-day retreats) in isolation, involving fasting and severe austerities to detach from worldly desires, a practice linked to figures like Baba Farid in remote settings. - 3. Recitation of holy songs to arouse a state of ecstasy in their audience: - Correct—Sufis, especially Chishtis, used "sama" (musical assemblies) with qawwalis—holy songs composed by poets like Amir Khusrau (Q28)—to induce "wajd" (ecstasy) in listeners, fostering spiritual union, as documented in medieval accounts. - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1 and 2 only: - Incorrect—1 (meditation) and 2 (asceticism) are true, but excludes 3 (sama), a well-known Sufi practice. - (b) 2 and 3 only: - Incorrect—2 (asceticism) and 3 (songs) are correct, but omits 1 (meditation/breath control), a core Sufi method. - (c) 3 only: - Incorrect—3 (holy songs) is true, but ignores 1 and 2, both integral to Sufi mysticism. - (d) 1, 2, and 3: - Correct—All three (meditation, asceticism, ecstatic songs) reflect Sufi practices in medieval India. - Answer: (c) The hall in which Akbar held discussions with scholars of various religions - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Fatehpur Sikri, built by Akbar (r. 1556-1605 CE) between 1571-1585 CE (Q25 context), was the Mughal capital reflecting his vision of religious tolerance. The Ibadat Khana (House of Worship), established in 1575 CE, was a key site for Akbar’s interfaith dialogues, documented in the Akbarnama by Abul Fazl (Q30 context). - Why Not Others?: - (a) The mosque for the use of Royal Family: - Incorrect—Fatehpur Sikri has a separate Jama Masjid for prayer, not the Ibadat Khana. The latter was not a mosque but a discussion hall, distinct from royal worship spaces. - (b) Akbar’s private prayer chamber: - Incorrect—The Ibadat Khana was a public venue, not a private chamber. Akbar’s personal prayers occurred elsewhere (e.g., his quarters), while this hall hosted scholars, as per historical records like Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh (Q32). - (c) The hall in which Akbar held discussions with scholars of various religions: - Correct—Initiated in 1575 CE, the Ibadat Khana was where Akbar debated with Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian, and Christian scholars (e.g., Jesuits like Rodolfo Acquaviva), shaping his syncretic policies, including the Din-i-Ilahi (Q13 context). - (d) The room in which the nobles belonging to different religions gathered to discuss religious affairs: - Incorrect—While nobles attended, the Ibadat Khana was specifically for scholars and religious leaders, not a general noble assembly. Akbar directed discussions, not delegating them to nobles. - Key Features: - Ibadat Khana: - Purpose: Interfaith dialogues. - Founded: 1575 CE, Fatehpur Sikri. - Outcome: Influenced Akbar’s Sulh-i-Kul (universal tolerance). - Related Figures: - Akbar: - Emperor (r. 1556-1605 CE), Ibadat Khana initiator. - Abul Fazl: - Historian (1551-1602 CE), chronicled discussions (Q30). - Badauni: - Historian (1540-1615 CE), criticized Akbar’s debates (Q32). - Birbal: - Advisor (1528-1586 CE), participated in talks. - Rodolfo Acquaviva: - Jesuit (1550-1583 CE), Christian delegate. - Other Notable Structures at Fatehpur Sikri: - Jama Masjid: - c. 1571 CE, grand mosque with Buland Darwaza. - Panch Mahal: - Five-tiered pavilion, architectural marvel. - Diwan-i-Khas: - Hall for private audiences, central pillar design. - Anup Talao: - Ornamental pool, Tansen’s performance site. - Hujra-i-Anup: - Small chamber, intricate carvings. - Broader Connection: - Links to Fatehpur Sikri (Q25), Mughal culture (Q10 [painting]), or Akbar’s policies (Q30 [Mansabdari]). - Key Takeaway: - The Ibadat Khana was the hall for Akbar’s discussions with scholars of various religions (c), not a mosque, prayer chamber, or noble meeting room. - Q86: In medieval India, the designations ‘Mahattara’ and ‘Pattakila’ were used for: - Options: (a) Military officers (b) Village headmen (c) Specialists in Vedic rituals (d) Chiefs of craft guilds - Answer: (b) Village headmen - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Medieval India (c. 6th-13th centuries CE, pre-Mughal) featured a decentralized agrarian society under dynasties like the Guptas, Cholas, and Rashtrakutas. Village administration relied on local leaders, often documented in inscriptions (e.g., Chola copper plates), managing land, taxes, and community affairs, distinct from military or ritual roles (e.g., Q35 [Jagirdari contrasts]). - Correct Option Explained: - (b) Village headmen: - Correct—In medieval India, ‘Mahattara’ (or Mahattaka) and ‘Pattakila’ referred to village headmen or elders. ‘Mahattara,’ derived from Sanskrit “mahattama” (great one), denoted a senior village official, often overseeing multiple villages, while ‘Pattakila’ (or Pattakil in South India) meant the head of a single village or settlement. These terms appear in inscriptions (e.g., Chalukya records, 7th-12th centuries CE) and denote local governance roles responsible for revenue collection, dispute resolution, and village administration. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Military officers: - Incorrect—Military officers had designations like ‘Senapati’ (army commander) or ‘Dandanayaka’ (general), not ‘Mahattara’ or ‘Pattakila.’ These terms lack martial connotations in historical records (e.g., Q14 [Mir Bakshi]). - (c) Specialists in Vedic rituals: - Incorrect—Vedic ritual specialists were called ‘Brahmins,’ ‘Purohitas,’ or ‘Hotris,’ not ‘Mahattara’ or ‘Pattakila.’ These roles were secular, not priestly, per texts like the Manusmriti (e.g., Q137 [Varna]). - (d) Chiefs of craft guilds: - Incorrect—Craft guild leaders were termed ‘Sreni-pramukh’ or ‘Jetthaka’ in medieval texts (e.g., Jataka tales, Gupta era). ‘Mahattara’ and ‘Pattakila’ are tied to village governance, not urban guilds (e.g., Q125 [Hundi]). - Term Details: - Mahattara: - Meaning: Senior village elder/official. - Context: North and Central India, 6th-13th centuries CE. - Pattakila: - Meaning: Village headman (often South Indian usage). - Context: Regional term, e.g., Chola administration. - Other Related Medieval Administrative Roles: - Gramani: - Context: Vedic-early medieval village head. - Features: Predecessor to Mahattara. - Vishayapati: - Context: Gupta era, district overseer. - Features: Above village level (Q135 [post-Gupta]). - Nadu Nadu: - Context: Chola, regional head. - Features: Supervised Pattakilas. - Deshmukh: - Context: Later medieval Deccan. - Features: Regional revenue officer (Q36 [Maratha]). - Muqaddam: - Context: Sultanate era village head. - Features: Post-Tughlaq evolution (Q65). - Historical Significance: - ‘Mahattara’ and ‘Pattakila’ reflect medieval India’s village-centric governance, ensuring local autonomy under feudal systems, a foundation later adapted by Sultanate and Mughal rulers (e.g., Q39 [Iqta, Jagir]). - Related Evidence: - Inscriptions: - Chalukya grants: Mahattara roles (7th-12th centuries CE). - Chola plates: Pattakila mentions (10th century CE). - Texts: - Arthashastra: Village officials (c. 300 BCE, influence). - Archaeology: - Village sites: Administrative traces (e.g., Tamil Nadu). - Related Figures: - Local Headmen: - Role: Mahattara/Pattakila, medieval period. - Chola Kings: - Context: Rajaraja I (r. 985-1014 CE); system patrons. - Gupta Rulers: - Context: Samudragupta (r. 335-375 CE); early framework. - Broader Connection: - Links to administration (e.g., Q35 [Jagirdari]), medieval society (e.g., Q137 [Varna]), or land tenure (e.g., Q39 [Amaram]). - Key Takeaway: - ‘Mahattara’ and ‘Pattakila’ were designations for village headmen (b) in medieval India. - [2015-I] - Q87: Consider the following pairs: - Pairs: 1. Champaka - Central India 2. Durgara - Jammu 3. Kuluta - Malabar - Question: Which of the above pairs is/are correctly matched? - Options: (a) 1 and 2 (b) 2 only (c) 1 and 3 (d) 1 and 3 only - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Medieval India (c. 6th-13th centuries CE) featured numerous small kingdoms, often hill states, documented in texts like the Rajatarangini and inscriptions. Geographical precision is key, as names can be confused or debated across regions (e.g., Q89 [Harihara], Q65 [Tughlaq]). - Evaluation of Pair 1: - 1. Champaka - Central India: - Incorrect (Revised)—Initially deemed correct, linking ‘Champaka’ to Central India (e.g., Malwa or Chhattisgarh) via Champakanagara or Champa references in Puranas. However, ‘Champaka’ is more accurately tied to Chamba, a hill state in modern Himachal Pradesh (North India), not Central India. Medieval sources (e.g., Rajatarangini, Chamba inscriptions) place it in the Himalayan region, not the central plains (e.g., Madhya Pradesh). This misalignment suggests Pair 1 is incorrect, per stricter regional definitions favored by sources. - Evaluation of Pair 2: - 2. Durgara - Jammu: - Correct—Durgara (or Trigarta) is consistently identified with the Jammu region in modern Jammu and Kashmir. The Rajatarangini (c. 1148 CE, Kalhana) and epigraphic evidence (e.g., 11th-century Chamba plates) confirm Durgara as a hill kingdom near Kashmir, ruled by Rajput clans, aligning precisely with Jammu (e.g., Q40 [Zain-ul-Abidin]). - Evaluation of Pair 3: - 3. Kuluta - Malabar: - Incorrect—Kuluta corresponds to the Kulu Valley in Himachal Pradesh, a Himalayan region, not Malabar on Kerala’s southwestern coast. Known from the Mahabharata and Gupta-era inscriptions, Kuluta was a northern kingdom, distinct from Malabar’s Chera or Zamorin domains (e.g., Q44 [Calicut]). This mismatch is clear. - Why (b) 2 only?: - Pair 1: False—Champaka is Chamba (Himachal Pradesh), not Central India. - Pair 2: True—Durgara matches Jammu. - Pair 3: False—Kuluta is Kulu (Himachal Pradesh), not Malabar. - Verification: - (a) 1 and 2: Wrong—1 is incorrect. - (c) 1 and 3: Wrong—Both 1 and 3 are incorrect. - (d) 1 and 3 only: Wrong—Same as (c). - Reassessment Rationale: - Initial error stemmed from a broader interpretation of ‘Champaka’ as Central India (e.g., Malwa), plausible in some medieval contexts. However, consensus sources (e.g., UPSC materials, testbook.com) favor Champaka as Chamba (North), aligning with hill states like Durgara and Kuluta. Only Durgara-Jammu holds as unequivocally correct, supporting (b). - Region Details: - Champaka: - Actual: Chamba, Himachal Pradesh (North). - Period: Medieval hill state. - Durgara: - Actual: Jammu, Jammu and Kashmir. - Period: Pre-13th century CE. - Kuluta: - Actual: Kulu Valley, Himachal Pradesh. - Period: Himalayan kingdom. - Other Related Medieval Regional Kingdoms: - Trigarta: Kangra, near Durgara. - Kumaon: Uttarakhand, hill state. - Garhwal: Uttarakhand, near Kuluta. - Chera: Malabar, South India (Q44). - Historical Significance: - Durgara’s correct match reflects medieval hill states’ distinct identities, while Champaka and Kuluta’s Himalayan ties clarify their northern context, not Central or Southern India (e.g., Q92 [Ajanta]). - Related Evidence: - Texts: Rajatarangini (Durgara, Champaka mentions). - Inscriptions: Chamba plates (Champaka as North). - Archaeology: Kulu Valley sites (Kuluta). - Related Figures: - Kalhana: Chronicler (c. 1148 CE). - Rajput Clans: Rulers of Durgara, Champaka. - Broader Connection: - Links to medieval geography (Q44), dynasties (Q65), culture (Q95). - Key Takeaway: - Only Durgara-Jammu (2) is correctly matched, making (b) correct. - Q88: Consider the following: - The arrival of Babur into India led to which of the above? - Statements: 1. Introduction of gunpowder in the subcontinent 2. Introduction of the arch and dome in the region’s architecture 3. Establishment of Timurid dynasty in the region - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2, and 3 - Answer: (b) 3 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Babur’s arrival in India (1526 CE) via the First Battle of Panipat marked the Mughal Empire’s inception, building on existing Sultanate traditions while introducing his Timurid lineage. The period saw technological and cultural shifts, but their attribution to Babur requires scrutiny (e.g., Q46 [Khanua], Q65 [Tughlaq]). - Evaluation of Statement 1: - 1. Introduction of gunpowder in the subcontinent: - Incorrect (Revised)—Previously considered true due to Babur’s effective use of gunpowder artillery and matchlocks at Panipat (1526 CE), as per the Baburnama. Babur enhanced its military application (e.g., tulughma tactics), but didn’t introduce it, per sources like Iqtidar Alam Khan’s studies. - Evaluation of Statement 2: - 2. Introduction of the arch and dome in the region’s architecture: - Incorrect—Arches and domes were introduced during the Delhi Sultanate, centuries before Babur (e.g., Qutb Minar, 1199 CE; Alai Darwaza, 1311 CE, Q38). Babur’s successors (e.g., Akbar) refined Mughal architecture with Persian influences, but he didn’t initiate this feature in 1526 CE. - Evaluation of Statement 3: - 3. Establishment of Timurid dynasty in the region: - Correct—Babur, a Timurid descendant of Timur, established the Timurid dynasty in India (Mughal Empire) with his victory at Panipat (1526 CE). This lineage, distinct from prior Lodi rulers, persisted until 1857 CE, a direct result of his arrival (e.g., Q46 [Babur’s victories]). - Why (b) 3 only?: - Statement 1: False—Gunpowder existed pre-Babur; he popularized its advanced use, not its introduction. - Statement 2: False—Arch and dome architecture predates Babur by centuries. - Statement 3: True—Timurid dynasty began with Babur’s arrival. - Verification: - (a) 1 and 2 only: Wrong—Both 1 and 2 are incorrect. - (c) 1 and 3 only: Wrong—1 is incorrect. - (d) 1, 2, and 3: Wrong—1 and 2 are incorrect. - Reassessment Rationale: - Initial choice of (c) overestimated Babur’s role in gunpowder’s introduction, conflating innovation with origin. Sources (e.g., UPSC materials, testbook.com) emphasize pre-existing gunpowder (Sultanate, Vijayanagara), leaving the Timurid dynasty as Babur’s sole unique contribution, aligning with (b). - Impact Details: - Gunpowder: - Pre-Babur: Sultanate cannons (14th century CE). - Babur: Enhanced use (1526 CE). - Arch and Dome: - Pre-Babur: Sultanate architecture (12th-13th centuries CE). - Timurid Dynasty: - Babur: Established 1526 CE. - Other Related Impacts: - Artillery Tactics: Babur’s innovation (Q46). - Persian Culture: Later Mughal influence (Q61). - Centralization: Mughal governance (Q49). - Historical Significance: - Babur’s Timurid legacy (3) defines his arrival’s lasting impact, unlike gunpowder or architecture, which evolved earlier (e.g., Q57 [Mughal decline]). - Related Evidence: - Texts: Baburnama (gunpowder tactics, not origin). - Archaeology: Qutb complex (pre-Babur domes). - Chronicles: Tabaqat-i-Nasiri (Sultanate gunpowder). - Related Figures: - Babur: Founder (d. 1530 CE). - Alauddin Khalji: Early gunpowder user (d. 1316 CE). - Ibrahim Lodi: Defeated foe (d. 1526 CE). - Broader Connection: - Ties to Mughal origins (Q46), architecture (Q38), warfare (Q94). - Key Takeaway: - Babur’s arrival led only to the Timurid dynasty (b), not gunpowder or architectural introductions. - Q89: Who of the following founded a new city on the south bank of a tributary to river Krishna and undertook to rule his new kingdom as the agent of a deity to whom all the land south of the river Krishna was supposed to belong? - Options: (a) Amoghavarsha I (b) Ballala II (c) Harihara I (d) Prataparudra II - Answer: (c) Harihara I - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Medieval South India (c. 9th-14th centuries CE) saw the rise of powerful dynasties like the Rashtrakutas, Hoysalas, Vijayanagara, and Kakatiyas, often centered around the Krishna River basin. The founding of cities and divine kingship were common, with rulers acting as agents of deities (e.g., Vishnu, Shiva) to legitimize their rule, a practice reflected in inscriptions and chronicles (e.g., Q64 [Vijayanagara]). - Correct Option Explained: - (c) Harihara I: - Correct—Harihara I (r. 1336-1356 CE), co-founder of the Vijayanagara Empire with his brother Bukka I, established the city of Vijayanagara (modern Hampi) on the south bank of the Tungabhadra River, a major tributary of the Krishna. He ruled as an agent of Lord Virupaksha (a form of Shiva), to whom the land south of the Krishna was dedicated, as per Vijayanagara tradition and inscriptions (e.g., 1336 CE Hampi records). This aligns with the empire’s origin story against Muslim incursions (e.g., Q56 [Saluva]). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Amoghavarsha I: - Incorrect—Amoghavarsha I (r. 814-878 CE), a Rashtrakuta ruler, developed Manyakheta (modern Malkhed, north of Krishna) as his capital, not a new city south of a Krishna tributary. He was a Jain patron, not tied to a deity claiming land south of the Krishna (e.g., Rashtrakuta inscriptions). - (b) Ballala II: - Incorrect—Ballala II (r. 1173-1220 CE), a Hoysala king, ruled from Halebidu (Dwarasamudra), south of the Krishna but not on a tributary’s south bank. He expanded Hoysala power but lacked the specific city-founding or divine-agent narrative tied to the Krishna (e.g., Hoysala records). - (d) Prataparudra II: - Incorrect—Prataparudra II (r. 1289-1323 CE), last Kakatiya ruler, reigned from Warangal (north of Krishna). He defended against Delhi Sultanate attacks (e.g., Q65 [Tughlaq]), not founding a new city south of a tributary or ruling as a deity’s agent for that region. - Ruler Details: - Harihara I: - Period: r. 1336-1356 CE. - Context: Vijayanagara founder, Tungabhadra, Virupaksha agent. - Amoghavarsha I: - Period: r. 814-878 CE. - Context: Rashtrakuta, Manyakheta, Jain focus. - Ballala II: - Period: r. 1173-1220 CE. - Context: Hoysala, Halebidu, expansion. - Prataparudra II: - Period: r. 1289-1323 CE. - Context: Kakatiya, Warangal, Sultanate foe. - Other Related Medieval South Indian Rulers: - Bukka I: - Date: r. 1356-1377 CE. - Context: Harihara’s brother, Vijayanagara co-founder. - Rajaraja Chola I: - Date: r. 985-1014 CE. - Context: Chola, Thanjavur, south of Krishna (Q86). - Pulakeshin II: - Date: r. 610-642 CE. - Context: Chalukya, Badami, pre-Vijayanagara. - Krishna Deva Raya: - Date: r. 1509-1529 CE (Q64). - Context: Vijayanagara peak, Harihara’s legacy. - Narasa Nayaka: - Date: d. 1505 CE (Q64). - Context: Tuluva transition, Vijayanagara. - Historical Significance: - Harihara I’s founding of Vijayanagara on the Tungabhadra, as Virupaksha’s agent, established a Hindu bulwark south of the Krishna, resisting northern invasions and shaping Deccan history (e.g., Q38 [Krishnadeva]). - Related Evidence: - Inscriptions: - Hampi records: Harihara’s Virupaksha link (1336 CE). - Texts: - Vidyaranya’s role: Spiritual guide (14th century CE). - Archaeology: - Vijayanagara ruins: Hampi, south bank site. - Related Figures: - Harihara I: - Founder (d. 1356 CE); Vijayanagara initiator. - Bukka I: - Co-founder (d. 1377 CE); Harihara’s ally. - Vidyaranya: - Sage (14th century CE); Vijayanagara mentor. - Broader Connection: - Links to Vijayanagara (e.g., Q64 [Saluva]), medieval South (e.g., Q86 [Pattakila]), or dynasties (e.g., Q65 [Tughlaq]). - Key Takeaway: - Harihara I (c) founded Vijayanagara on the Tungabhadra’s south bank, ruling as Virupaksha’s agent. - [2016-I] - Q90: Banjaras during the medieval period of Indian history were generally: - Options: (a) Agriculturists (b) Warriors (c) Weavers (d) Traders - Answer: (d) Traders - Analysis: - Historical Context: - During medieval India (c. 13th-18th centuries CE), spanning the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal periods, diverse social groups thrived, including nomadic communities like the Banjaras. Known as itinerant traders and transporters, they played a vital role in the economy, moving goods across regions under rulers like the Tughlaqs, Mughals, and Marathas (e.g., Q65 [Tughlaq], Q57 [Maratha]). - Correct Option Explained: - (d) Traders: - Correct—Banjaras (also called Lambanis or Lambadas) were generally traders and carriers during the medieval period. Originating as nomadic groups in North India (e.g., Rajasthan, Gujarat), they transported goods like grain, salt, and textiles using pack animals (e.g., bullocks), serving armies, merchants, and markets. Their role is noted in Mughal records (e.g., Ain-i-Akbari, 1590 CE) and British accounts (e.g., 18th-century trade logs), emphasizing their trading identity (e.g., Q44 [Surat]). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Agriculturists: - Incorrect—Banjaras were not primarily agriculturists. Unlike settled peasant communities (e.g., Q86 [Mahattara]), they were mobile, relying on trade rather than farming, though some later settled as cultivators under colonial pressures (post-18th century CE). - (b) Warriors: - Incorrect—Banjaras were not generally warriors. While they occasionally aided armies (e.g., Maratha campaigns, Q57), their primary role was logistical support as traders, not combat, unlike Rajputs or Maratha soldiers (e.g., Q14 [Mir Bakshi]). - (c) Weavers: - Incorrect—Weavers were distinct artisan groups (e.g., Julahas, Q42 [Kabir]), not Banjaras. Banjaras transported textiles but did not typically produce them, per medieval economic records (e.g., Q125 [Hundi]). - Group Details: - Banjaras: - Period: Medieval India (13th-18th centuries CE). - Role: Nomadic traders, transporters. - Features: Pack animal caravans, market links. - Other Related Medieval Social Groups: - Bhats: - Role: Bards, genealogists. - Context: Recorded Rajput histories (e.g., Q63). - Jats: - Role: Agriculturists, later warriors. - Context: North India, Mughal era (Q57). - Kaikadis: - Role: Nomadic artisans, thieves. - Context: Deccan, medieval fringe groups. - Gujjars: - Role: Pastoralists, traders. - Context: North-West India, mobile like Banjaras. - Pindaris: - Role: Irregular cavalry, plunderers. - Context: 18th-century Maratha allies (Q36). - Historical Significance: - Banjaras’ trading networks sustained medieval India’s economy, linking rural producers to urban centers and military campaigns, a role that persisted into the Mughal and Maratha periods before colonial disruption (e.g., Q44 [Babul Makka]). - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Ain-i-Akbari: Banjara trade role (1590 CE). - Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri: Caravan mentions (17th century CE). - Records: - British logs: Banjara grain transport (18th century CE). - Archaeology: - Trade routes: Banjara camp traces (e.g., Deccan). - Related Figures: - Akbar: - Emperor (r. 1556-1605 CE); trade patron (Q44). - Shivaji: - Maratha leader (r. 1674-1680 CE); Banjara allies (Q57). - Banjara Chiefs: - Leaders: Local tanda (group) heads, unnamed in texts. - Broader Connection: - Links to trade (e.g., Q44 [Surat]), medieval society (e.g., Q86 [Pattakila]), or military logistics (e.g., Q88 [gunpowder]). - Key Takeaway: - Banjaras were generally traders (d) in medieval India, not agriculturists, warriors, or weavers. - Q91: Who of the following had first deciphered the edicts of Emperor Ashoka? - Options: (a) Georg Buehler (b) James Prinsep (c) Max Muller (d) William Jones - Answer: (b) James Prinsep - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Emperor Ashoka’s edicts (c. 3rd century BCE), inscribed in Brahmi script across India, remained undeciphered until the 19th century CE, when British scholars in colonial India unlocked their meaning. These inscriptions, reflecting Ashoka’s Dhamma (e.g., Q138 [Ashokan pillars]), were pivotal in understanding Mauryan history, aided by the East India Company’s antiquarian efforts (e.g., Q130 [Shramana]). - Correct Option Explained: - (b) James Prinsep: - Correct—James Prinsep (1799-1840 CE), an English scholar and Assay Master at the Calcutta Mint, first deciphered Ashoka’s edicts in 1837 CE. Analyzing the Brahmi script from sites like the Delhi-Topra pillar (Firoz Shah’s relocation, Q38), he linked it to Pali and identified “Piyadasi” as Ashoka, using bilingual rock edicts (e.g., Shahbazgarhi). His work, published in the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, revolutionized Indian epigraphy. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Georg Buehler: - Incorrect—Georg Buehler (1837-1898 CE), a German Indologist, contributed to Sanskrit studies and epigraphy (e.g., Gupta inscriptions) later in the 19th century CE. He built on Prinsep’s work but was not the first to decipher Ashoka’s edicts. - (c) Max Muller: - Incorrect—Max Muller (1823-1900 CE), a German philologist, focused on Vedic texts and Sanskrit literature (e.g., Rigveda translations), not epigraphy. His work postdates Prinsep’s breakthrough and didn’t involve Ashokan edicts directly. - (d) William Jones: - Incorrect—William Jones (1746-1794 CE), founder of the Asiatic Society (1784 CE), pioneered Indo-European linguistics and Sanskrit studies (e.g., Q137 [Varna]). He died before the edicts were deciphered, lacking access to Brahmi’s key. - Scholar Details: - James Prinsep: - Period: 1799-1840 CE. - Contribution: Deciphered Brahmi, Ashoka’s edicts (1837 CE). - Georg Buehler: - Period: 1837-1898 CE. - Contribution: Later epigraphy, Sanskrit texts. - Max Muller: - Period: 1823-1900 CE. - Contribution: Vedic studies, not edicts. - William Jones: - Period: 1746-1794 CE. - Contribution: Early Indology, pre-Brahmi. - Other Related Scholars of Indian Antiquity: - Alexander Cunningham: - Role: Archaeologist (1814-1893 CE). - Context: Founded ASI, excavated Ashokan sites. - Henry Thomas Colebrooke: - Role: Sanskritist (1765-1837 CE). - Context: Pre-Prinsep, textual studies. - John Marshall: - Role: Archaeologist (1876-1958 CE). - Context: Later Indus Valley work (Q132). - Bhagwanlal Indraji: - Role: Epigraphist (1839-1888 CE). - Context: Post-Prinsep, Gupta inscriptions. - Charles Wilkins: - Role: Orientalist (1749-1836 CE). - Context: Early Sanskrit, pre-edict decipherment. - Historical Significance: - Prinsep’s decipherment of Ashoka’s edicts unveiled Mauryan governance and Buddhist principles, reshaping historical understanding of ancient India, a legacy built upon by later scholars (e.g., Q138 [Ashokan]). - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Journal of the Asiatic Society (1837 CE): Prinsep’s findings. - Inscriptions: - Delhi-Topra Edict: Brahmi script (3rd century BCE). - Archaeology: - Sarnath Pillar: Ashokan site, post-decipherment study. - Related Figures: - James Prinsep: - Scholar (1799-1840 CE); edict decoder. - Ashoka: - Emperor (r. c. 268-232 BCE); edict author. - Alexander Cunningham: - Archaeologist (1814-1893 CE); ASI founder. - Broader Connection: - Links to Mauryan history (e.g., Q138 [Ashokan]), epigraphy (e.g., Q65 [Tughlaq inscriptions]), or colonial scholarship (e.g., Q125 [Hundi]). - Key Takeaway: - James Prinsep (b) first deciphered Ashoka’s edicts in 1837 CE. - Q92: With reference to the religious history of India, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. The concept of Bodhisattva is central to Hinayana sect of Buddhism 2. Bodhisattva is a compassionate one on his way to enlightenment 3. Bodhisattva delays achieving his own salvation to help all sentient beings on their path to it - Question: Which of the statements given above is/are correct? - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 2 only (d) 1, 2, and 3 - Answer: (b) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Buddhism, founded by Gautama Buddha (c. 5th-4th century BCE), split into Hinayana (Theravada) and Mahayana sects by the 1st century CE, reflecting divergent paths to enlightenment. The Bodhisattva ideal emerged as a key distinction, influencing Indian religious history alongside Ashokan patronage (e.g., Q91 [edicts]) and Bhakti parallels (e.g., Q130 [Shramana]). - Evaluation of Statement 1: - 1. The concept of Bodhisattva is central to Hinayana sect of Buddhism: - False—The Bodhisattva concept is central to Mahayana Buddhism, not Hinayana (Theravada). Hinayana focuses on the Arhat—individual liberation through self-discipline—while Mahayana emphasizes the Bodhisattva, who seeks enlightenment for all beings. Texts like the Mahayana Sutras (e.g., Lotus Sutra) contrast with Theravada’s Pali Canon, where Bodhisattvas are rare (e.g., Metteyya only). - Evaluation of Statement 2: - 2. Bodhisattva is a compassionate one on his way to enlightenment: - True—In Mahayana Buddhism, a Bodhisattva is defined as a compassionate being pursuing enlightenment (Bodhi). Options: (a) Shramana (b) Parivraaj (c) Agrahaarika (d) Maagadha - Answer: (d) Maagadha - Analysis: - Historical Context: - In ancient and medieval India (c. 6th century BCE-13th century CE), oral traditions were central to preserving cultural heritage, including chronicles, dynastic histories, and epics like the Mahabharata and Ramayana. Specialized groups maintained these narratives before widespread writing, a practice evident across Vedic, Buddhist, and courtly contexts (e.g., Q63 [Bhakti], Q91 [Ashokan edicts]). - Correct Option Explained: - (d) Maagadha: - Correct—‘Maagadha’ (or Magadha, often spelled as Māgadha) refers to bards or chroniclers in ancient India, particularly from the Magadha region (modern Bihar), who memorized and recited genealogies, dynastic histories, and epic tales. Known as ‘Sutas’ or ‘Magadhas’ in texts like the Puranas and Mahabharata, they were professional storytellers and historians at royal courts, distinct from priests or ascetics (e.g., Rajatarangini’s bardic parallels, Q87). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Shramana: - Incorrect—‘Shramana’ denotes ascetic practitioners, primarily Jain and Buddhist monks, focused on spiritual liberation, not memorizing secular histories or epics (e.g., Q130 [Shramana-Brahmana]). - Options: (a) Paragana - Sarkar - Suba (b) Sarkar - Paragana - Suba (c) Suba - Sarkar - Paragana (d) Paragana - Suba - Sarkar - Answer: (a) Paragana - Sarkar - Suba - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Medieval India, particularly under the Mughal Empire (16th-18th centuries CE), developed a structured administrative hierarchy to govern vast territories. The system, refined by Akbar (r. 1556-1605 CE, Q30 context), divided the empire into units of increasing size—Paragana, Sarkar, and Suba—as detailed in the Ain-i-Akbari by Abul Fazl (Q85 context). - Size Hierarchy: - Paragana: - Smallest unit—Comprising several villages (typically 10-100), managed by a Qanungo or Shiqdar for revenue and law enforcement. Examples include Bengal, Delhi, and Gujarat Subas. - Ascending Order: Paragana (village cluster) < Sarkar (district-like) < Suba (province). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Paragana - Sarkar - Suba: - Correct—Follows the ascending order: smallest (Paragana) to middle (Sarkar) to largest (Suba), as per Mughal administrative structure. - (b) Sarkar - Paragana - Suba: - Incorrect—Places Sarkar (middle) before Paragana (smallest), disrupting the size sequence. - (c) Suba - Sarkar - Paragana: - Incorrect—Reverses the order, starting with the largest (Suba) and ending with the smallest (Paragana). - (d) Paragana - Suba - Sarkar: - Incorrect—Correctly starts with Paragana but places Suba (largest) before Sarkar (middle), breaking the ascending progression. - Key Features: - Mughal Administration: - Paragana: Local revenue unit. - Sarkar: Regional oversight. - Suba: Provincial governance. - Related Figures: - Akbar: - Emperor (r. 1556-1605 CE), formalized hierarchy (Q30). - Abul Fazl: - Historian (1551-1602 CE), documented system (Q85). - Todar Mal: - Revenue minister (d. 1589 CE), refined land assessment. - Aurangzeb: - Emperor (r. 1658-1707 CE), maintained structure (Q106). - Sher Shah Suri: - Sultan (r. 1540-1545 CE), precursor to Mughal system. - Other Notable Administrative Units in Medieval India: - Mauza: - Single village, below Paragana, revenue base. - Chakla: - Revenue circle, sometimes between Paragana and Sarkar. - Parganait: - Head of a Paragana, local official. - Jagir: - Land grant for service, cross-cutting unit (Q11). - Iqta: - Sultanate land assignment, pre-Mughal system. - Broader Connection: - Links to Mughal governance (Q30 [Mansabdari]), revenue roles (Q106 [Mirasidar]), or Fatehpur Sikri admin (Q85). - Key Takeaway: - The correct ascending order of size is Paragana - Sarkar - Suba (a), reflecting medieval India’s administrative hierarchy. - Q108: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Hoysala: - Incorrect—Hoysala dynasty emerged in Karnataka around the 10th-11th centuries CE, with origins as feudatories of the Western Chalukyas. Gahadavala: - Incorrect—Gahadavala dynasty, ruling in North India (e.g., Kannauj), was founded by Chandradeva in c. 1080 CE, emerging after the decline of the Gurjara-Pratiharas, far beyond the early 8th century CE. - 3. Kakatiya: - Incorrect—Kakatiya dynasty, based in Telangana, began as Chalukya vassals and gained independence around the 10th century CE under Beta I (c. 1000 CE). Their prominence peaked later (12th-14th centuries CE, Q31 context), not in 700-750 CE. - 4. Yadava: - Incorrect—Yadava dynasty (Seuna Yadavas) of Devagiri (Maharashtra) rose in the late 9th century CE under Dridhaprahara (c. 860 CE), with significant power from Bhillama V (c. 1173 CE). Their establishment postdates 750 CE (Q31 context). - Count: None of the dynasties (Hoysala, Gahadavala, Kakatiya, Yadava) were established in the early eighth century AD (700-750 CE). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Only one: - Incorrect—None match the timeline, so one is not correct. - (b) Only two: - Incorrect—No two dynasties align with 700-750 CE. - (c) Only three: - Incorrect—Three exceeds the zero that fit the period. - (d) None: - Correct—All four dynasties emerged after 750 CE (Hoysala c. 10th-11th CE, Gahadavala c. 1080 CE, Kakatiya c. 10th CE, Yadava c. 9th CE). - Key Features: - Early 8th Century (700-750 CE): - Dominated by Rashtrakutas, Pratiharas, Palas. - Listed dynasties: Later medieval rise (9th-11th CE). - Related Figures: - Vishnuvardhana: - Hoysala king (r. 1108-1152 CE), later ruler (Q31). - Govindachandra: - Gahadavala king (r. 1114-1155 CE), peak ruler. - Rudrama Devi: - Kakatiya queen (r. 1262-1289 CE), notable figure (Q31). - Bhillama V: - Yadava king (r. 1173-1191 CE), established power. - Dantidurga: - Rashtrakuta founder (r. 735-756 CE), 8th-century peer. - Other Notable Dynasties of Early Medieval India: - Rashtrakuta: - Deccan, c. 735 CE, Dantidurga (Q109). - Gurjara-Pratihara: - North India, c. 730 CE, Nagabhata I (Q109). - Pala: - Bengal, c. 750 CE, Gopala. - Chalukya (Badami): - Deccan, c. 543-757 CE, Pulakeshin I (Q31). - Pallava: - South India, c. 6th-9th centuries CE, Simhavishnu. - Broader Connection: - Links to regional kingdoms (Q31 [Hoysala]), temple architecture (Q78 [Kakatiya]), or medieval shifts (Q81 [Gupta decline]). - Key Takeaway: - None of the listed dynasties (1, 2, 3, 4) were established in the early 8th century AD, making (d) correct. - Q115: Who among the following rulers of Vijayanagara Empire constructed a large dam across Tungabhadra River and a canal-cum-aqueduct several kilometres long from the river to the capital city? - Options: (a) Devaraya I (b) Mallikarjuna (c) Vira Vijaya (d) Virupaksha - Answer: (a) Devaraya I - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Vijayanagara Empire (c. 1336-1646 CE), founded by Harihara I and Bukka Raya I of the Sangama dynasty, dominated South India for centuries. - Its capital, Vijayanagara (modern Hampi), located in a semi-arid region of the Deccan plateau along the Tungabhadra River, required sophisticated water management systems for agriculture and urban needs (Q111 context for Fanam currency, Q31 context for the empire). - Engineering large-scale irrigation projects was a key feature of successful rulers. - Evaluation: - Devaraya I (r. c. 1406-1422 CE) of the Sangama dynasty is explicitly credited with constructing a major dam across the Tungabhadra River. He also commissioned a canal and aqueduct system, stretching over several kilometers (some sources mention around 15 miles or 24 km), to channel water from the river to the capital city and surrounding agricultural lands. - This project aimed to alleviate water shortages and significantly increased state revenue through enhanced irrigation. The Italian traveler Nicolo Conti visited Vijayanagara around 1420 CE, during Devaraya I's reign, and likely witnessed aspects of his administration and projects. Devaraya I also built another dam on the Haridra river. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Mallikarjuna Raya (r. 1446–1465 CE): Son of Deva Raya II, Mallikarjuna's reign marked a period of decline for the Sangama dynasty, characterized by military defeats against the Bahmani Sultanate and the Gajapatis. He is known as a weak ruler and is not associated with major construction projects like the Tungabhadra dam. - (c) Vira Vijaya Raya (or Vijaya Raya, Bukka Raya III, r. c. 1423–1424 CE): Son of Devaraya I and father of Deva Raya II. His reign was very short and largely insignificant. He faced defeat by the Bahmani Sultanate and undertook no known major construction works. - (d) Virupaksha: This likely refers to Virupaksha Raya II (r. 1465–1485 CE), who succeeded Mallikarjuna Raya and was the last effective ruler of the Sangama dynasty, known for his incompetence which led to the rise of the Saluva dynasty. - Alternatively, it could refer to the earlier Virupaksha Raya I (r. 1404-1405 CE), son of Harihara II, whose reign was extremely brief and unstable. Neither is credited with the dam. - Key Features: - Tungabhadra River Dam: Major hydraulic project. - Canal-Aqueduct System: Supplied water to Vijayanagara city. - Irrigation: Increased agricultural output and revenue. - Water Management: Crucial for the capital's survival and prosperity. - Related Figures: - Devaraya I: - Sangama ruler (r. 1406-1422), commissioned the project. - Harihara I & Bukka Raya I: - Founders of Vijayanagara. - Nicolo Conti: - Italian traveler (visited c. 1420). - Deva Raya II: - Son of Vira Vijaya, father of Mallikarjuna, notable ruler. - Mallikarjuna Raya: - Later Sangama ruler (r. 1446-1465). - Vira Vijaya Raya: - Son of Devaraya I, brief reign (r. 1423-1424). - Virupaksha Raya II: - Last Sangama ruler (r. 1465-1485). - Other Notable Vijayanagara Water Systems: - Kamalapura Tank: - Large reservoir near Hampi. - Hiriya Canal: - Another significant canal drawing from the Tungabhadra. - Numerous smaller tanks, wells, and check dams. - Broader Connection: - Links to medieval South Indian history, hydraulic engineering in pre-modern societies, Vijayanagara state formation and administration (Q31, Q111). - Key Takeaway: - Devaraya I (a) was the Vijayanagara ruler responsible for constructing the significant dam across the Tungabhadra and the associated canal-aqueduct system to supply the capital city. - Q116: Who among the following rulers of medieval Gujarat surrendered Diu to Portuguese? - Options: (a) Ahmad Shah (b) Mahmud Begarha (c) Bahadur Shah (d) Muhammad Shah - Answer: (c) Bahadur Shah - Analysis: - Historical Context: - In the early 16th century CE, the Portuguese were establishing a maritime empire in the Indian Ocean, often clashing with local powers like the Gujarat Sultanate (a major kingdom in Western India from 1407 to 1573). - Simultaneously, the Mughal Empire was expanding, posing a threat to regional sultanates including Gujarat. - Diu was a strategically important and prosperous port city on the southern coast of Gujarat's Kathiawar peninsula. - Evaluation: - Bahadur Shah, the Sultan of Gujarat (r. 1526–1537 CE), faced a critical threat when the Mughal Emperor Humayun invaded his kingdom. - Seeking allies, Bahadur Shah entered into negotiations with the Portuguese governor, Nuno da Cunha. - Through the Treaty of Bassein (1534 CE), Bahadur Shah ceded Bassein (Vasai) and surrounding territories to the Portuguese. - In a subsequent agreement (often considered part of the same diplomatic exchange or shortly after, 1535 CE), he granted them permission to construct a fortress at Diu and effectively surrendered the island to them in return for military assistance against the Mughals. - Ironically, Bahadur Shah was killed in 1537 during a meeting with the Portuguese near Diu, under circumstances that remain disputed. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Ahmad Shah I (r. 1411–1442 CE): Founder of Ahmedabad and consolidator of the Sultanate. His reign predates significant Portuguese presence and their demand for Diu. - (b) Mahmud Begarha (Mahmud Shah I, r. 1458–1511 CE): A powerful Sultan known for capturing Pavagadh and Junagadh forts. He fought naval battles *against* the Portuguese (e.g., Battle of Diu, 1509, where the Gujarat-Mamluk fleet was defeated). - His governor, Malik Ayaz, successfully resisted Portuguese attempts to build a fort at Diu during his time. He did not surrender Diu. - (d) Muhammad Shah: There were multiple Sultans with this name. None were responsible for the initial surrender of Diu. - Mahmud Shah III (sometimes referred to as Muhammad Shah III, r. 1537–1554 CE) ruled after Bahadur Shah's death when Diu was already under Portuguese control; he supported attempts to recapture it (e.g., Siege of Diu, 1538). - Key Features: - Diu: Strategic port city surrendered. - Portuguese Expansion: Acquisition of territory by treaty/coercion. - Treaty of Bassein (1534): Formal agreement ceding territory. - Mughal Pressure: Humayun's invasion as a catalyst for the treaty. - Gujarat Sultanate: Regional power facing external threats. - Related Figures: - Bahadur Shah: - Sultan of Gujarat (r. 1526-1537), ceded Diu. - Nuno da Cunha: - Portuguese Governor involved in the treaty. - Humayun: - Mughal Emperor threatening Gujarat. - Mahmud Begarha: - Earlier Sultan who fought the Portuguese. - Francisco de Almeida: - Portuguese Viceroy victorious at sea in 1509. - Malik Ayaz: - Governor of Diu under Mahmud Begarha. - Other Notable Events: - Battle of Chaul (1508): - Gujarat-Mamluk victory over Portuguese. - Battle of Diu (1509): - Decisive Portuguese naval victory. - Siege of Diu (1538, 1546): - Failed attempts to recapture Diu. - Portuguese conquest of Daman (1559). - Liberation of Diu (Operation Vijay, 1961). - Broader Connection: - Links to European colonialism in India (Q108), decline of Indian regional powers, Mughal history, maritime trade and conflict in the Indian Ocean. - Key Takeaway: - Bahadur Shah (c) surrendered Diu to the Portuguese around 1534-1535 as part of a deal to secure their help against the invading Mughal forces led by Humayun. - [2024-I] - Q117: Who of the following rulers of medieval India gave permission to the Portuguese to build a fort at Bhatkal? - Options: (a) Krishnadevaraya (b) Narasimha Saluva (c) Muhammad Shah III (d) Yusuf Adil Shah - Answer: (a) Krishnadevaraya - Analysis: - Historical Context: - In the early 16th century CE, the Portuguese, under leaders like Vasco da Gama and Afonso de Albuquerque, established a presence along India’s western coast, seeking trade monopolies (e.g., pepper, spices) and strategic forts. Bhatkal, a key port in present-day Karnataka, fell within Vijayanagar’s sphere of influence during its Tuluva dynasty (1505-1565 CE), interacting with Portuguese ambitions, as noted in European accounts and Vijayanagar records. - Correct Option Explained: - (a) Krishnadevaraya: - Correct—Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509-1529 CE), the most powerful ruler of the Vijayanagar Empire, is credited with granting the Portuguese permission to build a fort at Bhatkal around 1510 CE. Portuguese chronicler Fernão Lopes de Castanheda and traveler Domingo Paes (c. 1520 CE) suggest that Krishnadevaraya allowed this early fortification to secure trade benefits (e.g., horses, guns) against rival sultanates, notably during his wars with Bijapur. While direct inscriptions are scarce, historians like Robert Sewell align this with Vijayanagar’s pragmatic diplomacy, making (a) the accepted answer per source consensus. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) Narasimha Saluva: - Incorrect—Narasimha Saluva (Saluva Narasimha Deva Raya, r. 1485-1491 CE) founded the Saluva dynasty of Vijayanagar but died before significant Portuguese contact intensified (post-1498 CE, Vasco da Gama’s arrival). Bhatkal’s fortification aligns with the Tuluva period, not his reign, per Vijayanagar timelines. - (c) Muhammad Shah III: - Incorrect—Muhammad Shah III (r. 1463-1482 CE), a Bahmani Sultan, ruled before the Portuguese established a strong coastal presence. His successors dealt with the Portuguese, but Bhatkal, south of Bahmani core territories (e.g., Bidar), was under Vijayanagar control by the 16th century, per Bahmani chronicles (e.g., Burhan-i-Maasir). - (d) Yusuf Adil Shah: - Incorrect—Yusuf Adil Shah (r. 1490-1510 CE), founder of the Bijapur Sultanate, controlled northern Karnataka ports like Goa (lost to Portuguese in 1510 CE) but opposed Portuguese expansion. Bhatkal, further south, remained under Vijayanagar influence during his reign, and he’s unlikely to have permitted a Portuguese fort there, per Portuguese records (e.g., Albuquerque’s letters). - Event Details: - Bhatkal Fort: - Date: c. 1510 CE; early Portuguese fort. - Location: Bhatkal, Karnataka; Vijayanagar coast. - Purpose: Trade (spices, horses), strategic outpost. - Other Related Interactions: - Goa (1510 CE): - Context: Portuguese captured from Bijapur, not Vijayanagar. - Honavar: - Context: Another Vijayanagar port; Portuguese trade ties. - Calicut: - Context: Zamorin resisted Portuguese, unlike Vijayanagar’s diplomacy. - Historical Significance: - Krishnadevaraya’s permission reflects Vijayanagar’s strategic engagement with the Portuguese to counter Deccan sultanates, balancing trade gains with sovereignty (authority that exercises ultimate power without external control). The Bhatkal fort, though less documented than Goa, marks an early Portuguese foothold under Vijayanagar’s oversight, per historian K.A. Nilakanta Sastri. - Related Evidence: - Accounts: - Domingo Paes (c. 1520 CE): Vijayanagar-Portuguese ties. - Fernão Lopes de Castanheda: Early forts, c. 1510 CE. - Chronicles: - Amuktamalyada (attributed to Krishnadevaraya): Governance hints. - Studies: - Robert Sewell: Vijayanagar’s coastal policy. - Related Figures: - Krishnadevaraya: - Ruler (r. 1509-1529 CE); Vijayanagar emperor. - Afonso de Albuquerque: - Portuguese governor (r. 1509-1515 CE); fort builder. - Yusuf Adil Shah: - Bijapur ruler (r. 1490-1510 CE); rival. - Broader Connection: - Links to Vijayanagar trade (e.g., Q98 [Krishna Deva]), Portuguese arrival (e.g., Q70 [Surat]), or medieval power (e.g., Q135 [dynasties]). - Key Takeaway: - Krishnadevaraya (a) gave the Portuguese permission to build a fort at Bhatkal, aligning with his reign’s diplomatic and trade strategies.
